# Papercusp Specification

> Open standard for autonomous-harness frameworks. Living document; pre-1.0.

> **Webapp retired (2026-05-14).** These docs are served *while the Tauri dev shell is running*. Start it with `cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev` — that boots embedded Postgres, the operator sidecar, and the Tauri webview together. Standalone `apps/operator` boots are no longer supported.

## What this is

[Section titled “What this is”](#what-this-is)

A specification for **autonomous-harness frameworks** — systems that drive AI agents through a structured loop (plan → work → validate → done) against a project goal.

Papercusp specifies:

* **The harness contract** — what shape an autonomous-harness must have for plugins to extend it
* **The plugin model** — how third parties contribute roles, lifecycle hooks, UI, API routes, DB schemas, and routines
* **The capability system** — declarative permissions enforced at the DI boundary
* **The state model** — Postgres-backed, atomic-checkout, hard-stop budget enforcement, goal-traceable tasks
* **Two reference apps** — Papercup (organization layer) and the coding harness (sheets-clone, etc.)

## Status

[Section titled “Status”](#status)

Pre-1.0. Most foundational phases have shipped — including **Phase 6b** (UI render of plugin contributions plus the Backstage-style DI runtime, shipped 2026-04-29) — alongside the postgres schema, plugin SDK + loader, capability framework, substrate runtime, routine ticker, and server-side contribution surface.

See the [implementation status table](/internal/docs/implementation/status) for the canonical state.

## What Papercusp is NOT

[Section titled “What Papercusp is NOT”](#what-papercusp-is-not)

* Not a hosted SaaS — it’s a framework you self-host
* Not a replacement for Claude Code / Cursor / etc. — it composes with them, doesn’t compete
* Not coupled to any specific LLM — uses whatever CLI you point it at
* Not opinionated about what kinds of harnesses exist — coding, org, research, marketing, all welcome

## How this doc is published

[Section titled “How this doc is published”](#how-this-doc-is-published)

This is an [Astro Starlight](https://starlight.astro.build) site at `apps/operator-docs/src/content/docs/`. Running `npm run build` from `apps/operator-docs` compiles it to `dist/` with `base: '/internal/docs'`, emits per-page `.md` twins, then `scripts/postbuild-copy.sh` mirrors `dist/` into `apps/operator/public/internal/docs/`. The operator serves it statically at `/internal/docs` on its Hono host (`http://localhost:3070/internal/docs`) — reachable only while the Tauri dev shell is running. (It was previously a Fumadocs site; the emit-md-twins step preserves the old per-page `.md` HTTP surface.)

After v1.0 freeze, the canonical spec moves to its own repo.

# Agent insights — overview

> What an insight is, when to write one, how to read them.

This section is the **agent knowledge base**: short, scannable notes about non-obvious things in this codebase that previous agents wished they’d known earlier.

Each insight answers three questions in three short sections:

1. **What** — the fact, in one paragraph.
2. **Why it matters** — the failure mode it prevents, with a citation to the incident or commit that revealed it.
3. **How to apply** — what an agent should *do differently* given this knowledge.

## Reading

[Section titled “Reading”](#reading)

* **At session start**, run `docs:outline` and skim this section. The whole collection should take under a minute. Most “weird bugs” have an insight written.
* **When investigating a confusing failure**, `docs:search` for the symptom before grepping code.

## Contributing

[Section titled “Contributing”](#contributing)

See [Agent policies §19](/internal/docs/agent-policies#19-agent-insights) for the full rule. Short version:

* Write one when you discover a non-obvious fact (PG quirk, library gotcha, subtle invariant, hidden cross-cutting rule).
* Don’t write one when the fix lives in code, or when the thing is already documented elsewhere — update the existing doc instead.
* Keep it short — three sections, under 50 lines total.

If something is obsolete, set `status: superseded` or `retired` in the frontmatter (don’t delete the file) and add an “Update:/Superseded:” note in the body. Entries stay in the sidebar and the generated [insights index](/internal/docs/reference/agent-insights-index) regardless of status — the index surfaces `status` as a column rather than hiding non-active pages.

# Adding a reactive table — the consolidated pattern

> How to make a new PG table push live updates to the UI. PG trigger → sync_invalidate → existing /api/zero-harness/sse → libs/sync invalidates the matching useSyncQuery.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

Papercusp’s UI gets live updates from PG through **one channel, two producers**:

```plaintext
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Application code     │── notifySyncInvalidate(name, args, data?) ─┐
  └──────────────────────┘                                            │
                                                                      ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐                              pg_notify('sync_invalidate', ...)
  │ PG trigger           │── emit_change_notify() ─────────┘          │
  │ (auto, every row)    │                                            │
  └──────────────────────┘                                            ▼
                            packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts → /api/zero-harness/sse
                                                                      ▼
                              libs/sync SSEAdapter → @tanstack/react-query
                                                                      ▼
                                                useSyncQuery refetches matching query
```

Both producers emit the same payload shape; consumers don’t care which fired. The 90-second dedupe window in `sync-sse.ts` collapses identical `(name, args)` notifies — so an app-code notify followed by a trigger-driven one for the same row hits the wire once.

## When to use which producer

[Section titled “When to use which producer”](#when-to-use-which-producer)

| Choice                                                | Use it for                                                                                                                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `notifySyncInvalidate(name, args, data?)` in app code | Fine-grained, intentional notifies after a meaningful write. Optional `data` payload pushes the new rows directly, saving the client a refetch. Used by 20+ writers. |
| `emit_change_notify` PG trigger                       | Coarse, automatic, fires on EVERY INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Catches writes that bypass app code — raw SQL from migrations, MCP-tool direct writes, agent-direct edits.   |

You usually want **both**: app code fires the targeted notify on the happy path; the trigger covers everything else.

## Recipe — add a reactive table

[Section titled “Recipe — add a reactive table”](#recipe--add-a-reactive-table)

### Step 1: define the table

[Section titled “Step 1: define the table”](#step-1-define-the-table)

In a `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/NNN-<name>.sql` migration (≥ `107`). **Update:** the old runtime-ensure path (`ensure-schema*.ts`, lazy-`CREATE TABLE`) is **removed** — schema is migrations-only now (`self-contained-migration-baseline-2026-06-02`). Add a migration; do not add an `ensureXxx()`.

### Step 2: attach the trigger

[Section titled “Step 2: attach the trigger”](#step-2-attach-the-trigger)

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER emit_change_notify_trg
  AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE
  ON harness_shared.your_new_table
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION harness_shared.emit_change_notify();
```

**Update:** the old runtime `wireDogfoodTriggers()` helper (in the removed `ensure-schema-dogfood.ts`) is gone. The dogfood trigger wiring now lives in a migration — `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/107-dogfood-reactivity-triggers.sql` attaches `emit_change_notify` to the reactive tables. Add your new table’s `CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER` line to a migration alongside those.

Idempotent (`CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER` is PG 14+), so re-applying the migration is safe.

### Step 3: in app code, also call `notifySyncInvalidate` after writes

[Section titled “Step 3: in app code, also call notifySyncInvalidate after writes”](#step-3-in-app-code-also-call-notifysyncinvalidate-after-writes)

After your route handler writes to the table:

```ts
import { notifySyncInvalidate } from '@papercusp/operator-core/lib/sync-sse';


// After the successful write:
void notifySyncInvalidate('your_table.changed', { workspace_id, op }).catch(() => {});
```

Best-effort — never let a notify failure break the write itself.

### Step 4: on the client, subscribe with `useSyncQuery`

[Section titled “Step 4: on the client, subscribe with useSyncQuery”](#step-4-on-the-client-subscribe-with-usesyncquery)

```tsx
import { useSyncQuery } from '@papercusp/sync';


const { data, loading } = useSyncQuery<YourRow>({
  // ...
});
```

`useSyncQuery` reads the SSE invalidate stream and refetches whenever a matching `name` arrives.

## Payload shape — never break this

[Section titled “Payload shape — never break this”](#payload-shape--never-break-this)

Both producers emit on `sync_invalidate` channel with:

```json
{
  "name": "<event-name>",
  "args": { "workspace_id": "<id|null>", "op": "INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE" }
}
```

Consumers filter on `name`. The format is the established `SyncEvent` contract in `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` — don’t invent a parallel channel; the trigger function was rewritten in commit `20609bb` to stop doing exactly that (was emitting on a new `papercusp_changes` channel; consolidated onto `sync_invalidate` for the 20+ existing consumers).

### Two name conventions exist — they don’t talk to each other yet

[Section titled “Two name conventions exist — they don’t talk to each other yet”](#two-name-conventions-exist--they-dont-talk-to-each-other-yet)

| Producer                                                | Name shape                 | Example                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Application code via `notifySyncInvalidate(name, args)` | camelCase noun + scope     | `plans.list`, `toastLog.recent`, `harnessTextArtifact.byHarness` |
| PG trigger `emit_change_notify` (this insight’s recipe) | `<schema>.<table>.changed` | `harness_shared.plan_runs.changed`                               |

Today’s existing `useSyncQuery` consumers subscribe with `queryName: 'harnessTextArtifact.byHarness'` (camelCase). My PG-trigger events fire with `harness_shared.harness_text_artifacts.changed` — clients filter on name, see no match, refetch nothing. Trigger events are **broadcast no-ops for existing clients today.**

**What this enables**: future code subscribing to `<schema>.<table>.changed` (the catch-all name shape) gets free coverage of any write to that table, including raw-SQL or MCP-tool writes that app code never notified about.

**Bridge work pending**: a future item should add a translator — “when `harness_shared.harness_text_artifacts.changed` arrives, also invalidate any subscriber to `harnessTextArtifact.*`.” That ties the trigger producer to the existing consumer surface. Until that lands, app-code `notifySyncInvalidate` calls remain the active path for known consumers; the trigger is the dormant safety net.

## Verifying it works

[Section titled “Verifying it works”](#verifying-it-works)

Live test that brings its own embedded PG, no shared-state risk:

```bash
node apps/operator/scripts/verify-trigger-consolidation.mjs
```

Runs in \~2s. Asserts the trigger fires on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, the payload shape is correct, the GUC workspace\_id is captured, and a coexisting trigger on the same table doesn’t block this one.

## Why it matters

[Section titled “Why it matters”](#why-it-matters)

Before the consolidation, agents were tempted to invent a new channel per concern (e.g., a new `/api/sync/stream` endpoint for a new feature). That fragments the SSE consumer surface (one EventSource per channel — and browsers cap HTTP/1.1 connections per host at 6). One channel + payload-filtered topic gives sub-second invalidation across the whole UI without exhausting the connection pool. See the [connection-pool insight](/internal/docs/agent-insights/webkit-connection-pool-exhaustion) for the failure mode if you stack multiple long-lived connections.

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` — `notifySyncInvalidate` + `subscribe`
* `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/zero-harness/sse.ts` — the SSE endpoint
* `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/000-baseline.sql` — the `emit_change_notify()` trigger function (originally `archive/078-emit-change-notify.sql`)
* `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/107-dogfood-reactivity-triggers.sql` — the trigger-attach migration (replaced the removed `wireDogfoodTriggers()` runtime helper)
* `apps/operator/scripts/verify-trigger-consolidation.mjs` — the live verifier

# Adding a query to the Zero-free sync resolver

> How to add a new useSyncQuery name to the v2 dispatcher. ~15 LOC drizzle entry, registry-style, no ZQL. Pairs with the reactive-table insight.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

The operator serves `useSyncQuery({ queryName: '<name>' })` reads through a switch-on-name dispatcher at `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts`. Each entry is a small async function that takes validated args and returns a flat row array. Adding a query is purely additive — \~15 LOC, no client-side changes needed for the dispatcher itself.

This replaced the legacy `@rocicorp/zero`-coupled ZQL resolver in P-022 (cutover commits `164671ed` + earlier batches). The legacy resolver is gone; this dispatcher is the only path.

## When to use it

[Section titled “When to use it”](#when-to-use-it)

Add an entry when:

* A UI component needs to subscribe to a PG-backed read with `useSyncQuery` and the queryName isn’t already registered.
* You’re moving a route from manual fetch + setInterval polling to push-driven reactivity.

Don’t add an entry for:

* One-shot reads that don’t need invalidation. Use a regular fetch
  * `useAsyncJson` or similar.
* Writes. The dispatcher is read-only; mutations stay on `POST /api/...` routes and fire `notifySyncInvalidate(...)` after the write succeeds.

## Recipe

[Section titled “Recipe”](#recipe)

### Step 1: confirm the table exists in drizzle’s generated schema

[Section titled “Step 1: confirm the table exists in drizzle’s generated schema”](#step-1-confirm-the-table-exists-in-drizzles-generated-schema)

The dispatcher uses `@papercusp/db-org`’s `generated` table registry for column → camelCase conversion. Check that your table is there:

```bash
grep "^export const yourTableNameInHarnessShared" \
  libs/papercusp/libs/db/src/schema/generated.ts
```

If missing: regenerate the schema via the drizzle generator, or add the table via `ensure-schema.ts` / a SQL migration first.

### Step 2: add a registry entry

[Section titled “Step 2: add a registry entry”](#step-2-add-a-registry-entry)

Open `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts`. Each entry has this shape (mirrors the legacy ZQL chain):

```ts
'yourQueryName.byScope': {
  argsSchema: z.object({
    harnessSlug: z.string(),
    limit: z.number().int().positive().max(500).default(50),
  }),
  resolve: async (args) => {
    const { harnessSlug, limit } = args as { harnessSlug: string; limit: number };
    const { getOrgPg, generated } = await import('@papercusp/db-org');
    const { desc, eq } = await import('drizzle-orm');
    const t = generated.yourTableNameInHarnessShared;
    const { db } = getOrgPg();
    return (await db
      .select()
      .from(t)
      .where(eq(t.harnessSlug, harnessSlug))
      .orderBy(desc(t.updatedAt))
      .limit(limit)) as unknown[];
  },
},
```

Key points:

* **`argsSchema`**: a zod schema. Validation runs before `resolve`. Bad args throw → route handler returns 400.
* **`resolve`** returns `unknown[]` — a FLAT row array. If your existing data helper returns `{rows: [...]}`, unwrap it here.
* **Dynamic `import()`** of `@papercusp/db-org` + `drizzle-orm` keeps the registry module lightweight and avoids cycles. The lazy import is per-call but the loader caches; no perf cost in practice.
* **`as unknown[]`** at the return — drizzle’s `select()` returns rich types; the dispatcher contract is `unknown[]`. The cast is intentional.

### Step 3: add the bridge entry (P-067)

[Section titled “Step 3: add the bridge entry (P-067)”](#step-3-add-the-bridge-entry-p-067)

Open `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts`. Add a line in `TABLE_TO_QUERY_NAMES` mapping your PG table to the new queryName:

```ts
'harness_shared.your_table_name': ['yourQueryName.byScope'],
```

This makes the PG trigger producer (P-018 `emit_change_notify`) fire your camelCase invalidation when ANY write touches the table — including raw SQL, MCP-tool writes, or migrations that bypass app code. Without this bridge, only app-code `notifySyncInvalidate` calls reach your subscribers.

If multiple queries scope on the same table (e.g. `byHarness` + `byFeature` over the same chunk plans), list both:

```ts
'harness_shared.harness_chunk_plans': [
  'chunkPlans.byHarness',
  'chunkPlans.byFeature',
],
```

### Step 4: update the registry-count assertion

[Section titled “Step 4: update the registry-count assertion”](#step-4-update-the-registry-count-assertion)

Open `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.test.ts`. Bump the running-count assertion (`expect(knownQueryNamesV2()).toHaveLength(N)`) and add the new name to the closest batch assertion. The count assertion exists so future drift surfaces: a registry entry added without the corresponding test update is treated as suspicious.

Same in `table-to-query-names.test.ts` — bump the `allBridgedQueryNames()).toHaveLength(N)` assertion.

**If the name you’re migrating is in the `FORWARD_DEFINED` set** (advance-mapped before its v2 entry existed — see [forward-defined-registry-entries insight](/internal/docs/agent-insights/forward-defined-registry-entries)), **remove it from `FORWARD_DEFINED` in the same commit**. The sanity assertion (“forward-defined names are NOT in v2”) will fail otherwise and tell you to do this; doing it as part of the migration commit keeps the drift signal accurate.

### Step 5: verify

[Section titled “Step 5: verify”](#step-5-verify)

```bash
cd packages/operator-core
npx vitest run lib/sync-resolver/    # 33+ tests
npx tsc --noEmit                     # check for type regressions
```

Optional live verification against running operator:

```bash
curl "http://127.0.0.1:3070/api/zero-harness/rest-query?name=yourQueryName.byScope&args=$(python3 -c 'import json,urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote(json.dumps({\"harnessSlug\":\"sheets\"})))')"
```

You should see `{"rows":[...], "version":"..."}` with the expected row shape.

## Why this design (not just calling notifySyncInvalidate on each write)

[Section titled “Why this design (not just calling notifySyncInvalidate on each write)”](#why-this-design-not-just-calling-notifysyncinvalidate-on-each-write)

Two complementary producers run side by side:

| Producer                                              | Trigger                                       | Use it for                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `notifySyncInvalidate(name, args, data?)` in app code | Application write paths                       | Fine-grained intentional notifies with optional row payload            |
| PG `emit_change_notify` trigger                       | Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on attached tables | Catch-all for raw SQL, MCP-tool writes, agent-direct edits, migrations |

Together they cover both planned writes (app code) and any other write (trigger). The 90s dedupe window in `sync-sse.ts` collapses the inevitable overlap so subscribers see one event per (name, args) per dedupe window.

The bridge (P-067, `table-to-query-names.ts`) is what makes the trigger producer reach the camelCase consumers. Without it, the trigger fires `harness_shared.your_table.changed` and clients subscribed to `yourQueryName.byScope` see no match.

## When to NOT add to this dispatcher

[Section titled “When to NOT add to this dispatcher”](#when-to-not-add-to-this-dispatcher)

Some reads don’t fit the registry shape:

* **Multi-table joins / aggregates**: legacy ZQL had limited join support too. Build a regular REST endpoint (e.g. `/api/admin/...`) and fire `notifySyncInvalidate` from the route.
* **File-system reads** (e.g. plans-admin’s markdown loading): these aren’t PG rows; the dispatcher’s `getOrgPg` shape doesn’t apply. Use `useAsyncJson` + push invalidation via `notifySyncInvalidate('plans.list', ...)` from the file-watcher.
* **Per-row scoped reads** (`one()` instead of an array): drizzle’s `.limit(1)` returns a single-element array, which matches the dispatcher contract. The client unwraps `rows[0]`. Don’t try to return a non-array — the SSE adapter expects `unknown[]`.

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts` — the dispatcher
* `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts` — the P-067 bridge
* [Adding a reactive table](/internal/docs/agent-insights/adding-a-reactive-table) — the producer side (PG trigger + `notifySyncInvalidate`)
* `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` — the LISTEN handler + SSE fan-out

# Calling defineTool tools from an in-process /admin route

> defineTool projections register POST-only and require identity via readIdentity(ctx). An admin route proxying them needs a synthesized POST + ?superuser=1 + ?client= + validateSuperuser, not a passthrough.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

When an admin route (loopback-only, `auth: 'public'`) wants to call a `defineTool` tool in-process via `handleHttpToolRequest`, the natural “just pass through the inbound method + searchParams” doesn’t work. Three traps:

1. **Every `defineTool` registers `methods: ['POST']`.** Both `registerLegacyAsProjected` and `registerRoleGatedAsProjected` in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/define-tool.ts` (the `defineTool` core was generalized out of `packages/agent-mcp` into `libs/generic/tooldef` / `libs/generic/tooldef-http`; `agent-mcp` re-exports them) hardcode it. A GET dispatch returns **405** at the methods gate inside `resolveToolAndContext` (now in `libs/generic/tooldef-http/src/http-projection.ts`). The browser side can keep cacheable GETs — the *internal* call must be POST.

2. **Tool args come from `req.body`, not `req.searchParams`.** The methods gate above is the obvious one; the more subtle one is that the dispatcher validates against `body` only. If you stay GET internally, your args never reach Zod and the tool runs with `{}`. Required fields fail validation.

3. **Writes (and `locks:queue`) need identity.** Tools using `with-plan-lock` or `readIdentity(ctx)` call into `resolveAgentIdentity`, which throws if ctx carries none of `isPowerUser` / `isSuperuser` / `principal`. The superuser branch *also* requires `ctx.uiClientId` to be set — otherwise it throws `"superuser context is missing uiClientId"`.

## The shape that works

[Section titled “The shape that works”](#the-shape-that-works)

```ts
// In your /admin/<surface>.ts route handler:


const ADMIN_UI_CLIENT_ID = 'pc-admin-<surface>-ui';


const HOST_EXTRAS: HttpToolHostExtras = {
  deps: PROJECTED_DEPS,
  log: () => {},
  // /admin/* is loopback-bound — that's the security boundary.
  validateSuperuser: () => true,
};


function adminSearchParams(inbound: URLSearchParams): URLSearchParams {
  const sp = new URLSearchParams(inbound);
  sp.set('superuser', '1');                       // → isSuperuser=true
  if (!sp.has('client')) sp.set('client', ADMIN_UI_CLIENT_ID); // → uiClientId
  return sp;
}


// For GETs from the browser — convert searchParams to args body:
function bodyFromSearchParams(p: URLSearchParams): Record<string, unknown> {
  const body: Record<string, unknown> = {};
  for (const key of new Set(p.keys())) {
    const all = p.getAll(key);
    if (all.length > 1) { body[key] = all; continue; }
    const v = all[0] ?? '';
    if (v === 'true') body[key] = true;
    else if (v === 'false') body[key] = false;
    else body[key] = v;
  }
  return body;
}


async function dispatchRead(req: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const url = new URL(req.url);
  const result = await handleHttpToolRequest({
    method: 'POST',                                       // ← always POST
    pathname: '/api/agent-tools/<group>/<verb>',
    searchParams: adminSearchParams(url.searchParams),    // ← superuser + client
    headers: collectHeaders(req),
    body: bodyFromSearchParams(url.searchParams),         // ← real args
  }, HOST_EXTRAS);
  return unwrap(result);
}
```

Browser-facing GETs stay cacheable / ergonomic; the proxy translates to the dispatcher’s expected POST + body + identity envelope. Writes (POST in, POST out) work the same way — just pass the inbound JSON body straight through.

## Required upstream support

[Section titled “Required upstream support”](#required-upstream-support)

`buildHttpSpawnContext` must read `?client=` into `uiClientId` (landed 2026-05-20 alongside the Plans admin tab). Without that, `?superuser=1` alone hits the `"superuser context is missing uiClientId"` throw. If you’re on an older revision and see that error from an admin proxy, that’s the symptom.

## Why this matters

[Section titled “Why this matters”](#why-this-matters)

The catchall at `/api/agent-tools/*` works because external callers ARE bearer-authed — they supply identity through bearer. An admin shell can’t present a bearer (the UI doesn’t have one). The “synthesize a superuser identity, gated by loopback” pattern is the local equivalent and the only working option short of moving the tools’ implementations behind a non-tool route.

The other working option is bypassing `handleHttpToolRequest` entirely and calling `tool.fn(input, ctx)` directly with a hand-built ctx — that works but loses the dispatcher’s role/quota/audit pipeline. Prefer the proxy pattern.

# An /adv dock panel must be registered in TWO places to be reachable

> Registering a panel type in HarnessesDock's panelRegistry only makes it restorable/openable-by-id — a user can only OPEN it from the "Add panel" catalog if its type is ALSO in the HarnessTopBar allowedTypes allowlist (and has a label/icon in AddPanelCatalog). Miss the second and the panel ships invisible.

## The trap

[Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap)

Adding a panel to the `/adv` harness dock feels like one step:

```ts
// app/adv/harnesses/HarnessesDock.tsx — ensureRegistered()
panelRegistry.register('adv:contributors', AdvContributorsPanel, { title: 'Contributors' });
```

That registration is **necessary but not sufficient**. It only lets the panel be (a) restored from a saved layout and (b) opened programmatically by type id. It does **not** put the panel in the **“Add panel” catalog** — so a user has no way to open it from a fresh layout. The panel ships *registered but invisible*.

This actually happened: P-048 Contributors and P-073 Insights were registered in `HarnessesDock` but omitted from the catalog allowlist, so they were unreachable in the UI until 2026-06-02 (commit on `main`; caught by the first live e2e of the `/adv` dock, `apps/operator/e2e/adv-contributors-panel.spec.ts`). Neither the jsdom render test nor the registration could catch it — only driving the real catalog flow did.

## The second place (and a third)

[Section titled “The second place (and a third)”](#the-second-place-and-a-third)

1. **Register** in `app/adv/harnesses/HarnessesDock.tsx` → `panelRegistry.register(...)`.
2. **Allowlist** the type in `app/adv/harnesses/HarnessTopBar.tsx` — the `allowedTypes={[...]}` prop passed to `<AddPanelCatalog>`. The catalog shows ONLY these types; this is the curated user-facing list.
3. **Label + icon** in `app/harness/dock/AddPanelCatalog.tsx` — add entries to the `HUMAN_LABELS` and `ICON_MAP` records (both fall back gracefully, but an unlabelled type reads as its raw `adv:foo` id and gets the `SquareDashed` placeholder glyph).

If you add an `/adv` panel and “it doesn’t show up in Add panel,” you skipped step 2. Verify with the e2e spec above (it asserts both Contributors and Insights appear in the catalog) or by opening the catalog in the prebuilt bundle — **not** the HMR dev server on `:3055`, which currently has a `'/@vite/client' … createHotContext` mismatch that renders `/adv` blank in a fresh browser (the desktop is unaffected — it loads the prebuilt bundle).

# A script that imports the agent-tools registry never exits — call process.exit

> Importing '@papercusp/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/index.ts' (the defineTool registry barrel) opens keep-alive handles, so a one-shot tsx script hangs after finishing instead of exiting — and a spawnSync caller blocks forever. End such scripts with an explicit process.exit.

## Symptom

[Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom)

A one-shot `tsx` script that imports the agent-tools barrel (`import '@papercusp/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/index.ts'` — e.g. to call `listAllProjectedTools()`) **prints its final output and then never exits**. Run standalone you may not notice (Ctrl-C, or a `timeout`/pipe masks it: a `timeout 180 npx tsx … | tail` pipeline still exits 0 because the *pipeline’s* last command succeeds). But any caller that **waits for the child** — `spawnSync`, a CI step, another script — blocks until an external timeout kills it. In `starlight-projection-generators-2026-06-05` this wedged the `gen:doc-projections` umbrella: the tool-catalog child printed its ✓, never exited, and the projectors queued behind it never ran (the outer `timeout` returned 124, which looked like the *next* script hanging).

## Root cause

[Section titled “Root cause”](#root-cause)

Importing the registry barrel side-effect-registers \~300 tools, and that import chain opens **keep-alive handles** (connection pools, timers), so Node’s event loop never drains. The script’s top-level code finishes; the process stays alive.

## Fix

[Section titled “Fix”](#fix)

End any one-shot script that imports the registry (or anything else that opens pools — e.g. a PG read via `withWorkspace`) with an explicit `process.exit(0)` (after your `--check` logic’s `process.exit(1)` paths). Both `scripts/gen-tool-catalog.ts` and `scripts/gen-doc-tool-catalog.ts` do this now; `scripts/gen-doc-plans-index.ts` always did (why it was wrongly cleared as the hang suspect first — it exits in \~1.4s).

Defense in depth for orchestrators: give `spawnSync` a `timeout:` + `killSignal: 'SIGKILL'` per child (see `scripts/gen-doc-projections.ts`) so one wedged child can never hang the whole run.

# Turn-lifecycle control: always-arm wake + turn-interrupt

> The two halves of turn-lifecycle control. WAKE: arming your inbox-wake watch is automatic at SessionStart — you are wakeable even if you never call coord:await-inbox (standing-row model, the woken:0 warning, the migration-183-rides-the-deploy hazard, why you still must not poll). INTERRUPT: turn:interrupt ends a RUNNING peer's turn — cooperative yield (glyph |) vs force, operator-mediated + audited + storm-limited.

## What changed

[Section titled “What changed”](#what-changed)

You no longer have to *remember* to make yourself wakeable. The operator now **arms your inbox-wake watch automatically at SessionStart** — server-side, in the lifecycle endpoint that `~/.papercusp/hooks/cc/lifecycle-report.sh` already POSTs to (`activity:report`, `kind:lifecycle`). It is client-agnostic (claude / omp / codex) and armed for the whole session, not just between turns. So every psu/Queen-launched agent is re-invokable on a `coord:send {wake:true}` **even when it has no idea it will ever be woken**.

Plan: `turn-lifecycle-control-2026-06-08` (Phase 1, D-001). The old rule — “call `coord:await-inbox` when you go idle or you won’t be wakeable” — is dead. Forgetting to arm no longer strands you.

## The model: one standing row per agent

[Section titled “The model: one standing row per agent”](#the-model-one-standing-row-per-agent)

Your watch is a single row in `harness_shared.event_awaits`, keyed `(workspace_id, subscriber_id, event_key)` with `event_key = coord:inbox-wake:<you>`.

* **Idempotent (D-002).** SessionStart re-arms by **upsert** (`upsertInboxWakeAwait`, `ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE`): re-arming refreshes the captured wake-handle + idle note + floor on the one row — it never inserts a duplicate. A partial unique index (migration 183) enforces exactly one live standing inbox-wake await per agent.
* **The rendezvous.** `coord:send {wake:true, to:[you]}` (and `coord:message-agent`) fires exactly `coord:inbox-wake:<you>` — a key only you watch. It is targeted, never a broadcast; `*`/`human` are not wakeable (no thunder-herd).
* **SessionEnd cancels it (D-003).** A clean session end cancels your standing watch, so a wake can’t race a just-exited session and phantom-resume it. If work arrives later, a fresh session is spawned by whoever needs it.

## `coord:await-inbox` is now just an annotation (D-005)

[Section titled “coord:await-inbox is now just an annotation (D-005)”](#coordawait-inbox-is-now-just-an-annotation-d-005)

Because arming is automatic, `coord:await-inbox` is **no longer the gate** that makes you wakeable. It survives as an *annotation*: it refreshes the “why I’m idle” note on your already-armed standing row (the note rides your wake turn) and lets you tune your `min_sleep_sec` floor. Call it to explain your idle state if you like — but forgetting to no longer makes you unwakeable, which was the whole point.

## You still must not poll

[Section titled “You still must not poll”](#you-still-must-not-poll)

Always-arm makes you *reliably wakeable*; it does not make polling OK. When you have no queued work: **end your turn.** You are re-invoked when someone `coord:send`s you with `{wake:true}` (bursts inside your floor coalesce into one wake). For a specific one-shot readiness (a lock grant, a peer’s artifact, a plan-run finishing) use `events:await` on that exact key and end the turn. A wake costs a whole turn — await only what genuinely blocks you; ambient interest stays a `topics:subscribe`.

## The woken:0 warning — don’t trust a silent ok (D-010)

[Section titled “The woken:0 warning — don’t trust a silent ok (D-010)”](#the-woken0-warning--dont-trust-a-silent-ok-d-010)

`coord:send {wake:true}` now returns a `wake.warning` when it fired but woke **nobody** (`woken: 0` while it had concrete targets):

```plaintext
wake fired but no live wake-watch was registered for the addressee(s) — the message
was injected to their inbox (seen on their next natural turn) but no session was
re-invoked now.
```

This is the exact gap that once made a wake *look* successful when nothing was listening. Always-arm makes `woken: 0` rare for fleet agents, but the warning still catches a not-yet-armed / non-fleet / dead-handle target. If you see it, your “wake” degraded to a plain inbox inject — the addressee sees it on their next natural turn, not now.

## The one deploy-time hazard: migration 183 rides the deploy (D-012)

[Section titled “The one deploy-time hazard: migration 183 rides the deploy (D-012)”](#the-one-deploy-time-hazard-migration-183-rides-the-deploy-d-012)

If you are deploying or debugging the live DB: **never manually apply migration 183 (the partial unique index) to the shared `papercusp` database.** The green-main operator (`:3070`, the live fleet) still *plain-inserts* `coord:inbox-wake:*` rows (no `ON CONFLICT`) until the Phase-1 upsert code is deployed. Applying the unique index first would dedup to one row/agent and then make green-main’s next idle insert throw a `unique_violation` → live-fleet idle-arm regression.

The index is correct and applies clean empty→head; it must land **coupled with the upsert code**, which only happens through the green-main deploy (green-checkpoint → release-trigger → `deploy-cli applyStagedMigrations`). It is not triggerable by accident: boot-migrate is gated off on `:3170`, and `:3070` reads the release SQL dir. So “apply 183 to live PG” is a no-op-by-design that rides the deploy — not a pending manual step.

## Where it lives

[Section titled “Where it lives”](#where-it-lives)

* `armInboxWake` / `cancelInboxWake` — `packages/operator-core/lib/events/await/inbox-wake-arm.ts`
* `upsertInboxWakeAwait` / `cancelInboxWakeAwaits` + the standing-row SQL — `packages/operator-core/lib/events/await/store.ts`
* SessionStart→arm / SessionEnd→cancel wiring — `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/activity/report.ts`
* The `woken:0` warning — `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/coordination/tools/send.ts`
* `coord:await-inbox` (annotation) — `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/coordination/tools/await-inbox.ts`
* Migration — `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/183-event-awaits-inbox-wake-one-per-agent.sql`

## The dual: turn-interrupt — ending a RUNNING peer’s turn

[Section titled “The dual: turn-interrupt — ending a RUNNING peer’s turn”](#the-dual-turn-interrupt--ending-a-running-peers-turn)

Wake re-invokes a *sleeping* agent; **`turn:interrupt`** ends a *running* one’s turn. It is **operator-mediated** (D-008): every fleet agent runs as the same OS user, so authorization / attribution / rate-limit can’t live at the OS socket — they live in the tool. `turn:interrupt { owner, mode, reason }` — `reason` is REQUIRED and audited.

**Two modes:**

* **`cooperative`** (the polite default) — injects a high-priority `yield` coord message (glyph `|`) into the peer’s `[coord+N]` block mid-turn. The peer follows the yield policy every role’s prompt now carries (the dual clause to this page’s wake guidance): reach a safe checkpoint, persist partial state to the work\_item, release locks, write a one-line successor note, end the turn. It is **not** killed. It **DEFERS** when the target holds file locks (a critical section) — a hard yield mid-edit can orphan a lock or half-write a file, so it lets the atomic edit finish and the lock release first, then you retry.
* **`force`** — ends the turn NOW, mid-thinking. A managed-pty session gets Ctrl+C over its control socket (the Phase-3 `interruptViaPty` seam); a headless spawn gets SIGINT to the session pid. The **turn** ends, not the agent — the session stays resumable by id. On a critical section `force` WARNS (orphaned-edit hazard) but proceeds.

**Guardrails (D-009):** `reason` required; every call audited (`turn.interrupt_cooperative` / `_force` / `_deferred` / `_rate_limited` / `_failed` in `harness_shared.audit_log`); storm-limited to 10/min/actor (the audit log is the rate source) so a confused or looping agent can’t halt the fleet; self-interrupt refused.

**Reach for cooperative first**; use `force` only when cooperative was ignored or there’s no time. To re-invoke an *idle* peer use `coord:send {wake:true}` — interrupt is for a *running* peer. The `yield` glyph + every other line type are sourced from the one `COORD_LEGEND`; see [the coord injection protocol](/internal/docs/agent-insights/coord-injection-protocol).

**Known gaps (2026-06-08):** the managed-pty typing-parity feel-check and the default-on flip (`PAPERCUSP_PSU_PTY` is opt-in today), and a full live interactive force-interrupt-mid-thinking e2e, are not yet run — the transport and the logic are each covered separately (`turn:interrupt` unit tests 8/8 + the Phase-3 control-socket e2e). Where it lives: `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/turn/interrupt.ts` (`performInterrupt` is the dep-injected, testable core).

# The attention/importance system (Planning tab)

> How plan-item importance + the unified AttentionItem feed fit together, and two non-obvious gotchas — parseWarnings become lint ERRORS, and the Plans tab has no in-app chat host.

## What it is

[Section titled “What it is”](#what-it-is)

Plan items carry an **importance** — a 4th axis orthogonal to status: `urgent | high | normal | low` (default `normal`), written as an `importance:` keyword on the item line and parsed glyph-agnostically like `blocked-by:`. It drives the Planning-tab sort/badges, the orchestrator’s halt-on-`urgent`, and (eventually) the push threshold. Source of truth: `@papercusp/plan-parser` (`IMPORTANCE_LEVELS`, `PlanItem.importance`); spec at [plan-format §Importance](/internal/docs/spec/plan-format#importance); rubric in [agent-policies §18](/internal/docs/agent-policies).

The Planning tab also shows a **unified attention feed**: one `AttentionItem` read-model (`packages/operator-core/lib/attention/`) that every “needs the human” surface adapts into — plan items, coord escalations, coord messages-to-human, smoke-test failures, plans-awaiting-review. The `plans:attention` tool unions them (best-effort per source), grouped by plan + a synthetic per-harness “Alerts” bucket, importance-sorted. The UI filter facets are ToDos / Needs Human / Blocked (plan-item statuses) + Escalations / Messages / Smoke / Reviews (the non-plan-item kinds).

## Gotcha 1 — parseWarnings become lint ERRORS

[Section titled “Gotcha 1 — parseWarnings become lint ERRORS”](#gotcha-1--parsewarnings-become-lint-errors)

`plans:lint` turns **every** `parsed.parseWarnings` entry into a hard `parse_warning` **error** (`lint.ts`). So the parser must NOT push a parseWarning for a recoverable condition like an unknown `importance:` value — that would fail CI on a typo. Instead:

* the parser **degrades silently** to `normal` (no parseWarning), and
* `plans:lint` re-scans the item’s `rawLine` and emits a soft `unknown_importance` **warning** (never an error).

If you add another tolerant item-keyword, follow the same split: degrade in the parser, warn (don’t error) in lint.

## Gotcha 2 — the Plans tab has no in-app chat host

[Section titled “Gotcha 2 — the Plans tab has no in-app chat host”](#gotcha-2--the-plans-tab-has-no-in-app-chat-host)

The in-app agent chat (`ChatPanel` via `AdvChatPanel`) is hosted **only by the `/adv` HarnessesDock**, opened by an `OPEN_CHAT_EVENT` that the dock listens for (`openFeatureChat` → `POST /api/harness/:slug/agent-chats` → dispatch event). The **Plans admin tab is not inside that dock**, so an `openFeatureChat`-style call there creates a chat that opens nowhere visible. The PlanItemPreview/PlanOtherList “Chat” buttons fall back to `launchAgent` (an external OMP/claude terminal session), which on desktop is invisible/no-op if the agent isn’t configured — hence “Chat does nothing.”

To make Chat work in the Plans tab you must add a host (e.g. a modal that creates a chat and renders `<ChatPanel slug chatId />` directly), and a chat needs a **harness** (`agent_chats` is per-harness-schema) — pure SU plans with no harness can’t host one. This is the open work in `planning-attention-importance-2026-05-31` P-017.

# Attention push-notification delivery

> How needs-human / escalation / smoke / plan-review notifications get delivered — event-driven at the source (notifyAttention), to mobile push + a native desktop notification. No more 60s poll.

## What it is

[Section titled “What it is”](#what-it-is)

The flip side of [the attention/importance system](/internal/docs/agent-insights/attention-importance-system): how an attention item that needs a human becomes a **push notification** on the user’s devices. Implemented by `planning-attention-importance-2026-05-31` P-020/P-021/D-007 (2026-05-31). This is the map.

## One helper, two channels, event-driven

[Section titled “One helper, two channels, event-driven”](#one-helper-two-channels-event-driven)

Everything funnels through **`notifyAttention()`** in `packages/operator-core/lib/attention-notify.ts`. Producers call it at the source the moment a ≥high attention item appears; it fans out to two independently fail-safe channels (a delivery error is logged and swallowed — it never propagates into the producer’s write path):

1. **Mobile** — `notifyWorkspace(wsId, payload)` → `packages/operator-core/lib/device-push-dispatcher.ts` → APNs/FCM to devices paired in `harness_shared.mobile_push_tokens`. No-op when none are paired. `data` must be string-valued and `kind` a `PushKind` — the helper coerces/maps.
2. **Desktop-native** — emits an `attention.notify` event on the sync SSE bus (`notifySyncInvalidate`). The webview’s `DesktopAttentionNotifier` (`apps/operator/app/_components/`, mounted once at the root, app-level so `@papercusp/sync` stays domain-free) shows an in-app **sonner toast** always, and in the Tauri shell invokes the **`show_attention_notification`** Rust command (`papercusp-desktop`, `tauri-plugin-notification`) for a native OS notification. Driven from Rust, so no JS-facing notification capability is needed; the command is app-defined → allowed by default.

**No 60s poll.** The old `device-intervention-watcher` (a `setInterval(60s)` catch-all that SELECTed the three tables) was **deleted** in P-021 — its triggers now emit at the source.

## Where those rows are written (the producer chokepoints)

[Section titled “Where those rows are written (the producer chokepoints)”](#where-those-rows-are-written-the-producer-chokepoints)

The fs-watcher mirror for these three tables is **retired** (see the long comment block in `harness-fs-watcher.ts`). They’re now written **at producer time** by three internal endpoints, called by `bash run.sh` / `bin/supervisor.sh` / `bin/service-smoke-test.sh`:

* `POST /api/internal/escalation-event` → `harness_escalations`
* `POST /api/internal/smoke-test-event` → `harness_smoke_test`
* `POST /api/internal/plan-review-event` → `harness_plan_review`

So an event-driven emit for these has a clean home (those 3 endpoints) — but see the coupling gotcha below.

## The importance map (what the ≥high gate includes)

[Section titled “The importance map (what the ≥high gate includes)”](#the-importance-map-what-the-high-gate-includes)

P-020 pushes only at importance **≥ high**. The per-kind importance lives in `packages/operator-core/lib/attention/adapters.ts`:

| Kind                   | importance                                                                      |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| smoke-fail             | `high` (fixed)                                                                  |
| plan-review            | `high` (fixed)                                                                  |
| coord escalation       | `severityToImportance(sev)` — blocker→`urgent`, question→`high`, advisory→`low` |
| coord message-to-human | `normal`                                                                        |
| plan item              | the item’s own `importance:` keyword                                            |

Note `harness_escalations` (the table the watcher polls) has **no severity column** — it’s a harness-level escalation, distinct from a *coord* escalation. Treat it as inherently high. Net: the watcher’s three triggers are all already high, so the watcher never pushed low-importance noise to begin with.

## The four producer call-sites + their once-per-event gating

[Section titled “The four producer call-sites + their once-per-event gating”](#the-four-producer-call-sites--their-once-per-event-gating)

`notifyAttention()` is called at exactly the points that *create* a ≥high attention item — there’s no poll, so each must fire **once per genuine event**:

| Source      | Where                           | Fire condition                                                                                 |
| ----------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| escalation  | `internal/escalation-event.ts`  | `escalation != null` (skip notes-only updates)                                                 |
| smoke-fail  | `internal/smoke-test-event.ts`  | **transition** into failing — reads prior `status`, fires only on `pass→fail` / first fail     |
| plan-review | `internal/plan-review-event.ts` | every call (the producer posts once per completed review)                                      |
| needs-human | `plans:set-status`              | transition INTO `needs-human` at importance ≥ high (`shouldPushNeedsHuman` + `itemImportance`) |

Why this was safe to do at once: each source is its own chokepoint, so there’s **no double-fire** (the poll that used to also push escalation/smoke/plan-review is gone). The gating above prevents re-pushing on idempotent re-writes. The trade vs the old poll: the poll was a catch-all that fired regardless of write path; source emits only fire from these four sites — if a *new* write path for those tables appears, wire `notifyAttention` into it too.

## Extending it

[Section titled “Extending it”](#extending-it)

* **New attention source:** call `notifyAttention({ kind, title, body, harnessSlug, importance })` at the write site. Add the kind to `AttentionNotifyKind` + `MOBILE_KIND` if it needs a distinct mobile route.
* **The desktop native notification needs a cargo rebuild** of `papercusp-desktop` to pick up `tauri-plugin-notification` + the `show_attention_notification` command. The toast + mobile push work without it; the native OS notification is a no-op (caught) until the rebuild.
* End-to-end delivery (APNs/FCM, native OS notification) is **not headless-testable** — verify in the desktop shell. The `notifyAttention` fan-out + the gates are unit-tested (`attention-notify.test.ts`, `set-status.test.ts`).

# The autoloop is the routines engine now (Pot operator + self-declared wake)

> After autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild, there is no setInterval autoloop ticker — the DBOS routines engine fires each harness's blueprint-declared schedule, and a Pot operator decides its own next wake via pot:declare-wake. autoloop:control flips routine rows, not a timer.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

`autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild-2026-06-05` removed the legacy in-process `setInterval` autoloop and reframed the whole loop around two ideas:

1. **The autoloop IS the durable routines engine** — not a process-local timer. A harness’s autoloop is its blueprint-declared schedule (`triggers.schedule` → `bp-schedule-*` routine rows, materialized at `harness:create`). The routines workflow fires those rows; there is no `setInterval` anywhere in `packages/operator-core/lib/autoloop.ts`.
2. **The Pot operator decides its own next wake** — there is no cadence trigger for the operator (D-002). Before ending a turn it calls `pot:declare-wake` to set a *time*, an *event-subscription*, or *nothing*; the manual/event fire target is `pot:wake`.

If your mental model is still “a ticker loops every N seconds and fires the director,” it’s wrong post-2026-06-05. The loop is event/schedule-driven and durable (survives restarts, no double-fire).

## Why it matters / the load-bearing facts

[Section titled “Why it matters / the load-bearing facts”](#why-it-matters--the-load-bearing-facts)

* **`autoloop:control` flips routine rows, not a timer.** `pause`/`resume` toggle the `bp-schedule-*` routine rows’ `active` column (durable, cross-process). `reset-errors` zeroes `consecutive_errors` in `autoloop_state`, closing the P-009 backoff circuit. There is no in-process handle to clear.
* **Error-backoff is real and READ at the fire point (P-009).** `autoloop.ts` exports `evaluateFireGate` / `checkFireGate` / `recordFire`. `routines-workflow.ts` calls `checkFireGate` *before* firing a role and `recordFire(...,'ok'|'error')` after — so a repeatedly-failing director gets exponential backoff and, at `circuitThreshold()` consecutive errors, the circuit OPENS (one attempt per `backoffCapSec()` window) until a fix + `autoloop:control reset-errors`. `consecutive_errors` used to be written-but-never-read; now it gates.
* **Enablement = the blueprint, not a flag or `director-config.json`.** A harness autoloops because its blueprint declares a schedule + a `dispatch:` policy (concurrency/priority/readiness/costCap/safetyCeiling — see `coding.yaml`/`research.yaml`). There is no `autoLoop:true` flag and the old `.papercusp/director-config.json` is detached.
* **The Pot is a real blueprint.** `blueprints/pot/blueprint.yaml` (`extends: base`, decider = the `operator` role) is the 14th built-in and a *launch* blueprint (fired via `system:blueprint-run` / the invoke route), not a feature pipeline. `blueprint:catalog` lists it with `launchable:true`.
* **`pot:declare-wake` has REPLACE semantics** (like `coord:declare-intent`): each call describes the *whole* next wake; omitted parts are cleared. Time wakes are clamped to a wake floor (`floorSec`, default 60) so a confused operator can’t spin; event wakes register a persisted `@papercusp/rules` reaction rule that fires `pot:wake` on match; `pot:wake` is floor-debounced (a burst collapses to one wake; `force` overrides).

## The operator’s superpower (discovery → create)

[Section titled “The operator’s superpower (discovery → create)”](#the-operators-superpower-discovery--create)

The Pot chooses what to run via `blueprint:catalog` (built-in + installed tiers; per-entry decider/roles/spineModel/triggers/dispatch; abstract parents like `base` flagged `abstract`, broken ones kept as `{id,tier,error}`) → `blueprint:validate`/`extend` → `harness:create`. The `operator` role carries the caps for all of these — granted both in `OPERATOR_CAPS` (provision.ts) AND `BLUEPRINT_ROLE_CAPS['operator']` (role-principal-caps.ts). The second is load-bearing: provisioning without `force` is a no-op on an existing principal row, so a pre-rebuild operator row would otherwise lack the new caps.

## Gotcha: harness read tools were org-table-only

[Section titled “Gotcha: harness read tools were org-table-only”](#gotcha-harness-read-tools-were-org-table-only)

`harness:list` / `harness:status` historically read ONLY `harness_shared.projects` (the org/department table). A harness created via `harness:create` writes the **registry** (`harness_shared.harness_registry`), so its own read-back returned “not found” — the Pot could create a harness it then couldn’t see. Both tools now read the registry first (merged with `projects` for budget/status enrichment; org-only rows kept as `source:'project'`). If you add another “what harnesses exist?” surface, read the registry, not just `projects`.

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* `packages/operator-core/lib/autoloop.ts` — the fire-gate + backoff state machine (no setInterval).
* `packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/routines-workflow.ts` — where `checkFireGate`/`recordFire` gate the fire.
* `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/pot/{declare_wake,wake,status}.ts` — the self-declared-wake surface.
* `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/blueprint/catalog.ts` — the blueprint discovery tool.
* `packages/agent-mcp/src/tools/harness/{list,status,registry-read}.ts` — the registry-aware harness read tools.
* Plan `autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild-2026-06-05` — the full design + decisions (D-001..D-009).

# await-event: don't poll or block — register a wake and sleep

> The universal subscription primitive (events:await/emit/cancel/status + locks:acquire{wake_on_grant}): durable one-shot wake subscriptions with liveness-adaptive delivery (pty-inject / session-resume / inbox-park). What to await, what never wakes, and the cost discipline.

## What it is

[Section titled “What it is”](#what-it-is)

Agents that needed X-to-happen-before-proceeding used to **poll, block, or pivot blind** — a lock conflict said “pivot/retry”, resource waits held the turn, plan-run completion was a poll-based sweep. As of `await-event-primitive-2026-06-05` there is ONE primitive:

```plaintext
events:await { event: '<key>', note, timeout_sec, on_timeout: 'wake'|'expire' }
→ END YOUR TURN. You are re-invoked when the key fires (or at the deadline).
```

Sources fire keys with `events:emit { event, summary, payload, to? }` (agents) or `emitAwaitedEvent(...)` (host code). The layering (plan D-001): the **source** resolves who an event concerns (a lock grants to ONE waiter and emits a targeted key; CI-green broadcasts); the **delivery** layer is dumb — per recipient, honor their declared policy. `wake` re-invokes you (one-shot by construction — it can never wake-loop); `notify` (topics, follows) goes to your coord inbox and **never** wakes.

## The delivery ladder (liveness-adaptive, D-003/D-009)

[Section titled “The delivery ladder (liveness-adaptive, D-003/D-009)”](#the-delivery-ladder-liveness-adaptive-d-003d-009)

The wake handle is stamped at **registration** (your coord SID → `adv_sessions`): it can’t be fetched at fire time because you’re asleep. On fire, the executor walks:

1. **Live managed pty** (pid-matched in pty-bridge) → the wake turn is injected directly.
2. **Process exited** → your session is **resumed** under a managed pty (`claude --resume <native-id>` / `omp -r <thread>`) with the wake reason as the prompt; `PAPERCUSP_SID` is re-exported so identity, lock hooks, and your other awaits survive. claude resume REQUIRES the native session UUID — `--continue` would resume a random peer’s conversation on the shared cwd.
3. **Alive but uninjectable** (a detached terminal — the common psu case, or a pid-less session row with fresh presence) → **parked** + a one-time inbox nudge; the parked wake converts to a resume when your process exits. **If the nudge reaches you while awake and you act on it, ACK it:** `events:cancel { delivery_id }` — otherwise you’ll also be resumed later (a wasted turn).
4. **Nothing live, nothing resumable** → dropped VISIBLY (logged + metered), never silently.

Delivery is durable (PG queue, at-least-once + idempotent wake): a host restart re-claims stuck deliveries; a missed lock-grant NOTIFY is re-derived from waiter-table truth each 30s sweep.

## The patterns

[Section titled “The patterns”](#the-patterns)

* **Blocked on a file lock:** `locks:acquire { paths, intent, wake_on_grant: true }` → returns `queued_for_wake` + a ticket — end your turn. The wake carries your `lock_id` with the TTL **already running**: edit, then `locks:release`. The old “pivot/retry” advice is retired.
* **Blocked on a peer:** they tell you a key (or you agree on one) → you `events:await`, they `events:emit`. Built-in keys that fire today: `work-item:done:<id>`, `work-item:unblocked:<id>` (last blocker settled), `plan-run:finished:<runId>`, `plan:draft-ready:<slug>`, `conversation:answered:<id>` (coord:ask’s miss path names it), `release:green`, `release:deployed` / `release:deploy-failed`, `escalation:resolved:<msgId>`, `handoff:accepted:<msgId>`, `rate-limit:paused/reset:gym-judge|gym-ab`, `lock:grant:<ticket>`.
* **Wake-at-reset for a rate limit:** you hold a `retryAfterMs` → `events:await { event: 'rate-limit:reset:<scope>', timeout_sec: ceil(ms/1000), on_timeout: 'wake' }` — the deadline IS the reset wake; an earlier reset emit just arrives sooner.
* **“Re-verify after the next deploy”:** await `release:deployed` instead of hand-tracking the deferral.

## Cost discipline (D-007) — and what NOT to await

[Section titled “Cost discipline (D-007) — and what NOT to await”](#cost-discipline-d-007--and-what-not-to-await)

A wake = a re-invocation = a turn = tokens. Hence: `notify` is the default and never wakes; `wake` requires the explicit verb; wakes are **metered** (`events:status { meter: true }` — per-agent counts by channel = the wake-storm detector); mass unblocks re-admit paced (per-tick resume cap + per-agent single-flight + the fleet governor’s `await-wake` admission scope). Don’t await sub-minute bounded waits (just block — a wake costs more than the wait), ambient interest (that’s `topics:subscribe`), or recurring schedules (the pot/routines own time-wakes; an await is one-shot).

## Gotchas

[Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas)

* **Workspace scoping is normalized.** Awaits/deliveries live in the ONE coord workspace regardless of your identity’s scoping — an early build registered ’\*‘-scoped awaits that never matched system emits. Event keys embed globally-unique ids, so one namespace is collision-free by construction.
* **Exact-key match, no globs.** `events:await` matches the literal string.
* **codex sessions park instead of resuming** (the per-session CODEX\_HOME isn’t re-derivable yet) — visible in the delivery row.
* The store + engine live at `packages/operator-core/lib/events/await/` (migration 163: `event_awaits` + `event_wake_deliveries`); the lock bridge at `agent-tools/locks/lock-grant-bridge.ts`.

# The command palette and the agent MCP catalog are two registries unified at projection, not merged

> Ctrl+P commands come from lib/commands (Action Registry, browser-reflexive); agent tools come from defineTool/tooldef (server, gated). The Capability contract (lib/capabilities) unifies them at the read/projection layer with a §3 safety filter — it does NOT merge the two definition systems. Key gotchas: persona-axis ≠ RBAC-axis, :3070 serves a static build, runsIn mirrors CommandDef.browser.

## The two registries (and why they look like one)

[Section titled “The two registries (and why they look like one)”](#the-two-registries-and-why-they-look-like-one)

There are **two** “invokable thing” registries, and they are easy to confuse:

1. **Action Registry** — `packages/operator-core/lib/commands/`. `CommandDef`s registered via `register()`. **Browser-reflexive**: they run in the tab (mutate DOM / nuqs / URL), `browser: 'required'|'optional'|'none'`. Surfaces: the ⌘K palette, keyboard shortcuts, voice, the mobile webhook. Discovery: `list({ kind:'command', agent:'palette' })`.

2. **tooldef / endpoint catalog** — `defineTool()` in `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/` (+ `libs/generic/tooldef`, `packages/agent-mcp`). **Server-side, gated, audited**. Surfaces: the MCP transport (`papercusp-su` + in-app agents) and HTTP routes. Discovery: `getCatalog()` / `listAllProjectedTools()`.

They share **no** definition substrate. The only long-standing seam is `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/agent-mcp/run-command.ts` — itself a `defineTool` route that bridges an agent’s command id to a live browser tab (`session-registry.deliver`). The Action Registry’s `types.ts` header still claims it’s “the single source of truth for Oracle/Pi MCP” — that’s **stale**; conversational agents read the tooldef `mcp__agentmcp__*` catalog (`packages/operator-core/lib/operator-mcp-tools.ts`).

## What `packages/operator-core/lib/capabilities/` does

[Section titled “What packages/operator-core/lib/capabilities/ does”](#what-packagesoperator-corelibcapabilities-does)

Plan `capability-metadata-contract-2026-05-31`. The `Capability` contract unifies the two **at the read/projection layer only** — it does **not** merge the definition systems (a merge would re-couple browser concerns into the now-extracted host-agnostic `@papercusp/tooldef`). Two read-only adapters map each registry into one `Capability[]`: `from-action-registry.ts` and `from-tooldef.ts`. The palette then lists both; `Ctrl+P` spans browser commands **and** the server tool catalog.

* `GET /api/agent-mcp/capabilities` — the §3-eligible, principal+role-gated server catalog.
* `POST /api/agent-mcp/run-tool` — loopback-only invoke; runs the tool through the **full dispatch stack with NO gate-bypass** (`lookupByMcpName` + `dispatchProjectedToolToMcp` + `PROJECTED_DEPS`), so role/capability/authorize/quota/audit all apply.
* `app/_components/use-server-capabilities.ts` — client fetch + execute + toast.

## Gotchas that will bite you

[Section titled “Gotchas that will bite you”](#gotchas-that-will-bite-you)

* **Persona/surface axis ≠ principal RBAC axis.** A `CommandDef.agents` entry like `'palette'`/`'operator'` is the **persona/surface** axis (→ `Capability.gating.agentRoles`

  * the `surfaces` overlay), **never** principal `auth.roles`. Conflating them is the exact bug RFC `tooldef-auth-rfc-2026-05-31`’s decision D-E forbids. The first draft of this plan’s §4 made that mistake; see D-004.

* **The palette principal is just the request principal — no escalation.** On the desktop, `tryResolvePrincipal` → `principalFromLoopback` yields `kind:'loopback'`, `trust:'unverified-loopback'`, `capabilities: Set(['*'])`. Do **not** mint a higher-trust “trusted” palette principal — trust-gated tools correctly reject loopback, and the dispatch stack is the real boundary (D-005).

* **One-keystroke ≠ safe.** “principal-allowed + no-args” is NOT “safe to fire from a fuzzy palette with a toast.” `safety-filter.ts` (`paletteEligibility`) excludes streaming/interactive/required-arg tools and forces a **confirm** step for destructive/`tier:high`. `run-tool` re-enforces this **server-side** (never trust the client) — destructive tools 409 without `confirmed:true`.

* **`runsIn` is 3-valued, mirroring `CommandDef.browser`** (`required`→browser, `none`→server, `optional`→hybrid). A binary server/browser split silently drops `browser:'optional'` (e.g. `chat.dispatch`).

* **`ToolDefinition` (from `getCatalog()`) has `tier` + `args`; `ProjectedTool` (from `listAllProjectedTools()`) has `agentRoles` + `expose` but NOT `tier`.** Use the catalog for risk/args, the projection for the role allowlist. Tooldef’s `CapabilityTier` is `'low'|'medium'|'high'` — note **`medium`**, not `med`.

## Why your route change “doesn’t show up” in the running desktop

[Section titled “Why your route change “doesn’t show up” in the running desktop”](#why-your-route-change-doesnt-show-up-in-the-running-desktop)

The desktop webview loads **`:3070`, which serves a static pre-built `operator-vite/dist/`** (hashed `/assets/index-*.js`, no Vite HMR). `:3055` is the live HMR dev server but the webview does **not** use it. Consequences:

* **Client (UI) changes** need `npm --workspace @papercusp/operator-vite run build` **and** a webview reload (`DevReloadGate` suppresses auto-reload — `Ctrl/Cmd+R` is manual).
* **Server route changes** (`routes/index.ts`) need the **`:3070` hono host to restart** — it does not hot-reload new routes. Don’t restart it casually: it’s a shared service that also backs the `papercusp-su` MCP and other agents’ sessions. Announce/get authorization first (see how the dogfood agents restarted `papercup-dev-api.service`).

This is why a freshly-added route can read `404` on `:3070` even though it’s correctly registered and the build is green — it’s live only after the host restarts.

# claude-code headless permission model (what --allowed-tools / --permission-mode actually do)

> Verified vs claude 2.1.158 — --allowed-tools is NOT a whitelist by itself; only --permission-mode dontAsk makes it one, and even then gating is non-uniform (CronCreate/EnterWorktree bypass it). --disallowed-tools is the hard block. How the fleet spawn is locked down.

## Why this exists

[Section titled “Why this exists”](#why-this-exists)

The headless fleet (orchestrator `invoke()` → `claude -p`) needs to run unattended without (a) hanging on a permission prompt or (b) being able to do anything destructive. The flag semantics that achieve this are **surprising and contradict the docs in places** — every claim here was tested empirically against claude 2.1.158 with external side-effects, because a doc-only read sent an earlier pass down the wrong path. If you’re changing the fleet’s permissions (`claudeMcpArgs` in `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/invoke.ts`), read this first.

## The model (all verified, not assumed)

[Section titled “The model (all verified, not assumed)”](#the-model-all-verified-not-assumed)

1. **`--allowed-tools` is NOT a whitelist on its own.** It’s a *pre-approval* list (don’t-prompt-for-these). What an *un-listed* tool does depends on `--permission-mode`:

   * Under **`bypassPermissions`** the allow-list is **ignored entirely** — everything runs. (Verified: Bash wrote a file with only `Read` allow-listed.)
   * Under **`default`** the tool still *runs*, but `default` applies a **sandbox** that blocks filesystem-writes-outside-workdir + network. (Verified: a CWD write was blocked.) → `default` breaks file-writing roles; do not use it for the fleet.

2. **`--permission-mode dontAsk` makes `--allowed-tools` a true default-deny whitelist** — an un-listed *gated* tool is denied, the model is told, and it continues (no hang). Unlike `default`, `dontAsk` does **not** sandbox the allowed tools, so writes/edits work. **This is the posture the fleet uses.**

3. **`dontAsk` gating is NON-uniform.** A class of session-local / “meta” built-ins is **exempt** from the allow-list and runs even when omitted. Verified: with the exact fleet allow-list, `CronCreate` still created a job and `EnterWorktree` still ran. A `claude -p` spawn carries 250+ tools incl. `CronCreate/Delete/List`, `Workflow`, `Enter/ExitWorktree`, `RemoteTrigger`, `PushNotification`, `Monitor`, `ScheduleWakeup`, `Task`, `Skill`, `LSP`. **The allow-list alone is not a complete boundary.**

4. **`--disallowed-tools` is the hard block.** It removes a tool from the spawn entirely (“No such tool exists in this environment”), wins over the allow-list AND over `bypassPermissions`, and supports command granularity: `Bash(git push:*)` blocks `git push` while `echo` still runs. This is what closes the dangerous *exempt* tools (#3) and dangerous Bash *commands*.

5. **The per-role MCP boundary is already server-side**, belt-and-suspenders: `tools/list` is surface-filtered by `listMcpProjections(role)` (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/tool-projection.ts`) AND call-time-denied by the dispatch stack’s `role-allowlist` step (`dispatch-stack.ts`, skipped only for `gateBypass.role` = superuser). So a fleet worker only ever sees/calls its role’s MCP tools — `--allowed-tools "mcp__papercusp"` (server wildcard) grants exactly that, no per-role enumeration needed.

## What the fleet spawn ships (invoke.ts `claudeMcpArgs`)

[Section titled “What the fleet spawn ships (invoke.ts claudeMcpArgs)”](#what-the-fleet-spawn-ships-invokets-claudemcpargs)

```plaintext
--mcp-config <cwd>/.mcp.json --strict-mcp-config
--permission-mode dontAsk
--allowed-tools "mcp__papercusp Read Edit Write Bash Glob Grep WebFetch WebSearch"
--disallowed-tools CronCreate CronDelete CronList ScheduleWakeup \
  EnterWorktree ExitWorktree Workflow Task RemoteTrigger PushNotification \
  Monitor "Bash(sudo:*)" "Bash(git push:*)"
```

Allow-list is one space-joined arg (claude splits it); deny patterns are separate argv elements so internal spaces (`Bash(git push:*)`) survive — `claudeMcpArgs` is the **tail** of `finalArgv` for claude-code, so the variadic `--disallowed-tools` swallows nothing unintended. Defers the whole posture if the user set any permission flag in `AGENT_CMD`.

The allow-list is **per-role** (`fleetAllowedToolsForRole(role)`): most roles get the kit above, while any role in `FLEET_NO_WRITE_ROLES` drops `Edit`/`Write` (mechanically enforcing an “API/MCP-only — do NOT use `Write`/`Edit`” prompt instruction). **Update (2026-06): `FLEET_NO_WRITE_ROLES` is currently EMPTY** — the former `expert`/`feedback` API-only roles were removed, so no role is cut today; the mechanism stays for when such a role returns. That’s the *only* per-role built-in cut that’s safe from a prompt read (other review/gate roles write legit output via `Write`). It’s a nudge, not a boundary — `Bash` is still granted, so a shell redirect could write; deeper per-role cuts need a real fleet-spawn run, not a prompt read. An unknown role gets the full kit.

**No-push** is *really* enforced by a spawn-env-scoped pre-push hook (`gitConfigNoPushEnv` injects `core.hooksPath` via `GIT_CONFIG_*` into the spawn env only — the shared checkout’s config and the user’s/other agents’ pushes are untouched). The `Bash(git push:*)` deny is the evadable backstop (`git -C … push`, aliases, `&& git push` slip past command-string matching; the hook does not).

## Honest limits (the deny-list alone is not a sandbox)

[Section titled “Honest limits (the deny-list alone is not a sandbox)”](#honest-limits-the-deny-list-alone-is-not-a-sandbox)

**Update (`fleet-spawn-sandbox-2026-06-01`, P-013/D-015): there is now a DEFAULT-ON sandbox layered on top of this deny-list** — claude-code’s OWN built-in sandbox (Linux bubblewrap + socat egress proxy; macOS Seatbelt), injected via `--settings`, opt-out with `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX=0`. It closes the two gaps the deny-list cannot: it hides credential dirs (`FLEET_SANDBOX_DENY_READ` — `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.config/gcloud`, `~/.papercusp`, `~/.npmrc`) from sandboxed Bash and confines egress to an allow-listed set of package registries (`resolveFleetAllowedDomains()`; strip-all with `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX_DENY_ALL_EGRESS=1`). The bullets below describe the **deny-list layer in isolation** — i.e. the posture *before* that sandbox, which is now the default container for those reads/egress.

* **Credential reads are not closed by the deny-list** — the allow-listed `Read` tool reaches any path. **Network egress is not closed by the deny-list** — `WebFetch` is allow-listed. True containment of those needs a network/fs sandbox, not a deny-list — which is what the default-on sandbox above now is.
* **Worktree isolation is conditional** — `invoke.ts` falls back to `ctx.projectDir` (the shared main checkout) when there’s no feature-worktree, so “the worker is contained in a worktree” is not universally true.
* Per-role *tightening* of the built-in dev kit (e.g. deny `Write` to read-only roles) is deliberately NOT done — it needs per-role real-spawn verification because withholding a needed built-in silently breaks a role mid-pipeline.

## How to re-verify (don’t trust the docs here)

[Section titled “How to re-verify (don’t trust the docs here)”](#how-to-re-verify-dont-trust-the-docs-here)

Test against the real CLI with an **external side-effect** (a file on disk, not just a `tool_use` block in the stream — a denied call still shows an attempt). Use a pristine `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` (copy in only `.credentials.json`, no settings) so a stray `settings.local.json` allow-rule can’t confound the result. Pattern that settled it:

```plaintext
claude -p "use a shell command to create file X containing Y" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk --allowed-tools "Read" --output-format json
# then check whether file X exists — exists = the tool ran, absent = denied.
```

# claude-file memory: MEMORY.md is a capped projection — and over-cap it goes silently STALE

> The session-start index has a ~24.4KB hard cap. The projector evicts oldest project entries to fit a 20KB soft cap, PHYSICALLY ARCHIVING them (they leave the searchable store) — and when durables alone exceed the hard cap it ABORTS, leaving MEMORY.md stale. Measured at 111/1k/10k by the memory bench's index-cap probe.

## The three-layer trap

[Section titled “The three-layer trap”](#the-three-layer-trap)

The Claude Code file memory has **three different visibility layers**, and they diverge at scale:

1. **Topic files** (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/*.md`) — the store. The `ClaudeFileMemoryBackend` searches these (full re-read + lexical score per query; `archive/` is invisible to it).
2. **`MEMORY.md`** — an auto-generated *projection* of the topic files (`~/.claude/scripts/memory-compact.mjs`, a SessionStart hook). This is what a booting agent actually loads. Native hard cap **\~24.4 KB** — past it Claude silently drops the tail.
3. **`archive/`** — where the projector moves evicted files. Recoverable, but **invisible to both the index and the backend’s search**.

The gotcha: the projector keeps the index under a **20 KB soft cap** by **physically archiving** overflow `project`-type files (oldest first; `user`/`feedback`/`reference` are never auto-evicted). So the cap doesn’t just bound session-start visibility — **one compaction pass shrinks the searchable store itself**.

Danger

When the durable set *alone* renders over the hard cap, the projector has nothing mechanical left to shed and **ABORTS: it archives nothing and leaves the existing MEMORY.md untouched — i.e. STALE**. New memories stop appearing in the index entirely, with only a session-start `memory-hygiene` notice as the signal. The real store on this box already hit this state (113 durables → 26.3 KB > 24.4 KB).

## Measured (memory-backend-benchmark P-010, D-004)

[Section titled “Measured (memory-backend-benchmark P-010, D-004)”](#measured-memory-backend-benchmark-p-010-d-004)

The bench’s index-cap probe (`packages/operator-core/lib/memory/bench/index-cap-cli.ts`, pure FS — temp-dir stores seeded through the seam) recorded, with the simulation pinned **exactly** to the real script’s dry-run output:

| store size        | indexed | index KB | indexed % | behavior                                                    |
| ----------------- | ------- | -------- | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| 114 (real corpus) | 113     | 26.3     | 99.1%     | over BOTH caps → projector aborts; index stale              |
| 1,000             | 113     | 26.3     | 11.3%     | 887 would-be-archived; durables still over hard cap → abort |
| 10,000            | 113     | 26.3     | 1.1%      | 9,887 would-be-archived; abort                              |

i.e. the file backend’s *session-start reach* is bounded at roughly **\~115–200 entries regardless of store size** (whatever fits \~20 KB of one-line hooks), and on an all-durable store the index stops updating altogether.

## What to do with this

[Section titled “What to do with this”](#what-to-do-with-this)

* **Don’t design features assuming the file store scales** — anything past a few hundred entries is invisible at boot and, after compaction, unsearchable. PG-backed memory (mem0) is the scale path; this is one of the falsifiable predictions the memory bench scores (D-006).
* **A stale MEMORY.md is a signal, not a bug in your change** — check the `memory-hygiene` SessionStart notice; the fix is deliberate curation of durables (merge/retire/tighten), never hand-editing the index.
* **Reproduce / re-measure** with `npx tsx packages/operator-core/lib/memory/bench/index-cap-cli.ts --sizes 1000,10000` (no PG, no keys needed). The simulation lives in `index-cap.ts` and its fidelity to the real script is pinned by `index-cap.test.ts` (auto-skips where `~/.claude/scripts/memory-compact.mjs` doesn’t exist).

## See also

[Section titled “See also”](#see-also)

* [`mem0-unavailable-outage-or-swallowed-bug`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/mem0-unavailable-outage-or-swallowed-bug/) — the mem0 side’s swallowed-failure trap (same benchmark arc).

# Parsing tagged compact tool results (TOON / CSV)

> Tool results are no longer always JSON — the MCP transport delivers compact TOON by default, prefixed with a `format: <fmt>` marker. How to read each format, where the pagination cursor + row count went, and how to force JSON when you need it.

## What changed

[Section titled “What changed”](#what-changed)
