Tool results you read over MCP are **no longer always JSON**. To save tokens, the server picks a compact format from each tool’s output shape and serializes `ToolResponse.data` into `content[0].text` accordingly. You don’t request this — it’s delivered. Plan: `token-efficient-tool-result-formats-2026-06-06`.

Every compact payload **self-identifies** with a marker on its first line, so you never have to guess:

```plaintext
format: toon
[3]{id,state,title}:
  WI-001,todo,Wire the encoder
  WI-002,passed,Add the schema
  WI-003,wip,Backfill list tools
```

* **No marker → it’s JSON** (the assumed default; unmarked so bytes are unchanged).
* **`format: toon`** → TOON. The `[N]{cols}:` header names the row count `N` and the columns; each following indented line is one row, comma-separated, in column order. Nested values indent YAML-style. It is a lossless JSON superset — read a cell as the JSON value it represents (`null` is `null`, `42` is a number, a quoted `"…"` is a string with escapes).
* **`format: csv`** / **`format: tsv`** → a header row then comma/tab-separated rows, RFC 4180 quoted (a field with a delimiter/quote/newline is `"…"`, embedded quotes doubled). CSV is **lossy** — every cell is a string; there are no types or nulls. Only flat tools opt into it.

## Where the envelope went

[Section titled “Where the envelope went”](#where-the-envelope-went)

Compact tabular formats can’t hold a pagination cursor inside the table, so the **envelope rides in `_meta`**, not the body:

* `_meta.format` — the format that was actually served.
* `_meta.nextCursor` — the pagination cursor (was `ToolResponse.nextCursor`).
* `_meta.degraded` / `_meta.degradedReasons` — partial-result flags.
* `_meta.formatFallback: true` — the server downgraded from the requested/ideal format (e.g. you asked for CSV on a nested shape, or TOON couldn’t represent the data losslessly). The payload in `content[0].text` is still correct; just note it isn’t what was nominally requested.

**The row count is in the TOON header** (`[N]{…}`), not a `count` field — list tools dropped their `{ ok, count, items }` wrapper; `data` is the array directly.

## Forcing JSON (or another format)

[Section titled “Forcing JSON (or another format)”](#forcing-json-or-another-format)

The format is a **client-process knob**, never something you put in tool *args*. If you (or a programmatic consumer) need lossless JSON for round-tripping or exact parsing:

* **MCP** — pass `_meta.format: "json"` on the `tools/call`, or add `?format=json` to the MCP connection URL. `?format=csv` / `compact` also work.
* **HTTP** — `?format=json` (or `Accept: application/json`) on the request.
* **structuredContent** — `?structured=1` (or `_meta.structured: true`) also attaches the lossless structured JSON as `structuredContent` alongside the compact text, for clients that render it separately. Off by default.

## The lossless guarantee (why a list sometimes comes back as JSON)

[Section titled “The lossless guarantee (why a list sometimes comes back as JSON)”](#the-lossless-guarantee-why-a-list-sometimes-comes-back-as-json)

`@toon-format/toon` is lossless in the common case but has round-trip bugs on pathological keys and on certain string values containing structural characters (backticks, colons, `→`) in its nested-list form. The encoder **verifies the round-trip** (encode → decode → compare) and falls back to JSON whenever it doesn’t hold — so you are **never handed a compact payload that doesn’t decode back to the original**. Practical consequence: a list whose rows carry rich markdown text or nested blobs (e.g. `work_items:list` with non-null `payload`) may arrive as JSON with `_meta.formatFallback: true`. That’s the safety net working, not a bug. Flat/uniform list tools (e.g. `audit:list`) reliably arrive as TOON.

Implementation: `libs/generic/result-encoding` (encoder + eligibility) and `libs/generic/tooldef/src/serialize-result.ts` (the single serializer every transport calls). Contract reference: [Transports → Result formats](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/transports).

# Split a budget conditionally on which pools are actually active

> When fanning out a `limit` across N optional pools (user / workspace / N harnesses), the per-pool slice must depend on which pools are non-empty THIS call — not a fixed compile-time ratio.

## The trap

[Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap)

`buildMemoryContextBlock` fans out one `limit` across multiple optional pools:

* per-user pool (skipped when `userId` is `null` — workspace-bearer routes)
* legacy `workspace:<wsId>` pool (was present during the deprecation window — **since drained, D-005**; the live `buildMemoryContextBlock` no longer pulls it, so the concrete user-vs-workspace example below is now historical)
* N per-harness pools (zero when no harness slugs supplied)

The original code hardcoded:

```ts
const userLimit = input.limit ?? 6;
const workspaceLimit = Math.ceil(userLimit / 2);
```

`workspaceLimit` is *always* half the budget, even when there’s no user pull to share with. A workspace-bearer caller that passed `limit: 9` got `workspaceLimit = 5` — wasting 44 % of its budget on a pool that didn’t exist.

This was caught only because a unit test asserted the expected `limit: 9`.

## The pattern

[Section titled “The pattern”](#the-pattern)

When the budget split is supposed to share a pool budget, **condition the share on which pools are actually firing**, not on a fixed ratio:

```ts
// Fixed split — wrong when pools are optional
const workspaceLimit = Math.ceil(userLimit / 2);


// Conditional split — correct
const workspaceLimit = input.userId ? Math.ceil(userLimit / 2) : userLimit;
```

The principle generalises: for **N optional pools**, divide by the count of pools that will actually fire this call:

```ts
const activePools = [
  input.userId ? 'user' : null,
  needLegacyWorkspace ? 'workspace' : null,
  ...harnessSlugs.map((s) => `harness:${s}`),
].filter(Boolean);
const perPoolLimit = Math.ceil(userLimit / activePools.length);
```

Or — when each pool has a meaningful natural cap (`PER_HARNESS_LIMIT = 3` in the same file), don’t divide at all; sum the caps and let the caller bound the merged total.

## How to spot this

[Section titled “How to spot this”](#how-to-spot-this)

Greppable signature: any `const fooLimit = Math.ceil(<budget> / 2)` near a `client.search(... { limit: fooLimit })`. If the *other* pool can be empty or unset, the divisor is wrong.

In tests, the signal is: a test that fixes the budget at `limit: N`, isolates one pool, and asserts the *exact* request limit. If that test expects `N` but the implementation passes `N/2`, this bug is present.

## Why it stuck around

[Section titled “Why it stuck around”](#why-it-stuck-around)

The fixed `/ 2` worked correctly when both pools were always present — that was the codebase invariant before the memory-harness-scope plan turned the per-user pull optional. The bug only became visible once `buildMemoryContextBlock` started accepting `userId: null`.

This is a recurring shape: **a new optional shape introduced, while a legacy assumption about co-presence stays implicit.** Audit any other budget / quota / ratio constant when adding an optional pool. The `forward-defined-registry-entries` pattern has the same flavor — adding a new variant breaks the assumption that the variant list is closed.

## See also

[Section titled “See also”](#see-also)

* `packages/operator-core/lib/memory/injection.ts` — the canonical fix (commit `5b0e48ee`). **Update:** the legacy `workspace:` pool this split fed has since been **drained** (D-005), so the live code no longer divides a budget here — it pulls the user pool at `limit` and each harness pool at `PER_HARNESS_LIMIT`, with no `workspaceLimit`. The pattern above still holds for any future multi-pool fan-out.
* `packages/operator-core/lib/memory/injection.test.ts` — the test that caught it was replaced (now `pulls user + harness scopes only — no deprecated workspace pull (D-005)`).
* [`pure-decision-functions-pulled-from-daemons`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/pure-decision-functions-pulled-from-daemons/) — extracting `decideBudgetSplit(input)` as a pure function with tests would have caught this on the first variant.

Tip

“Half the budget for workspace” is a *defaulted assumption*, not a specification. Encode the assumption as a function whose inputs include the set of active pools — then the next person adding a pool can’t accidentally silently misallocate the budget.

# Coord lifecycle auto-emits are subscription-scoped (not broadcast)

> Lifecycle auto-emits (claim/intent/finding/completion) deliver only to agents watching the plan/topic/work-item via audience selectors, not to '*'. How the @plan/@topic/@object/@file selectors resolve, and the PAPERCUSP_COORD_EMIT_SCOPE kill-switch.

## What it is

[Section titled “What it is”](#what-it-is)

The coord **lifecycle auto-emits** — claim (“Taking X”), intent (“now working on X”), finding (a filed bug), completion (“DONE + tested”) — used to broadcast to `to: ['*']`, landing in **every** agent’s inbox (\~360 events/6h). As of `coord-emit-subscription-scoping-2026-06-05` (Brief 28) they deliver only to the agents **watching** the relevant plan / topic / work-item. The coordination signal is preserved; the firehose is gone.

## How it works — audience selectors expanded at send time

[Section titled “How it works — audience selectors expanded at send time”](#how-it-works--audience-selectors-expanded-at-send-time)

The rule `args` functions are synchronous, so watcher-resolution (which needs PG) can’t happen there. Instead the lifecycle rules emit **audience selectors** in the `to[]`, and `sendMessage` (`agent-tools/coordination/messages.ts`, the single async choke point every `coord:emit`/`coord:send` flows through) expands them to concrete ownerIds before persisting. The expanded set is stored on the one envelope, so the inbox filter (`to.includes(ownerId) || '*'`) is unchanged.

Selectors (pure resolver in `agent-tools/coordination/audience.ts`, PG wiring in `audience-host.ts`):

* `@plan:<slug>` — plan subscribers ∪ **active presence on the plan** (`coord_presence.current_plan_slug`) ∪ subscribers of topics the plan is tagged to. The presence half is load-bearing: it makes scoping work **without** every agent explicitly subscribing — an agent that merely declared intent on plan X still receives X’s events.
* `@topic:<slug>` — subscribers of that topic.
* `@object:<kind>:<ref>` — subscribers of that coord object (the full stored subscription `target_ref`, e.g. `feature:<harness>#<id>` / `issue:<id>`) ∪ its tagged-topic subscribers. Build it with `objectSelector(workItemObjectRef(wi))`.
* `@file:<path>` — active presence whose `current_files` includes `<path>` (the file-collision signal, used by intent).

Plain ownerIds, `*`, and `human` pass through untouched (a normal `coord:send` is zero-overhead). Which category emits which selectors:

| Lifecycle     | selectors                                             |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| intent        | `@plan:<slug>` + one `@file:<path>` per file in scope |
| completion    | `@plan:<slug>` + `@object:<ref>`                      |
| claim         | `@object:<ref>`                                       |
| finding (bug) | `@object:<ref>`                                       |

An empty resolution (no subscribers, nobody present on the plan) → empty `to` → the row still persists (queryable plan history) but reaches **no inbox**. We never fall back to `*` — that would re-open the firehose. `coord:emit`’s `to` therefore allows an empty array (a selector that resolves to nobody), though omitting `to` on a hand-call still defaults to `['*']`.

## Kill-switch — `PAPERCUSP_COORD_EMIT_SCOPE`

[Section titled “Kill-switch — PAPERCUSP\_COORD\_EMIT\_SCOPE”](#kill-switch--papercusp_coord_emit_scope)

This changes coordination delivery for the whole fleet, so there’s a one-flag revert (`audience-host.ts:audienceMode()`):

* unset / `scoped` (default) — selectors resolve to watchers.
* `broadcast` — every selector collapses back to `['*']` (legacy global broadcast). Set it + restart the host if scoping ever starves real coordination; no code change or redeploy needed.

## Gotchas

[Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas)

* It deploys to the **live fleet** via the release gate (`:3070` green), not on a bare restart — test server edits on staging `:3170` first.
* Claim/finding scope to **object** subscribers only (no plan in the event), so they’re quiet unless someone explicitly `work_items:subscribe`d. That’s fine: collision-avoidance is via the work-item’s `assignee`/state, not a push. The high-volume wins are intent + completion (both carry plan context).
* The companion owner directive (`autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild` D-013): the Pot operator triages its inbox first each wake and subscribes a wake on need-human arrival — so what *does* reach the operator’s inbox is acted on promptly.

# Coord injection protocol — the positional [coord+N] block + single-source schema

> How the continuous [coord] push surface is encoded. One coord-schema module drives both the server-side injection renderer and the psu-prompt legend; the cc/omp hooks are dumb pipes. Read before touching render.ts glyphs, the COORD_LEGEND, or the coord hooks.

## The idea

[Section titled “The idea”](#the-idea)

The `[coord …]` blocks injected after **every** psu tool call are the highest- leverage token surface in the system — pushed continuously, not pulled. A coord line has **one fixed schema, identical every injection**, with the operator (renderer) and the model (reader) both ours. So the schema does not belong on the wire: it is declared **once, out-of-band, in the psu prompt** (the `## Coord injection protocol` legend), and only VALUES travel — a positional line `<glyph> <handle> <text>`. Plan: `token-efficient-coord-injection-2026-06-06`.

Measured cut vs the legacy format: **−70%** (5-message block) to **−80%** (single message) — most of it from killing the per-injection footer, the double-UUID, and the per-block header.

## The pieces (one source of truth)

[Section titled “The pieces (one source of truth)”](#the-pieces-one-source-of-truth)

`packages/operator-core/lib/coord-schema.ts` is the **single source**:

* **`COORD_LEGEND`** — `lineType → { glyph, name }`, keyed by the lifecycle category (`intent`/`completion`/`claim`/`window`/`handoff`/`finding`) plus the base `CoordKind`s. Glyphs are **1-token ASCII** (`>` `*` `+` `#` `<` `!` `-` `^` `=` `.` `~`) — emoji (`▶ ↪ ⚠`) tokenize to 2–3 tokens, pure waste here.
* **`glyphFor(entry)`** — the glyph for one entry: its lifecycle category if it has one (keyed on the **`lifecycle`** envelope field that `coord:emit` stamps — NOT `category`, which is reserved for ambient tags), else its `kind`.
* **`shortHandle(from)`** — `su-ab53332d-…` → `ab533`; shown ONCE per line.
* **`renderInjection(entries)`** (Projection 1, the wire) — the `[coord+N]` block: capping + overflow count, digest-notify coalescing, latest-per-peer intent collapse, no header, no footer.
* **`renderCoordLegend()`** (Projection 2, the prompt) — the once-per-session legend (grammar + glyph key + the relocated footer), spliced into the psu playbook at `<!-- PAPERCUSP-SU:COORD-LEGEND -->` by `renderSuPlaybook`.

Because the wire and the legend **both derive from `COORD_LEGEND`**, they cannot desync — the anti-desync test (`coord-schema.test.ts`) asserts every glyph `renderInjection` can emit is documented in the legend. A positional format can’t self-correct a schema mismatch (no inline header), so this is load-bearing.

## How a delta flows

[Section titled “How a delta flows”](#how-a-delta-flows)

1. A lifecycle event (`work_items:complete`, `coord:declare-intent`, …) emits a coord message via `coord:emit`, stamped `auto:true` + `lifecycle:'<category>'`. `render.ts` produces **glyph-free, sender-free** prose (the glyph + handle are presentation, added downstream — P-003/P-010).
2. The cc/omp hook calls `coord:inbox { since_ts: <cursor> }`. The handler computes `injection = renderInjection(entries)` server-side and returns it alongside `entries`.
3. The hook is a **dumb pipe**: it echoes `result.injection` into its envelope (Claude `additionalContext` / OMP `<system-reminder type="coord">`) and advances the cursor from `summary.newest_ts`. All formatting/capping/collapse is server-side — one edit re-tunes every client.

## Rules when you touch this

[Section titled “Rules when you touch this”](#rules-when-you-touch-this)

* **Never hardcode a glyph.** Add/change it in `COORD_LEGEND`; the renderer + legend both read it, and the anti-desync test enforces coverage.
* **`render.ts` stays glyph-free + sender-free.** The stored summary is content only; `renderInjection` adds the glyph (from the line type) and the handle (once). Re-baking either double-emits it on every injection.
* **The glyph keys on `lifecycle`, not `category`.** `coord:emit` stamps the lifecycle category on the envelope’s `lifecycle` field; `category` holds ambient tags (`service-health`) that `coord:inbox` default-excludes. (`categorizeCoordMessage` is unaffected by the glyph-strip — it short-circuits on the `lifecycle`/`auto` flag before any glyph-sniffing.)
* **Hooks are dumb pipes.** Keep only transport + the per-launch cursor. Do NOT re-add formatting/capping/footers client-side — that’s the divergence this replaced (the cc + omp footers had already drifted apart).
* **The footer lives once, in the prompt legend** — not per injection.
* **The legend is in BOTH prompt pipelines** (`renderSuPlaybook` for psu + `assembleRolePrompt` for role agents). Don’t assume coord injection is psu-only: the coord hook lives in the GLOBAL `~/.claude/settings.json` and `bootstrap-role` sets `PAPERCUSP_SID`, so **Claude role agents receive injection too** — they need the legend to read the positional format (the pre-positional prose was self-describing; this format isn’t). Codex role homes omit the coord hook (the hook is added only for the SU `coordSid`), so codex roles don’t inject — but the legend is harmless accurate guidance for them.

# Mid-turn coord delivery (Claude / Codex / OMP)

> How new coord:inbox messages reach a RUNNING agent between tool calls — not just at session/turn start — per client, why it's prompt-cache-safe, and the holder-intent enrichment on lock blocks.

## What it is

[Section titled “What it is”](#what-it-is)

A peer’s `coord:send` used to reach an agent only at **session start** (the prompt tells SU agents to call `coord:inbox` once) or, for OMP, at **turn start** (the `coord-hook.ts` reminder). A long turn could run for minutes — many tool calls — blind to “stop, I’m refactoring that file.”

Mid-turn delivery closes that: after **each tool call**, the agent’s own tool cadence is used to poll `coord:inbox` for messages newer than a cursor and inject any new ones. No model discipline (an LLM can’t keep a wall-clock timer); the **system** rides the tool stream.

## Per client — three mechanisms, one behavior

[Section titled “Per client — three mechanisms, one behavior”](#per-client--three-mechanisms-one-behavior)

| Client     | Where                                                                                 | Mechanism                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Claude** | `~/.claude/settings.json` PostToolUse, matcher `*`                                    | `apps/operator/scripts/hooks/cc/posttooluse-coord-inbox.sh` → `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` (exit 0, **no** `decision`).                                                                                                                                            |
| **Codex**  | per-session `$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json` PostToolUse, matcher `.*` (**SU sessions only**) | same script, written by `role-codex-home.ts` `writeSuCodexHome` with a **baked `PAPERCUSP_SID`**. Codex fires PostToolUse for **Bash / apply\_patch / MCP** (not WebSearch) — independent of the PreToolUse-on-edits gap (#20204) that keeps the *lock* hook inert on codex. |
| **OMP**    | `coord-hook.ts` `tool_result` handler                                                 | `pollInboxDelta()` → `pi.sendMessage(…, { deliverAs: 'steer' })`. `ToolResultEvent` carries no content, so steer-append is the vector (not content-replacement).                                                                                                             |

The shell hook **gates on `PAPERCUSP_SID`** (psu sessions only) + the su-token, so a plain `claude`/`codex` on the box no-ops. `owner == PAPERCUSP_SID`, which is the same id baked into the agent’s MCP `&client=`, so the hook reads the *right* inbox/watermark.

## The cursor / dedup protocol

[Section titled “The cursor / dedup protocol”](#the-cursor--dedup-protocol)

* **Per-owner cursor.** Claude/Codex: a local file `coord-cursor-<owner>.json` in `~/.papercusp/locks-cache/`. OMP: a module var seeded at `turn_start` to the newest ts surfaced, advanced on each `tool_result`, persisted to the watermark at `turn_end`.
* **First run seeds to “now”** and injects nothing — the session-start `coord:inbox` already showed the backlog; only *new* arrivals inject.
* Each message injects **exactly once** (cursor advances past it); newest are shown when capping (8), older summarized as a count.
* **Fail-open + best-effort:** operator unreachable / no baseline → no-op, never blocks the tool, never crashes the turn.

## Why it does NOT bust the prompt cache

[Section titled “Why it does NOT bust the prompt cache”](#why-it-does-not-bust-the-prompt-cache)

The injection is a **tail append** — it lands *after* the latest tool result, past every cache breakpoint. The cached prefix (system prompt, tools, prior turns) is untouched, so you keep the cache hit on the bulk of the context; only the injected tokens (capped, and only when there’s new mail) are processed once as part of the new suffix, then themselves cached. What *would* bust it is inserting/modifying content **earlier** in the conversation — the hook never does that. So freshness is essentially free on cache terms.

## Companion: holder-intent on lock blocks

[Section titled “Companion: holder-intent on lock blocks”](#companion-holder-intent-on-lock-blocks)

`locks:acquire` busy rows now carry **`holder_intent`** + **`holder_focused`** (`acquire.ts` `enrichBusy` → `coord:presence`). The auto-acquire hook stamps a generic `intent: 'PreToolUse:Edit'`, so a blocked peer used to see junk; now it sees the holder’s **declared** `coord:declare-intent` one-liner (and a flag when the contended path is in their `current_files`). **Declare a real intent** so your locks explain themselves.

## Gotchas

[Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas)

* **No MCP `tools/list_changed`** is emitted, so a tool-surface change (add/remove a verb) leaves *running* agent sessions with a **stale cached catalog** until they relaunch. New sessions are correct.
* **Codex coord hook is SU-only** (pipeline-role sessions coordinate via `messages:send`/`inbox`, not the SU coord bus) and activates server-side on the next operator restart (the `:3070` host has no hot-reload).
* **OMP `deliverAs:'steer'`** delivering mid-turn is verify-at-deploy — the fetch/format/dedup path is live-verified, but steer-into-a-running-turn needs a real OMP turn to observe.

To integration-test their EXPORTS (not just the underlying lib stores):

# PG is canonical state, not a transport

> Don't poll PG to send messages between apps. Use HTTP/SSE/in-process; persist to PG after the message is delivered, never as the channel itself.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

Postgres holds **canonical state** in this codebase, but it is **not a transport**. The common anti-pattern is having app A write a row to PG that app B polls for, treating the row as a “message.” This is wrong for our topology.

The right shape:

```plaintext
app A  ──HTTP/SSE/in-process call──►  app B
                                       │
                                       └─►  persist outcome to PG
```

Not:

```plaintext
app A  ──INSERT INTO messages──►  PG
                                   ▲
                                   └── app B SELECT…WHERE handled=false
```

## Why it matters

[Section titled “Why it matters”](#why-it-matters)

PG-as-transport has bitten us in three concrete ways:

1. **Polling latency.** B has to choose between polling often (CPU burn) and rarely (user-visible delay). Neither is acceptable.
2. **Backpressure invisibility.** If B is slow, A keeps writing rows that pile up. There’s no flow control, no backpressure, no signal to A that B is overloaded.
3. **Coupling on schema.** A and B share table layout. Schema migrations require coordinated deploy; a column rename breaks the channel.

Live HTTP/SSE/in-process calls give you backpressure, structured errors, request/response correlation, and decoupled schemas for free.

The other shape that looks like PG-as-transport but isn’t: `pg_notify`. That’s a real PG-level publish/subscribe with kernel- level wakeups, not polling. It’s fine for *event* notification (use case: “tell me when a row changed”) but not for *request/response* (use case: “send this command and tell me the result”).

## How to apply

[Section titled “How to apply”](#how-to-apply)

* **Cross-app communication**: HTTP (with a typed endpoint via `defineTool`, which also produces the route projection) or in-process call. SSE for streaming.
* **Persist outcomes to PG** after the call returns. PG holds the authoritative state, not the message itself.
* **`pg_notify` is OK** for “wake up and re-read state” patterns — e.g., a UI subscribing to row changes. Not for command dispatch.
* **If you find yourself writing a polling loop**, stop and ask whether the right answer is an HTTP call or an SSE subscription.

The endpoint system docs at [`/docs/endpoint-system/overview`](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/overview) describe the canonical “function as truth, transports as projections” shape. Use it.

# DBOS durable execution — the eight gotchas that bite on first integration

> Hard-won findings from wiring DBOS Transact into the operator (dbos-durable-jobs-2026-05-31) — boot path, PG connect-probe, version pinning, scheduled-workflow registration, dedup vs concurrency, interrupted-step re-execution, and why the durable pipeline is sequential-only.

DBOS Transact (`@dbos-inc/dbos-sdk`) gives us Postgres-backed durable execution: a workflow checkpoints each step, so a crash resumes mid-flight without re-running completed work. Wiring it into the operator (`dbos-durable-jobs-2026-05-31`) surfaced eight non-obvious traps. Each cost real debugging time; none is in the SDK’s quickstart.

The bootstrap lives at `packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/bootstrap.ts` (`startDbos()`), gated by `PAPERCUSP_DBOS_ENABLE=1` (default off). Read that file alongside this page — the comments there cross-reference the plan’s decision IDs.

## 1. Boot from the live host path, not the retired instrumentation hook

[Section titled “1. Boot from the live host path, not the retired instrumentation hook”](#1-boot-from-the-live-host-path-not-the-retired-instrumentation-hook)

The instinct is to launch DBOS from `apps/operator/instrumentation-node.ts` — that’s the Next.js instrumentation hook, the “run once at server start” idiom. **It’s retired.** The operator is served by the `operator-vite` + Hono host (`bin/hono-host.ts` → `bin/host-bootstrap.ts`), not by Next any more. A DBOS launch wired into `instrumentation-node.ts` simply never runs in the desktop product.

`startDbos()` must be called from **`bin/host-bootstrap.ts`** (the live boot path). The tell that you got this wrong: the `dbos` schema never appears in the embedded PG even though `PAPERCUSP_DBOS_ENABLE=1`. See also `operator-next-is-retired`.

## 2. Probe the resolved PG — the source label can’t tell dead from live

[Section titled “2. Probe the resolved PG — the source label can’t tell dead from live”](#2-probe-the-resolved-pg--the-source-label-cant-tell-dead-from-live)

`getHarnessAdminUrlWithSource()` returns a `source` label (`native-fallback`, `embedded`, …). The first instinct is to **refuse to launch on `native-fallback`** — on the desktop product `:5432` is the retired `papercusp_legacy` and connecting there is a bug (`embedded-pg-discovery`). But on a **dev box**, `:5432/papercusp` IS the live operator DB, and `source==='native-fallback'` there is correct. A label check blocks DBOS on exactly the box you’re developing on.

The fix is a **connect-probe**, not a label check: open the resolved DSN, run `SELECT 1`, launch if it succeeds, skip cleanly if it doesn’t. Reachability is the real signal; the label is advisory.

```ts
const probe = postgres(url, { max: 1, connect_timeout: 5, prepare: false });
try { await probe`SELECT 1`; } catch { /* skip launch */ return; }
finally { await probe.end({ timeout: 2 }).catch(() => {}); }
```

## 3. Turn off the admin server — it defaults to :3001 and EADDRINUSE-es

[Section titled “3. Turn off the admin server — it defaults to :3001 and EADDRINUSE-es”](#3-turn-off-the-admin-server--it-defaults-to-3001-and-eaddrinuse-es)

DBOS starts an HTTP admin server on **:3001** by default. This box also runs Restart, whose shop-api binds :3001 — so `DBOS.launch()` dies with `EADDRINUSE` before any workflow runs. We don’t use the admin server. Set `runAdminServer: false` in `DBOS.setConfig`. (Even without a port clash, leave it off unless you’re using it.)

## 4. Pin `applicationVersion` or recovery silently stops across app updates

[Section titled “4. Pin applicationVersion or recovery silently stops across app updates”](#4-pin-applicationversion-or-recovery-silently-stops-across-app-updates)

DBOS tags every workflow with the running `applicationVersion`, and on restart it **only recovers workflows whose version matches the current process.** The default version is content-derived, so any code change bumps it — and after a deploy, every in-flight workflow from the previous version is left `PENDING`, never resumed. For an always-on operator with long-lived scheduled workflows, that’s silent data loss.

Pin it: `applicationVersion: process.env.DBOS__APPVERSION || 'papercusp-jobs-v1'`. Bump the constant deliberately only when you intend to orphan old workflows. This was proven in the Phase-0 gate: an unpinned version change left the prior workflow stuck.

## 5. A scheduled function must ALSO be registered as a workflow

[Section titled “5. A scheduled function must ALSO be registered as a workflow”](#5-a-scheduled-function-must-also-be-registered-as-a-workflow)

`DBOS.registerScheduled(fn, { crontab })` is not enough on its own — the scheduled function has to be a **registered workflow** too, or the scheduler has nothing durable to bind to. Register the workflow first, then schedule it.

Also note the default firing semantics: DBOS **skips missed intervals** by default (if the process was down over a scheduled tick, that tick is dropped). Backfill is opt-in via `ExactlyOncePerInterval` / `automaticBackfill`. For our timers (telemetry flush, scratch GC, …) skip-missed is the right default — don’t add backfill reflexively, or a process that was off for a day will stampede a day’s worth of ticks on boot.

## 6. Single-fire dedup is `deduplicationID`, not `concurrency: 1`

[Section titled “6. Single-fire dedup is deduplicationID, not concurrency: 1”](#6-single-fire-dedup-is-deduplicationid-not-concurrency-1)

To guarantee a feature/slug isn’t double-dispatched, the reach is for a queue with `concurrency: 1`. Wrong tool: concurrency throttles *parallelism*, it doesn’t dedup — two enqueues of the same logical job still both run, just one-at-a-time. The dedup primitive is per-enqueue:

```ts
await DBOS.startWorkflow(wf, {
  workflowID,
  queueName: q.name,
  enqueueOptions: { deduplicationID: workflowID }, // ← this is the single-fire guard
})(input);
```

Combined with a **deterministic `workflowID`** (we use `pipeline:<slug>:<feature>`), a re-dispatch resumes the same workflow instead of starting a second one.

## 7. An *interrupted* step re-executes on resume; a *completed* one does not

[Section titled “7. An interrupted step re-executes on resume; a completed one does not”](#7-an-interrupted-step-re-executes-on-resume-a-completed-one-does-not)

This is the one that looks like a bug. Crash a workflow mid-step and resume: that step runs **again** (we observed the agent spawn count go to 2). That’s correct — DBOS only checkpoints a step’s *result* when it **completes**; an interrupted step has no checkpoint, so resume re-runs it. Completed steps are never re-run (their result is replayed from the checkpoint).

The consequence for agent steps: a crash mid-`worker` re-spawns the worker. We make that safe two ways — (a) DBOS’s own checkpoint prevents re-running *completed* roles, which is the primary resume mechanism; (b) for the interrupted-but-side-effecting case, `invoke()` takes an `idempotencyKey` (the durable pipeline passes `<slug>:<feature>:<role>:t<turn>`) and reuses a prior *completed* run row from `harness_shared.harness_run_output` instead of re-spawning.

Caution

Don’t over-rely on the `harness_run_output` reuse as the resume mechanism — DBOS checkpointing already handles completed steps. The idempotency key is the **belt** for re-dispatch / non-DBOS callers and for a run that finished but crashed before its checkpoint landed. The braces-and-belt is intentional; the checkpoint is primary. Agents also re-read live git state on a fresh spawn (parent D-003), so a re-run worker converges rather than duplicating work.

## 8. Keep workflow code deterministic — and the pipeline sequential-only

[Section titled “8. Keep workflow code deterministic — and the pipeline sequential-only”](#8-keep-workflow-code-deterministic--and-the-pipeline-sequential-only)

DBOS replays a workflow’s orchestration code from the checkpoint log on resume, so **all non-determinism (agent spawns, the LLM decision, clocks, randomness) must live inside steps**, never in the workflow body. Our dispatch loop calls `parseDecision` (a *pure* function — see `pure-decision-functions-pulled-from-daemons`) on a checkpointed step output, so replay is deterministic.

That purity is also why the durable pipeline is **sequential-only**. The moment a decision is a parallel fan-out (`NEXT_WORKER` with `N=k`, branch isolation, the synthesizer), the clean per-feature workflow-ID claim and the linear checkpoint chain stop modelling the work. The durable workflow handles the common sequential pipeline (scoper → worker → validator → …) and **stops** on any parallel/branch verb, leaving that feature to the legacy main loop. Don’t try to model parallel lanes as nested DBOS workflows without first redesigning the ownership/claim model — that’s the live-integration boundary the plan stops at, not a quick extension.

***

**Where this is wired:** `packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/` — `bootstrap.ts` (launch + probe + flags), `orchestrator-workflow.ts` (the durable pipeline), `orchestrator-runner.ts` (spawns `invoke-once` with the idempotency key), `periodic-workflows.ts` (the timers). Full design + decision log: the plans `dbos-durable-jobs-2026-05-31` and `dbos-orchestrator-durability-2026-05-31`.

Note

**Update (2026-06-06):** Two things in this footer drifted. (1) The DBOS dir moved from `apps/operator/lib/dbos/` to `packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/`. (2) The `autoloop-workflow.ts` (AutoLoop as scheduled + dedup-keyed) is **retired** (`autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild-2026-06-05` P-010/D-009 — it read a `director-config.json` enablement surface nothing wrote). (3) The Phase-3 durable pipeline is now the **default** orchestrator (on unless `PAPERCUSP_DBOS_ORCHESTRATOR=0`), and the **legacy main loop is retired** — archived to `libs/papercusp/_retired/orchestrator-run-loop/` on 2026-06-06; setting `PAPERCUSP_DBOS_ORCHESTRATOR=0` no longer reverts to it (there is no legacy loop left), it just registers no DBOS orchestrator at all. Gotcha #8’s “leaving that feature to the legacy main loop” no longer applies — a parallel/branch verb now simply stops the durable pipeline.

# Desktop IPC transport map — what rides IPC, what's dormant, how to turn it on

> The desktop routes webview /api traffic over Tauri IPC to dodge WebKitGTK's ~6-conn libsoup cap. Three mechanisms, all gated behind PAPERCUSP_DESKTOP_IPC + a release-only sidecar spawn. Here's the whole map + the turn-on recipe + the SSE-over-IPC reconnect/churn contract (D-006) + how to verify with window.__ipcInspector + the gotchas.

## Why IPC exists here

[Section titled “Why IPC exists here”](#why-ipc-exists-here)

The desktop is Tauri/WebKitGTK. WebKitGTK’s libsoup HTTP stack caps **\~6 connections per host**, so the operator’s long-lived SSE streams (sync, log/provision streams, agent-thinking, UI-intents, …) camp every slot and starve on-demand `fetch()`. The fix: route the webview’s same-origin `/api/*` traffic over **Tauri IPC** (a Unix domain socket to the Node sidecar) instead of real HTTP sockets, dodging the cap entirely.

## The three IPC mechanisms

[Section titled “The three IPC mechanisms”](#the-three-ipc-mechanisms)

1. **`sys:http` blanket bridge** — `installDesktopIpcPolyfills()` (`libs/generic/desktop-ipc/src/desktop-bootstrap.ts`, installed at module-eval in `apps/operator/app/_components/RootSyncProvider.tsx`) patches:

   * `window.fetch` → `ipcFetch` for **same-origin `/api/*`, string/URL input, string body**.
   * `window.EventSource` → `IpcEventSource` (all EventSources). Any component using `fetch('/api/...')` or `new EventSource('/api/...')` rides IPC with **zero per-call changes**. Falls back to native when IPC is unavailable. **Gaps it does NOT cover:** cross-origin, non-`/api/` paths, `Request`-object input, binary/Blob/FormData bodies, and WebSockets.

2. **Typed `endpoint_invoke` dispatch** — `dispatchEndpointStream` (`libs/generic/desktop-ipc/src/index.ts`): picks IPC on Tauri for typed event-stream tools, gated by a host **allowlist** in `apps/operator/bin/host-bootstrap.ts` (the IPC server start logic moved there from the retired `instrumentation-node.ts`; it calls `startEndpointIpcServer` from `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-ipc/server.ts`). Returns the same `EndpointStreamEvent` union on both transports, so a consumer migrated to it keeps a working HTTP fallback in the browser.

3. **`expose.ipc: true`** — declarative per-tool flag in `ToolExposure` (`libs/generic/tooldef` `tool-projection.ts`). The intended successor to the hardcoded allowlist; `defineTool`’s auto-projection must thread `input.expose?.ipc` for it to reach the registry.

## It is OFF by default in dev — the dormancy gates

[Section titled “It is OFF by default in dev — the dormancy gates”](#it-is-off-by-default-in-dev--the-dormancy-gates)

A live probe will usually find `endpoint_invoke` → **“state not managed”**. Three gates must all be satisfied for IPC to actually run:

* **`PAPERCUSP_DESKTOP_IPC`** (desktop env, `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs`): the desktop only sets `PAPERCUSP_IPC_ENABLE=1` on the sidecar + pipes its stdout to parse the handshake when this is on. **As of 2026-05-31 it defaults ON** (disable with `=0`).
* **Release vs dev build** — the sidecar is spawned **only in release** (`cfg!(debug_assertions) == false`). A `tauri dev` / `cargo build` (debug) run prints *“dev mode — skipping sidecar spawn”* and the operator runs separately on `:3055`/`:3070` with **no IPC server**. So a debug binary can never complete the handshake — you need `cargo build --release`.
* **The handshake** — the sidecar boots its IPC server only when `PAPERCUSP_IPC_ENABLE=1` (`apps/operator/bin/host-bootstrap.ts`, which starts `startEndpointIpcServer`), prints `PAPERCUSP_IPC_READY socket=<path>`; Rust parses it, `IpcClient::connect` + `app.manage`. Until `app.manage` runs, `endpoint_invoke` errors with “state not managed”, and `ipcFetch` falls back to native HTTP while `IpcEventSource` falls back to a native EventSource (commit `7ef90807`).

## Turn-on / verify recipe

[Section titled “Turn-on / verify recipe”](#turn-on--verify-recipe)

```bash
cd papercusp-desktop/src-tauri && cargo build --release      # NOT debug — dev skips the sidecar
PAPERCUSP_DESKTOP_IPC=1 ./target/release/papercusp-desktop   # redundant now it defaults on
```

Release/bundled mode spawns its own sidecar on a **free port** (no `:3070`/systemd conflict — `find_free_port`), and points the webview at `window.__papercuspBase`. Verify on the new window via the dev bridge (`tauri-agent-tools eval --port <p> --token <t>`): `endpoint_invoke('dev:ipc_echo')` returns a result (not “state not managed”); `window.EventSource`/`window.fetch` are the patched polyfills; `~/.papercusp/sockets/<pid>.sock` exists.

**But connectivity is NOT the real check** — see the churn contract below. A `dev:ipc_echo` that returns a result proves the wire works; it does **not** prove the long-lived SSE streams are stable, which is what actually broke (flashing).

## SSE-over-IPC reconnect — the churn contract (D-006, 2026-06-01)

[Section titled “SSE-over-IPC reconnect — the churn contract (D-006, 2026-06-01)”](#sse-over-ipc-reconnect--the-churn-contract-d-006-2026-06-01)

Turning IPC on once surfaced a sharp regression: **the desktop flashed — constant full reloads.** Root cause was a reconnect-ownership conflict between the transport and its consumer, now fixed across three layers. The invariant to preserve when touching any of them:

> **The transport auto-reconnects on a transient drop (readyState CONNECTING); a consumer recreates the EventSource only when it is genuinely dead (readyState CLOSED).** Recreating on a CONNECTING drop discards a stream that was about to resume — and over IPC that means a brand-new channel + a sync-layer re-subscribe + a re-render on *every* blip. That is the flashing.

What went wrong + the fix (`@papercusp/desktop-ipc` + `@papercusp/sse`):

1. **`IpcEventSource` was one-shot** — a dropped stream (`done` / transient error) called `close()` (terminal). Native `EventSource` instead auto-reconnects (CONNECTING, resumes with `Last-Event-ID`). Fixed: it now reconnects internally, terminal only on `close()` or a fatal head. (`8f2da9a`)
2. **A fatal error fired BEFORE `close()`** — so readyState still read CONNECTING when a consumer’s error handler ran, hiding the death. Fixed: a `terminate()` helper sets readyState CLOSED *then* dispatches `error` (faithful to native), so a recreate-on-CLOSED consumer rebuilds — and on the IPC-unavailable latch, the rebuild yields a native EventSource fallback. (`5da236d`)
3. **`createResilientEventSource` force-recreated on EVERY error** — it closed the underlying ES and span up a fresh one on every blip. Fixed: it recreates only on readyState CLOSED, leaving CONNECTING drops to the underlying ES; the zombie watchdog stays the safety net and escalation still counts every error. (`c6927b3`)

`DesktopAttentionNotifier` got the same recreate-on-CLOSED alignment (`7b827b2c1`). All four changes are unit-proven (66 tests) but **not yet live-verified** — the verification below is the open step.

**Verify it (the real check):** open **/dev → IPC tab → churn**, or in the desktop devtools console:

```js
window.__ipcInspector.churn()
// PASS → [{ path:'/api/zero-harness/sse', constructions:1, drops:>0,
//           verdict:'OK — one persistent channel (N internal reconnects)' }]
// FAIL → constructions climbing for one URL = a consumer is still recreating it.
```

The inspector (`packages/operator-core/lib/dev/ipc-inspector-client.ts` + the zero-cost seam in `libs/generic/desktop-ipc/src/ipc-inspector.ts`) is on automatically in dev. **But IPC only runs in a *release* build** (debug skips the sidecar spawn — see the dormancy gates), and a release build is `NODE_ENV=production`, where the inspector is off by default — so to observe the actual fix you must opt in: **`localStorage['papercusp.ipcInspector'] = '1'` then reload** the release window (real users never set it). IPC traffic is invisible to the devtools Network panel (it rides the unix socket, not HTTP), so the inspector is the *only* way to see the reconnect cadence — `constructions` (new channels) vs `connects`/`drops` (internal reconnects) is exactly the churn signal. Plan: `calltool-endpoint-seam-2026-06-01` (Phase C/D, D-006).

**LIVE-CONFIRMED (2026-06-02).** Drove a release build via the dev bridge: navigated the window to `papercusp://localhost` → `window.location.origin === 'papercusp://localhost'`, `isSecureContext`, `window.EventSource`/`window.fetch` are the minified `IpcEventSource`/`ipcFetch` polyfills, and `GET /api/desktop/ version → 200` round-tripped over IPC with **no `ipc://` access-control block**. A 4-min run showed every healthy SSE stream rock-stable (`es_drop=0`, 0 reconstructions, no flashing). The off-HTTP-on-IPC goal is met. (The unique transient-drop → one-channel-reconnect is test-proven, 72 tests; it can’t be *staged* live because the sync SSE is LISTEN-fanout drop-resistant and killing the sidecar is a *fatal* event — the fix classified that correctly: `drops=0`, recreate + native fallback.)

## The audit conclusion (2026-05-31)

[Section titled “The audit conclusion (2026-05-31)”](#the-audit-conclusion-2026-05-31)

Because `sys:http` blankets all same-origin `/api/*` fetch + EventSource, **per-call-site “migrate to IPC” work is tiny** — once IPC is on, \~everything rides it automatically. The only genuine residual gaps: console-launch’s old `Image().src`/absolute-`:3055` hacks (fixed to a relative same-origin POST), and the Deepgram STT WebSocket (external `wss://`, not reachable over the local socket). The terminal PTY — the one full-duplex webview channel — already uses a dedicated native Tauri pty command, not a WS. The IPC framing is **server-push-only** (Request + Cancel are the only client→server frames), so full-duplex channels can’t map onto it as-is.

## Resumability

[Section titled “Resumability”](#resumability)

`libs/generic/tooldef/src/replay-buffer.ts` (Phase-4 T2.2) already buffers per `(workspaceId, toolName, runId)` and the HTTP SSE routes already honor `Last-Event-ID + X-Papercusp-Run-Id` (`parseLastEventId`; `agent-tools/catchall.ts` sets the run id). The remaining work for the typed dispatch path is wiring that cursor through `http-stream.ts` / `ipc-stream.ts` so a reconnect resumes from the buffer.

## Gotchas that cost time

[Section titled “Gotchas that cost time”](#gotchas-that-cost-time)

* **`cargo build … | tail` masks the exit code** — the pipeline reports `tail`’s status, not cargo’s. A failed compile looks like “exit 0”. Read the actual log tail for `error[E...]`.
* **`open_devtools()` doesn’t exist in release** — it’s compiled out unless the tauri `devtools` feature is on; gate it `#[cfg(debug_assertions)]` (fixed 2026-05-31). This had kept the release binary \~3 weeks stale.
* **A debug binary launched directly is still “dev mode”** — the sidecar-spawn gate is the compile profile (`debug_assertions`), not how you launch it. Don’t expect IPC from `target/debug/papercusp-desktop`.
* **Raw `cargo build --release` keeps the DEV frontend.** A bare `cargo build --release` produces a release-*profile* binary (so it takes the IPC/sidecar path) but bakes in the `tauri.conf.json` **`devUrl` (`:3055`)**, not the production bootstrap — so the window loads `http://localhost:3055`, never navigates to `papercusp://localhost`, and the polyfill stays *native* (no IPC). Use `tauri build` (or `npm run build`) to bake the production frontend; only that path navigates to `papercusp://localhost` (verified 2026-06-02).
* **`build.rs` re-assembles the sidecar on every cargo build — don’t run it while a sidecar is live.** Each `cargo build` copies sidecar binaries (`code-server/lib/node`, `embedded-postgres/bin/postgres`, …); if a prior desktop’s sidecar/code-server is still running it triggers `Text file busy (ETXTBSY)`, and `kill -9` mid-copy can leave the binaries corrupt → `embedded-postgres did not accept TCP` / code-server `Exec format error`. Kill ALL release/sidecar processes first, then build; re-run `bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh` to restore if a copy got interrupted (verified 2026-06-02).
* **Embedded-PG boot can crash on a migration `42P01`→`42703` chain.** A migration whose one-`BEGIN…COMMIT` file `ALTER`s a table created by *ensure-schema* (not by a migration — e.g. `feature_queue`) throws `42P01` at embedded-boot (migrations run BEFORE ensure-schema), rolling back the WHOLE file → a later migration that uses the un-added column hard-crashes the entire PG boot with `42703` (no database at all). Fix: `ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS` on ensure-schema tables (graceful no-op at boot). Found + fixed in 097/098 on 2026-06-02.

See the plan `desktop-ipc-transport-completion-2026-05-20` for the broader effort.

# Desktop webview localStorage is unreliable for persistence — per-user prefs belong in PG

> A preference stored only in localStorage silently fails to persist on the Tauri/WebKitGTK desktop — the operator origin churns (random sidecar port per launch → a fresh localStorage partition) and in-session writes don't reliably flush across a reload. Symptom is "my setting doesn't stick after reload/restart". Move per-user prefs to operator_user_profile (PG via /api/profile) with localStorage as a pre-paint cache + host injection. Includes the React-snapshot gotcha and how to diagnose on disk.

## The trap

[Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap)

A preference stored **only in the desktop webview’s `localStorage`** silently fails to persist. The user changes it, it applies in-session, then on the next reload/restart it’s back to the default. Reported as *“the theme switch doesn’t persist”* (it was the active-theme selection; the same applies to any localStorage-only pref).

It is **not** a bug in the read/write/apply code — that’s usually correct. The problem is that **localStorage in the Tauri/WebKitGTK webview is not a reliable durable store on this app.** Three compounding reasons:

1. **Origin churn across launches (dominant).** The desktop binds a *random free* sidecar port each launch (`papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs` → `find_free_port()`), and the webview loads `http://localhost:<port>`. WebKitGTK partitions localStorage by **origin = scheme + host + port**, so **every launch on a new port = a brand-new, empty localStorage partition.** On a long-lived dev box you can see the history pile up:

   ```sh
   ls ~/.local/share/com.papercusp.desktop/localstorage/*.localstorage \
     | grep -oE 'localhost_[0-9]+' | sort -u | wc -l    # → dozens of ports
   ```

   (The `papercusp://localhost` custom protocol — default-on since 2026-06-01, `src-tauri/src/custom_protocol.rs` — gives the *packaged* app a **stable** origin while keeping the port dynamic. But the **dev shell loads the HTTP `devUrl` directly**, bypassing it, so dev still gets the unstable origin.)

2. **`localhost` vs `127.0.0.1` are different origins** → different partitions. `devUrl` (`http://localhost:3070`) and `frontendDist` (`http://127.0.0.1:3070`) do not share localStorage.

3. **In-session writes don’t reliably flush across a reload.** Even on a fixed port, a `localStorage.setItem` followed (seconds later) by a real reload can come back empty — the on-disk SQLite stays un-checkpointed (observed a 34 MB abandoned `…localstorage-wal` whose main DB hadn’t been written in a day), so the reload re-hydrates from a stale snapshot that lacks the write. Several `com.papercusp.desktop` instances sharing one WebKit data dir on a busy box makes this worse.

This is exactly why the storage policy says **per-user preferences belong in Postgres, not localStorage** (see `/internal/docs/system/storage-policy`).

## The fix / the pattern

[Section titled “The fix / the pattern”](#the-fix--the-pattern)

Make **Postgres the source of truth** and keep localStorage as a *non-authoritative per-device cache* for instant first paint. The blessed in-repo pattern (already used by `auto_accept` in `operator-shared-state.ts` and `toast_last_seen_ms` in `NotificationCenter.tsx`, and generalized in `lib/profile-pref.ts`):

1. **First paint** — read the localStorage cache synchronously (instant).
2. **On mount** — `GET /api/profile`; if PG differs, adopt it (overwrite cache + apply + notify). `reconcileProfilePref()` does this, with a guard so a concurrent local edit isn’t clobbered by a slow GET.
3. **On change** — write the cache + apply + notify, **and** `POST /api/profile` (fire-and-forget). PG is the durable copy.

For **pre-paint** prefs (theme, visual-effects — read before React mounts to avoid a flash), the host **injects the PG value into `index.html`** alongside `window.__PAPERCUSP_WS__` / `__PAPERCUSP_FLAGS__` (`apps/operator/bin/host-spa.ts`), and the boot scripts read the injected value first, cache as fallback.

Adding a field is just a new key on the `operator_user_profile` JSONB (no SQL migration) — extend the `Profile` type in `lib/session.ts` **and** the `ALLOWED` allowlist in `endpoint-route/routes/misc/profile.ts` (the POST silently strips keys not on the list).

## The React-snapshot gotcha (don’t stop at host injection)

[Section titled “The React-snapshot gotcha (don’t stop at host injection)”](#the-react-snapshot-gotcha-dont-stop-at-host-injection)

Host injection makes the **boot script** paint the right value — but React can still reset it. `useSyncExternalStore`’s synchronous snapshot (`readActiveTheme()` / `readVisualEffectsMode()`) reads the localStorage cache, which is **cold right after a desktop reload**, so it falls back to the default and overwrites the freshly-injected value on first render. data-theme flips injected → default a beat after load.

Fix: the synchronous read must fall back **cache → injected (`window.__PAPERCUSP_PREFS__`) → default**, so the snapshot agrees with what the boot script painted. See `injectedPref()` in `lib/profile-pref.ts`.

## How to diagnose

[Section titled “How to diagnose”](#how-to-diagnose)

* “Setting doesn’t persist after reload” on the desktop → suspect localStorage, not your read/write logic. Confirm: drive the running webview’s dev bridge (`tauri-agent-tools eval`), write the key, do a **genuine** reload (`window.__papercuspOriginalReload()` — `location.reload` is suppressed on the static host), then re-read. If a freshly-written key vanishes while *old* keys survive, it’s the flush/origin problem, not your code.
* Inspect on disk: `~/.local/share/com.papercusp.desktop/localstorage/` — many `http_localhost_<port>.localstorage` files (one per past port) is the origin-churn smoking gun; a large, stale-mtime `…-wal` next to an old `.localstorage` is the unflushed-write smoking gun.

## Rule of thumb

[Section titled “Rule of thumb”](#rule-of-thumb)

If a value is a **per-user preference that should survive a reload/restart**, it goes in **PG** (`operator_user_profile` via `/api/profile`), with localStorage only as a pre-paint cache. localStorage-only is fine for **caches** (recomputable — git logs, custom-theme CSS) and **ephemeral one-shot UI flags** (onboarding “seen”, hint dismissals), where losing it on a reset is harmless.

See `lib/profile-pref.ts`, `/internal/docs/system/storage-policy`, and the related [headless-desktop-testing-needs-gl](/internal/docs/agent-insights/headless-desktop-testing-needs-gl) insight for the desktop-webview context.

# Gate dev-only UI on import.meta.env.MODE, not .DEV

> The desktop dev shell runs `vite build --mode development`, so import.meta.env.DEV is FALSE there. Gate dev-only UI on MODE !== 'production' or it never appears in the desktop. Verified by build-grep.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

To gate a dev-only UI surface so it ships in the desktop **dev** shell but is **absent from the production build**, gate on `import.meta.env.MODE !== 'production'` — **not** `import.meta.env.DEV`.

```tsx
// ✅ shows in the desktop dev shell, tree-shaken out of production
const DevAdminRail =
  import.meta.env.MODE !== 'production'
    ? lazy(() => import('../components/dev-admin-rail/DevAdminRail'))
    : null;


// ❌ NEVER appears in the desktop — DEV is false in a `vite build`
const DevAdminRail = import.meta.env.DEV ? lazy(...) : null;
```

## Why (the trap)

[Section titled “Why (the trap)”](#why-the-trap)

Vite ties `import.meta.env.DEV` / `.PROD` to the **command** (`vite` serve vs `vite build`), while `.MODE` follows `--mode`. The desktop’s three run modes (see [Dev modes](/internal/docs/desktop/dev-modes)) are:

| Run mode                                | command                                 | `MODE`        | `DEV`       |
| --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------- | ----------- |
| `bin/desktop-dev` (HMR)                 | `vite` (serve)                          | `development` | `true`      |
| `bin/desktop-dev-nohmr` (rebuild-watch) | `vite build --watch --mode development` | `development` | **`false`** |
| shipped (`tauri build`)                 | `vite build`                            | `production`  | `false`     |

`bin/desktop-dev-nohmr` is the **default** `npm run dev` for the desktop, and it is a `vite build` — so `import.meta.env.DEV` is `false` there. A `DEV`-gated surface compiles away and **never appears in the desktop you’re testing in**, even though you’re “in dev”. `MODE` is the only flag that is `development` in **both** dev shells and `production` only in the shipped build.

(Empirically confirmed on this repo’s rolldown-vite: a `DEV`-gated rail was absent from both a `--mode development` build and a production build; the `MODE`-gated rail was present in the dev build and absent in the prod build.)

## How to verify the gate (build-grep)

[Section titled “How to verify the gate (build-grep)”](#how-to-verify-the-gate-build-grep)

`MODE` is a static string Vite replaces at build time, so a `MODE`-gated lazy chunk is dead code in prod — Rollup drops it. Prove both directions by building to throwaway dirs and grepping for a marker unique to your surface:

```bash
cd apps/operator-vite
npx vite build                          --outDir /tmp/p --emptyOutDir   # production
npx vite build --mode development       --outDir /tmp/d --emptyOutDir   # dev
grep -rho "<your-unique-class-or-string>" /tmp/p/   # → 0 (absent in prod)
grep -rho "<your-unique-class-or-string>" /tmp/d/   # → >0 (present in dev)
```

Run the two builds **sequentially** to separate `--outDir`s — concurrent `vite build`s share the vite cache dir and cross-contaminate each other’s output.

## Two more gotchas this surfaced

[Section titled “Two more gotchas this surfaced”](#two-more-gotchas-this-surfaced)

* **CSS imported by a dead lazy module still leaks.** Vite eagerly collects a `import './x.css'` into the output stylesheet even when the importing module is a tree-shaken dynamic chunk — the JS goes, the class names stay. Carry dev-only CSS as a JS string injected via `<style>{CSS}</style>` (a JS import tree-shakes with the dead module) instead of a `.css` import. (FeaturesAdmin’s inline `<style>` pattern, for the same reason.)
* **Pick a unique class prefix.** `pc-dev-*` is already heavily used by the `/dev` page (`pc-dev-rail-*`, `pc-dev-panel`, `pc-dev-row`, `pc-dev-kv`). Reusing it bleeds CSS onto that page. The dev admin rail uses `pcdar*`.

## Where this came from

[Section titled “Where this came from”](#where-this-came-from)

The dev admin rail (`apps/operator-vite/src/components/dev-admin-rail/`, plan `dev-admin-sidebar-2026-06-05`). Its plan named `import.meta.env.DEV`; that would have made the rail invisible in the very desktop it’s meant for. The mount in `apps/operator-vite/src/routes/__root.tsx` carries the corrected gate + rationale.

# How the papercusp-workspace + papercup-self-registration boot path works

> Two fire-and-forget bootstrap helpers run on every operator boot to make Papercusp dogfood itself — sentinel workspace ensure + papercup repo auto-register. Idempotent + non-disruptive to existing installs.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

Two helpers make Papercusp dogfood itself:

1. **`ensurePapercuspWorkspace()`** — guarantees a workspace called `papercusp-workspace` (literal name) exists in the workspace registry. Idempotent.
2. **`registerPapercupHarness()`** — if running from the papercup source repo, auto-registers it as a harness named `papercup` inside that sentinel workspace, `state: private`. Idempotent
   * no-op for packaged installs.

Together: Papercusp dogfoods itself. The user finds `papercup` in their harness dropdown when they switch to `papercusp-workspace` — no manual `harness create` step.

Files:

* `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/papercusp-workspace.ts`
* `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/register-papercup.ts`
* `apps/operator/scripts/run-dogfood-bootstrap.ts` (one-shot manual driver)

Caution

**Update (2026-06):** The original boot wiring was `apps/operator/instrumentation-node.ts` (the Next.js instrumentation hook), which is **retired** along with the Next standalone operator. The two helper modules moved from `apps/operator/lib/harness/` to `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/`. As of this audit there is **no live boot-time caller** of `ensurePapercuspWorkspace()` / `registerPapercupHarness()` in the operator source — they are exercised only by the one-shot driver `apps/operator/scripts/run-dogfood-bootstrap.ts` (npm `verify:dogfood-bootstrap`) and their unit tests. Run the driver manually to flip dogfooding on; the rest of this page (sentinel name, the scoped-write trick, `detectPapercupRoot`) is still accurate.

## Why two helpers, not one

[Section titled “Why two helpers, not one”](#why-two-helpers-not-one)

They do different things:

* **`ensurePapercuspWorkspace`** writes to `~/.papercusp-workspaces/registry.json` (file-backed) — the user’s list of workspaces.
* **`registerPapercupHarness`** writes to PG (`harness_shared.harness_registry`) **scoped to** the sentinel workspace (not the active workspace) — the harness list within that workspace.

Splitting them keeps each helper testable in isolation. The bootstrap calls them in order: sentinel ensure → register papercup as harness.

## The “scoped to the sentinel workspace, not active” trick

[Section titled “The “scoped to the sentinel workspace, not active” trick”](#the-scoped-to-the-sentinel-workspace-not-active-trick)

When you have multiple workspaces, the harness registry is per- workspace: each workspace has its own list of harnesses. The operator’s existing `saveHarnessRegistry()` defaulted to writing to the **active** workspace.

If P-024 wrote to the active workspace, it would silently dump `papercup` into whichever workspace the user happened to be looking at — usually `default`. Bad: pollutes the user’s workspace.

The fix (commit `b53185ee`): add an optional `workspaceId` param to `saveHarnessRegistry()` (additive, 100% back-compat across 52 call sites). The dogfood bootstrap passes `PAPERCUSP_WORKSPACE_ID` explicitly so the write lands in the sentinel workspace regardless of which one is active.

A symmetric `wsOverride?` was already on `readOperatorState`; this just closes the API asymmetry at the underlying `writeOperatorState` helper.

## How the papercup-root auto-detector works

[Section titled “How the papercup-root auto-detector works”](#how-the-papercup-root-auto-detector-works)

`detectPapercupRoot(start)` in `register-papercup.ts` walks UP from the given directory looking for both markers:

```ts
existsSync(join(dir, 'apps', 'operator', 'package.json'))
  && existsSync(join(dir, 'libs', 'papercusp', 'package.json'))
```

Two markers because either alone could be coincidental in unrelated projects. Both together pin the directory to “this is the papercup repo.” Bounded to 8 levels up so it can’t unbounded-walk a weird filesystem.

Returns `null` for packaged desktop installs where neither marker exists — the bootstrap silently skips with a `state: 'skipped'` result.

## When you touch this code

[Section titled “When you touch this code”](#when-you-touch-this-code)

* **Renaming the sentinel** (`papercusp-workspace` → anything else)? Bad idea: many future surfaces (Cupboard, plan dogfood docs, multi-machine reconciliation) hardcode the name as a stable reference. The constant is in `papercusp-workspace.ts` for the one place that needs it; don’t make it a per-install variable.
* **Changing the markers** in `detectPapercupRoot`? Be conservative — the two-marker rule was chosen specifically to avoid false positives. Adding a 3rd marker is fine; removing one is risky.
* **Adding a 3rd bootstrap helper** (e.g. auto-register sub-harnesses for papercup’s submodules)? Add it to the one-shot driver (`run-dogfood-bootstrap.ts`), alongside the existing two. Keep each helper idempotent.

## Verifying it works without restarting the operator

[Section titled “Verifying it works without restarting the operator”](#verifying-it-works-without-restarting-the-operator)

There’s a one-shot driver at `apps/operator/scripts/run-dogfood-bootstrap.ts`:

```bash
cd apps/operator && npx tsx scripts/run-dogfood-bootstrap.ts
```

Runs the same code paths the boot path runs. Prints the registry + PG state. Useful when:

* You just made a change to the bootstrap helpers and want to verify it works against the live PG.
* The running operator predates your changes (memory rule: don’t restart the user’s running dev server). The script exercises your new code without touching the operator process.
* You’re debugging a “papercup isn’t showing up in the dropdown” symptom and want to confirm the PG row is there.

Sample output:

```plaintext
=== STEP 1: ensurePapercuspWorkspace ===
workspace entry: id=papercusp-workspace, name=papercusp-workspace, createdAt=...
workspaces total: 6, current: default
✓ sentinel 'papercusp-workspace' present in registry
=== STEP 2: registerPapercupHarness ===
state: already-registered
path: /home/marsh-office/papercupai-workspace/papercup
=== STEP 3: verify PG row ===
harness_registry@papercusp-workspace: 1 projects
  - papercup  →  /home/marsh-office/papercupai-workspace/papercup
✓ papercup registered in sentinel workspace
=== PASS — dogfooding flipped on ===
```

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/classify-tree.ts` — the 5-rule classifier for nested `.git` entries; uses the same `existsSync`-on-markers pattern. See [the classifier insight](/internal/docs/agent-insights/harness-tree-classifier).
* v5 plan Phase 1a P-014 (workspace bootstrap) + Phase 4 P-024 (papercup self-registration).
* `packages/operator-core/lib/workspace-registry.ts` — the underlying file- backed registry helpers.
* `packages/operator-core/lib/operator-state-pg.ts` — `readOperatorState` / `writeOperatorState` with optional `wsOverride` for per-workspace scoping.

# Dogfood go-live runbooks — P-026 orchestrator run + P-051b Cupboard deploy

> Step-by-step runbooks for the two remaining user-driven dogfood items. P-026 is the first end-to-end orchestrator run on a real papercup feature; P-051b is the Cupboard server deploy. Both require user creds or live UI interaction — autonomous agents cannot complete them.

## When this applies

[Section titled “When this applies”](#when-this-applies)

You (a human) want to drive Papercusp’s dogfood plan to substantial completion. The two remaining items below need either live UI clicks or external credentials (Cloudflare, DNS, GitHub OAuth secrets) that no agent has. Everything else is shipped + tested — these are the last threads.

If you’re an agent reading this: do NOT try to run either runbook end-to-end. P-026 requires GitHub merges from the user’s account. P-051b requires Cloudflare + DNS creds. Both are user steps. Prep the surrounding code + verify the substrate is healthy, then hand off to a human.

## P-026 — first end-to-end orchestrator run on papercup

[Section titled “P-026 — first end-to-end orchestrator run on papercup”](#p-026--first-end-to-end-orchestrator-run-on-papercup)

**Plan:** `apps/operator/docs/plans/papercusp-dogfood-phase4-single-engineer-dogfood-2026-05-24.md`.

### Pre-flight

[Section titled “Pre-flight”](#pre-flight)

1. **Substrate is on**: `PAPERCUSP_DOGFOOD_SUBSTRATE_ENABLE=1` in the running hono-host env. Check via `curl -s http://localhost:3070/api/admin/dogfood-substrate-status` → `enabled: true`.
2. **Papercup harness is registered**: see `harness_papercup` schema in PG. Check via `curl -s http://localhost:3070/api/harness/projects/lite | jq '.projects[] | select(.slug=="papercup")'`.
3. **F-DOGFOOD-001/002/003 exist in queue**: check via `curl -s http://localhost:3070/api/harness/papercup/features | jq '.[] | .id'`.
4. **Director config is set**: `papercup/.papercusp/director-config.json` should have `autoLoop: true` + `autoIntervalSeconds: 60` (or shorter for the run).

Caution

**Update (2026-06):** The `director-config.json` + `autoLoop:true` / `autoIntervalSeconds` cadence mechanism in pre-flight step 4 and run-sequence step 4 is **retired** (`autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild-2026-06-05`, P-009/P-010 D-009). Both director-cadence loops (the legacy in-process `setInterval` ticker in `autoloop.ts` and its DBOS twin `dbos/autoloop-workflow.ts`) are GONE — they read a `director-config.json` enablement surface nothing wrote. The surviving cadence path is the **blueprint** one: a harness’s blueprint declares `triggers.schedule`, `harness:create` materializes them into `harness_shared.routines`, and the durable DBOS `routinesTick` fires them. So ignore step 4 and “let autoloop pick it” — drive the feature manually (“Start working” + a deliberate dispatch) for the first run, or schedule it via the blueprint. The per-`(workspace, harness, role)` fire-state still lives on `harness_shared.autoloop_state` (now with read `consecutive_errors` backoff).

### Run sequence

[Section titled “Run sequence”](#run-sequence)

1. **Open the papercup harness in the operator** (live Tauri shell): `http://localhost:3070/harness/papercup`.

2. **Pick the feature** to run end-to-end. F-DOGFOOD-002 or 003 are safer than 001 (which is the observations-capture feature itself and should stay in the queue indefinitely).

3. **Click “Start working”** on the feature’s row in the Queue column (P-038a). This adds you to the working\_users set; the orchestrator will exclude the feature from auto-pickup.

4. **OR: let autoloop pick it.** Skip step 3 if you want the orchestrator to drive autonomously. The autoloop fires the director every `autoIntervalSeconds`. Within \~5 min the director should dispatch a worker on the feature.

5. **Watch the lanes panel** in the harness dashboard. A new worker run should appear with `role: worker` + the feature id.

6. **When the worker finishes**, review the produced diff against the papercup repo (it’s a commit on the user’s branch under `<papercup-clone>/.papercusp/user-trees/<your-github-user-id>/`).

7. **Push + open a PR manually** (Phase 7 auto-PR is wired but the path is verified per-harness; manual is fine for the first run):

   ```bash
   cd /home/marsh-office/papercupai-workspace/papercup/.papercusp/user-trees/<github_user_id>
   git push -u origin user/<github_user_id>
   gh pr create --fill
   ```

8. **Merge on GitHub** via the normal review flow.

9. **Within 60s of merge**, the Phase 2 verifier daemon stamps `completion_ref` on the feature row + flips status to `shipped`. Verify via the operator UI (tier-B ✓ badge appears) or `curl -s http://localhost:3070/api/harness/papercup/features/F-DOGFOOD-002 | jq '.feature.completion_ref'`.

### Verification checklist (P-026a–e)

[Section titled “Verification checklist (P-026a–e)”](#verification-checklist-p-026ae)

* [ ] P-026a — orchestrator picked the feature within 5 min OR I manually triggered it.
* [ ] P-026b — worker run completed with a real diff.
* [ ] P-026c — PR opened (auto or manual).
* [ ] P-026d — PR merged on GitHub by me.
* [ ] P-026e — `completion_ref` populated + status flipped to shipped within 60s of merge.
* [ ] P-026f — record total wall-clock time as a data point.

### Likely friction points

[Section titled “Likely friction points”](#likely-friction-points)

* **Orchestrator pick latency**: if no worker dispatched after 5 min, check `harness_shared.autoloop_state` and the director config.
* **Worker prompt quality on a real codebase**: papercup is large + has 175+ tables. First run may produce a noisy diff. Note in F-DOGFOOD-001 observations.
* **`completion_ref` not stamping**: confirm the verifier daemon is running. Check `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/completion-ref-verifier.ts`
  * the daemon’s logs.

### Then update Phase 4 plan

[Section titled “Then update Phase 4 plan”](#then-update-phase-4-plan)

After P-026 lands (or fails meaningfully), run P-027 (observe pain points → F-DOGFOOD-001 comments) + P-028 (gate verdict). Update `papercusp-dogfood-phase4-single-engineer-dogfood-2026-05-24.md`’s `## Now` accordingly.

## P-051b — Cupboard server deploy to Cloudflare Workers + D1

[Section titled “P-051b — Cupboard server deploy to Cloudflare Workers + D1”](#p-051b--cupboard-server-deploy-to-cloudflare-workers--d1)

**Plan:** `apps/operator/docs/plans/papercusp-dogfood-phase9-cupboard-discord-sync-2026-05-24.md`. **Code:** `apps/operator-public/` (already shipped 2026-05-25 — Hono on Cloudflare Workers + D1, 18 server tests + 14 indexer tests).

### Pre-flight

[Section titled “Pre-flight”](#pre-flight-1)

1. **Cloudflare account** with Workers + D1 enabled.
2. **`wrangler` CLI** authenticated: `wrangler whoami`.
3. **DNS for the hostname** you’ll bind (e.g. `cupboard.papercusp.dev`).
4. **GitHub OAuth app** with client id + secret. Used for the `gh-bearer` auth on publish / claim / report endpoints.

### Deploy sequence

[Section titled “Deploy sequence”](#deploy-sequence)

```bash
cd apps/operator-public


# 1. Create D1 + KV resources. Paste the returned ids into wrangler.toml.
wrangler d1 create papercusp-cupboard
wrangler kv:namespace create papercusp-cupboard-counters


# 2. Apply schema to remote D1.
npm run d1:apply:remote


# 3. Set secrets.
wrangler secret put GITHUB_CLIENT_ID
wrangler secret put GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET
wrangler secret put IP_HASH_PEPPER   # random 32+ chars


# 4. Bind DNS + Workers route in the Cloudflare dashboard:
#    Workers → your-worker → Triggers → Add Custom Domain → cupboard.papercusp.dev


# 5. Deploy.
npm run deploy


# 6. Wire the desktop operator to point at the deployment.
echo 'PAPERCUSP_CUPBOARD_URL="https://cupboard.papercusp.dev"' >> ~/.papercusp/env


# 7. Verify.
curl -s https://cupboard.papercusp.dev/healthz   # → {"ok": true}
curl -s https://cupboard.papercusp.dev/harnesses # → {"harnesses": [], "next_cursor": null}
```

### Verification checklist (P-051b-1/2/3)

[Section titled “Verification checklist (P-051b-1/2/3)”](#verification-checklist-p-051b-123)

* [ ] P-051b-1 — Worker live at chosen hostname with TLS (`curl https://<hostname>/healthz` returns 200).
* [ ] P-051b-2 — D1 backups: D1 has automatic point-in-time recovery enabled by default; verify in CF dashboard. No additional config needed for v1 volumes.
* [ ] P-051b-3 — `PAPERCUSP_CUPBOARD_URL` set + desktop operator picks it up. Test by opening the ShareWizard, picking `shared-public`, and confirming the publish goes through.

### Cron + indexer

[Section titled “Cron + indexer”](#cron--indexer)

The hourly stats indexer runs as a Workers Cron Trigger (configured in `wrangler.toml` as `0 * * * *`). The first cron tick after deploy will refresh tier-A stats for any listed harnesses. Check via `wrangler tail` or the CF dashboard Cron logs.

### What deploys today even with zero listings

[Section titled “What deploys today even with zero listings”](#what-deploys-today-even-with-zero-listings)

The endpoints are live but `GET /harnesses` returns `[]` until someone publishes via the ShareWizard. That’s expected. Publish flow: desktop operator’s ShareWizard step 9 → POST `/api/harness/cupboard/publish` (operator proxy) → POST `https://<hostname>/harnesses` (Cupboard) with the user’s gh token. Browser never sees the token.

### After deploy: update Phase 9 plan

[Section titled “After deploy: update Phase 9 plan”](#after-deploy-update-phase-9-plan)

Flip `papercusp-dogfood-phase9-cupboard-discord-sync-2026-05-24.md` frontmatter `status: shipped` (or wait until first real publish lands successfully end-to-end).

## Why these are NOT autonomous agent pickups

[Section titled “Why these are NOT autonomous agent pickups”](#why-these-are-not-autonomous-agent-pickups)

Both items require state outside the agent’s reach:

* **P-026** needs (a) a GitHub merge to happen, which only the user’s GitHub identity can authorize, and (b) judgment on whether the worker’s diff is acceptable (the user owns the gate before merging).
* **P-051b** needs (a) a Cloudflare account the agent can’t auth into, (b) DNS that only the domain owner can edit, and (c) GitHub OAuth secrets that should never leave the user’s secret store.

An agent CAN: verify the substrate is healthy, document the runbooks (this file), prep + commit any code changes that make the runbooks shorter. The agent CANNOT push the deploy or merge the PR.

# Dogfood v5 readiness map — what's wired, what's gated, what's user-driven

> Concrete index of every Phase 5a / 5b / 6 / 8 / 9 surface shipped during the autonomous loop. For each plan item — file path, test coverage, and the exact condition that activates it.

## How to read this

[Section titled “How to read this”](#how-to-read-this)

Three categories per item:

* **Wired** — code shipped + tested + idempotently dormant until the gate flips.
* **Gated** — wired, but never actually fires until `PAPERCUSP_DOGFOOD_SUBSTRATE_ENABLE=1`.
* **User-driven** — requires a behavioural decision (e.g. “run a feature”, “deploy Cupboard”) only the user can make.

Path convention below (updated post-`operator-core` extraction): UI surfaces (`app/**/*.tsx`, `scripts/*`) are in **`apps/operator/`**; every non-`app` `lib/**` path moved to **`packages/operator-core/lib/**`** (so `lib/sync/hyperbee/…` → `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/…`, `lib/orchestrator/…`, `lib/harness-insights/…`, `lib/user-profile/…`, etc.). Routes are HTTP paths registered in `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/index.ts`. The `instrumentation-node.ts` boot-wiring rows are **retired** (the Next.js instrumentation hook is gone) — see the Phase-5a note below.

# Dropping a harness_shared column — the 4-place procedure

> A DROP COLUMN migration alone fails the fresh-migrate STRICT gate. Sync 4 places (migration, 000-baseline, generated.ts, schema.ts), unfreeze SELECT* views, grep pg_proc bodies, and boot-apply via dev:restart.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

Dropping a `harness_shared.*` column in papercup touches **4 places**, not 1 — a plain `DROP COLUMN` migration alone fails the `fresh-migrate.integration` STRICT gate.
