First proven on migration **155** (drop `harness_features_consolidated.blocked_by`, plan `harness-blueprint-orchestration-2026-06-03` P-020/EI-1).

## The 4 consistency points (same change, same tick)

[Section titled “The 4 consistency points (same change, same tick)”](#the-4-consistency-points-same-change-same-tick)

1. **The migration** — `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/<NNN>-*.sql`. Reserve the number via `db:next-migration` (never max-on-disk+1; it collides with peers’ reservations).
2. **`000-baseline.sql`** — the squashed dump still defines the column + its indexes. Re-applying baseline RAW on the post-drop head fails (`CREATE INDEX … (col)` → “column does not exist”; the `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` is a no-op so it doesn’t re-add the column). The fresh-migrate “re-applying 000-baseline.sql RAW is a clean no-op” gate catches this. → **Surgically remove the column def + any index from baseline.** There is no baseline-regen CI compare (`verify-baseline.ts` only counts tables), so a hand-edit is safe. A full live-dump regen is the WRONG scope — it folds in every peer’s un-regenerated migration.
3. **`src/schema/generated.ts`** — the canonical drizzle mirror (runtime imports it via `schema/index.ts`). `pull-schema.mjs` regenerates it but the file is stale fleet-wide (peers don’t run it), so **surgical-edit** the column + index out; don’t full-regen.
4. **`src/schema/schema.ts`** — the raw drizzle-kit introspect intermediate (not imported, but keep it consistent). Same surgical edit.

## Two hazards that bite

[Section titled “Two hazards that bite”](#two-hazards-that-bite)

* **`SELECT *` views freeze their column list at CREATE.** `work_items` is `SELECT * FROM harness_features_consolidated` (migration 136) — created after the column existed, so it froze it and PG refuses the `DROP COLUMN` while the view lists it. The migration must `DROP VIEW` → `DROP COLUMN` → recreate the view. Views frozen *before* the column existed don’t list it — verify live with `information_schema.view_column_usage WHERE column_name='<col>'`.
* **Function/trigger bodies aren’t in pg\_depend.** Grep `pg_proc.prosrc ILIKE '%<col>%'` live before dropping — `DROP … CASCADE` does not rewrite function bodies that name the column.

## Applying live

[Section titled “Applying live”](#applying-live)

The native `:5432` dev box **boot-applies pending migrations on `dev:restart`** (`papercup-dev-api.service`). Restart FIRST so new code stops reading the column before the drop lands (no error window), then check `notifications:recent { level: 'error' }`.

## Provenance

[Section titled “Provenance”](#provenance)

Lifted from the Claude memory archive (`project_drop_baseline_column_procedure`, 2026-06-04) during the claude-memory-projection-integration boundary split — runbooks live here, not in per-client memory.

# Never hardcode PG port — read embedded-pg.json

> Embedded Postgres uses a discovered port written to ~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json on desktop boot. Hardcoding :5432 or :16534 breaks on any machine that wasn't the one you wrote the code on.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

Papercusp ships with **embedded Postgres**, not a host-installed PG. On desktop boot, the embedded-pg process picks an available port and writes its connection info to:

```plaintext
~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json
```

Agents and the webapp resolve the connection via `getHarnessAdminUrl()` (from `packages/operator-core/lib/embedded-pg-discovery.ts`; the generic resolver is `resolvePgUrl` in `libs/generic/embedded-pg-discovery`), which reads this file. `getHarnessPg(slug)` (per-harness scoped) lives in `libs/papercusp/libs/db/src/connection.ts`. The port is **not** stable — it can shift between boots, machines, and Papercusp installs.

## Why it matters

[Section titled “Why it matters”](#why-it-matters)

Code that hardcodes `:5432` (host PG default) or `:16534` (an older embedded-pg default we’ve seen) works on the developer’s laptop and **breaks silently on every other machine**. Symptoms:

* “Connection refused” on a freshly cloned machine.
* Tests that pass locally and fail in CI.
* An agent’s `psql` invocation that returns nothing because it connected to the *wrong* PG instance — possibly the user’s unrelated host PG, leading to confusing query results.

The native-PG path (`:5432`) is also being retired (memory: `project_papercusp_pg_topology` — “public release = desktop + embedded-pg only; native PG :5432 + webapp are dev crutches going away”). Don’t assume it’ll be there.

## How to apply

[Section titled “How to apply”](#how-to-apply)

* **Always resolve PG connections through `getHarnessAdminUrl()`** (admin role) or `getHarnessPg(slug)` (per-harness scoped).

* **For shell scripts**, read the JSON directly. The discovery file holds a single resolved DSN under `.url` (the resolver reads `parsed.url`), so feed it straight to psql:

  ```bash
  psql "$(jq -r .url ~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json)"
  ```

* **Never write a config file** that bakes a PG port at install time. Resolve at runtime.

* If embedded-pg.json doesn’t exist, the desktop hasn’t been booted yet — surface that to the user rather than falling back to `:5432`.

# Porting Next route.ts files to defineRoute

> The non-obvious patterns from migrating all 243 operator endpoints off Next route handlers onto the Hono-mounted defineRoute primitive.

The R5 endpoint migration moved every `app/api/**/route.ts` in the operator onto `defineRoute` (mounted on the Hono `app` via `registerAllRoutes`). 243 routes, 24 family batches. A few things that bite if you don’t know them:

## Catch-all routes must register LAST

[Section titled “Catch-all routes must register LAST”](#catch-all-routes-must-register-last)

Hono’s parametric/wildcard matches (`/:transport`, `/plugins/*`, `/agent-tools/*`) will shadow literal paths registered after them in some router configs. Register every literal route first, then the family catch-all, then the absolute-last `:transport` MCP catch-all. In `routes/index.ts` the spread order in `ALL_ROUTES` is load-bearing — the comment markers there are not decoration.

## A route module importing the barrel can deadlock the registry

[Section titled “A route module importing the barrel can deadlock the registry”](#a-route-module-importing-the-barrel-can-deadlock-the-registry)

`routes/openapi-json.ts` needs `allRouteFragments()`. Importing it from the package barrel (`@/lib/endpoint-route`) creates a cycle: `routes/index.ts → openapi-json.ts → barrel → register.ts → routes/index.ts`. Import the **leaf module** directly (`../openapi`) instead. Any route module that needs something from the endpoint-route package must reach for the specific file, never the barrel.

## Port at the route’s *current* auth posture — don’t tighten mid-port

[Section titled “Port at the route’s current auth posture — don’t tighten mid-port”](#port-at-the-routes-current-auth-posture--dont-tighten-mid-port)

Most legacy `route.ts` files were `auth: 'public'` with an inline `isLoopback()` / `getSessionUser()` / `requirePrincipal()` check. A mechanical port keeps exactly that: `auth: 'public'` + the same inline check. Tightening (e.g. making `credentials` require `trust: 'trusted'`) is a **separate, auditable pass** — never smuggled into a migration diff. Reviewers can’t see a behavior change hidden inside 200 lines of faithful copy.

## Colocated route.test.ts → Hono in-process app.request()

[Section titled “Colocated route.test.ts → Hono in-process app.request()”](#colocated-routetestts--hono-in-process-apprequest)

Old tests imported `{ GET, POST }` from `./route` and called them with a fake `NextRequest`. The ported test builds a Hono app, `registerAllRoutes`, and drives `app.request('/api/...')`. Move the file to `lib/endpoint-route/__tests__/`. Two recurring fixes:

* **Flag-gated routes** (`gateApiRoute(FLAGS.X)`) 404 in tests unless you `vi.mock('@/lib/require-flag', () => ({ gateApiRoute: async () => null }))`.
* **Never `vi.mock('node:fs')`** — `registerAllRoutes` transitively loads prompt-assembly, which `existsSync`/`readFileSync`s real persona files. A blanket fs mock breaks unrelated routes. Mock the specific lib instead.

## getSessionUser / getSessionUserOrDefault are header-aware

[Section titled “getSessionUser / getSessionUserOrDefault are header-aware”](#getsessionuser--getsessionuserordefault-are-header-aware)

`defineRoute` handlers get a plain `Request`. The Next-free cookie substrate (`lib/auth.ts`) exposes `getSessionUser(headers?)` / `getSessionUserOrDefault(headers?)` — pass `req.headers`. The no-arg form falls back to `next/headers` `cookies()`, which is the thing being removed.

## Enforcement is a script, not a lint rule

[Section titled “Enforcement is a script, not a lint rule”](#enforcement-is-a-script-not-a-lint-rule)

`apps/operator/scripts/endpoint-route-progress.mjs --check` exits non-zero if any raw `route.ts` exists under `app/api/**` outside the `[[...route]]` host-seam floor. That catches a re-introduced route regardless of contents — strictly better than a contents-matching ESLint rule. Wire it into CI next to `tsc`.

# Reading failed-tool-call history (forensics)

> Where the history of failed tool calls lives (dev:telemetry + harness_shared.tool_invocations), how to classify the failures, and why the restart-window connection-refused mode is invisible in that table.

When someone says “tool calls were failing,” don’t assume — the history is recorded and cheap to read. There are **two failure surfaces** and they do **not** overlap; check both.

## Surface 1 — recorded tool errors (`tool_invocations`)

[Section titled “Surface 1 — recorded tool errors (tool\_invocations)”](#surface-1--recorded-tool-errors-tool_invocations)

Every dispatched tool call (including `?superuser=1`) writes a row to `harness_shared.tool_invocations` in the **`papercusp`** DB. On the standing dev box that’s the embedded PG the operator connects to on **port 5432** (`harness_admin` / `harness_admin_pwd`; resolve the DSN via `getHarnessAdminUrl()` / [embedded-pg-discovery](/internal/docs/agent-insights/embedded-pg-discovery) in code — don’t hardcode).

Quick triage without SQL: the **`dev:telemetry`** MCP tool returns a per-tool rollup (`call_count`, `error_count`, p50/p95) over the last N hours. Narrow the window (e.g. 3h vs 168h) to localize *when* a burst happened.

Row-level columns that matter: `tool_name, status, error_message, invoked_at, duration_ms, role, transport, principal_kind, workspace_id, args_json`. `status` is one of `ok | error | role-not-allowed | timeout`.

### Classify before you fix

[Section titled “Classify before you fix”](#classify-before-you-fix)

In a 2026-05-31 audit, \~234 errors / 7 days bucketed as (most → least):

| Bucket                            | Signature                                                                                                               | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Bad arg shape**                 | `invalid_args: …` (surfaces as `handler_error`/HTTP 500, *not* 400 — the Zod throw is inside the projected fn)          | Caller sent the wrong arg shape. Not a backend fault.                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Missing harness scope**         | `No harness in scope` / `resolveHarnessPlansDir: no harness in ctx`                                                     | A harness-scoped tool called without the `harness` arg.                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Missing bearer/workspace auth** | `built-in tool "X" requires authenticated request (bearer + workspace tx)`; `Principal "loopback" lacks capability "…"` | A principal-gated built-in invoked without a principal/tx, or a principal whose caps don’t include the one required. See [tooldef-authorization-model](/internal/docs/agent-insights/tooldef-authorization-model). |
| **Timeout**                       | `status='timeout'`, `duration_ms ≈ 60000`                                                                               | Usually `chat:ask_choice` — the user never answered the card. Not a bug.                                                                                                                                           |
| **Real bug**                      | `permission denied for table …`, `column "…" does not exist`, `spawn npx ENOENT`, `features_import_failed:404`          | The small genuine set.                                                                                                                                                                                             |

The lesson: most “failures” are caller-side (bad args, missing scope) or a specific auth-wiring gap — **not** a backend that fell over. `p50≈0–1ms` with 100% error rate ⇒ an instant throw (validation/auth gate), not a crash.

## Surface 2 — the restart window (NOT in `tool_invocations`)

[Section titled “Surface 2 — the restart window (NOT in tool\_invocations)”](#surface-2--the-restart-window-not-in-tool_invocations)

The `:3070` Hono host has **no hot-reload** for `lib/**`, so picking up a server-side edit means restarting it (`systemctl --user restart papercup-dev-api.service`, or the Tauri reload). During each boot window the port **refuses connections**, and every in-flight tool call + lock-hook call across the fleet fails with `ECONNREFUSED` — which never reaches the host, so **it is never logged in `tool_invocations`.**

Where to see it instead:

* `~/.papercusp/locks-cache/last-error.json` — the lock hook’s last failure (`phase:"connect"`, `detail:"<urlopen error [Errno 111] Connection refused>"`).
* `journalctl --user -u papercup-dev-api.service` — `Stopping/Started` lines; match their timestamps against the lock-cache error to the second.

If agents report a *burst* of failures that don’t appear in `tool_invocations`, it was almost certainly a restart window, not a tool bug. (This is the self-referential cost of agents editing the backend they run on.)

## postgres-js gotchas when writing regression tests against PG

[Section titled “postgres-js gotchas when writing regression tests against PG”](#postgres-js-gotchas-when-writing-regression-tests-against-pg)

Two that bit while adding the regression tests for these bugs:

* **`int8`/`BIGINT` comes back as a string.** `payload->>…` and bigint columns (e.g. `harness_registry.updated_at`) deserialize to `string`, not `number`. Coerce with `Number(...)` if the tool’s contract is numeric.
* **`${JSON.stringify(obj)}::jsonb` double-encodes.** postgres-js re-serializes the string, storing a quoted JSON *string scalar* (so `payload->'projects'` is `null`). Insert JSON with **`sql.json(obj)`** instead.

## Live-DB checks are fair game

[Section titled “Live-DB checks are fair game”](#live-db-checks-are-fair-game)

You can `psql` the embedded PG (5432, `harness_admin`) read-only to reproduce a query or confirm a `has_table_privilege(...)`. For a faithful migration test, execute the **real** `NNN-*.sql` files against a testcontainer DB (see `apps/operator/test/harness-plan-status-grants.integration.test.ts`) rather than re-stating the DDL.

# Don't infer the fleet's inference plan from credential presence — check the wire

> Agents repeatedly conclude "the fleet runs on the Claude Max subscription" from the presence of a `subscriptionType: max` OAuth in `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, without checking what the spawned `claude -p` bee actually presents on the wire. Credential presence ≠ the subscription serving the workload. Cost telemetry and 429s reinforce the wrong conclusion. Run `npm run check:fleet-auth` for the ground truth.

## The recurring mistake

[Section titled “The recurring mistake”](#the-recurring-mistake)

When the fleet is rate-limited and someone asks “are we on the API or the Max plan?”, agents check `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, see a `claudeAiOauth` block with `subscriptionType: max`, and conclude **“we’re on Max, this is just a transient throttle.”** This conclusion is reached over and over, and it skips the one thing that actually answers the question: **what the spawned `claude -p` process authenticates with on the wire, and whether that auth is the right one for a headless fleet.**

The presence of OAuth credentials does **not** prove the subscription is usefully serving the workload. Two signals actively mislead:

1. **Cost telemetry looks like API billing.** claude-code reports a **non-zero `total_cost_usd` even on a subscription** — it’s an *equivalent-cost estimate* (tokens × list price), not a bill. `harness_shared.agent_usage_samples` stores it with `cost_source: provider`. So agents see real dollar figures and conclude “API key.” Wrong — the number is the same shape on both plans.
2. **It 429s, so it “looks like it’s working, just busy.”** A rate-limited bee is *authenticated* (429, not 401), so the auth obviously “works” — which gets read as “Max is fine, back off and retry.” But on a consumer subscription driven headless at fleet concurrency, the throttle is the **structural** symptom, not a transient blip.

## The ground truth: check the wire, not the config

[Section titled “The ground truth: check the wire, not the config”](#the-ground-truth-check-the-wire-not-the-config)

Run:

```bash
npm run check:fleet-auth        # scripts/check-fleet-auth.mjs
```

It runs one real `claude -p` call with `ANTHROPIC_LOG=debug` (the SDK’s HTTP logging — **this**, not the `--debug` flag, dumps the request) and classifies the **actual request auth**:

* **`x-api-key` header present** ⇒ an **API key** (pay-per-token, proper API rate-limit tiers).
* **`authorization: Bearer …` + `anthropic-beta: oauth-…`** ⇒ the **subscription OAuth**.

It also greps every spawn-relevant env (`process.env`, `.env.local`, the `papercup-{dev,staging}-api` host process envs via `/proc`) for `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` — the only thing that flips a `claude` spawn off the OAuth path (claude precedence: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env → `apiKeyHelper` → OAuth file).

## What was verified on this box (2026-06-08)

[Section titled “What was verified on this box (2026-06-08)”](#what-was-verified-on-this-box-2026-06-08)

Every layer was traced, not inferred:

| Layer           | Finding                                                                                                                                |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Command         | `AGENT_CMD=claude` on both hosts → bees run raw `claude -p` (not omp/Meridian)                                                         |
| API key         | **None** anywhere — host envs, `.env.local`, shell, `~/.claude.json`, `settings.json`, no `apiKeyHelper`/`forceLoginMethod`            |
| Per-spawn creds | `writeSpawnClaudeConfig` (spawn-mcp.ts) **symlinks `~/.claude/.credentials.json`** (the Max OAuth) into each bee’s `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` |
| **Wire**        | request sends `authorization: Bearer …` + `anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20` — **subscription OAuth, not `x-api-key`**                 |

So the fleet **does** authenticate with the Max OAuth. But that is the trap’s other half:

## The part that matters — a consumer subscription is the wrong auth for a headless fleet

[Section titled “The part that matters — a consumer subscription is the wrong auth for a headless fleet”](#the-part-that-matters--a-consumer-subscription-is-the-wrong-auth-for-a-headless-fleet)

A consumer **Pro/Max** subscription is gated for **interactive, single-session** Claude Code. Driving it **headless (`claude -p`) at fleet concurrency** (a hive of opus-xhigh agents + N bees through one OAuth) gets throttled hard — `"Server is temporarily limiting requests (not your usage limit)"`. The subscription is technically the auth, but the fleet is **not getting usable Max throughput** from it. In the sense that matters, *the Max subscription is not actually serving the fleet* — which is the real thing to discover, and the thing the “creds exist → Max → fine” shortcut misses.

**The fix for a production fleet is a real `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`** (or Bedrock / Vertex) with an appropriate rate-limit tier — set it in the spawning host’s env so `claude` picks it up (`x-api-key`), and lean on the API’s proper rate-limit headers instead of fighting a consumer throttle. The fleet’s AIMD concurrency back-off + the Apiary runner’s rate-limit relaunch (`bee-instance.ts`) mitigate the throttle but cannot fix an auth/workload mismatch.

## TL;DR for the next agent

[Section titled “TL;DR for the next agent”](#tldr-for-the-next-agent)

* **Do not** answer “API vs subscription” from `~/.claude/.credentials.json`. Run `npm run check:fleet-auth`.
* A non-zero `total_cost_usd` does **not** mean API billing (it’s an estimate even on a subscription).
* A 429 means *authenticated-but-throttled*, not “working fine.”
* If the fleet is persistently rate-limited on subscription OAuth, that’s a structural mismatch — recommend a real API key, don’t just back off.

# Fleet OS sandbox (default-on) — what it confines, how to opt out / extend egress, and what breaks

> The headless claude-code fleet runs inside claude's built-in OS sandbox by DEFAULT (PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX, default-on). It confines Bash-subprocess writes to the cwd + an allow-listed cache dir, hides credential dirs, and allowlists egress. claude's MCP/model connections are OUTSIDE its sandbox. codex is contained too — via an external srt-wrap (its native sandbox cancels MCP); omp gets the same srt-wrap. So all three backends are contained. How to opt out, extend the egress allowlist, the npm-install cache gotcha, the bwrap fail-loud mode, and omp's writable agent-dirs.

## What it is

[Section titled “What it is”](#what-it-is)

Every **claude-code** fleet spawn (orchestrator `invoke()` → `claude -p`) runs inside claude-code’s **own built-in OS sandbox** (Linux bubblewrap + socat proxy; macOS Seatbelt), injected via `--settings`. It is **default-on** as of 2026-06-01 (plan `fleet-spawn-sandbox-2026-06-01`, P-013). Source of truth: `fleetSandboxEnabled()` / `fleetSandboxSettingsForRole()` / `resolveFleetAllowedDomains()` / `fleetSandboxCacheEnv()` in `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/invoke.ts`.

What it confines (the **Bash tool + its children only** — see the boundary note):

* **Filesystem writes** → the cwd (`allowWrite: ['.']`) plus one allow-listed package-manager cache dir (`~/.cache/papercusp-fleet-sandbox`). Everything else, including `$HOME`, is read-only.
* **Credential reads** → `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.config/gcloud`, `~/.papercusp`, `~/.npmrc` are `denyRead` (hidden from Bash) **and** denied to the `Read`/`Edit` tools via `permissions.deny` (the sandbox does not cover the Read/Edit tools — they go through the permission system).
* **Network egress** → allowlisted to package registries (npm/yarn/pypi/crates)
  * GitHub + the common toolchain CDNs (Playwright `cdn.playwright.dev` / `playwright.download.prss.microsoft.com`, node-gyp `nodejs.org`). Everything else is blocked.
* Subprocess env is scrubbed of cloud creds (`CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB`).

## The boundary that matters

[Section titled “The boundary that matters”](#the-boundary-that-matters)

For **claude-code**, the sandbox wraps the **Bash tool and its child processes — nothing else.** The agent’s own **MCP, model, WebFetch and WebSearch** connections run in claude’s main process, **outside** the sandbox, so they are unaffected (verified live: a papercusp MCP call from inside a sandboxed spawn reached the server normally).

**codex** is different and needs a different mechanism. codex’s *native* sandbox gates the MCP transport itself — under `-s workspace-write`/`read-only` it client-cancels MCP tool calls (re-verified on codex 0.135; `network_access` doesn’t help; no MCP-trust knob exists), so codex can’t self-sandbox. The way around (P-015/D-017): run codex with its native sandbox **bypassed** (`codexSandboxArgs` keeps `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, so MCP works) and wrap the **whole** codex process in **`srt`** (`@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime`: bubblewrap `--unshare-net` + a host-side allowlisting proxy) via `wrapSpawnWithSrt`. srt confines codex’s shell commands (writes → cwd+cache+CODEX\_HOME, egress → an allowlist of operator + model endpoints + registries, creds hidden) while codex’s MCP+model traffic routes **through** srt’s proxy. One gotcha baked into the impl: srt injects a `no_proxy` that excludes loopback + RFC1918, which would send the operator MCP directly into the isolated netns (unreachable) — the wrap clears `no_proxy` inside the srt shell so it goes through the proxy. So under `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX`, **both claude-code and codex are contained.**

**omp** (no native sandbox) gets the **same srt-wrap** as codex (D-018/D-019). Its model + MCP are loopback on this box (ollama / the meridian bridge), the same loopback-through-srt’s-proxy transport codex uses, so its egress allowlist is operator + localhost + registries; a cloud-model omp adds its host via `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` (omp’s provider is deployment-set, so there’s no single host to hardcode like codex’s OpenAI). Its writable agent dirs (`~/.omp` + `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` = `<project>/.papercusp/pi-sessions`, which holds omp’s agent/auth/models SQLite DBs) are added to `allowWrite` — miss that and omp dies at startup with `SQLiteError: attempt to write a readonly database`. Verified under srt: omp **starts cleanly + reaches its model**. (Caveat unrelated to containment: omp can’t *complete* a tool-using task against **ollama** due to an omp↔ollama tool-schema bug — `cannot unmarshal bool into ToolFunctionParameters.properties` — present with or without srt, on every ollama model; needs a tool-capable local server or a working cloud/meridian provider.) So under `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX` **all three backends are contained.**

## Knobs (env, read per-spawn from the trusted orchestrator env)

[Section titled “Knobs (env, read per-spawn from the trusted orchestrator env)”](#knobs-env-read-per-spawn-from-the-trusted-orchestrator-env)

| Env var                                        | Effect                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX=0` (or `false`/`off`) | **Opt out** — run the fleet unsandboxed (the pre-2026-06-01 behavior).                                                                 |
| `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`      | Comma/space-separated hosts **appended** to the base egress allowlist (a private registry, an internal mirror, an extra CDN). Deduped. |
| `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX_DENY_ALL_EGRESS=1`    | **Lockdown** — emit `[]` for the allowlist (block ALL sandboxed-Bash egress). Wins over the append var.                                |

Changes take effect on the **next `:3070` operator restart** — the Hono host has no hot-reload.

## What breaks, and the fix

[Section titled “What breaks, and the fix”](#what-breaks-and-the-fix)

* **`npm install` / `pip install` / `cargo build` fail `EROFS`** writing `~/.npm/_cacache` (etc.). Root cause: package managers cache under `$HOME`, which the sandbox makes read-only. **This is already handled** — `fleetSandboxCacheEnv()` redirects npm/yarn/pip/cargo/go/XDG caches into a per-project subdir of the allow-listed cache root. If you add a new ecosystem whose cache lives in `$HOME`, add its cache env var there. (Gotcha for reviewers: an isolation test that only writes a file *inside* cwd will pass while real installs are broken — always test a **real package install** under a write-confining sandbox.)
* **A build/test command hits a host not in the allowlist** → that command’s egress fails (curl exit 6/7/28/56, HTTP 000). Add the host via `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`, or (for a known-common toolchain) to the base `FLEET_SANDBOX_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`.
* **Host without `bubblewrap`** → the sandbox is `failIfUnavailable: true`, so the spawn fails **loudly** rather than silently running unsandboxed. A host that genuinely can’t sandbox (e.g. a container without user-ns nesting) opts out with `PAPERCUSP_FLEET_SANDBOX=0`. (Wiring `enableWeakerNestedSandbox` for the containerized case is unbuilt — see the plan’s P-011.)

## Threat model (don’t oversell it)

[Section titled “Threat model (don’t oversell it)”](#threat-model-dont-oversell-it)

Defense-in-depth, **not** a hard boundary. The egress proxy filters by client-supplied hostname **without** terminating TLS, so a broad allowlist is a potential domain-fronting exfil channel — keep additions minimal. A Bash shell-redirect can still write inside cwd. The guarantee is: a sandboxed claude-code Bash command can’t read the listed credential dirs, can’t write outside cwd + the cache dir, and can’t reach a non-allowlisted host.

## See also

[Section titled “See also”](#see-also)

* [claude-code headless permission model](/internal/docs/agent-insights/claude-code-headless-permissions) — the `--allowed-tools` / `--permission-mode dontAsk` posture the sandbox composes with.
* Plan `fleet-spawn-sandbox-2026-06-01` (decisions D-001..D-015) — the full design + the real-fleet-pass findings.

# Forward-defined registry entries — advance-mapping without losing the drift signal

> When you need to map something before its target exists, the cheap path is a `FORWARD_DEFINED` set + a sanity assertion that flips when the target lands. Keeps the drift visible.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

Sometimes you want to add an entry to a registry **before** the thing it references exists. Example from P-067 (bridge module):

The bridge maps `harness_shared.<table>` → camelCase queryNames that consumers subscribe to. When v5 plan addendum 3 added two new tables (`contributor_usage_events` + `insights_first_visit`), the matching camelCase queryNames (`contributorUsageEvents.byHarness` + `insightsFirstVisit.byHarness`) don’t exist in the v2 sync-resolver registry YET — those will land with P-073 (Insights tab) work.

Three options for the bridge:

1. **Wait.** Add nothing to the bridge until v2 entries exist. Problem: when the consumer lands, someone has to remember to also wire the bridge. Easy to forget — drift.
2. **Map anyway, ignore the consistency assertion.** Bridge fires `contributorUsageEvents.byHarness` events that nothing listens to. Harmless, but the consistency assertion (“every bridged name is in v2”) flips to false, becomes noise, gets disabled.
3. **Forward-define with explicit tracking.** Map the names + add them to a `FORWARD_DEFINED` set + add a sanity assertion that inverts the consistency check.

Option 3 is what shipped. It preserves the drift signal.

## The pattern

[Section titled “The pattern”](#the-pattern)

```ts
describe('TABLE_TO_QUERY_NAMES vs v2 registry consistency', () => {
  /**
   * Forward-defined names — mapped in the bridge BEFORE the
   * corresponding v2 registry entry exists. Trigger events for
   * these tables fire (as expected) but currently invalidate
   * nothing; the matching consumer + v2 entry will land later.
   *
   * REMOVE an entry from this set as soon as its v2 registry
   * entry lands — otherwise drift between intent ("this should
   * land soon") and reality ("it never did") stops being visible.
   */
  const FORWARD_DEFINED = new Set<string>([
    'contributorUsageEvents.byHarness',
    'insightsFirstVisit.byHarness',
  ]);


  it('every bridged query name is either in v2 OR explicitly forward-defined', () => {
    const v2 = new Set(knownQueryNamesV2());
    const bridged = allBridgedQueryNames();
    const unaccountedFor = bridged.filter((n) =>
      !v2.has(n) && !FORWARD_DEFINED.has(n)
    );
    expect(unaccountedFor).toEqual([]);
  });


  it('forward-defined names are NOT in v2 registry (sanity)', () => {
    const v2 = new Set(knownQueryNamesV2());
    const stillForward = Array.from(FORWARD_DEFINED).filter((n) => !v2.has(n));
    // If this assertion fails, a forward-defined name has been
    // implemented and its entry in FORWARD_DEFINED should be removed.
    expect(stillForward.sort()).toEqual(Array.from(FORWARD_DEFINED).sort());
  });
});
```

The two assertions work together:

* The first **passes** as long as every bridged name is EITHER in v2 OR explicitly forward-defined. Drift in either direction surfaces.
* The second **fails the moment a forward-defined name lands in v2**. The failure message tells you to remove the entry from `FORWARD_DEFINED`. The drift signal is preserved.

## Why this matters

[Section titled “Why this matters”](#why-this-matters)

The naïve “I’ll just disable the consistency check while it’s forward-defined” pattern destroys the drift signal:

* No way to tell what’s intentionally-pending vs accidentally-broken.
* When the v2 entry lands, no test fires; the forward-define becomes obsolete vestigial code.
* New agents reading the code can’t tell what’s intent vs bug.

The `FORWARD_DEFINED` set is documentation in code: “these names are deliberately mapped before their target exists.” The sanity assertion makes that documentation **load-bearing** — the test suite forces you to update it.

## When to use this

[Section titled “When to use this”](#when-to-use-this)

Whenever you’re tempted to:

* Add a value to a registry/map ahead of its consumer landing.
* Suppress a lint/test failure with `// @ts-expect-error` or `// eslint-disable-next-line` for “this will be fixed in a follow-up.”
* Add a `TODO` for “remove this when X lands” — the comment is passive; the assertion is active.

In each case: the question is “how will future-you/future-agent know this is still pending vs forgotten?” `FORWARD_DEFINED` + an inverted assertion answers it.

## What it looks like in the wild (this codebase)

[Section titled “What it looks like in the wild (this codebase)”](#what-it-looks-like-in-the-wild-this-codebase)

* `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.test.ts` — the canonical example. 2 entries: `contributorUsageEvents.byHarness` + `insightsFirstVisit.byHarness` for P-073 Insights tab work.

## Variations

[Section titled “Variations”](#variations)

* **`FORWARD_DEFINED` with expiration**: if you also know a target date, fail when current date > expiration with “this should have been resolved by N.” Stronger signal at the cost of brittleness.
* **Inverted-only**: if you can’t easily list every value (e.g., a pattern instead of a finite set), invert: `expect(orphans).toEqual([])` with a comment explaining “if a real orphan appears, decide whether to add to FORWARD\_DEFINED or fix the registry.”
* **Per-domain**: large registries can have multiple `FORWARD_DEFINED` sets keyed by purpose (e.g., `FORWARD_DEFINED_PLANNED_THIS_QUARTER` vs `FORWARD_DEFINED_DEFERRED_INDEFINITELY`). Helps prioritization.

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts` — the bridge that uses this pattern.
* `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts` — the v2 registry the bridge maps INTO.
* [Adding a query to the sync resolver](/internal/docs/agent-insights/adding-a-sync-query) — when you migrate a forward-defined name, removing it from `FORWARD_DEFINED` is step 4 of the recipe.

# Generalizing a Papercusp lib into a borrowable one — the host-seam pattern

> How to take a lib that's tied to Papercusp and make it project-agnostic without changing the operator's behavior: the package names no project, the host injects domain values through a configure*()/props seam, and the operator maps its domain onto that seam at the boundary. Includes the soft-coupling checklist (schema/db names, fs paths, env vars, global keys, domain vocab in public types, generated-output banners — the ones grep misses), the cross-repo contract gotcha, and the borrowable-libs catalog + regroup tooling.

When you make a Papercusp lib reusable by any project — or notice domain coupling leaking into one that’s supposed to be generic — follow this pattern. It’s the one used across the 2026-05-31 generalization pass (plan `papercusp-systems-abstraction-2026-05-29`, D-011).

## The pattern, in one line

[Section titled “The pattern, in one line”](#the-pattern-in-one-line)

> **The package names no project. The host injects domain values through a small seam (a `configure*()` call or a React prop). The operator maps its own domain onto that seam at the boundary** — so the live app stays byte-identical while the lib becomes borrowable.

Concretely, three shapes recur:

* **`configure*()` host seam** (server libs). The lib exposes `configureX({ ... })` and reads the injected values at runtime; the operator calls it once in a `lib/<x>/configure.ts` imported for side effect. Examples: `configureMemory({ schema, defaultDbName, localStoreDir })`, `configureDesktopIpc({ forceHttp })`, `configureBackup`, `configureLocks`.
* **Options on the entry function.** When there’s a natural call site, add options instead of a global: `startEndpointIpcServer({ readyToken, socketPath, upstreamBaseUrl })`. The operator passes its branded values; the lib defaults to neutral ones.
* **React props + a config Context** (UI libs). Add props with neutral defaults; thread them to memo’d children via a small Context so you don’t prop-drill. Example: LogView’s `appLinks` / `primarySource` / `bookmarkKeyPrefix`.

The operator keeps the brand. e.g. `@papercusp/ipc-endpoint-server` emits a generic `IPC_READY` handshake by default; the operator injects `readyToken: 'PAPERCUSP_IPC_READY'` to satisfy the papercusp-desktop Rust client. The lib names nothing; the host owns the wiring.

## The soft-coupling checklist (what to hunt for)

[Section titled “The soft-coupling checklist (what to hunt for)”](#the-soft-coupling-checklist-what-to-hunt-for)

Compile-time imports of domain packages (`@papercusp/db-org|harness| orchestrator|agent-mcp|zero-harness|papercup-shared`) are the obvious coupling and usually already gone. The **soft** coupling is what hides:

1. **Hardcoded PG schema / db names** in SQL — `harness_shared.*`, default db `papercusp`. → inject a `schema` / `defaultDbName`.
2. **Filesystem paths** — `~/.papercusp`, `.papercusp/`, `apps/operator/...`. → inject a dir, default to `os.tmpdir()`.
3. **Branded env-var names** — `PAPERCUSP_*`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_PAPERCUSP_*`. → a `configure()` field, or a generic-named env fallback.
4. **Branded global / window keys** — `__restart*__`, `__papercusp*__`. Make them fully neutral (`__sse_channel_registry__`), not just renamed to your own scope. “Self-namespaced by the package” still reads as coupling — go neutral.
5. **Domain vocab in a PUBLIC type/field** — `harnessSlug`, `harness_slug`, `feature_id`. → rename to neutral (`scope`, `scopeFilter`); the operator maps its column onto it and maps back in its output.
6. **Generated-output banners / strings.** A tokens/codegen lib that prepends `AUTO-GENERATED by @papercusp/...` brands *the consumer’s* files. → neutral default + an override option.

grep is not enough

Items 4 and 6 are routinely missed by a string grep over imports/paths — a global key looks like any identifier, and a banner is a generated string, not an import. **Read the source.** The 2026-05-31 deep audit (four parallel Explore agents reading source, not grepping) caught the `token-kit` banner, the `sse`/`sync` global keys, and confirmed the rest clean — after a grep-level pass had marked them “clean”.

## Verify the host still behaves identically

[Section titled “Verify the host still behaves identically”](#verify-the-host-still-behaves-identically)

For each generalized lib: run its own test suite + a typecheck, and run the **one operator test that exercises the seam end-to-end** if it exists (e.g. `dev_ipc_echo_e2e.test.ts` confirmed the operator still emits the real `PAPERCUSP_IPC_READY` handshake through the new `readyToken` option). The `npm run test:affected` walker is **not** a usable gate in a bare sandbox — the operator’s integration suite needs Docker/embedded-PG and mass-times-out without it. Verify per-lib instead.

## What stays coupled — and why that’s correct

[Section titled “What stays coupled — and why that’s correct”](#what-stays-coupled--and-why-thats-correct)

Not everything should be generalized. Keep the tie-in when the lib *is* the domain contract: the plugin SDK/loader (`PapercuspContext`, the `papercusp.json` manifest), the flag registry (the keys *are* the product), `host-platform` (the designated host layer). Generalizing those would just recreate a generic shell with none of the value (plan D-008). Some seam’d libs (`locks`, `coordination`, `backup`, `docs-engine`) keep a Papercusp tie-in by decision even though they have a host seam.

## Discoverability + grouping tooling

[Section titled “Discoverability + grouping tooling”](#discoverability--grouping-tooling)

* **Catalog:** `BORROWABLE.md` at the repo root, generated by `scripts/gen-borrowable-catalog.mjs` (`npm run gen:borrowable`, and `:check` as a CI staleness guard). Membership is curated in the script (not a package.json keyword) so adding a submodule never needs a submodule commit. When you make a lib generic, add it there.
* **Physical grouping** under `libs/generic/`: `scripts/regroup-borrowable-libs.sh` does the atomic move (git mv each submodule + repoint every `node_modules/@papercusp/*` symlink + rewrite workspace globs + regen the catalog). It is **safe because consumers import by package name, not path**. It self-aborts unless the operator is stopped and every target submodule is clean. **Executed 2026-05-31** (plan D-012) — the 9 borrowable submodules now live at `libs/generic/`.

A path move is more than symlinks — three gotchas (D-012)

Repointing `node_modules/@papercusp/*` symlinks makes the *running* operator resolve fine, but it is **not** the whole job:

1. **Path refs beyond symlinks go stale.** Repointing symlinks + the root workspace globs is not enough — a path move must also rewrite: `file:` workspace deps (`apps/operator/package.json`, `packages/agent-mcp/package.json` declare `"@papercusp/x": "file:../../libs/x"` — breaks a fresh `npm install`), `.github/workflows` working-dirs, `scripts/scaffold-tests.mjs` dirs, docs `--workspace` paths, **`Dockerfile` `COPY` lines**, and **test-discovery globs** (`packages/operator-core/lib/testing-domains-registry.ts`). Grep every file type, not just `*.json`/`*.yml`. (Skip refs that are example harness sub-slugs like `papercup/libs/sync`, and `Dockerfile.papercup` — bannered “do not fix”.)
2. **The operator services are transient `systemd-run --user` units** (`papercup-dev-api` = :3070 host, CWD `apps/operator`; `papercup-dev` = operator-vite watcher, CWD repo root). `systemctl --user stop` **destroys** a transient unit — you can’t `start` it back. Recreate with `systemd-run --user --unit=<name> --working-directory=<dir> --property=Restart=always /usr/bin/bash -c '<exec>'`.
3. **Shared-index commit hazard:** `git commit` commits the whole index — in this multi-agent checkout another session may have left files staged. **Always `git diff --cached --name-only` before committing.**

## Going-forward: start generic-first (the lint)

[Section titled “Going-forward: start generic-first (the lint)”](#going-forward-start-generic-first-the-lint)

Migrating a batch of misfiled cores out of the app is a one-time cleanup; the *recurring* failure is writing the next generic core inside the app again. The 2026-06-05 audit (`generalize-libs-to-generic-2026-06-05`, D-005) added a guard so the debt doesn’t re-accrue:

* **`npm run lint:generic-first`** (advisory; `:all` for a full-tree sweep, `--strict` to exit non-zero) — `scripts/check-generic-first.mjs`. It flags a *substantial* file in `operator-core/lib` / `apps/operator/lib` that **both** (a) has zero papercusp coupling (no relative import, no domain `@papercusp/*`, no DB/IO client) **and** (b) *names* a textbook CS concept (supervision tree, fencing token, topological sort, token bucket, φ-accrual, saga…). It nudges the file toward `libs/generic/<name>` behind a seam.
* **Both signals are required on purpose.** Structural decoupling alone flags \~200 files (most app code imports little); the concept name is the precision filter that separates a real misfiled algorithm from ordinary decoupled glue. The tradeoff is that a generic algorithm with an unlisted name is a false negative — acceptable for an advisory lint; a 200-candidate cry-wolf is not. Extend `CONCEPT_RE` when a new concept family recurs.
* **Default mode is diff-scoped** (mirrors `affected-tests.mjs`: added/modified `.ts` since the merge-base with `origin/main`, plus working-tree edits) so it nudges at the point of introduction in a PR. `--all` audits the whole tree.
* A genuinely app-local file whose concept keyword is incidental (e.g. ElevenLabs MSE “backpressure” = browser audio buffering) goes in the `ALLOW` set in the script — not a blanket suppression.

Informational by default (like `lint:knip` — never gates a merge). The convention it guards is the “Borrowable libraries” section of the repo `CLAUDE.md` + `BORROWABLE.md`.

# GTK tree surgery during Tauri setup() wedges VTE's grid geometry — defer until the window is mapped

> Re-parenting the webview / inserting native-windowed widgets (VTE) into the Tauri window's GTK tree during setup() runs mid-realization and permanently wedges VTE's internal grid (it latches a boot-time inset while every GTK allocation reports correct). Defer the surgery until the window is mapped + ~2s settled.

## The trap

[Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap)

The D-009 embedded native terminal (`native-terminal-desktop-2026-06-06`) packs a **VTE widget beside the WebKitWebView** inside the Tauri window’s default GTK vbox (a `GtkPaned` split — one window, Wayland-safe). The obvious place to do that surgery is `start_native_terminal()` from Tauri’s `setup()` hook, via `window.run_on_main_thread`.

Doing it there **silently breaks VTE’s geometry forever**: the terminal’s grid computes rows against a latched boot-time inset (e.g. a constant 540px subtracted from every height), so zellij renders a \~67×15 strip pinned to the pane’s bottom corner while the rest stays black. The failure is maddening to diagnose because **every GTK-side observation reports correct**:

* `widget.allocation()` → full pane (`538x800+0+0`)
* `translate_coordinates(toplevel)` → `(0,0)`
* the widget’s `GdkWindow` position/size → correct
* the webview half works (its JS `innerWidth` matches the pane)

Forcing the grid by hand (`vte_terminal_set_size` on every `size-allocate`) does **not** recover it; nor does `unrealize()` + `show()` re-realization. The wedge happens because the surgery runs **mid-realization** — wry/tauri are still doing their post-create bootstrap (webview sizing + bounds passes) when the tree is cut.

## The fix

[Section titled “The fix”](#the-fix)

Defer the surgery until the window is **fully realized + mapped, plus a settle delay**. The shipped pattern (`main.rs` `start_native_terminal`, `EmbeddedView(Vte)` arm): poll `gtk_window.is_mapped()` on a 250ms `glib::timeout_add_local`, then wait \~2s more, then embed. Verified empirically: 500ms after map still hits the wedge; \~2s is safe.

The same surgery a beat after map renders perfectly — full-pane grid, pty reflows on every resize.

## Related gotchas in the same path

[Section titled “Related gotchas in the same path”](#related-gotchas-in-the-same-path)

* **Spawn order matters too**: `vte_terminal_spawn_async` before the widget is packed + shown leaves the pty stuck at the boot-time 80×24-ish grid. Pack → `show_all()` → then spawn.
* **No vte-rs bindings for GTK3** (tauri/wry are GTK3; `vte4` is GTK4-only and two GTKs can’t share a process). The embed hand-rolls \~6 C symbols and **dlopens `libvte-2.91.so.0` at runtime** (`libloading`) — no dev headers, no link-time/.deb dependency; when the lib is absent the strategy downgrades to `NewWindow` (`downgrade_unbuilt_with`).
* **Verifying “Wayland-only” work on the X11 box**: the embed is display-server-agnostic, so `PAPERCUSP_NATIVE_TERMINAL_FORCE=embedded-vte` exercises the whole path under the standard isolated Xvfb rig (`/internal/docs/testing/agent-e2e` §15.4) — no Wayland compositor needed for the widget-tree mechanics.

# The gym is a blueprint (gym-as-blueprint port)

> How the self-improving "gym" became the third built-in Harness Blueprint (D-022). A gym is a harness whose work is "improve another harness's blueprint"; the target declares its own rubric/signals/collectTrace; the lib/gym primitives are re-exposed as engine-primitives + gym:* tools; live-edit = commit→reproject.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

The “harness gym” (eval-driven prompt/orchestration optimizer) is no longer bespoke machinery — it is the third **built-in Harness Blueprint** (`gym`), alongside `coding` and `research` (`harness-blueprint-orchestration-2026-06-03` Phase D / D-022). A **gym is just a harness whose work is “improve *another* harness’s blueprint.”** Everything special about it is data in a blueprint, not a separate code path.

The split that makes this work:

* **The `gym` blueprint** owns the optimization **spine**: `generate-tasks → run-target-variant (sub-harness) → judge → propose → A/B-gate → accept (commit the target blueprint)`. Roles: `task-generator` / `variant-runner` / `judge` / `proposer` / `committer`, driven by a `gym-director`. It is layer-4 **recursive** (`recursion.spawnOn: variant-runner`) — running a target variant spawns the target as a durable sub-harness. It is `requiresRepo:false` and `gym.collectTrace: work-item-output` (the gym is itself gym-able). File: `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/gym/blueprint.yaml`.

* **The *target* blueprint** owns its own gym rubric: `blueprint.gym.collectTrace` (the trace seam), `blueprint.gym.signals` (the deterministic guardrails), and `blueprint.gym.rubric` (the judge’s dimensions/weights). The gym **reads the target’s** gym block — so a `coding` target is judged on a git diff and a `research` target on its work-item output, with no gym-side change.

## How the pieces map (Phase D)

[Section titled “How the pieces map (Phase D)”](#how-the-pieces-map-phase-d)

| Concern                                    | Where                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The `gym` blueprint                        | `harness/blueprints/gym/blueprint.yaml` + role prompts at the package-level `harness/prompts/{gym-director,task-generator,variant-runner,judge,proposer,committer}.md` (NOT a per-blueprint `gym/prompts/` dir) | Validates clean (engine `loadBuiltinBlueprint('gym')`).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Re-exposed primitives                      | `packages/operator-core/lib/gym/primitives.ts`                                                                                                                                                                  | One import surface: the **signal registry** (`resolveSignals`/`evaluateSignals` over `GYM_SIGNAL_REGISTRY`) + the **rubric mapper** (`rubricFromBlueprintGym` → a concrete `GymJudgeRubric`, falling back to `GYM_JUDGE_RUBRIC_V1`) + re-exports of `judgeGymRun`/`runAbEvaluation`/`collectTrace`.                                                                                                                       |
| Gym tools                                  | `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/gym/{judge,signals}.ts`                                                                                                                                                 | `gym:judge` (frozen Opus judge, target’s rubric — testable inner `runGymJudge`) + `gym:signals` (resolve a target’s declared signals by name). The judge/proposer roles call these.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| A/B eval-matrix                            | `packages/operator-core/lib/gym/ab-matrix.ts`                                                                                                                                                                   | The matrix `variants × tasks × repeats` as a **Level-2 runtime DAG** (cells = wave 0, all parallel; `aggregate` = wave 1) — maps onto the planner’s wave + `blocked_by` model. `aggregateAbMatrix` / `compareVariantsFromOutcomes` are the pure comparison/aggregation primitive (mean-based, excludes non-scored cells).                                                                                                 |
| collectTrace seam (D-015)                  | `packages/operator-core/lib/gym/collect-strategies.ts`                                                                                                                                                          | `collectTraceByStrategy('git-diff' \| 'work-item-output' \| <custom>)` breaks the gym’s repo-coupling: `git-diff` diffs the clone (coding); `work-item-output` collects the work-item output + transcripts with **NO git** (research/gym). Wired into `ab-runner-real.ts` `collectAndDistill`, dispatching on the target’s `gym.collectTrace`.                                                                            |
| Live-edit = commit→reproject (D-007/D-021) | `packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint/commit-reproject{,-real}.ts`                                                                                                                                              | An accepted edit writes the target’s `.papercusp/blueprint.yaml` / `.papercusp/prompts/<role>.md`, **commits it** (the target’s own git tree), then **reloads + re-projects** via `projectBlueprintToPg`. Order is the contract: file → commit → project (the cache is never ahead of the committed file). `acceptProposalViaCommit` is the gym-accept path that replaces the ungated `PUT /harness/:slug/prompts/:role`. |

## Gym extensions = harness plugins (P-015)

[Section titled “Gym extensions = harness plugins (P-015)”](#gym-extensions--harness-plugins-p-015)

Because the gym is now a blueprint, you do **not** extend it by editing core gym code. Two extension points:

1. **New gym behavior → a harness plugin.** Custom signals, custom collectors, or custom proposer strategies are added as `<plugin>.<verb>` harness plugins (the plugin host), not as new branches in `packages/operator-core/lib/gym`. The built-in signal registry (`GYM_SIGNAL_REGISTRY`) and the `collect-strategies` dispatch both have a clear “unknown name → error” boundary, so a custom name must be host/plugin-registered — it never silently no-ops.

2. **The control plane stays.** `packages/operator-core/lib/gym/control-plane.ts` (`gym_proposals` + `gym_autoloop_config`, migration 110) is **retained as the gym blueprint’s UI/state surface** — the persistent, user-facing review queue + autoloop config the `/api/gym/*` routes read. The gym’s heavy *execution* data still lives in the ephemeral gym run DB; the small control plane the human acts on persists in `harness_shared`, scoped by `(workspace_id, harness_slug)`. The accept action is what changed: it now goes through commit→reproject, not a direct `harness_prompt_overrides` write.

## Gotchas

[Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas)

* **The judge reads the *target’s* rubric, not a constant.** Use `rubricFromBlueprintGym(targetBlueprint.gym)` — a target that declares only `weights` still gets a complete rubric (the rest falls back to V1).
* **`plantedBugCaught` is fuzzy by design** — it matches on location tokens of length ≥ 4, so `src/x.ts` (no ≥4 token) never matches. Use a real path.
* **A signal that lacks its inputs reports `applicable:false`, not `false`** — a repo-less (work-item-output) target has no pre/post tests, so `regressionsFromTests` is inapplicable, never a misleading “no regression.”
* **commit→reproject commits the TARGET repo, not the operator tree.** The target harness is its own git repo; committing its `.papercusp/` files is D-007, not a violation of the “git-sync owns the papercup tree” rule.
* **A failed commit or reprojection leaves the proposal PENDING.** Never mark a proposal accepted on a half-applied edit — that discipline is what the old ungated PUT lacked.

## See also

[Section titled “See also”](#see-also)

* Plan `harness-blueprint-orchestration-2026-06-03` (Phase D: P-011–P-016, D-022 / D-015 / D-007 / D-021). Absorbs `harness-gym-eval-optimizer-2026-06-02`.
* The engine: `@papercusp/orchestrator/blueprint` (`GymSchema`, `RecursionSchema`, `deriveNext`, the loader) — **frozen**; the gym needed no schema change.

# Harness tests gate feature approval, and link to plans through the VAL

> The V2 tester writes one black-box test per VAL; the validator runs them as the approval gate. VALs live in harness_plan_assertions (inline plan bullets via plans:promote) — NOT validation-contract.md or a validation_criteria table. The plan↔test link is a rollup join on the VAL.

How the harness testing system fits together after `harness-tests-tab-and-tester-promotion-2026-05-26` (phases A–E + G). If you’re touching the tester, validator, the harness Tests tab, or anything that reads VAL assertions, start here.

## The VAL is the single join key

[Section titled “The VAL is the single join key”](#the-val-is-the-single-join-key)

A **VAL** (`VAL-{plan-slug}-{NNN}`) is one binding behavioral assertion. It is the only thing that links plans, features, tests, and the validator:

* **Plan item** authors VALs as inline `[VAL-…]` sub-bullets (`Verify:` / `Evidence:` / `Status:` / optional `RequiresTest:`). `plans:promote` parses them (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/plans/val-assertions.ts`) and writes them to PG.
* **Feature** carries them in `claims[]` (set by `plans:promote`).
* **Test** declares `coversVALs[]` in `.papercusp/tests.json`.
* **Validator** resolves them by id to decide pass/fail.

VALs live in harness\_plan\_assertions

Do **not** read `.papercusp/validation-contract.md` (retired by plans-central-harness-ux-2026-05-26 D-005) and do **not** add a `validation_criteria` table (the original plan proposed one; it was dropped). The canonical store is `harness_shared.harness_plan_assertions`, keyed by `(workspace_id, harness_slug, val_id)`, with `plan_slug` / `item_id` / `verify_text` / `evidence_text` / `status` / `requires_test`. Resolve a VAL via `GET /api/harness/:slug/assertion/:valId`.

## The gate: tester writes, validator runs, approval requires green

[Section titled “The gate: tester writes, validator runs, approval requires green”](#the-gate-tester-writes-validator-runs-approval-requires-green)

The staging loop (`libs/papercusp/.../prompts/staging/`) gates feature approval on tests:

1. A feature is `validating` (worker committed). The orchestrator’s **C0** decision emits `NEXT_TESTER <F> <VAL>` for each claim VAL with no passing covering test. (`NEXT_TESTER` is wired in the **DBOS pipeline** — `packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-decide.ts` dispatches the `tester` role; bash `run.sh` AND the TS run-loop (`main-loop.ts`, archived 2026-06-06 to `_retired/orchestrator-run-loop/`) are both retired. The prompt just needed to start emitting it.)
2. The **tester** (`staging/tester.md`) writes one black-box test per VAL, registers it in `.papercusp/tests.json` with `coversVALs`, exits.
3. Once every test-requiring VAL has a passing test, the orchestrator sends the feature to the **validator** (`staging/validator.md` V2), whose primary gate is **running** the VAL-covering tests. An untested required claim is a FAIL.

A VAL with `requires_test: false` (copy, design-spec, judgement) is **exempt** — the gate skips it; the validator verifies it by inspection. Default is `true`.

## The plan↔test link is a rollup, not a new edge

[Section titled “The plan↔test link is a rollup, not a new edge”](#the-plantest-link-is-a-rollup-not-a-new-edge)

There is **no** `test → plan-item` foreign key. The link is computed by joining through the VAL (`packages/operator-core/lib/harness-test-rollup.ts`, pure + unit-tested):

* `/api/internal/test-snapshot` drives `harness_plan_assertions.status` from covering-test outcomes (`deriveAssertionStatus`) and stamps `plan_slug` / `item_ids` onto each test row.
* `GET /api/harness/:slug/plan-items-test-status` and `plans:get`’s `planItemTests` both call `computePlanItemTestStatus` → per-plan-item `{ valsTotal, valsRequiringTest, valsCovered, valsPassing }`.
* The Plans UI badge (`decoratePlanItemTestBadges`) and the harness Tests tab’s Acceptance view render from that.

No-VAL tests stay harness-level

Built-in/universal tests (lint, typecheck, smoke — the `universalDomains` tier from `@papercusp/testing-shell`, formerly “generalized”) have no `coversVALs`, so they match no assertion and contribute to no plan item. Only behavioral/Project tests link to plans.

## Where things live

[Section titled “Where things live”](#where-things-live)

* **`@papercusp/testing-shell`** — `TestingShell` (left-rail + panel host), `DomainTestPanel`, the `universalDomains` registry (Built-in/Universal tier, pure data — `src/registry/universal.ts`), and the `TestingDataSource` interface. The lib↔operator boundary *is* the universal↔Papercusp boundary.
* **operator** — `packages/operator-core/lib/testing-domains-registry.ts` (`papercuspRegistry`, \~30 Papercusp domains, composed with the lib’s universal tier into `adminRegistry`), the harness `/testing/*` routes, and the `/adv` `HarnessTestsView` + `AcceptancePanel`.

The harness Tests tab is an `/adv` dock panel (`adv:tests`), not a `HarnessDashboard` tab — that monolith was deleted by the `/adv` migration.

# Harness Tests-tab domains are harness-owned, not operator-hardwired

> The harness Tests tab's domain nav comes from the harness's OWN contract at <worktree>/.papercusp/testing-domains.json (served by GET /api/harness/:slug/testing/domains), falling back to the generic generalized+Acceptance set. Do not special-case a harness in operator code. Also — harness endpoints resolve against reg.current (the global active workspace), so a CLI curl can silently hit the wrong workspace.

Two things to know before you touch the harness **Tests** tab (`/adv` → `HarnessTestsView` → `@papercusp/testing-shell`, backed by `/api/harness/:slug/testing/*`).

## The domain nav is HARNESS-owned data, not an operator registry

[Section titled “The domain nav is HARNESS-owned data, not an operator registry”](#the-domain-nav-is-harness-owned-data-not-an-operator-registry)

`/admin/testing` reads `adminRegistry` (the 8-domain Universal tier — formerly “generalized” — plus \~30 Papercusp domains, i.e. `[...operatorUniversal, ...papercuspRegistry]`) from `packages/operator-core/lib/testing-domains-registry.ts` — operator-internal code. The **harness** Tests tab does NOT import that. Each harness declares its own test domains in its contract surface:

```plaintext
<worktree>/.papercusp/testing-domains.json   ->  { domains: TestDomain[], tierLabels?: {} }
```

served by `GET /api/harness/:slug/testing/domains` (`endpoint-route/routes/harness/testing.ts` → `loadHarnessDomains(root)`). A harness that declares **no** file falls back to the generic `harnessTestingRegistry` (Built-in *Universal* tier + Acceptance — `[...universalDomains, ACCEPTANCE_DOMAIN]`, in `packages/operator-core/lib/harness-testing-registry.ts`). The frontend fetches that route for its nav; it does not import a static registry.

Don't special-case a harness in operator code

The wrong fix (rejected) was `isSelfHarness(slug) ? adminRegistry : …` wired into the view/route. That hard-wires the operator’s internal registry into a harness surface. The right place for a harness’s test config is the harness’s own `.papercusp/` contract — the same surface where `tests.json` (tester-created tests) lives. To give a harness more domains, write its `.papercusp/testing-domains.json`; don’t edit operator code.

The **papercup dogfood harness** (its worktree IS the operator repo) ships a `.papercusp/testing-domains.json` **generated from `adminRegistry`** (so there’s no hand-maintained drift) — that’s why its Tests tab shows the full `adminRegistry` set while a generic harness shows the sparse Universal tier + Acceptance. Regenerate it the same way (load `adminRegistry` + the Acceptance domain, serialize) if the domains change. Note that several Universal-tier domains are `admin-suite` runners that are non-functional in the harness data-source, and others (`live-web`/`chaos-web`/`routes`) glob operator-internal paths — so for a *non-papercup* harness the Built-in tier is mostly empty; that’s expected, not a bug. Default the nav to the first non-`universal` (content-bearing) tab.

## Harness endpoints resolve against `reg.current` — your curl can hit the wrong workspace

[Section titled “Harness endpoints resolve against reg.current — your curl can hit the wrong workspace”](#harness-endpoints-resolve-against-regcurrent--your-curl-can-hit-the-wrong-workspace)

`resolvePhasedProject(slug, phase)` resolves the harness from the registry scoped to `activeWorkspaceId()`, which reads `current` from `~/.papercusp-workspaces/registry.json` — a **single global** value, not per-request. The `:3070` host serves whatever `reg.current` is *right now*.

This bites hard when debugging: a `curl /api/harness/papercup/...` returns `{"error":"unknown project"}` not because the harness is gone, but because `reg.current` is a workspace that doesn’t contain it (it switches under you — the desktop, or a concurrent agent, flips it). I burned real time concluding “the papercup harness was deleted” when it was simply that `reg.current` had moved from `papercusp-workspace` to `default` mid-session.

Before concluding a harness is missing

Check the active workspace and where the harness actually lives:

```bash
python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('$HOME/.papercusp-workspaces/registry.json'));print('current:',d['current'])"
```

To list a *specific* workspace’s harnesses (the `?workspace=` query param on `projects/lite` is ignored — it uses `reg.current`), call `loadHarnessRegistry('<workspace-id>')` directly via a one-off `tsx` script. The papercup self-harness lives in the `papercusp-workspace` workspace, pointed at the operator repo.

Corollary: server-side edits to `harness/testing.ts` need a host restart (`systemctl --user restart papercup-dev-api.service`) — the `:3070` host has no hot-reload — and frontend edits to `HarnessTestsView` ship via the operator-vite watch-build + a desktop reload.

# The 5-rule harness-tree classifier

> When walking a git repo's nested .git entries, classify each as submodule / worktree / standalone / plain-dir. Used by the harness-creation flow to decide what becomes a sub-harness.

## What

[Section titled “What”](#what)

When you point the harness-creation flow at an existing git repo (Entries 1, 2, or 3 of the §3 create-harness wizard), it walks the directory looking for nested `.git` entries and decides whether each one becomes a sub-harness, a separate root harness, or part of the parent. The classifier lives at `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/classify-tree.ts` (papercusp-dogfood-v5 P-007).

There are **five outcomes**, ordered by precedence:

1. **Submodule** — `.git` is a *file* whose contents point into the parent repo’s `.git/modules/<name>/`. → Becomes a **sub-harness**.
2. **Worktree** — `.git` is a *file* whose contents point into the same repo’s `.git/worktrees/<name>/`. → **NOT a new harness** (it’s an additional checkout of the same repo, which is what phases already are).
3. **Standalone** — `.git` is a *directory* with its own `HEAD` etc. → Becomes a **separate root harness**, not a sub-harness.
4. **Plain dir** (no `.git`) — just part of the parent repo. → No harness, no recursion needed.
5. **Tree root** — the entry point of the walk; gets its own harness with the unified queue. Sub-harnesses share that queue (`parent_slug` link) tagged by component path.

## Why distinguishing matters

[Section titled “Why distinguishing matters”](#why-distinguishing-matters)

The three “has-nested-.git” cases (1, 2, 3) all look superficially the same: there’s a `.git` somewhere below the root. But they mean completely different things:

* **Submodule**: the parent repo deliberately references a separate upstream repo, pinned to a commit. It IS a logical sub-project of the parent. Sub-harness is right.
* **Worktree**: the parent repo has multiple checked-out branches living side by side, sharing one object store. Each worktree is the SAME project. Treating it as a sub-harness would duplicate the harness for every phase the user has materialized.
* **Standalone**: someone happened to clone an unrelated repo inside the parent’s directory. Not part of the parent’s project at all. Should be a separate root, not a sub of the parent.

Getting this wrong creates ghost harnesses, double-counts work, or makes the harness tree feel arbitrary.

## How the rules detect each case

[Section titled “How the rules detect each case”](#how-the-rules-detect-each-case)

The classifier reads the first line of `<dir>/.git` and pattern-matches:

```plaintext
.git is a directory          → standalone (rule 3)
.git contents start with
  "gitdir: <abs>/.git/modules/" → submodule (rule 1)
  "gitdir: <abs>/.git/worktrees/" → worktree (rule 2)
  anything else              → standalone (rule 3, fallback)
```

For directories without `.git`, the walker descends into them *unless* it hits a `.git` directory in a child — at which point the classifier fires and a single decision is made for that subtree.

## Real-world layout (papercup itself)

[Section titled “Real-world layout (papercup itself)”](#real-world-layout-papercup-itself)

papercup has (after the 2026-05-31 borrowable-submodule regroup under `libs/generic/` + the `test-config`/`testing-shell` promotions):

* 1 tree root: the papercup repo at `/home/marsh-office/papercupai-workspace/papercup`
* 7 direct-child submodules under `libs/`: `agent-chat`, `papercup-db`, `papercup-shared`, `papercusp`, `test-config`, `testing-shell`, `zero-harness` (the formerly-direct `git-graph`/`papergrid`/`sync`/`ui-primitives` submodules now live under `libs/generic/`)
* 7 plain dirs under `libs/`: `flags`, `generic`, `holepunch-spike`, `host-platform`, `marketplace-public-ui`, `papercusp-export-state`, `papercusp-publish-auth` (`generic/` itself is plain at depth 0 — it holds the regrouped borrowable submodules below it)
* Many worktrees in siblings of the papercup repo (`papercup-backup`, `papercup-design-migration`, etc.) — those are detected if a future walk starts above papercup, but the classifier never confuses them for new harnesses.

Total direct `libs/` count: 14 dirs (7 submodules + 7 plain), exactly what the test asserts against:

packages/operator-core/lib/harness/classify-tree.test.ts

```ts
it('matches the libs/ layout: 7 submodules + 7 plain (borrowable submodules regrouped under libs/generic/)', ...)
```

## When you touch this code

[Section titled “When you touch this code”](#when-you-touch-this-code)

* **Adding a 6th rule** (e.g. `git-annex` repos, fossil repos)? Add to the precedence list and update the test count. The classifier is a pure function over (path, fs) → outcome; tests are cheap.
* **Changing the walker boundary**? The current default stops recursion at the first nested `.git` entry. If you change that, you’ll start materializing harnesses for every git repo at every depth (probably not what you want for nested monorepos).
* **Changing the slug derivation**? Sub-harness slugs are path-qualified relative to the tree root (e.g. `papercup/libs/sync`). Changing this collides with existing harness registry entries.

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/classify-tree.ts` — the classifier
* `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/register-papercup.ts` — uses `detectPapercupRoot` (same shape) to find the papercup repo for Phase 4 dogfood self-registration
* v5 plan §2 — the architectural treatment of harness hierarchy reflecting submodule hierarchy

# Headless desktop testing needs real GL — bare Xvfb gives blank screenshots

> WebKitGTK on a plain Xvfb has no GPU/GL, so it never paints the webview — every screenshot comes back uniformly blank-white regardless of the DOM. Looks like a broken/blank app; it isn't. Use VirtualGL (vglrun -d egl0) on an isolated Xvfb, or run on :0. Verified recipe + the exact gotchas.

## The trap

[Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap)

When you drive the Tauri desktop on a headless box by spawning a bare `Xvfb` and screenshotting it (`import -window …`), **every screenshot comes back uniformly blank white — regardless of what the webview’s DOM actually contains.** It looks exactly like a broken or non-rendering app. It is not. The DOM is fine; the *pixels* never render.

Why: a plain `Xvfb` is a software framebuffer with **no DRI3 / no GL**. The tell is in the app log:

```plaintext
libEGL warning: DRI3 error: Could not get DRI3 device
```

WebKitGTK’s accelerated compositor can’t get a GL context, so it never paints the webview to the framebuffer. The window chrome (titlebar, drawn by the WM) shows up; the webview content area is blank.

This burned \~hours in the desktop-ipc Phase-4 packaged smoke (2026-06-01): the “blank window” across every boot was read as a render failure, when it was purely the GL-less Xvfb. The giveaway was that **every screenshot was the exact same byte size** — the framebuffer never changed because nothing ever painted into it.

## Why it’s easy to miss

[Section titled “Why it’s easy to miss”](#why-its-easy-to-miss)

* On a **release** build there’s no dev bridge (`#[cfg(debug_assertions)]`), so a screenshot is your *only* introspection — and it lies (blank).
* On a **debug** build the bridge (`tauri-agent-tools`) reads the **DOM**, not pixels, so it works fine GL-less — which is why DOM-level checks pass while screenshots look broken. The two disagree, and the screenshot is the wrong one.
* `WEBKIT_DISABLE_COMPOSITING_MODE=1` / `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1` / `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` do **not** fix it here (NVIDIA box; mesa software paths don’t drive the NVIDIA card).

## The fix — get real GPU GL

[Section titled “The fix — get real GPU GL”](#the-fix--get-real-gpu-gl)

Two options:

1. **Run on `:0`** (the real GPU X server): `DISPLAY=:0 …`. Simplest, but opens a window on the operator’s actual screen (focus-steal).
2. **VirtualGL on an isolated Xvfb** — *recommended* (no focus-steal, real GPU). `vglrun` routes GL to the GPU’s EGL render node while the app displays to the isolated Xvfb.

VirtualGL isn’t in Ubuntu apt; install the GitHub release once:

```sh
curl -sSL -o /tmp/vgl.deb \
  https://github.com/VirtualGL/virtualgl/releases/download/3.1.4/virtualgl_3.1.4_amd64.deb
sudo dpkg -i /tmp/vgl.deb
```

**Always confirm you got the real GPU, not `llvmpipe`/`swrast`:**

```sh
Xvfb :90 -screen 0 1920x1080x24 -nolisten tcp & sleep 2
DISPLAY=:90 vglrun -d egl0 glxinfo | grep -i "OpenGL renderer"
# → OpenGL renderer string: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090/...   ✅
# → ...llvmpipe / swrast                                  ❌ still software
```

Then launch the app **under `vglrun`** so WebKitGTK composites on the GPU:

```sh
( cd papercusp-desktop && DISPLAY=:90 vglrun -d egl0 npm run dev ) &
DISPLAY=:90 import -window root /tmp/shot.png   # now shows REAL content
```

## Gotchas

[Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas)

* Use **`-d egl0`** — the EGL **device index**. Do **not** pass the `/dev/dri/renderD128` path: VGL rejects it with `[VGL] ERROR: Invalid EGL device`.
* If you see `libEGL ... failed to create dri2 screen` with `-d egl0`, the mesa loader is fighting NVIDIA; `-d egl0` already selects the NVIDIA EGL device (`EGL_NV_device_cuda` in `eglinfo`), so it still works — the warning is noise as long as `glxinfo` reports `NVIDIA`.
* The render node is `/dev/dri/renderD128` (`crw-rw----+ root render`); the invoking user must be in the `render` group (or it’s ACL-granted).

See the full cookbook in [testing/agent-e2e §15.4](/internal/docs/testing/agent-e2e#154-xvfb--xdotool--ocr-fallback-cookbook).

# Hive-scoped federation (re-key from harness → Hive identity)

> How a shared project's substrate federates at HIVE scope, not harness scope — the Ed25519-pubkey topic re-key, per-Hive admission (revoked-pubkey union), Track A coord/presence, and Track B lock authority. Read before touching lib/hive-federation.ts, lib/authority/*, lib/sync/hyperbee/{boot,boot-all,wire-presence}.ts, or anything that resolves a swarm topic / lock authority. Includes the complete P-003 anchor inventory — every capture trigger, PEER_LOG_TAG_TO_TABLE tag, drain-routing site, and lib/authority scope-key. Plan — shared-hive-federation-2026-06-08.

## One paragraph

[Section titled “One paragraph”](#one-paragraph)

Federation used to key on `harness_slug` (migs 144/150 — a pre-redesign artifact). As of `shared-hive-federation-2026-06-08` the sharing boundary is the **Hive** (the project = harnesses + plans + settings, identified by a stable **Ed25519 keypair**), not the harness.
