Rate limit: **30 RPS per session user**, sliding window. Bursts past that return 429. The bucket key is the session’s user id (not the caller-supplied `workspaceId`, which is untrusted) so a single workspace-hopping client cannot evade the limit.

## Client-side companion: `askUserLocal`

[Section titled “Client-side companion: askUserLocal”](#client-side-companion-askuserlocal)

For render-time-only prompts that never cross the wire (tab pickers, settings dialogs, “are you sure?” confirmations):

```ts
import { askUserLocal } from '@/lib/chat-cards/ask-user-local';


const r = await askUserLocal({
  prompt: 'Switch to a new chat?',
  dataSchema: z.object({ choice: z.enum(['yes', 'no']) }),
  presentation: { kind: 'radio', options: [...] },
});
```

Same `CardSpec` / `CardResponse` types. Different transport: a global subscriber registry in the React tree.

To **render** an `askUserLocal` prompt, mount a `LocalCardHost` somewhere in the React tree:

```tsx
import { LocalCardHost } from '@/app/_components/chat/LocalCardHost';


function MyLayout() {
  return (
    <>
      {/* …app chrome… */}
      <LocalCardHost />
    </>
  );
}
```

`LocalCardHost` subscribes to the `askUserLocal` registry on mount, queues incoming cards, and reuses the same `AskChoiceCard` / `InputCard` renderer dispatch as `PendingCardsBar` (so cards look identical regardless of which path emitted them). The operator chat sidebar already mounts one `LocalCardHost`; without any host mounted, every `askUserLocal` call immediately resolves `{action:'cancel'}`.

`askUserLocal` and `ctx.askUser` are **not interchangeable**. Use `ctx.askUser` when the prompt is in flight inside a tool execution; use `askUserLocal` when the prompt is purely a UI affordance.

## Idempotency

[Section titled “Idempotency”](#idempotency)

```ts
const r = await ctx.askUser({
  prompt: '...',
  dataSchema: ...,
  idempotencyKey: 'pick-flavor',
});
```

If the tool reaches this point again within the same `runId` (e.g. re-entrant flow), the cached response is returned without re-prompting. Keys are scoped per-run — two different runs ask independently.

## Timeouts

[Section titled “Timeouts”](#timeouts)

`timeoutMs` is on the card, not the tool. The card’s deferred is resolved `{action:'cancel'}` when the timeout fires; the handler decides what to do next.

The tool’s own `timeoutSec` is independent — it aborts the entire run, which cascades cancel to every open card under it.

## State retention across reconnects

[Section titled “State retention across reconnects”](#state-retention-across-reconnects)

`state-snapshot` for a `runId` is retained for 5 minutes after the run ends (success or abort). A late reconnect within that window receives the final snapshot. Past 5 minutes the entry is GC’d.

## Limitations

[Section titled “Limitations”](#limitations)

* **In-process only.** The PENDING map lives in the operator’s Node process. Dev-mode HMR drops it; a server restart drops it. v1 accepts this — the same bound applies to `/turn-answer` today. PG-backed persistence is a v1.x follow-up.
* **One card visible at a time.** The renderer shows `openCards[0]`; additional concurrent cards queue behind it with an indicator. This avoids the multi-card chat-surface cliff. If you need a multi-question flow, prefer one card with a multi-field `dataSchema` instead of multiple sequential `ctx.askUser` calls.
* **No bidirectional state sync.** `ctx.publishState` handles server-to-client state (snapshot-only in v1; JSON-Patch deltas deferred to v1.1). The reverse (client-edits-server-state) is not in scope — it’s the same shape as a regular tool call, which already covers that direction.

## See also

[Section titled “See also”](#see-also)

* [Function-as-truth](./function-as-truth.mdx) — how `defineTool` projects to every transport.
* [Voice modality](./voice-modality.mdx) — how cards collapse to plain text on voice surfaces.
* Plan: `apps/operator/docs/plans/bespoke-card-improvements-2026-05-13.md`

# Function-as-truth

> The architectural decision that makes the rest of the system work. Why the function comes first, the manifest second, the transports last.

## The decision

[Section titled “The decision”](#the-decision)

The function is the source of truth. The manifest declares which transports project it. The framework auto-mounts both HTTP and MCP without per-tool route code.

This is *not* “HTTP-first wrapped by MCP.” It’s not “MCP-first wrapped by HTTP.” Both transports are equal-weight projections of one underlying function.

## What that means in practice

[Section titled “What that means in practice”](#what-that-means-in-practice)

A tool author writes this:

libs/papercusp/plugins/repomix/index.ts

```ts
export const tools: PluginToolMap = {
  pack: async (input, ctx) => {
    const result = await ctx.spawn('repomix', ['--stdout', ...]);
    return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: result.stdout }] };
  },
};
```

And this:

```json
// libs/papercusp/plugins/repomix/papercusp.json (excerpt)
{
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "pack",
      "description": "Pack a project into a single LLM-friendly document.",
      "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "target_dir": { "type": "string" } } },
      "capabilities": ["compute:exec:repomix"],
      "roles": ["worker", "scoper", "architect"],
      "rolesQuota": { "worker": { "perChunk": 1 }, "architect": { "perRun": 5 } },
      "timeoutSec": 120
    }
  ]
}
```

That’s it. No route file. No `app/api/plugins/repomix/pack/route.ts`. The framework reads the manifest, finds the matching `tools.pack` handler, registers it in the projected-tool registry, and the catch-all routes do the rest.

A new caller — UI, agent over MCP, or another module — gets the function with all gating and telemetry intact.

## The pivot away from per-route code

[Section titled “The pivot away from per-route code”](#the-pivot-away-from-per-route-code)

Before this design we had \~50 hand-written `app/api/agent-mcp/*/route.ts` files. Each one re-implemented its own auth check, its own JSON parse, its own try-catch, its own logging, its own error mapping. They drifted: some returned 500 where they should have returned 401; some forgot RLS scoping; some accepted GET when only POST made sense; some had quotas, most didn’t.

The function-as-truth approach replaces all that with a single dispatcher (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-projected.ts`). A new tool inherits correct behavior because there’s only one place that behavior is defined.

## Why we didn’t just generate routes from the manifest at build time

[Section titled “Why we didn’t just generate routes from the manifest at build time”](#why-we-didnt-just-generate-routes-from-the-manifest-at-build-time)

We considered codegen — read the manifests, emit one route file per tool. We chose dynamic catch-all routes instead because:

* **No build step.** Adding a tool is editing a manifest + restarting the host. Codegen would mean re-running a generator and committing generated files; the next agent edit always clashes.
* **Single dispatcher invariant.** With codegen, behavior diverges if anyone hand-edits a generated file. Dynamic routing forces all tools through the same code path.
* **Plugin hot-reload is possible.** A new plugin registered at runtime appears in the catch-all on next request. Codegen would require a rebuild.
* **About 10 lines of routing magic.** The Hono catch-all routes (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/plugins/catchall.ts` and `…/agent-tools/catchall.ts`, serving `/api/plugins/*` and `/api/agent-tools/*`) look up the tool by path in the registry at request time. No magic, easy to debug.

The trade is one extra registry lookup per request. Compared with auth + RLS + database I/O, it’s noise.

## Why we kept mcp-handler

[Section titled “Why we kept mcp-handler”](#why-we-kept-mcp-handler)

We use Vercel’s `mcp-handler` library as the MCP transport. We do not rebuild `StreamableHTTPTransport`. The bridge between two existing transports (mcp-handler for MCP, Hono route handlers for HTTP) is \~150 lines, both share the same `dispatchProjectedTool`, both populate the same `UnifiedToolContext`. Building our own MCP transport would have been weeks of work for no win.

## What “decoupling” actually means in our codebase

[Section titled “What “decoupling” actually means in our codebase”](#what-decoupling-actually-means-in-our-codebase)

Three rules a function must follow to be projection-ready:

1. **No transport awareness.** A function does not know whether it’s serving HTTP or MCP. It does not read headers, it does not write `Response` objects. It receives `(input, ctx)` and returns `ToolResult` or throws.
2. **Cancel via `ctx.signal`.** If a function does long work it watches `ctx.signal.aborted` and bails. Both transports thread the abort signal through the dispatcher’s timeout mechanism.
3. **Progress via `ctx.progress()`.** Optional. If called, MCP transport emits `notifications/progress`; HTTP SSE emits an `event: progress` line. No transport branching in the function.

When you migrate a route, you’re really doing two things: (a) writing the function in this shape, (b) deleting the legacy route. The MCP-callable part is automatic.

## The six known tool shapes

[Section titled “The six known tool shapes”](#the-six-known-tool-shapes)

After the foundation pivot we shipped four plugins to validate the model. A fifth (MCP-proxy) is designed but not yet shipped. The sixth (interactive-card) was originally a render-only emergent pattern but consolidated into a first-class framework primitive (`ctx.askUser`) in the bespoke-card-improvements arc (2026-05-13). Each shape stresses a different corner:

| Shape                                          | Example                                 | What it stresses                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Subprocess single-tool                         | `repomix.pack`                          | `ctx.spawn`, capability `compute:exec:*`, large output to scratch dir                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| HTTP fetch with optional secret                | `fetch_plus.fetch_clean`                | `ctx.secret` returning null, capability `http:fetch:<host>`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Subprocess multi-tool                          | `code2prompt.diff` + `code2prompt.pack` | Two tools sharing a manifest, dynamic templates                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| HTTP fetch with required secret                | `firecrawl.scrape` + `extract` + `map`  | Three tools sharing a manifest, `secrets:read:<NAME>`, JSON-schema-driven extraction                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **MCP-proxy plugin** *(designed, not shipped)* | future GitNexus wrapper                 | Forwards to an external MCP server. Needs manifest extension `dynamicTools()` so the proxy can list at runtime instead of hard-coding.                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Interactive card**                           | `chat:ask_choice`                       | Tool calls `ctx.askUser(spec)` and blocks until the user submits/declines/cancels. The card travels on the **state channel** (`state-snapshot` SSE), not the per-tool event ring buffer — so reconnect-resilient by construction. Handler returns the user’s response value, not echoed args. See [ctx.askUser](./ask-user.mdx). |

If your work doesn’t fit one of those shapes, stop and discuss before inventing a seventh. See [Operations → When to stop and ask](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/operations#when-to-stop-and-ask).

### Interactive-card conventions

[Section titled “Interactive-card conventions”](#interactive-card-conventions)

For tools that pause execution to ask the user something via the chat sidebar:

1. **Call `ctx.askUser(spec)`** — the handler blocks on a deferred Promise. The card-correlator registers a `correlationId`, the state-channel publishes a snapshot containing the card, and the SSE stream ships it to subscribed clients. The handler resumes with `r.action` ∈ `'submit' | 'decline' | 'cancel'` and a Zod-validated `r.payload`.
2. **No client-side `renderToolCard` registry.** The chat surface (`PendingCardsBar`) reads `openCards` straight from the `state-snapshot` SSE and renders the appropriate component (`AskChoiceCard`, `InputCard`) keyed off `presentation.kind`. There’s nothing per-tool to register — adding a new card-emitting tool just calls `ctx.askUser`; no client code changes.
3. **Persistence** — `state-snapshot` payloads are in-process for the run’s lifetime + a 5-min reconnect window. Past 5 min the snapshot GCs. The handler’s *return value* (after `ctx.askUser` resolves) is persisted as a normal `assistant` turn in `operator_turns` if the caller is an LLM agent.
4. **Voice modality** — voice surfaces don’t render cards. If a card-emitting tool runs during a voice turn, the operator-converse SSE forwarder appends each card’s `fallbackText` to the spoken response (gated on `body.modality === 'voice'` to prevent cross-conversation leak). Voice users still can’t *send* a structured `/card-response` payload — they’d have to click via the chat surface. See [Voice modality → Cards on voice](./voice-modality.mdx#cards-on-voice--fallbacktext).
5. **Naming** — use the `chat:` namespace for tools whose only purpose is to ask via card (`chat:ask_choice`, `chat:ask_text`, …). `ui:` namespace is for browser-control side-effect tools (`ui:dispatch`) that don’t produce a server return value.
6. **Reserved event name** — `'card'` is rejected at register time (`registerProjectedTool` throws). Plugins cannot intercept the askUser flow by declaring `events: { card: ... }`.

## Where the model is *not* the right answer

[Section titled “Where the model is not the right answer”](#where-the-model-is-not-the-right-answer)

* **Bidirectional audio streams** (voice WSS, agent ↔ user mid-call audio). Those go through the ElevenLabs Conv AI integration, not the endpoint system. The `(input, ctx) → ToolResult` shape *does* support mid-run question/answer via `ctx.askUser` (server publishes a card on the state channel; the handler awaits a deferred until the user clicks) and LLM token streams via `ctx.emit`. What it does NOT support is a long-lived bidirectional audio/binary channel — those need WebRTC or raw WebSockets.
* **File uploads >5MB.** The dispatcher is JSON-in / JSON-or-SSE-out. Multipart isn’t wired.
* **Browser-state actions.** Things like “expand left panel” or “set voice mode.” Those don’t have a server-side function to project; they’re client commands. Use `ui:dispatch` instead.
* **Anything that needs a real bearer principal *and* is callable by spawned agents.** Today, agents pass URL spawn context — no bearer. The HMAC-signed URL scheme provides workspace/role attribution but doesn’t carry an enforceable capability set. If a tool genuinely needs principal-bound capabilities and agent-callability, that’s separate auth work.

# Gating

> The ordered gates every tool call runs through — signature, default-deny, roles, capabilities, RBAC, harness, quota, resource authorization, declarative preconditions, timeout — and the error codes they emit.

## The gates, in order

[Section titled “The gates, in order”](#the-gates-in-order)

Every projected tool call runs through `tryBuildSpawnContext` → `dispatchProjectedTool` and faces these gates in order. The first one that fails short-circuits with the matching error code. The dispatch-stack gates are defined once in `DEFAULT_DISPATCH_STACK` (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-stack.ts`); signature verification runs earlier, in `tryBuildSpawnContext`.

```plaintext
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 0. Signature verification (per-spawn)           │  → request_rejected: spawn_sig_<reason>
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Default-deny (opt-in; off by default)        │  → ungated (403)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. Role allowlist (agent role vs tool.roles)    │  → role_not_allowed (403)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. Capability check (principal capabilities)    │  → unauthorized (401) | missing_capability (403)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 4. RBAC role requirement (tool.requireRoles)    │  → missing_role (403)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 5. Harness-required gate                        │  → harness_required (400)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 6. Per-window quota                             │  → quota_exceeded (429)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 7. Resource authorization (tool.authorize)      │  → authorization_denied (403)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 8. Declarative preconditions (tool.requires)    │  → precondition_failed (412)
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 9. Per-tool timeout (during execution)          │  → timeout (504)
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

If every gate passes, the function runs. Whatever it returns or throws is recorded with one of the post-execution statuses (`ok`, `error`, `timeout`).

Gates **1, 4, 7** and the **authorization audit trail** are the [RFC tooldef-auth](/internal/docs/spec/plan-format) layer: a fail-closed default-deny posture, declarative RBAC roles, resource-level “can THIS principal act on THIS resource”, and an audit event for every authz decision. Gates 0, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8 are the original coarse checks. Each is detailed below.

## Signature verification (gate 0)

[Section titled “Signature verification (gate 0)”](#signature-verification-gate-0)

Before any other gate fires, the dispatcher verifies the per-spawn URL’s HMAC signature. A worker that rewrites `?role=worker` → `?role=operator` produces an `invalid_signature` and is rejected with `request_rejected: spawn_sig_invalid_signature`. The attempt is persisted to `harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures` for on-call review.

This check is **not** wired into `tools/list` — listing returns what the *claimed* role would see, so an agent can introspect what tools exist before invoking. Verification happens at `tools/call`.

The `?superuser=1` door bypasses this check entirely; it has its own loopback + bearer envelope. See [Superuser mode](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/superuser-mode).

Full scheme, reason codes, rotation, and observability live in [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing).

## Default-deny (gate 1)

[Section titled “Default-deny (gate 1)”](#default-deny-gate-1)

A **fail-closed posture**: when the host sets `deps.defaultDeny`, a tool that declares **no gate at all** — no capabilities, no agent `roles`, no `requireRoles`, no `authorize` hook — is denied as `ungated` (403) unless it is explicitly marked `public: true` (the `[AllowAnonymous]` equivalent).

The *engine* default is off (the legacy allow-by-omission posture), but **the Papercusp host turns it ON** — `PROJECTED_DEPS` in `packages/operator-core/lib/projected-tool-deps.ts` sets `defaultDeny: true` (audited 2026-05-31). It currently denies nothing registered, because every first-party `defineTool` (which *requires* a `capability`) and every bundled plugin tool already declares a gate; it’s the fail-closed floor for a future / third-party tool that forgets to. It is **not bypassable** by `GateBypass` — an ungated tool is a declaration gap regardless of caller, so the fix is to declare a gate or mark it `public`.

`defineTool` *requires* a `capability`, so every first-party built-in tool already declares a gate and is never `ungated`. The posture exists to catch plugin / direct `registerProjectedTool` registrations that forgot to gate themselves. Since `defaultDeny` is already on, re-verify before/after installing a plugin by running `listUngatedProjectedTools()` (with the full registry loaded) — an empty result means nothing is silently denied; anything it returns must declare a gate or be marked `public`.

## Role allowlist (gate 2)

[Section titled “Role allowlist (gate 2)”](#role-allowlist-gate-2)

Tools declare `roles[]` — the **agent**-role allowlist (worker / scoper / architect / …), checked against `ctx.role` from the URL spawn param. This is orchestration gating, distinct from the RBAC role requirement below.

```jsonc
{
  "roles": ["worker", "scoper", "architect"]
}
```

A `validator` calling this tool gets:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "role_not_allowed",
    "message": "Role \"validator\" cannot call tool \"plugin.tool\" (allowed roles: worker, scoper, architect)"
  }
}
```

HTTP status: 403. The check only runs when *both* `tool.roles` and `ctx.role` are set, and is skipped when `GateBypass.role` is set. Tools without `tool.roles` skip this check.

## Capability check (gate 3)

[Section titled “Capability check (gate 3)”](#capability-check-gate-3)

Built-in tools declare a single capability string per tool. When a request arrives with a bearer token, the framework resolves it to a principal with a `Set<string>` of granted capabilities. The dispatcher checks `tool.capabilities[]` ⊆ `principal.capabilities`.

Two distinct failure modes:

* **No principal at all** (no bearer or invalid bearer) → `unauthorized` (401). The wrapper around legacy `defineTool` handlers throws `UnauthorizedToolError`; the dispatcher catches it and maps to 401.
* **Principal present but missing the required capability** → `missing_capability` (403).

The check is skipped when there is no principal (the agent path gates via the role allowlist instead) or when `GateBypass.capability` is set. Plugin tools have `capabilities[]` declared too, but they’re descriptive-only today — used by the Intel UI and tooling, not enforced.

## RBAC role requirement (gate 4)

[Section titled “RBAC role requirement (gate 4)”](#rbac-role-requirement-gate-4)

A tool declaring `requireRoles` is callable only by a principal whose **RBAC `roles`** (`principal.roles`) include at least **one** of them (any-of). This is the typed, declarative, audited replacement for ad-hoc `requireAdminKey` / `requireStaff`-style checks.

```jsonc
{ "requireRoles": ["staff", "admin"] }   // caller must hold staff OR admin
```

`principal.roles` is a **distinct axis** from `kind` (how the caller authenticated), from `capabilities` (OAuth-scope-like grants), and from the agent `roles` allowlist above (which is checked against `ctx.role`, not the principal).

* **Principal holds a required role** → pass.
* **Principal lacks every required role, or there is no principal (anonymous)** → `missing_role` (403). The gate is **fail-closed**: a role requirement can’t be satisfied without an identity.
* Skipped when `GateBypass.role` is set — a superuser passes RBAC role gates as it passes the agent-role allowlist.

Every denial emits an authorization audit event (see below).

## Harness-required gate (gate 5)

[Section titled “Harness-required gate (gate 5)”](#harness-required-gate-gate-5)

A tool declaring `harness: 'required'` (a ctx-only harness-scoped tool — one with no slug arg, so `ctx.harnessSlug` is its only harness source) is rejected with `harness_required` (400) when no harness is in scope. This gate **fails closed even for privileged callers** — `GateBypass.papercusp` is deliberately *not* set by the superuser/power-user mapping, because a `harness: 'required'` tool genuinely can’t function without a harness; the point is to return the uniform “harness required” hint rather than push the failure into the handler.

## Per-window quota (gate 6)

[Section titled “Per-window quota (gate 6)”](#per-window-quota-gate-6)

A window is a counter scoped by `(workspace, tool, role, window_key)` against `harness_shared.tool_invocations`. The window key depends on role:

* **Worker** → `chunk:<chunkId>` (resets per chunk)
* **Anyone else** → `run:<runId>` (resets per orchestrator run)

`tool_invocations` rows that count against quota have `status='ok'` only. Failures (`error`, `timeout`, `quota-exceeded`, `role-not-allowed`) don’t consume a slot, so a tool that returns 500 doesn’t burn the budget.

Manifest declares the limit per role:

```jsonc
{
  "rolesQuota": {
    "worker":    { "perChunk": 1 },
    "architect": { "perRun": 5 },
    "scoper":    { "perRun": 3 }
  }
}
```

When a call exceeds, the dispatcher returns:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "quota_exceeded",
    "message": "Tool \"plugin.tool\" exceeded worker quota (1/1) in window \"chunk:Q1\"",
    "meta": { "tool": "plugin.tool", "role": "worker", "windowKey": "chunk:Q1", "used": 1, "limit": 1 }
  }
}
```

HTTP status: 429. Skipped when `GateBypass.quota` is set.

### Quota under concurrency

[Section titled “Quota under concurrency”](#quota-under-concurrency)

Five simultaneous requests with `perChunk=1` produce one ok and four `quota-exceeded`. This holds in practice because Node’s event loop serializes through the JS code paths and the first INSERT lands before the others reach `readQuotaState`.

There is a theoretical TOCTOU window: all five readers could see `count=0` before any of them inserts. Closing this rigorously would require a PG advisory lock or `INSERT ... RETURNING` with a check constraint. Today the soft guarantee is good enough for the workloads the framework handles. If you have a tool where a one-call-over-quota bug is catastrophic, file an issue.

### Don’t quota reads

[Section titled “Don’t quota reads”](#dont-quota-reads)

Read-only tools (`roles:list`, `snapshots:get`) shouldn’t have a `rolesQuota`. Quotas exist for: external API spend, PG write bursts, subprocess fan-out. Counting every read produces noise without protection.

## Resource authorization (gate 7)

[Section titled “Resource authorization (gate 7)”](#resource-authorization-gate-7)

The coarse gates above answer “may this *kind* of caller use this tool”. The `authorize` hook answers the **fine-grained** question the others can’t express: “may THIS principal act on THIS *resource*” (ownership / ReBAC / ABAC).

```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'orders:get',
  capability: 'orders:read',
  authorize: ({ principal, input }) =>
    input.ownerId === principal?.slug
      ? { allow: true }
      : { allow: false, reason: 'not the owner' },
  // …
});
```

It runs **after** the coarse gates and **before** the handler, **fail-closed** (a throw denies → `authorization_denied`), and is **additive** — a tool with no `authorize` skips this gate entirely. Because it runs in-process with the tool’s `ctx`, it can load the resource it needs to decide (“authorize close to the data”) and can return `obligations` (e.g. a row filter) for list endpoints rather than checking each row.

The framework is the **policy-enforcement point**; it ships the contract (`AuthzQuery` / `AuthDecision` / `PolicyDecisionPoint`, plus a trivial `ownerOnly` helper) and **no policy engine** — the decision is the host’s, supplied as an in-process closure or by delegating to an external PDP (OPA / Cedar / OpenFGA / Cerbos / an AuthZEN engine).

### Break-glass: `GateBypass.policy`

[Section titled “Break-glass: GateBypass.policy”](#break-glass-gatebypasspolicy)

Unlike the role/capability/quota bypasses, the resource-`authorize` gate is **not** skipped by them — resource ownership is a separate decision a host opts out of explicitly, per call, via `GateBypass.policy` (default off). And even then **the bypass is audited**: skipping the hook still emits an authz audit event recording the bypass. Break-glass best practice is “policy-governed *and* mandatorily logged” — a bypassed check that isn’t logged is the silent super-admin the standard forbids.

## Declarative preconditions (gate 8): `requires:`

[Section titled “Declarative preconditions (gate 8): requires:”](#declarative-preconditions-gate-8-requires)

The **preInvoke mirror of `emits:`** (autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild-2026-06-05 D-006). A tool declares `requires: [ToolRequireSpec, …]` — each spec a declarative condition (a `@papercusp/rules` MatchMap / `all`/`any`/`not` combinator over `{ tool, args, ctx, state }`) that must **hold** for the call to proceed, plus a response when it doesn’t:

* `{ error }` — **reject** the call with `precondition_failed`.
* `{ fire, then: 'retry' }` — **auto-correct, visibly**: fire a corrective tool through the host’s injectable `deps.firePrecondition` port (Papercusp wires it to the same dispatch path reactions use — auth-gated, audited, cause-chained), re-resolve state, re-evaluate **once**, and reject if it still fails.

```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'autoloop:status',
  // The former in-handler `if (!slug) throw` guard, lifted (the proof migration):
  requires: [{
    id: 'harness-slug',
    when: { any: [
      { 'args.harnessSlug': { truthy: true } },
      { 'ctx.harnessSlug':  { truthy: true } },
    ]},
    error: 'autoloop:status — harness slug required (passed or in spawn ctx)',
  }],
  // …
});
```

Host state enters through the spec’s optional `state(args, ctx)` resolver (re-resolved before the retry); conditions are **declarative only** — there is deliberately no JS-predicate hatch here, because inspectability/serializability is the point of the lift. Everything fails **closed**: a throwing resolver, a malformed condition, a missing fire port, or a failed retry all deny. Denials and auto-corrections are audited with `gate: 'precondition'` through the same `deps.auditAuth` sink as gates 4/7 (first-try passes are not audited — they’re the overwhelmingly common case).

It runs **after** `authorize` — a corrective fire must only happen for an authorized caller, and a functional gap must not mask an auth denial — and **before** `timeout` (it’s a gate; no timers or buffers exist yet on the deny path).

**What belongs in `requires:`:** *functional* preconditions — an arg/scope shape the handler can’t proceed without, a resumable resource that a corrective fire can fix (the reject/auto-correct/delete choice is D-006’s safety-vs-convenience judgment: auto-correct ergonomic preconditions visibly; reject ones the caller must fix; delete artificial ones instead of migrating them).

### Safety invariants are EXCLUDED by design (D-007)

[Section titled “Safety invariants are EXCLUDED by design (D-007)”](#safety-invariants-are-excluded-by-design-d-007)

**`requires:` must never absorb a safety invariant.** The rule (autoloop-pot-operator-rebuild D-007): *the operator proposes, the gate disposes* — an agent gets maximal agency **inside** a small set of hard, coded guardrails it cannot reason past. A safety gate in a declarative rule table is a safety gate an agent (or a rule edit) can weaken; these stay imperative, fail-closed, audited **code**. The inventory (verified 2026-06-05):

| Gate                    | Where (imperative code)                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Audit sink                                                          | Bypass                                                                       |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Don’t-deploy-on-red** | `apps/operator/lib/release/green-checkpoint.ts` (ready advances only on green) + `deploy-cli.ts` (refuses un-green targets)                                                                                                                | coord broadcast per checkpoint/deploy                               | `--force` / `--deploy-commit` — loudly audited (`🚨 FORCED un-green deploy`) |
| **Protected-paths**     | `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/improvements/policy.ts` `classifyImprovement()` — glob patterns route protected surfaces to the human queue                                                                                            | tier decision in the improvements digest/queue                      | none (kind-graduation only widens `auto` kinds, never the protected paths)   |
| **Budget / quota caps** | `libs/papercusp/libs/db/src/budget-enforcement.ts` (row-locked atomic budget check, fail-closed) + `orchestrator-loop.ts` `SAFETY_CEILING` (hard constant; blueprint `dispatch.safetyCeiling` may only tighten) + the quota gate (6) above | `tool_invocations` (quota); `BudgetExceededError` carries detail    | quota: `GateBypass.quota`; budget/ceiling: none                              |
| **Auth perimeter**      | gates 0–4 + 7 above (`dispatch-stack.ts`, `tryBuildSpawnContext`)                                                                                                                                                                          | `harness_shared.tool_authz_log` + `spawn_sig_verification_failures` | per-gate `GateBypass`, `policy` bypass audited                               |
| **No-double-allocate**  | `work-items.ts` atomic CAS (`UPDATE … WHERE taken_by IS NULL`), `orchestrator/feature-claim.ts` append-only claim log, `authority/lock-authority.ts`                                                                                       | `harness_shared.claim_audit` (won/lost/timeout/error)               | none — atomic by construction                                                |

None of the five flows through `@papercusp/rules`, the event-reaction tables, or `requires:` — and that’s load-bearing, not an accident. When migrating a hardcoded guard to `requires:` (or a reaction to `emits:`), first ask: *is this gate’s failure mode harm?* If yes, it stays code.

## The authorization audit trail

[Section titled “The authorization audit trail”](#the-authorization-audit-trail)

Gates 4 and 7, and every `GateBypass.policy` bypass, emit an `AuthAuditEvent` through the optional `deps.auditAuth` sink — every allow, deny, and bypass. The Papercusp host persists them to `harness_shared.tool_authz_log` (`packages/operator-core/lib/tool-authz-audit.ts`), a security-decision stream distinct from the login-scoped `auth_audit_log` and the per-call `tool_invocations` telemetry. It answers “show me every denial / every break-glass bypass / everything this principal was denied”.

## Per-tool timeout (gate 9)

[Section titled “Per-tool timeout (gate 9)”](#per-tool-timeout-gate-9)

Each manifest entry has `timeoutSec` (default 60). The dispatcher creates an `AbortController`, hands `controller.signal` to the function as `ctx.signal`, and aborts after the configured time. Functions doing long work should watch `ctx.signal.aborted` and bail.

A timed-out call gets:

```json
{
  "error": { "code": "timeout", "message": "tool \"plugin.tool\" exceeded timeout of 60s" }
}
```

HTTP status: 504. The `tool_invocations` row records `status='timeout'`.

## The whole error code → HTTP status table

[Section titled “The whole error code → HTTP status table”](#the-whole-error-code--http-status-table)

For HTTP transport, `statusForErrorCode` in `http-projection.ts` maps:

| Error code             | HTTP | Source                                                                                              |
| ---------------------- | ---- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ungated`              | 403  | Default-deny on; tool declares no gate and isn’t `public`                                           |
| `unauthorized`         | 401  | Built-in tool, no bearer / invalid bearer                                                           |
| `role_not_allowed`     | 403  | Agent role not in the tool’s allowlist                                                              |
| `missing_capability`   | 403  | Principal missing required capability                                                               |
| `missing_role`         | 403  | Principal missing a required RBAC role (`requireRoles`)                                             |
| `harness_required`     | 400  | `harness:'required'` tool with no harness in scope                                                  |
| `quota_exceeded`       | 429  | Window count ≥ limit                                                                                |
| `authorization_denied` | 403  | The tool’s `authorize` hook denied (or threw → fail-closed)                                         |
| `precondition_failed`  | 412  | A declarative `requires:` precondition failed (after the auto-correct retry, when one was declared) |
| `invalid_input`        | 400  | Function threw a typed input-validation error                                                       |
| `timeout`              | 504  | AbortController fired before function returned                                                      |
| `unknown_tool`         | 404  | No projection registered at this path/name                                                          |
| `method_not_allowed`   | 405  | HTTP method not in `expose.http.methods`                                                            |
| anything else          | 500  | Function threw an unhandled error → `handler_error`                                                 |

For MCP transport, errors are returned as a normal `tools/call` result with `isError: true` and a `content[].text` describing the error. There’s no JSON-RPC-level rejection — the MCP spec puts tool errors in the result envelope.

## A worked example

[Section titled “A worked example”](#a-worked-example)

Here’s what happens when a `worker` tries to call `firecrawl.scrape` with `chunk=Q1` for the second time:

1. **Default-deny.** On in Papercusp (`defaultDeny: true`), but `firecrawl.scrape` declares a role allowlist, so it’s gated → pass.
2. **Role check.** `firecrawl.scrape.roles = [scoper, architect, operator, reviewer, debugger, worker]`. Worker is in. Pass.
3. **Capability check.** Plugin tool — no principal — skipped.
4. **RBAC role requirement.** No `requireRoles` → skip.
5. **Harness gate.** Not `harness:'required'` → skip.
6. **Quota check.** Window `chunk:Q1`, role `worker`. Manifest says `worker: { perChunk: 2 }`. Read state: `count=1` (the first call already landed as ok). 1 < 2, pass.
7. **Resource authorization.** No `authorize` hook → skip.
8. **Preconditions.** No `requires:` declared → skip.
9. **Timeout.** AbortController set to 60s.
10. **Execute + record.** `scrape` runs, completes in 800ms; insert `tool_invocations` row with `status='ok', duration_ms=800`.

Same call a third time: gates 1–5 pass/skip as before, then the quota check reads `count=2`, `2 ≥ 2`, **fails**, inserts a quota-exceeded row, returns 429.

## Where the dispatcher lives

[Section titled “Where the dispatcher lives”](#where-the-dispatcher-lives)

`libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-stack.ts` defines `DEFAULT_DISPATCH_STACK` — the one ordered list these checks run in; `dispatch-projected.ts` drives it. If you find yourself wanting to add a custom gate inside a tool function, you’re probably making a mistake. The dispatcher is the canonical place for cross-cutting concerns.

# Operations

> Day-to-day workflows for the endpoint system. Hot reload, host refresh, common failure modes, and when to stop and ask.

> **Webapp retired (2026-05-14).** Any `localhost:3055` or `localhost:3070` URL on this page is only reachable while the **Tauri dev shell** is running. Start it with `cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev`.

## After every plugin manifest or handler edit

[Section titled “After every plugin manifest or handler edit”](#after-every-plugin-manifest-or-handler-edit)

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3055/api/plugins/host/refresh
```

The projection registry is module-level state. HMR is unreliable for it. If you don’t refresh after editing a plugin, you’re testing stale code and you won’t know.

The endpoint returns the host status:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "status": {
    "loaded": 15,
    "errors": 2,
    "plugins": [...],
    "loadErrors": [...]
  }
}
```

`errors=2` is the steady-state baseline (two unrelated pre-existing manifest issues). If you push a change and `errors` goes up, your edit broke discovery — read the `loadErrors[]` list.

## Where the registry lives

[Section titled “Where the registry lives”](#where-the-registry-lives)

Three module-level Maps in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/tool-projection.ts`:

* `REGISTRY` — keyed by `mcp:<name>` or `http:<path>`, value is the full `ProjectedTool`
* `BY_MCP_NAME` — `Map<string, ProjectedTool>` for `tools/call` lookups
* `BY_HTTP_PATH` — `Map<string, ProjectedTool>` for the catch-all routes

These are populated at startup as a side effect of:

1. Importing `@papercusp/agent-mcp` — every `defineTool(...)` auto-registers into the registry (PR 0c.D extension).
2. The first call to `getPluginHost()` — runs `loadPlugins({ projectDir, harnessSlugs, globalPluginsDir })`, then `registerPluginTools(loaded)` walks each plugin’s `toolDefinitions[]` and calls `registerProjectedTool` per entry.

`registerPluginTools` is **idempotent** for same-plugin re-registration: it calls `unregisterProjectedToolsForPlugin(pluginName)` first, then re-registers. This means `/api/plugins/host/refresh` works correctly without producing collision errors. **Cross-plugin collisions still throw** — two different plugins claiming the same MCP name fails with `ToolRegistrationError`.

## Discovery sources

[Section titled “Discovery sources”](#discovery-sources)

`loadPlugins` searches in this order:

1. `<projectDir>/plugins/<name>/` — for in-repo bundled plugins. The operator wires this via `findBundledPluginsParent()` in `packages/operator-core/lib/plugin-host-runtime.ts`.
2. `~/.papercusp/harnesses/<slug>/plugins/<name>/` — per-harness plugins.
3. `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/<name>/` — globally installed plugins.

Dedupe by `plugin.name` with priority `project > harness > global`. So if you have both `libs/papercusp/plugins/repomix/` and `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/repomix/`, the in-repo one wins.

This is why you don’t need to symlink plugins into `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/` during development. Just put them in `libs/papercusp/plugins/` and they’ll be discovered.

## Hot-reload watcher

[Section titled “Hot-reload watcher”](#hot-reload-watcher)

`watchPluginsForReload` (in `plugin-host-runtime.ts`) sets up a debounced fs.watch over the global-plugins directory. Triggers on changes to `papercusp.json`, `index.{js,mjs,ts}`, or `dist/index.js`. On a hit, it calls `_resetPluginHostForTests()` which clears the host cache; next request to the host re-runs discovery.

It’s gated behind `PAPERCUSP_DEV_PLUGIN_WATCH=1`. Off by default because filesystem-watch overhead is unwanted on shared hosts. Turn it on for plugin development if you don’t want to keep curling `/api/plugins/host/refresh`.

## Migrations don’t run on the system PG

[Section titled “Migrations don’t run on the system PG”](#migrations-dont-run-on-the-system-pg)

The embedded-postgres-server has a migration runner that walks `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/*.sql` on boot and applies missing files via `harness_shared.schema_migrations`. The system PG (`localhost:5432`) does not — there’s no boot hook.

Every new SQL file requires manual application:

```bash
PGPASSWORD=harness_admin_pwd psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U harness_admin -d papercusp \
  -f libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/048-my-table.sql


PGPASSWORD=harness_admin_pwd psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U harness_admin -d papercusp \
  -tAc "SELECT to_regclass('harness_shared.my_table')"
```

This bites every time. If your tool depends on a table that doesn’t exist, the queries throw, the dispatcher catches and continues, the tool returns 200 with `output` text — and your quota tracking + telemetry are silently dead until you apply the migration. **Verify with `to_regclass` before testing the tool.**

## Common failure modes

[Section titled “Common failure modes”](#common-failure-modes)

### Tool returns 404 `unknown_tool` after a manifest edit

[Section titled “Tool returns 404 unknown\_tool after a manifest edit”](#tool-returns-404-unknown_tool-after-a-manifest-edit)

You forgot to refresh. `curl -X POST /api/plugins/host/refresh`.

Or HMR wiped the registry. Same fix.

### Tool returns 200 but `tool_invocations` is empty

[Section titled “Tool returns 200 but tool\_invocations is empty”](#tool-returns-200-but-tool_invocations-is-empty)

Two likely causes:

1. **Workspace GUC not set.** The HOST\_EXTRAS.deps insert calls `SELECT set_config('app.workspace_id', $1, true)` — but if the request didn’t include `?workspace=<id>`, `ctx.workspaceId` is `undefined`, and the insert silently fails. Make sure the test request has the workspace param.
2. **Migration not applied.** The table doesn’t exist. See above.

### Tool returns 500 `handler_error`

[Section titled “Tool returns 500 handler\_error”](#tool-returns-500-handler_error)

The function threw an unhandled error. Check the `tool_invocations.error_message` for that call. If the message is `spawn <bin> ENOENT`, the binary isn’t installed on the machine running the operator (e.g. `code2prompt` not present in dev). Either install it or skip that tool.

### Tool returns 401 `unauthorized` for a tool you expected to work without bearer

[Section titled “Tool returns 401 unauthorized for a tool you expected to work without bearer”](#tool-returns-401-unauthorized-for-a-tool-you-expected-to-work-without-bearer)

You wrote a built-in (`defineTool(...)`) when you needed a plugin. Built-ins require `ctx.principal`; agents over MCP only have URL spawn context, no bearer. Move the tool to `libs/papercusp/plugins/<name>/`.

### `/api/plugins/host/refresh` shows error count > 2

[Section titled “/api/plugins/host/refresh shows error count > 2”](#apipluginshostrefresh-shows-error-count--2)

Something in your manifest broke discovery. The response body has `loadErrors[]` — read it.

Common causes: `name` collision with an existing tool from a different plugin; `expose.mcp.name` missing the namespace separator (must contain `.` or `:`); orphan handler (manifest declares `tools[].name = 'foo'` but `index.ts` has no `tools.foo` export).

### Tool works on MCP but returns “ctx.X is unset” on HTTP

[Section titled “Tool works on MCP but returns “ctx.X is unset” on HTTP”](#tool-works-on-mcp-but-returns-ctxx-is-unset-on-http)

The HTTP catch-all needs the same `ctx.spawn` / `ctx.secret` / `ctx.projectDir` resolvers as MCP. Check that the plugins catch-all (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/plugins/catchall.ts`) builds its `HttpToolHostExtras` with `spawn` (`pluginSpawnImpl`), `secret` (`secretImpl`/`makeSecretResolver`), and `resolveHarnessPaths`. If it doesn’t, that’s a regression of audit-2/3 fixes.

### Tool works on dev but agents in spawned subprocesses don’t see it

[Section titled “Tool works on dev but agents in spawned subprocesses don’t see it”](#tool-works-on-dev-but-agents-in-spawned-subprocesses-dont-see-it)

Check the orchestrator’s `.mcp.json` URL. In dev (`NODE_ENV=development`) it should point at `http://localhost:3055/api/sse`; in prod, `http://localhost:3070/api/sse`. Override with `PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_URL` if neither default applies.

### Search-provider env vars don’t reach spawned agents

[Section titled “Search-provider env vars don’t reach spawned agents”](#search-provider-env-vars-dont-reach-spawned-agents)

The orchestrator’s `invoke()` path (`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/invoke.ts`) decrypts search-provider keys from PG via `buildSearchProviderSpawnEnv` (`spawn-env-from-pg.ts`) and attaches them to `InvokeContext.extraSpawnEnv`. They land in every `invoke()` call’s spawn env.

The operator harness-launch path does this independently: `packages/operator-core/lib/harness-launch.ts` calls `buildSpawnEnv` from `packages/operator-core/lib/search-provider-credentials.ts`. Both paths are wired; if a worker doesn’t see `TAVILY_API_KEY` etc., the keys aren’t in PG (check `harness_shared.operator_search_provider_credentials`) or the encryption key is missing (`~/.papercusp/db-encryption-key`).

## Spawn-signing admin endpoints

[Section titled “Spawn-signing admin endpoints”](#spawn-signing-admin-endpoints)

The HMAC signing scheme (see [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing)) ships with two loopback + superuser-bearer-gated admin routes for incident response and observability.

### Rotate the signing key

[Section titled “Rotate the signing key”](#rotate-the-signing-key)

```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)
curl -X POST http://localhost:3070/api/admin/spawn-signing/rotate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

Rotates the PG row **and** bumps the operator’s in-process cache. Every in-flight signed URL fails its next call with `invalid_signature`. The orchestrator must re-spawn affected workers. Wrapper script: `bun run rotate:spawn-key`.

### Read the verification audit log

[Section titled “Read the verification audit log”](#read-the-verification-audit-log)

```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)
curl "http://localhost:3070/api/admin/spawn-signing/failures?limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

Query params: `limit` (max 1000, default 100), `since` (ISO timestamp), `reason` (filter). Returns `{ rows, summary: { byReason, window } }`.

A non-zero rate of `invalid_signature` outside explicit test runs is a real signal. Correlate `claimed_spawn` with orchestrator spawn IDs to identify the culprit.

## When to stop and ask

[Section titled “When to stop and ask”](#when-to-stop-and-ask)

You should stop and ask before doing any of these:

* The component you want to wrap doesn’t fit one of the four shipped plugin shapes (subprocess single-tool, HTTP+optional-secret, subprocess multi-tool, HTTP+required-secret-with-schema). Don’t invent a fifth shape; the function-as-truth design doc lists which patterns are blessed.
* You want to extend the manifest contract with a new field. Each existing field corresponds to a dispatcher behavior; adding one is an architecture decision, not a cleanup.
* You hit one of the known open issues and need to work around it. The workaround usually masks a real bug — better to surface it and get the framework fix.
* The handler signature you’d want isn’t `(input, ctx) => ToolResult`. The framework can’t accommodate exotic shapes. If you want a callback-based contract, a multi-response stream, or anything else non-request/response, it doesn’t belong here.
* You’re tempted to delete a legacy `app/api/agent-mcp/*/route.ts` route that the dashboard fetches from. **Always grep for UI callers first.** The same JSON is now served at `/api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>`; UI can switch URLs in the same PR. Delete only when zero UI callers remain.

## Per-tool migration checklist

[Section titled “Per-tool migration checklist”](#per-tool-migration-checklist)

When you’re moving an existing route to the endpoint system, run through this list. Each step is mandatory; skip any and you ship a broken tool:

1. Grep for UI callers of the legacy route. Decide replace-with-redirect or full-delete.
2. If new PG schema, write the SQL file in `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/` and apply it manually.
3. Write the typed function with no transport awareness.
4. Write the manifest entry. JSON Schema directly. No `zodToJsonSchema`.
5. `curl` the HTTP transport. Verify status code + body shape.
6. `curl` the MCP transport. Verify the same.
7. `psql` the telemetry row. Verify `status='ok'` and `app.workspace_id` was set.
8. Quota smoke test: fire perChunk+1 → second is 429.
9. Role gate smoke test: wrong role → 403.
10. `curl /api/plugins/host/refresh`. Confirm error count unchanged.
11. Delete the legacy route in the same commit (only if step 1 said zero UI callers).
12. Submodule commit first if you touched `libs/papercusp/`, then bump the parent’s submodule pointer in a second commit.

## Per-turn commit discipline

[Section titled “Per-turn commit discipline”](#per-turn-commit-discipline)

When you’re working across the operator app and the `libs/papercusp/` submodule:

* Commit the submodule first.
* Bump the parent’s submodule pointer in a second commit.

Otherwise the parent commit references a submodule SHA that isn’t pushed and the next agent sees a broken checkout. This is observed-from-experience guidance; multiple agents have shipped half-broken trees by inverting the order.

# Overview

> One function, three transports — what the endpoint system is and why we built it this way.

## The one-line version

[Section titled “The one-line version”](#the-one-line-version)

You write **one typed function**. The framework projects it onto:

* An **HTTP route** at `/api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>` (or `/api/agent-tools/<tool>` for built-ins)
* An **MCP `tools/call` entry** under `<plugin>.<tool>` (or `<scope>:<verb>` for built-ins)
* An **in-process call** any TypeScript caller can `await` directly

You declare exposure, role allowlist, capabilities, and quotas in a manifest. The framework handles auth gating, role enforcement, quota windows, telemetry persistence, streaming progress, and per-spawn URL context — none of which you write per tool.

## Why “endpoint system” not “MCP migration”

[Section titled “Why “endpoint system” not “MCP migration””](#why-endpoint-system-not-mcp-migration)

The first instinct was to call this an MCP migration. That framing is wrong.

**The function is the source of truth.** HTTP and MCP are projections of it. Once a function is decoupled from any specific transport, all three callers — your dashboard, an AI agent over MCP, another module in the same Node process — get it for free, with the same auth/role/quota/telemetry behavior.

The hard part isn’t writing the MCP wrapper. The hard part is pulling a function out of its current transport-coupled form so that the wrapper *can be* generated. The “MCP-callable” part is the smallest-and-easiest consequence of that decoupling.

## What this gets you

[Section titled “What this gets you”](#what-this-gets-you)

* **No duplicated route+handler code.** A new feature is one typed function plus six lines of manifest. Both the dashboard and the agent get it.
* **Single test surface.** You test the function. Both transports inherit correct behavior because they both go through the same dispatcher.
* **Uniform observability.** Every invocation lands in `harness_shared.tool_invocations` with role, window key, status, duration, output size — regardless of transport. You can answer “which agents called which tools when” without per-route instrumentation.
* **Uniform gating.** Role allowlist, capability check, and per-window quota all enforce in the same dispatcher. Adding a new sensitive tool means setting `roles: ["operator"]` + `rolesQuota: { operator: { perRun: 5 } }` and you’re done.
* **Stream-or-not, no rewrite.** A function that calls `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` automatically gets MCP `notifications/progress` events on the MCP transport and SSE events on the HTTP transport. No transport-specific wiring.
* **Token-efficient by default.** A function returns structured `data`; the dispatcher serializes it in the most compact format the data’s shape allows (TOON for arrays, lossless JSON otherwise) — agents read ≈ −20–35% fewer tokens on list results with no change to how they call. Declaring `result: <schema>` unlocks CSV + MCP `outputSchema` advertisement. See [Transports → Result formats](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/transports).

## What this is not

[Section titled “What this is not”](#what-this-is-not)

* Not a replacement for SSE chat, WebSocket voice, or anything else that holds a long-lived bidirectional connection. Those stay on dedicated routes; the endpoint system is for request → response (with optional streamed progress).
* Not a way to expose your dashboard to the public internet. The trust model is **loopback bind + HMAC-signed per-spawn URL params** (see [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing)), suitable for local dev + Tauri desktop. Off-loopback exposure needs a real principal/auth layer in front, since same-UID code can still read the signing key from PG.
* Not a generic RPC framework. The contract is narrow on purpose: `(input, ctx) => ToolResult`. Trying to make it accommodate exotic shapes (callbacks, multi-response, file uploads >5MB) defeats the point of having one function as truth.

## The route projection — `defineTool` also defines plumbing

[Section titled “The route projection — defineTool also defines plumbing”](#the-route-projection--definetool-also-defines-plumbing)

Not every endpoint is an agent tool. The browser, the desktop shell, an orchestrator, a webhook — they call **routes**: HTTP plumbing that must *not* appear in the agent tool catalog. `defineTool` produces those too.

`defineTool` accepts a **route-shaped** input — discriminated by the `method` field — and returns a `RouteDefinition` instead of a `ToolDefinition`:

```ts
defineTool({
  method: 'GET',
  path: '/desktop/version',
  auth: 'public',                    // or a PrincipalRequirements gate
  input: z.object({ verbose: z.coerce.boolean().optional() }), // optional
  handler(req, ctx) {                // Web-standard Request in, Response out
    return Response.json({ version: '…' });
  },
});
```

A route runs through the same cross-cutting machinery — auth, input validation, timeout, telemetry, uniform errors — but it is **not** projected onto the MCP catalog. `tools/list` never sees it; an agent cannot call it. That guarantee is what keeps plumbing out of the agent surface.

Route files import `defineTool` directly — the former `defineRoute` alias was **removed** when the primitives were unified (Phase E6, `endpoint-unification-2026-05-21`). A route is *declared* with `defineTool` and *mounted* host-side by `registerRoute` (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/`).

### Paired-phone routes — `auth: { kind: ['device'] }` + `cors`

[Section titled “Paired-phone routes — auth: { kind: \['device'\] } + cors”](#paired-phone-routes--auth--kind-device---cors)

A route reachable from the paired phone declares the device-JWT auth gate and opts into cross-origin reachability — there is no implicit folding:

```ts
defineTool({
  method: 'POST', path: '/device/heartbeat',
  auth: { kind: ['device'] },        // gate on the device-JWT principal
  cors: true,                        // CORS allowlist (paired-device + tauri + localhost)
  handler(req, ctx) { /* ctx.principal is the device */ },
});
```

`cors: true` mounts the shared CORS middleware (OPTIONS preflight + headers); `auth: { kind: ['device'] }` makes the route-stack reject anything that doesn’t resolve to a device principal. Paired-phone routes live under `/api/device/*`. Built-in tools are reachable from the phone for free — the device JWT is a bearer token, and the `/api/agent-tools/*` catch-all resolves it like any other.

## Two channels at a glance

[Section titled “Two channels at a glance”](#two-channels-at-a-glance)

A tool handler has two outbound channels available, projected uniformly across transports:

| Channel    | API                                                   | Wire                                                   | Replay on reconnect                               |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| **Events** | `ctx.emit('name', payload)`, `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` | typed SSE events / MCP notifications                   | Ring buffer (T2.2), bounded by `replayBufferSize` |
| **State**  | `ctx.askUser(spec)`, `ctx.publishState(snapshot)`     | `state-snapshot` SSE on `/api/operator/state-snapshot` | Current snapshot only — replay does not re-prompt |

Cards (`ctx.askUser`) and tool state (`ctx.publishState`) live on the state channel because they’re not append-only — a reconnecting client wants the latest answered/unanswered card state, not history of every snapshot. The framework auto-installs `askUser` / `publishState` on the ctx when the call has a `workspaceId + runId` (always present for HTTP-projected calls). See [ctx.askUser](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/ask-user) and [state-shaped tools](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/state-tools).

## How it’s packaged

[Section titled “How it’s packaged”](#how-its-packaged)

The endpoint system started life inside `@papercusp/agent-mcp`. It has since been **carved into a host-agnostic engine plus thin adapters** (plan `papercusp-tooldef-extraction-2026-05-29`), so the same dispatcher can be used outside Papercusp:

| Package                              | Role                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **`@papercusp/tooldef`**             | The engine — `defineTool`, the registry, the dispatch pipeline, the state/card/replay channels, OpenAPI assembly, core types. **Zero** Papercusp / PG / Next / `@restart` deps. Validator-agnostic ([Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev)); every host-specific rule is injected (table below).                                                                                                           |
| **`@papercusp/tooldef-http`**        | The HTTP transport adapter (`handleHttpToolRequest` / `…Streaming`). Resolves a request → tool, builds the ctx from `X-Papercusp-*` headers, dispatches. Depends only on the engine + `@papercusp/sse`.                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **`@papercusp/ipc-endpoint-server`** | The IPC (unix-socket) transport adapter.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **`@papercusp/agent-mcp`**           | The **Papercusp host adapter** — supplies the injected deps (PG-backed quota/telemetry, the role config, quota-window policy, capability→tier table, gate-bypass mapping, HMAC spawn verification) and re-exports the engine + HTTP surface so existing import sites are untouched. The **MCP bridge** (Vercel `mcp-handler` glue + spawn-context auth) currently still lives here / in the operator route layer. |

Everything Papercusp-specific is a **host-injected seam** with a generic engine default:

| Concern                          | Seam                                                                              | Engine default                |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Roles                            | augment the `RoleRegistry` interface → shapes `AgentRole`                         | `string` (any role)           |
| Quota window + ceiling           | `DispatchProjectedDeps.computeQuotaWindow(ctx, roleQuota)`                        | run-scoped / `perRun`         |
| Capability → tier                | `setCapabilityTierResolver` (read via `tierFor`)                                  | `'low'`                       |
| Gate bypass (privileged callers) | `ctx.gateBypass { role?, capability?, quota? }`                                   | absent ⇒ all gates enforce    |
| Schema validation                | `args` / `state` / card `dataSchema` typed `StandardSchemaV1`; `standardValidate` | any Standard Schema validator |
| Schema → JSON Schema             | `setJsonSchemaAdapter` (read via `toJsonSchema`)                                  | Zod 4 `toJSONSchema`          |
| Quota / telemetry I/O            | `DispatchProjectedDeps.readQuotaState` / `recordInvocation`                       | no-ops                        |
| Transaction handle               | `ToolContext<Tx = any>`                                                           | `any`                         |

The engine is provably standalone — see `libs/generic/tooldef/examples/standalone-inprocess.ts` (registers + dispatches a tool importing **only** `@papercusp/tooldef`). It is also mirrored to a standalone `Papercusp/tooldef` repo for external consumers.

# Reference

> Manifest schema, error codes, file map, capability conventions. Lookup material.

## Manifest schema (plugin tool entry)

[Section titled “Manifest schema (plugin tool entry)”](#manifest-schema-plugin-tool-entry)

```jsonc
{
  // Required
  "name":        "do_thing",                   // Identifier within the plugin
  "description": "One-sentence description.",  // Shown in tools/list to agents
  "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "..." },  // JSON Schema — use Zod 4's z.toJSONSchema, never zodToJsonSchema


  // Strongly recommended
  "capabilities": ["http:fetch:example.com"],  // Descriptive on plugins, enforced on built-ins
  "roles":        ["worker", "architect"],     // Role allowlist — empty/missing means "no role gate"
  "rolesQuota":   { "worker": { "perChunk": 1 } },  // Per-window quota; reads usually don't need this
  "timeoutSec":   60,                          // Default 60 if omitted


  // Streaming + state
  "events": {                                  // Typed event vocabulary; surfaced on tools/list
    "delta":     { "type": "string" },         // z.string() → raw text on the SSE wire
    "tool_call": { "type": "object", "..." }   // any object → JSON-encoded
  },
  "replayBufferSize":  100,                    // Ring-buffer size for Last-Event-ID resume. Default 0 = no replay.
  "idleTimeoutSec":    120,                    // Abort if no event emitted for N seconds. Default unset.
  "state":             { /* JSON-Schema for ctx.publishState payload */ },  // Declares state-shaped tool (auto opt-out of replay buffer; auto-streamable)
  "modality":          ["text", "voice"],      // Surface filter for prompt-assembly catalog. Default ["text"].
  "guidance": {                                // Rendered into prompt-assembly tools catalog
    "when":      "User asks to <X>; pair with <Y> for the chained-list case.",
    "notWhen":   "Not for <Z> — use <other_tool> instead.",
    "chaining":  "After <prerequisite_tool>; before <successor_tool>."
  },


  // Optional — exposure overrides
  "expose": {
    "http": {
      "path":    "/api/plugins/my-plugin/do_thing",  // Default: /api/plugins/<short-name>/<tool.name>
      "methods": ["POST"]                            // Default: ["POST"]
    },
    "mcp": {
      "name":         "my-plugin.do_thing",          // Default: <short-name>.<tool.name>
      "streaming":    true,                          // Explicit streamability opt-in. Also implied by declared events or state.
      "largeOutput":  true                           // Hint that output may be written to scratch dir
    }
  }
}
```

If `expose.*` is omitted entirely, the framework picks defaults for both. If you want only one transport, declare only that one.

Built-in `defineTool` calls accept the same fields as TS/Zod (`state: z.object({...})`, `events: { delta: z.string(), ... }`, etc.). The `RoleToolDefinitionInput` shape is the canonical authority — see `libs/generic/tooldef/src/types.ts`.

## Error codes

[Section titled “Error codes”](#error-codes)

| Code                      | HTTP | Meaning                                              |
| ------------------------- | ---- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `unauthorized`            | 401  | Built-in tool, no bearer / invalid bearer            |
| `role_not_allowed`        | 403  | Plugin tool, role not in allowlist                   |
| `missing_capability`      | 403  | Built-in tool, principal missing required capability |
| `quota_exceeded`          | 429  | Window count ≥ limit                                 |
| `invalid_input`           | 400  | Function threw a typed input-validation error        |
| `timeout`                 | 504  | AbortController fired before function returned       |
| `unknown_tool`            | 404  | No projection registered at this path/name           |
| `method_not_allowed`      | 405  | HTTP method not in `expose.http.methods`             |
| `handler_error`           | 500  | Function threw an unhandled error                    |
| `invalid_request_context` | 400  | MCP call missing required URL spawn params           |
| `invalid_bearer`          | 401  | (MCP) Bearer didn’t resolve to a principal           |

For MCP transport, errors return `{ result: { content: [{ type: 'text', text: 'code: message' }], isError: true } }` rather than HTTP status codes. The codes are the same.

## Capability conventions

[Section titled “Capability conventions”](#capability-conventions)

Capability strings should namespace by intent. Existing patterns:

* `tools:<plugin>:<verb>` — ownership marker for plugin-contributed tools (`tools:repomix:pack`, `tools:web:fetch_clean`)
* `compute:exec:<bin>` — subprocess execution (`compute:exec:repomix`, `compute:exec:npx`); enforces `ctx.spawn(bin, ...)` to a basename match
* `http:fetch:<host>` — outbound HTTP fetch to a specific host (`http:fetch:r.jina.ai`, `http:fetch:api.firecrawl.dev`)
* `secrets:read:<NAME>` — explicit secret access (`secrets:read:FIRECRAWL_API_KEY`)
* `<scope>:read` / `<scope>:write` — built-in tool capabilities (`audit:read`, `tasks:write`)
* `events:emit:<name>` / `events:listen:<name>` — pub-sub event bus

Don’t consolidate capabilities into a single `secrets:*` or `compute:*` namespace. Granular grants exist so a future principal/auth model can selectively allow `secrets:read:FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` without granting access to all secrets.

## Role names

[Section titled “Role names”](#role-names)

Agents pass one of these as the `?role=` URL param:

| Role         | Quota window | Typical use                                    |
| ------------ | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `worker`     | `chunk:<id>` | Implements one feature per chunk               |
| `validator`  | `run:<id>`   | Tests the worker’s output                      |
| `scoper`     | `run:<id>`   | Generates feature plans + validation contracts |
| `architect`  | `run:<id>`   | Routes work, owns the loop                     |
| `reviewer`   | `run:<id>`   | Code review pass                               |
| `debugger`   | `run:<id>`   | Debugs failing validations                     |
| `operator`   | `run:<id>`   | UI-mode reads/writes                           |
| `documenter` | `run:<id>`   | Doc generation                                 |
| `curator`    | `run:<id>`   | Curates artifacts                              |

The framework doesn’t care if you invent a new role — `tool.roles[]` is a string list, not a typed enum at runtime. But sticking to the established set keeps quotas comparable across runs.

## Window keys

[Section titled “Window keys”](#window-keys)

`window_key` (and the quota ceiling) in `tool_invocations` is computed by the host-injected `DispatchProjectedDeps.computeQuotaWindow(ctx, roleQuota)` (plan P-011). The engine default (`defaultComputeQuotaWindow` in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-types.ts`) is run-scoped / `perRun`; Papercusp’s policy (`papercuspComputeQuotaWindow` in `packages/agent-mcp/src/quota-policy.ts`, wired via `PROJECTED_DEPS`) is:

* `worker` → `chunk:<chunkId>` (cap `perChunk`) if `ctx.chunkId` set, else null (no window, no quota)
* power-user session → `power-user:<uiClientId>` (cap `perRun`) — keyed on the stable auth session, not the per-request run
* anyone else → `run:<runId>` (cap `perRun`) if `ctx.runId` set, else null

Null window means no quota check (and no telemetry insert path that requires the key). In practice every real call has both `?run=` and either a worker chunk or a run-scoped role, so windows are always set.
