## URL spawn params

[Section titled “URL spawn params”](#url-spawn-params)

Read by `buildHttpSpawnContext` in `http-projection.ts` and the equivalent on the MCP route.

| Query param    | Header                     | Field                                                   |
| -------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `workspace`    | `X-Papercusp-Workspace`    | `ctx.workspaceId`                                       |
| `harness`      | `X-Papercusp-Harness`      | `ctx.harnessSlug` (also drives `projectDir` resolution) |
| `role`         | `X-Papercusp-Role`         | `ctx.role`                                              |
| `feature`      | `X-Papercusp-Feature`      | `ctx.featureId`                                         |
| `chunk`        | `X-Papercusp-Chunk`        | `ctx.chunkId`                                           |
| `run`          | `X-Papercusp-Run`          | `ctx.runId`                                             |
| `spawn`        | `X-Papercusp-Spawn`        | `ctx.spawnId`                                           |
| `parent_spawn` | `X-Papercusp-Parent-Spawn` | `ctx.parentSpawnId`                                     |

Header form takes precedence over query form when both are present. The orchestrator uses query form when writing per-spawn `.mcp.json` because mcp-handler clients don’t have a clean way to attach custom headers.

## Operations endpoints

[Section titled “Operations endpoints”](#operations-endpoints)

| Endpoint                                             | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET /api/plugins/tools`                             | List every projected tool. Used by `/settings/plugins/tools`.                                                                                                                                                       |
| `POST /api/plugins/host/refresh`                     | Re-run discovery. Returns full host status.                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `GET /api/credentials/search-providers`              | Read masked search-provider keys + provider list (UI-only).                                                                                                                                                         |
| `POST /api/credentials/search-providers`             | Update keys (UI-only).                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `POST /api/agent-tools/<scope>/<verb>`               | Built-in tool catch-all.                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `POST /api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>`                  | Plugin tool catch-all (HTTP).                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `GET/POST /api/mcp`                                  | MCP transport (Streamable HTTP).                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `GET /api/sse`                                       | MCP transport (SSE). Same handler.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `GET /api/operator/state-snapshot`                   | SSE stream of `state-snapshot` events for the active workspace. Carries `openCards` (from `ctx.askUser`) + `toolState` (from `ctx.publishState`). Session-cookie required (401).                                    |
| `POST /api/operator/conversations/:id/card-response` | Resolves a pending `ctx.askUser` card. Body: `{ correlationId, action: 'submit'\|'decline'\|'cancel', workspaceId, payload?, reason? }`. 30 RPS per session user. 404 on cross-workspace replay (defense-in-depth). |
| `POST /api/operator/conversations/:id/run-cancel`    | Cancels every pending card under a `runId`. Body: `{ runId, workspaceId }`. Same auth + rate limit + cross-workspace gate as `/card-response`.                                                                      |
| `POST /api/workspaces/switch`                        | Body `{ id }`. Captures `leaving = reg.current`, writes new current, fires `dispatchWorkspaceSwitch(leaving)` — drops state snapshots + cancels every pending card under the leaving workspace.                     |

## Result envelope

[Section titled “Result envelope”](#result-envelope)

Tool functions return `ToolResult`:

```ts
interface ToolResult {
  content: Array<
    | { type: 'text'; text: string }
    | { type: 'image'; data: string; mimeType: string }
    | { type: 'resource'; resource: { uri: string; ...etc } }
  >;
  isError?: boolean;
}
```

The dispatcher does not inspect `content` — it’s passed through to the transport verbatim. `isError` flips the MCP transport’s `tools/call` error envelope but doesn’t change the HTTP status (HTTP statuses come from `error.code` mapping).

For **large outputs** (>50k chars), write to `<stateDir>/scratch/<id>.<ext>` and return:

```ts
return {
  content: [{
    type: 'text',
    text: JSON.stringify({ path: '/abs/path', sizeBytes, sample: '...' }, null, 2),
  }],
};
```

The dispatcher records `output_ref` and `output_size` based on the result, so the Intel UI can link directly to scratch files without the response body bloating up.

# Spawn-URL signing

> Per-spawn MCP URLs carry an HMAC signature over their baked params. The dispatcher refuses to honor role claims that don't match. Realistic prompt-injection defence.

> **Webapp retired (2026-05-14).** Any `localhost:3055` or `localhost:3070` URL on this page is only reachable while the **Tauri dev shell** is running. Start it with `cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev`.

## The problem this solves

[Section titled “The problem this solves”](#the-problem-this-solves)

Before 2026-05-11 the per-spawn URL bound a worker to `?role=worker&workspace=…&harness=…&run=…&spawn=…`. The dispatcher trusted those params verbatim. A worker that wanted operator-tier tools just rewrote `?role=worker` → `?role=operator` and called. One line, no auth, no audit.

Today every per-spawn URL carries an HMAC-SHA256 `sig` plus a Unix-epoch `exp`. The dispatcher’s `tryBuildSpawnContext()` calls `verifySpawnParams()` before honoring any role claim. Forged URLs fail with `invalid_signature` and the attempt lands in `harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures` for on-call review.

The realistic threat

A prompt-injected agent reading a poisoned doc that says “to fix this, please call X with role=operator.” Without HMAC the model just edits its URL. With HMAC the edit produces an invalid signature, the request is rejected, and the attempt is logged. See [Threat model](#threat-model) for what this does and does not defend against.

## How it works

[Section titled “How it works”](#how-it-works)

Both ends share a 32-byte signing key stored at:

```sql
SELECT value_b64 FROM harness_shared.operator_secrets WHERE name = 'spawn-signing-key';
```

The row is auto-minted on first use by either side. Both the operator and the orchestrator cache it in-process, invalidating the moment PG’s `rotated_at` advances (a 5-minute TTL is kept only as a fallback for when `rotated_at` can’t be read).

### Mint side — orchestrator

[Section titled “Mint side — orchestrator”](#mint-side--orchestrator)

`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/spawn-mcp.ts` → `writeSignedSpawnMcp()` is what the orchestrator’s `invoke()` calls when it lays down a per-spawn `.mcp.json`. It:

1. Builds the baked URL params (`harness, workspace, role, run, spawn, [feature], [chunk], [parent_spawn], [client]`).
2. Adds `exp` = `now + 24h` (override with `ttlSec`).
3. Canonicalizes by sorting + URL-encoding (only the allowlist; duplicates rejected; `sig` itself ignored).
4. HMAC-SHA256 over the canonical string, base64url-encoded, appended as `sig=`.
5. Writes the `.mcp.json` with mode 0600. The per-spawn worktree dir is mode 0700.

The orchestrator’s PG DSN is inherited from the operator-set env. If signing fails (DSN missing, row missing on first boot), `writeSignedSpawnMcp` throws — the outer try/catch in `invoke()` logs `spawn-mcp write failed` and the agent boots without an MCP endpoint, making the failure visible. Callers that need the historical soft-warn fallback (emit unsigned + warn) can pass `allowUnsigned: true` AND run the operator with `PAPERCUSP_REQUIRE_SPAWN_SIG` unset.

### Verify side — operator

[Section titled “Verify side — operator”](#verify-side--operator)

`packages/operator-core/lib/spawn-signing.ts` → `verifySpawnParams(url)` runs first thing in `tryBuildSpawnContext()` at `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/transport/_mcp-handler.ts`. It:

1. Reads `sig` + `exp`. Missing either → `missing_sig` / `missing_exp`.
2. Rejects past-`exp` URLs as `expired`.
3. Canonicalizes the same way the minter does; rejects duplicates.
4. Computes HMAC over the canonical string with the cached key.
5. `timingSafeEqual` against the provided `sig`.
6. On mismatch → `invalid_signature`. On encoding error → `invalid_sig_encoding`.

Any non-`ok` result is persisted to `harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures` (reason + claimed role/harness/workspace/spawn + remote\_addr + user\_agent + exp\_claim) and the request is rejected with `request_rejected: spawn_sig_<reason>`.

tools/list mirrors tools/call in strict mode

Both `tools/list` and `tools/call` reject when the URL claims a spawn context (role/workspace/spawn) without a valid sig. `tools/list` on a bare `/api/mcp` URL with no claims still returns the full catalog — that’s anonymous discovery, not an escalation attempt. (Prior behavior returned the claimed-role catalog even for forged URLs; that leaked the operator-tier surface to anyone setting `?role=operator` and left no audit trace.)

## Operating modes

[Section titled “Operating modes”](#operating-modes)

### Strict (default)

[Section titled “Strict (default)”](#strict-default)

`PAPERCUSP_REQUIRE_SPAWN_SIG=1` in `apps/operator/.env.local`. Unsigned URLs that claim a spawn context (any of `role=`, `spawn=`, `workspace=`) hard-reject with `request_rejected: spawn_sig_missing_sig_required_mode`. Bare URLs with no claims are accepted (tools/list returns the full catalog, tools/call fails on `invalid_request_context` from the dispatcher).

### Soft-warn (rollout-only)

[Section titled “Soft-warn (rollout-only)”](#soft-warn-rollout-only)

`PAPERCUSP_REQUIRE_SPAWN_SIG` unset or `!= '1'`. Unsigned-with-claims URLs accepted with a console warning. Was the default during the 2026-05-11 rollout window for in-flight spawn compatibility.

## Coarse revocation

[Section titled “Coarse revocation”](#coarse-revocation)

If a key may be compromised, or a bad batch of prompts shipped and you want every in-flight spawn to fail closed, rotate. There is **no per-spawn revocation** — rotation invalidates everything.

### Preferred: admin endpoint (immediate effect)

[Section titled “Preferred: admin endpoint (immediate effect)”](#preferred-admin-endpoint-immediate-effect)

```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)
curl -X POST http://localhost:3070/api/admin/spawn-signing/rotate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# → { "ok": true, "rotatedAt": "2026-05-11T04:00:00.000Z" }
```

The endpoint rotates the PG row **and** bumps the operator’s in-process cache, so revocation takes effect on the very next MCP call (not the 5-minute lazy-cache lag).

Loopback + superuser-bearer gated. Off-loopback returns 403; missing/bad bearer returns 401.

Multi-instance cache coherence

Each process caches the key, but every cache honors PG’s `rotated_at`: a rotate on *any* process (or a direct PG `UPDATE` that bumps `rotated_at`) is picked up by every other operator process and orchestrator subprocess on its **next** signing/verifying call — not after a 5-minute lag. The 5-minute TTL is only a fallback for when `rotated_at` can’t be read, so you do **not** need to call `/rotate` on each port.

### CLI wrapper

[Section titled “CLI wrapper”](#cli-wrapper)

```bash
bun run rotate:spawn-key                # confirmation prompt
bun run rotate:spawn-key -- --yes       # no prompt
```

(`apps/operator/scripts/rotate-spawn-signing-key.mjs`. Prefers the HTTP endpoint when the operator is reachable; falls back to direct PG when not — the direct `UPDATE` bumps `rotated_at`, so every other process still picks up the new key on its next call.)

### Direct PG (only when the operator is down)

[Section titled “Direct PG (only when the operator is down)”](#direct-pg-only-when-the-operator-is-down)

```sql
UPDATE harness_shared.operator_secrets
SET value_b64 = encode(gen_random_bytes(32), 'base64'),
    rotated_at = now()
WHERE name = 'spawn-signing-key';
```

After rotation: every in-flight `.mcp.json` URL is now invalid. The orchestrator must re-spawn affected workers. Use sparingly.

## Observability

[Section titled “Observability”](#observability)

### From the operator admin API

[Section titled “From the operator admin API”](#from-the-operator-admin-api)

```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)
curl "http://localhost:3070/api/admin/spawn-signing/failures?limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

Returns the audit log + a summary count by reason for the configured window (default last 24h). Query params:

* `limit` — max rows (default 100, max 1000)
* `since` — ISO timestamp; only rows with `ts > since`
* `reason` — filter by reason string

### From SQL

[Section titled “From SQL”](#from-sql)

```sql
-- Recent failures by reason (last 24h)
SELECT reason, count(*) FROM harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures
WHERE ts > now() - interval '24 hours'
GROUP BY reason ORDER BY 2 DESC;


-- Most-recently failed spawns
SELECT ts, reason, claimed_role, claimed_harness, claimed_spawn
FROM harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures
ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 20;
```

A non-zero rate of `invalid_signature` outside explicit test runs is a real signal. Correlate `claimed_spawn` with the orchestrator’s spawn IDs to identify which spawn produced the forgery.

## Reason codes

[Section titled “Reason codes”](#reason-codes)

| reason                      | When                                                                                        |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `missing_sig`               | URL has `exp` but no `sig` (typically a logged-only warning unless in strict mode)          |
| `missing_exp`               | URL has `sig` but no `exp`                                                                  |
| `invalid_exp`               | `exp` not parseable as a positive integer                                                   |
| `expired`                   | `exp < now()`                                                                               |
| `invalid_sig_encoding`      | `sig` isn’t valid base64url                                                                 |
| `invalid_signature`         | HMAC mismatch — the realistic forgery signal                                                |
| `duplicate_param:<k>`       | Same allowlisted key appears twice (forger appending `&role=operator` after the signed one) |
| `missing_sig_required_mode` | Unsigned URL hit the verifier with `PAPERCUSP_REQUIRE_SPAWN_SIG=1`                          |

## Threat model

[Section titled “Threat model”](#threat-model)

### Defends against

[Section titled “Defends against”](#defends-against)

* **Prompt-injected worker rewriting URL params.** The HMAC is over the canonical original; the agent doesn’t have the key. Edits produce `invalid_signature`.

### Does NOT defend against

[Section titled “Does NOT defend against”](#does-not-defend-against)

* **Same-UID code that queries PG for the key.** The agent runs as the operator’s UID and has libpq access. HMAC is friction, not enforcement.
* **Replaying another spawn’s `.mcp.json`.** Each URL is a valid bearer for its `exp` window (24h default). `.mcp.json` is 0600 and worktrees are 0700, but same UID means same OS user can read across them.
* **The `?superuser=1` door.** Separate envelope (loopback + superuser-bearer); see [Superuser mode](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/superuser-mode). HMAC doesn’t change that surface.
* **Editing `~/.papercusp/granted-capabilities.json`.** Plain JSON, same UID, writable. The capability gate trusts what it finds.
* **Operator memory dump** (`gcore <pid>`). Key is in the heap.
* **Replacing the operator binary or PG client.** Far beyond prompt injection but in scope for same-UID ownership.

### What actually closes the loop

[Section titled “What actually closes the loop”](#what-actually-closes-the-loop)

OS-level isolation per worker (`bwrap` / `firejail` / a separate UID with file ACLs). Real fix; bigger lift. Eventual landing spot.

## Signed-param allowlist

[Section titled “Signed-param allowlist”](#signed-param-allowlist)

Only these keys participate in the HMAC. Adding others has no effect on the signature.

```plaintext
harness, workspace, role, run, spawn, feature, chunk, parent_spawn, client, exp
```

Reorder, URL-encoding variants, and duplicates are all canonicalized before signing/verification.

The suites are Vitest, under `packages/operator-core/lib/`. The integration ones need Docker (testcontainers Postgres); run them from the package dir (e.g. `cd packages/operator-core && npx vitest run <name>`):

| Test                                              | Kind        | What it proves                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `spawn-signing.test.ts`                           | unit        | sign/verify canonicalization + every reason code                         |
| `__tests__/spawn-signing-e2e.integration.test.ts` | integration | full path through the MCP boundary                                       |
| `__tests__/mint-roundtrip.integration.test.ts`    | integration | orchestrator’s `writeSignedSpawnMcp` ↔ operator’s verifier agree on HMAC |
| `__tests__/admin-rotate.integration.test.ts`      | integration | rotation endpoint auth + revocation semantics                            |
| `__tests__/admin-failures.integration.test.ts`    | integration | audit-read endpoint (filter + summary)                                   |

Run them before promoting any change to the signing pipeline.

[Section titled “File map”](#file-map)


(The `operator_secrets` + `spawn_sig_verification_failures` tables are defined by SQL migrations under `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/`, not by runtime DDL — the old `ensure-schema.ts` lazy-`CREATE TABLE` path was removed.)

# ctx.publishState — state-shaped tools

> Tools that publish their current state instead of streaming events. Reconnect-resilient by construction; clients see the latest snapshot, never event history.

# `ctx.publishState` — state-shaped tools

[Section titled “ctx.publishState — state-shaped tools”](#ctxpublishstate--state-shaped-tools)

A **state-shaped tool** publishes its current snapshot rather than streaming events. Clients reconnecting mid-run receive the latest snapshot — never event history.

```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'search:semantic',
  state: z.object({
    results: z.array(z.object({ id: z.string(), score: z.number() })),
    progress: z.number(),
    phase: z.enum(['embedding', 'querying', 'ranking', 'done']),
  }),
  handler: async (args, ctx) => {
    ctx.publishState({ results: [], progress: 0, phase: 'embedding' });
    const embedded = await embed(args.query);
    ctx.publishState({ results: [], progress: 0.4, phase: 'querying' });
    const results = await query(embedded);
    ctx.publishState({ results, progress: 1, phase: 'done' });
    return results;
  },
});
```

## Why state-shaped instead of events?

[Section titled “Why state-shaped instead of events?”](#why-state-shaped-instead-of-events)

Most streaming tools today emit events (`ctx.emit('progress', …)`, `ctx.emit('text-delta', …)`) and rely on a replay ring buffer (T2.2) to recover from disconnects. That’s the right shape when output is **append-only** (LLM token streams). But for tools whose output is a **current value that supersedes prior values**, replay is the wrong shape:

| Aspect                | Event-shaped (`ctx.emit`)      | State-shaped (`ctx.publishState`)    |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| Wire form             | typed events on the wire       | one `state-snapshot` per change      |
| Replay on reconnect   | Last N events from ring buffer | Latest snapshot                      |
| Memory                | Linear in stream length        | Bounded by state shape               |
| Long-lived disconnect | Buffer evicts past 5000 events | Snapshot persists across disconnects |
| Workspace switch      | Buffers cleared                | Snapshots cleared                    |

For a search tool with 100 results, state-shape is \~10KB regardless of how many internal updates happened. For a token stream, that same encoding would be lossy.

## Declaring a state-shaped tool

[Section titled “Declaring a state-shaped tool”](#declaring-a-state-shaped-tool)

Add `state: ZodType<S>` to `defineTool`. The schema is the source of truth for the snapshot shape:

```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'whatever',
  state: z.object({ /* your shape */ }),
  ...
})
```

Tools that declare `state` automatically:

* Get `ctx.publishState` installed (when the call has both `workspaceId` and `runId` — the HTTP catch-all defaults a `runId` per-request, so plain JSON / SSE callers both work).
* Opt **out** of the replay ring buffer (no double-storage — state snapshots replace events on the wire).
* Become **streamable** — the HTTP catch-all’s strict-streamable predicate recognizes `tool.state` as a valid trigger for `Accept: text/event-stream`, so the runId-bearing SSE path is reachable even when no `events` are declared.
* Persist snapshots for 5 minutes after run-end (reconnect window).

## Handler API

[Section titled “Handler API”](#handler-api)

```ts
ctx.publishState(snapshot)
```

* **Validated** against `tool.state` at publish time. Bad shapes throw synchronously.
* **Replaces** the run’s current snapshot (v1 is snapshot-only).
* **Reactive** — every call bumps the run’s `version` and re-emits to subscribed clients.

### v1 limitations

[Section titled “v1 limitations”](#v1-limitations)

* **Snapshot-only.** Passing a JSON-Patch array throws. Deltas are deferred to v1.1 once we measure full-snapshot perf on real tools.
* **In-process state.** Snapshots live in the operator’s Node process. Dev HMR / server restart drops them. PG-backed persistence is a follow-up.

## Client-side consumption

[Section titled “Client-side consumption”](#client-side-consumption)

The state-snapshot SSE stream (`GET /api/operator/state-snapshot`) carries `toolState` alongside `openCards`. Use `useStateSnapshots()` to subscribe and `selectToolStates()` to filter:

```ts
import { useStateSnapshots, selectToolStates } from '@/lib/use-state-snapshots';


function MyComponent() {
  const { byRun } = useStateSnapshots();
  const states = selectToolStates(byRun);
  // states is Map<runId, toolState>
}
```

The `useStateSnapshots` hook owns one EventSource per mount. `selectToolStates` is a pure helper — do not call `useStateSnapshots()` from inside it.

## How state-shape absorbs T4.3

[Section titled “How state-shape absorbs T4.3”](#how-state-shape-absorbs-t43)

The original Phase-4 plan had T4.3 “long-lived disconnected tools” as a separate Tier-4 item: detach `AbortSignal` from disconnect, manage the ring buffer’s lifetime, decide when to *actually* abort.

State-shape collapses T4.3 to **zero engineering**:

* State outlives any single SSE connection.
* Reconnect serves the current snapshot — no buffer to evict, no history to replay.
* “Long-lived” is the default for state-shaped tools.

The tool author opts in by declaring `state`. The framework handles the rest.

## When NOT to use state

[Section titled “When NOT to use state”](#when-not-to-use-state)

* **LLM token streams** (`runAgentChat` etc.) — those are inherently append-only. Use `ctx.emit('text-delta', …)` with `replayBufferSize` for reconnect.
* **One-shot tools** with a final result — no streaming, no need for state.
* **Tools that need to emit ordered events** (notifications, log lines) — state collapses ordering into “latest only.”

For a tool that mixes a state-shaped result (`results`) with an append-only side stream (`log_lines`), declare `state` AND `events` — both surfaces work together.

## See also

[Section titled “See also”](#see-also)

* [ctx.askUser](./ask-user.mdx) — interactive prompts on the same state channel.
* Plan: `apps/operator/docs/plans/bespoke-card-improvements-2026-05-13.md` §5

# Superuser mode

> Give an agent shell launched outside Papercusp full access to MCP tools across every workspace and harness, with a single token.

## What this is

[Section titled “What this is”](#what-this-is)

A way to point any `omp`, `claude`, or `codex` shell — running in any directory, on any of your workspaces — at Papercusp’s MCP server. Plugin tools (Repomix, GitNexus, Firecrawl, Phase 9 spawn primitive, …) and built-ins (intel:*, artifacts:*, …) all become available. The agent picks the workspace per call.

This is the opposite of the orchestrator’s per-spawn URL: instead of locking the agent into one (workspace, harness, role, run, spawn), the agent gets superuser access and chooses workspace per tool invocation.

Threat model: friction, not enforcement

Loopback alone can’t tell a user-shell agent apart from a papercusp-spawned agent — both run on the same machine, same user, same loopback. Superuser requires a bearer token from `~/.papercusp/superuser-token` (mode 0600). A spawned agent that wants to escalate its gates can `cat` the token file. Same way it can `rm -rf` your home directory.

Superuser is for *honest* user shells, not for *enforced* isolation. For real isolation, run shell-omp under a different OS user with file ACLs that prevent the orchestrator user from reading the token.

(The orchestrator-spawned path has a separate envelope — see [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing). Forging a worker URL into operator-tier fails the HMAC verifier; pasting the superuser token into your own shell does not, by design.)

## One-time setup

[Section titled “One-time setup”](#one-time-setup)

```bash
$ apps/operator/scripts/install-standalone-mcp.sh
✓ Minted ~/.papercusp/superuser-token (mode 0600)
✓ Merged 'papercusp-su' into ~/.omp/agent/mcp.json (mode 0600)
✓ Installed ~/.local/bin/psu (tracked picker launcher)
✓ Endpoint responded 200
```

The script:

1. Generates a 32-byte random token (only on first install — a re-run **reuses** the existing token so live shells keep working)
2. Writes it to `~/.papercusp/superuser-token` (mode 0600, owned by you)
3. Registers the `papercusp-su` MCP server for OMP (`~/.omp/agent/mcp.json`) and Claude Code (`~/.claude.json`), each with the operator URL + `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
4. Renders the per-client playbooks into `~/.papercusp/` and installs the `psu` launcher (plus the `ptool` defineTool CLI) into `~/.local/bin` (see [below](#the-psu-launcher-and-playbooks))
5. Verifies the operator is running and accepts the token

Re-run any time to refresh the playbooks and launcher — it **reuses** the existing token, so live shells keep working. To rotate the token deliberately, delete `~/.papercusp/superuser-token` first, then re-run; the operator picks up the new token without restart (file mtime triggers a cache refresh). Add `--profile=power` for the power-engineer subset.

## The `psu` launcher and playbooks

[Section titled “The psu launcher and playbooks”](#the-psu-launcher-and-playbooks)

The MCP registration above makes the SU tools *available* to a raw `omp` / `claude` shell; a second layer — the **engineer-collaborator playbook** — teaches a shell how to use them. That layer is delivered by a single launcher, **`psu`** (the older `omp-su` / `claude-su` / `codex-su` wrappers are retired). Plain `omp` / `claude` / `codex` stay vanilla; only `psu` loads the playbook.

`psu` records a tracked `/adv` session, then execs the **raw** agent CLI with the playbook + the `papercusp-su` MCP + the right per-client flags assembled per launch (`buildLaunchSpec`):

```bash
psu                                                          # interactive picker
psu --no-picker --agent=claude --harness=papercup --no-plan  # scripting
psu --resume                                                 # resume a tracked session
```

| Agent    | Playbook injection                                                                                                        |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `omp`    | `--append-system-prompt ~/.papercusp/<profile>-collaborator.md` (+ `-e ~/.papercusp/papercusp-coord.ts` for coordination) |
| `claude` | `--append-system-prompt-file ~/.papercusp/<profile>-collaborator.claude.md`                                               |
| `codex`  | a per-session `CODEX_HOME` whose `AGENTS.md` *is* the playbook                                                            |

**One base, per-client overlays.** The shared base playbook (`prompts/papercusp-su-<profile>.tools.md`) carries all client-neutral guidance. The client-specific task/workflow tooling — which differs by client (OMP `todo_write` / `omp:sessions`; Claude Code `TodoWrite` / `Task`; Codex `update_plan`) — lives in a small overlay (`papercusp-su.{omp,claude,codex}.md`) that is spliced into the base at a `<!-- PAPERCUSP-SU:CLIENT-TOOLING-OVERLAY -->` marker. This keeps one source of truth for the base and prevents, e.g., OMP-only “don’t use the Claude task tools” guidance from landing in the Claude or Codex playbook.

**Codex is special.** Codex has no `--append-system-prompt`; it injects instructions through `AGENTS.md` within its `CODEX_HOME`. So for a Codex launch `psu` mints a dedicated per-session `CODEX_HOME` whose `AGENTS.md` *is* the playbook and whose `config.toml` registers the `papercusp-su` server with the bearer supplied at launch — so plain `codex` (`CODEX_HOME=~/.codex`) never sees the server, and the token is never written into shared config.

Re-run `install-standalone-mcp.sh` (optionally `--profile=power`) any time to refresh the playbooks and the launcher.

## How the request flows

[Section titled “How the request flows”](#how-the-request-flows)

```plaintext
omp shell anywhere on the box
  └─ reads ~/.omp/agent/mcp.json
  └─ POST http://localhost:3070/api/mcp?superuser=1
       Authorization: Bearer <token>
       Accept: application/json, text/event-stream


operator
  └─ /api/mcp route detects ?superuser=1
  └─ checks: loopback origin + bearer matches superuser-token file
  └─ on failure: tool-shaped error from tools/call (`request_rejected: superuser_invalid_bearer`).
  │  (initialize + tools/list remain open per MCP spec; the gate fires at dispatch.)
  └─ on success: builds spawn ctx { isSuperuser: true,
                                    workspaceId: '*',
                                    role: 'operator', ... }


projected-tool dispatcher
  └─ ctx.gateBypass (from isSuperuser) → bypass role allowlist
  └─ ctx.gateBypass (from isSuperuser) → bypass capability gate
  └─ ctx.gateBypass (from isSuperuser) → bypass quota window
  └─ tool runs
  └─ tool_invocations row recorded with role='operator',
     run_id='<uuid>' (fresh per request),
     spawn_id='ephemeral-<hex>', window_key='run:<uuid>'
```

## Workspace switching

[Section titled “Workspace switching”](#workspace-switching)

The endpoint URL is workspace-agnostic. Tools that need a workspace take a `workspace` argument; the dispatcher uses `args.workspace ?? ctx.workspaceId`, and `ctx.workspaceId` defaults to `'*'` in superuser mode.

To discover what workspaces exist:

```typescript
papercusp:list_workspaces()
// → { workspaces: [
//      { slug: "default", harnesses: ["sheets","papercup-org"], lastActiveTs: 1778... },
//      { slug: "scratch", harnesses: [], lastActiveTs: 1778... }
//    ],
//    defaultWorkspace: "default" }
```

Then any subsequent call:

```typescript
intel.spawn_tree({ harness: "sheets", workspace: "default", limit: 50 })
orchestrator.spawn({ workspace: "default", harness: "sheets",
                     role: "worker", featureId: "F-FILL-001",
                     chunkId: "C-1" })
```

Tools that don’t care about workspace (`repomix.pack`, `fetch_plus.fetch_clean`, `firecrawl.scrape`, `gitnexus.list_repos`) ignore the missing `workspace` arg — they’re path-driven or URL-driven.

## What’s NOT bypassed

[Section titled “What’s NOT bypassed”](#whats-not-bypassed)

These still apply to superuser:

1. **Per-tool input validation** — invalid args still return `invalid_input` 400.
2. **Per-tool timeout** — long-running tools still get killed at the tool’s `timeoutSec`.
3. **Workspace requirement on first-party tools.** Most first-party tools (`harness:*`, `tasks:*`, `messages:*`, …) need a concrete workspace to open a PG transaction. Pass `?superuser=1&workspace=<slug>` in the URL — the default `workspaceId='*'` doesn’t satisfy them and you’ll get `handler_error: built-in tool "..." requires authenticated request (bearer + workspace tx)`.

What **is** bypassed: role allowlist, capability gate (the dispatcher’s `isSuperuser` short-circuits in both), per-window quota, and the spawn-URL signature check (superuser has its own bearer envelope).

## Troubleshooting

[Section titled “Troubleshooting”](#troubleshooting)

| Symptom                                                                                  | Cause                                                                                  | Fix                                                                                                       |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `request_rejected: superuser_invalid_bearer` on `tools/call` (and an empty `tools/list`) | Token mismatch, token file missing, or `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header not sent | Re-run `install-standalone-mcp.sh`; check the header is set in `~/.omp/agent/mcp.json` / `~/.claude.json` |
| `request_rejected: superuser_non_loopback`                                               | Request didn’t originate from loopback (127.0.0.1 / ::1 / localhost)                   | Call the operator over loopback                                                                           |
| `unknown_tool` 404                                                                       | Plugin didn’t load                                                                     | `curl /api/plugins/host/refresh` to see load errors                                                       |
| `harness_required` / `workspace required` from a tool                                    | Tool needs a real workspace/harness; `*` doesn’t work for it                           | Pass `workspace: "default"` (or other slug from `list_workspaces`) explicitly                             |

## Telemetry

[Section titled “Telemetry”](#telemetry)

Every superuser tool call writes a `harness_shared.tool_invocations` row with:

* `role = "operator"`
* `run_id = "<uuid>"` — a fresh per-request UUID, **not** a fixed `"standalone"` sentinel (the shared sentinel was dropped to avoid a cross-cancellation hazard)
* `spawn_id = "ephemeral-<random hex>"`
* `window_key = "run:<uuid>"`

Quota is bypassed for superuser, but the invocation row is still recorded — the stable marker for superuser activity is the `ephemeral-` `spawn_id` prefix.

## Revoking access

[Section titled “Revoking access”](#revoking-access)

```bash
$ rm ~/.papercusp/superuser-token
```

The next `tools/call` is rejected with `request_rejected: superuser_invalid_bearer` (and `tools/list` returns an empty catalog). To replace it with a fresh token instead, delete it and then re-run `install-standalone-mcp.sh` (a plain re-run reuses the existing token).

# Telemetry

> Every tool call lands in `harness_shared.tool_invocations`. Schema, queries, and the Phase 9 spawn-lineage forward-look.

## The single table

[Section titled “The single table”](#the-single-table)

`harness_shared.tool_invocations` is where every projected-tool call goes. One row per dispatch attempt, regardless of transport, regardless of outcome. The table originally shipped in migration 046 (now folded into the squashed `000-baseline.sql`, with the original at `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/archive/046-tool-invocations.sql`); later migrations added the `args_json` / `transport` / `event_count` / `metadata_json` / `principal_*` columns and two views (below).

```sql
CREATE TABLE harness_shared.tool_invocations (
  id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  workspace_id    TEXT NOT NULL,
  harness_slug    TEXT NOT NULL,
  plugin_name     TEXT NOT NULL,
  tool_name       TEXT NOT NULL,
  role            TEXT NOT NULL,
  feature_id      TEXT NULL,
  chunk_id        TEXT NULL,
  run_id          TEXT NULL,
  spawn_id        TEXT NOT NULL,
  parent_spawn_id TEXT NULL,                 -- Phase 9 lineage
  window_key      TEXT NOT NULL,             -- 'chunk:<id>' or 'run:<id>'
  invoked_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  duration_ms     INT NULL,
  status          TEXT NOT NULL,             -- enum below
  output_ref      TEXT NULL,                 -- papercusp://scratch/... URI for large outputs
  output_size     BIGINT NULL,
  error_message   TEXT NULL,
  args_json       JSONB NULL,                -- the call's input args (truncated past 32 KB)
  transport       TEXT NULL,                 -- 'http' | 'mcp' | 'ipc' | 'in_process'
  event_count     INT NULL,                  -- number of ctx.emit calls during the run
  metadata_json   JSONB NULL,                -- ctx.metadata() payload + reaction cause-chain
  principal_kind        TEXT NULL,           -- Principal audit fields (bearer/MCP path only;
  principal_auth_method TEXT NULL,           -- NULL → surfaces as 'unknown' in /dev)
  principal_trust       TEXT NULL
);
```

The squashed schema also ships two views over the table: `tool_invocations_artifacts` (successful calls that wrote a scratch `output_ref` — feeds the Intel Pack/Diff sub-tabs) and `tool_invocations_spawn_tree` (recursive `parent_spawn_id` lineage, `depth=0` for roots).

Two indexes:

* `tool_invocations_quota_idx` on `(workspace_id, tool_name, role, window_key) WHERE status='ok'` — partial index, makes the dispatcher’s quota read O(log n) per call.
* `tool_invocations_telemetry_idx` on `(workspace_id, harness_slug, invoked_at DESC)` — feed for Intel UI’s recent-activity panel.

## The status enum

[Section titled “The status enum”](#the-status-enum)

| Status             | Meaning                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ok`               | Function returned successfully. Counts against quota.                                                                        |
| `error`            | Function threw. Doesn’t count against quota. `error_message` populated.                                                      |
| `timeout`          | Dispatcher’s AbortController fired before function returned.                                                                 |
| `quota-exceeded`   | Pre-dispatch quota check rejected. Function never ran.                                                                       |
| `role-not-allowed` | Pre-dispatch role check rejected. Function never ran. Also covers the `missing_capability` denial (both map to this status). |
| `invalid-input`    | Function threw a typed input-validation error (`invalid_input`).                                                             |

Add a new status only by editing the dispatcher; do not let tool functions return arbitrary status values.

## Reading the table

[Section titled “Reading the table”](#reading-the-table)

The table has RLS — every read needs `app.workspace_id` set first:

```sql
SELECT set_config('app.workspace_id', 'default', false);
SELECT tool_name, role, status, duration_ms, error_message
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE invoked_at > now() - interval '1 hour'
ORDER BY invoked_at DESC;
```

`harness_admin` is `BYPASSRLS` and sees every workspace; `harness_app` is RLS-bound and sees only the configured workspace.

## Useful queries

[Section titled “Useful queries”](#useful-queries)

### Per-tool success rate this run

[Section titled “Per-tool success rate this run”](#per-tool-success-rate-this-run)

```sql
SET app.workspace_id = 'default';
SELECT
  tool_name,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='ok') AS ok,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='error') AS errors,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='timeout') AS timeouts,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='quota-exceeded') AS quota_hits
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE run_id = 'r-2026-05-10-001'
GROUP BY tool_name
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;
```

### What did role X do in this run

[Section titled “What did role X do in this run”](#what-did-role-x-do-in-this-run)

```sql
SELECT invoked_at, plugin_name, tool_name, status, duration_ms
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE run_id = 'r-2026-05-10-001' AND role = 'architect'
ORDER BY invoked_at;
```

### Quota near-limits (architect at 4/5)

[Section titled “Quota near-limits (architect at 4/5)”](#quota-near-limits-architect-at-45)

```sql
SELECT tool_name, role, window_key, count(*) AS used
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE status = 'ok' AND window_key LIKE 'run:%'
GROUP BY tool_name, role, window_key
HAVING count(*) >= 4;
```

### Slowest calls

[Section titled “Slowest calls”](#slowest-calls)

```sql
SELECT tool_name, role, duration_ms, output_size, invoked_at
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE status = 'ok' AND duration_ms > 5000
ORDER BY duration_ms DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

### Failed calls with messages

[Section titled “Failed calls with messages”](#failed-calls-with-messages)

```sql
SELECT invoked_at, tool_name, role, status, substring(error_message, 1, 200)
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE status IN ('error', 'timeout')
ORDER BY invoked_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

## Output reference for large results

[Section titled “Output reference for large results”](#output-reference-for-large-results)

Tools that produce a large result write it to the scratch tree at `~/.papercusp/scratch/<workspace>/<toolName>/<runId>/<basename>` and return `outputRef` as a `papercusp://scratch/<workspace>/<toolName>/<runId>/<basename>` URI (see `scratch-uri.ts`); the dispatcher persists it to the `output_ref` column. The body of the tool result still includes a small sample + the ref. Repomix uses this pattern; expect code2prompt and any future packing tools to do the same.

This keeps the table queryable without bloating it with 1MB+ payloads.

## `parent_spawn_id` lineage

[Section titled “parent\_spawn\_id lineage”](#parent_spawn_id-lineage)

`parent_spawn_id` captures the spawn-of-spawn relationship: a child call’s rows reference the parent’s `spawn_id`. It is **now populated** (not the always-`null` placeholder it once was) on two paths:

* The `parent_spawn` spawn-URL param, parsed into `ctx.parentSpawnId` by the MCP transport (`routes/transport/_mcp-handler.ts`). The fleet spawner (`fleet/operator-spawn.ts` + `fleet/parent-wake.ts`) is what threads it through — superseding the never-installed, now-retired `@papercupai/orchestrator-spawn` plugin.
* The event-reaction cause chain (`lib/events/dispatch-reaction.ts` sets `parentSpawnId` to the triggering call’s `spawnId`).

The `harness_shared.tool_invocations_spawn_tree` view (recursive CTE over `parent_spawn_id`, `depth=0` for roots) already exists for querying this lineage.

## How the row is written

[Section titled “How the row is written”](#how-the-row-is-written)

`recordTelemetry` runs in the `finally` of `runDispatchStack` (`dispatch-stack.ts`) on every termination path and calls the host-injected `deps.recordInvocation` — whose Papercusp implementation (`recordInvocationImpl` in `packages/operator-core/lib/projected-tool-deps.ts`) does the actual `INSERT`:

* After every successful tool execution: insert `(status='ok', duration_ms, output_size, ...)`.
* After every thrown error: insert `(status='error', duration_ms, error_message)`.
* After a quota check rejection: insert `(status='quota-exceeded', error_message='quota X/Y for role Z in window W')`. Function did not run.
* After a role rejection: insert `(status='role-not-allowed', error_message)`. Function did not run.

Best-effort: every insert is wrapped in try/catch. A PG outage doesn’t break the dispatcher; the call still resolves, but the row is lost. The HTTP catch-all logs a warning when this happens.

The `app.workspace_id` GUC is set before every insert via `SELECT set_config('app.workspace_id', $1, true)` — never `SET LOCAL = $1` (PG doesn’t accept binds in SET, audit-2 silently broke this for two days before we caught it).

## Where to read in code

[Section titled “Where to read in code”](#where-to-read-in-code)

* Schema: `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/000-baseline.sql` (original at `archive/046-tool-invocations.sql`)
* Quota read + insert (shared across all three transports): `packages/operator-core/lib/projected-tool-deps.ts` — the single `PROJECTED_DEPS` object (`readQuotaStateImpl` + `recordInvocationImpl`), passed to the plugins / agent-tools / transport Hono routes under `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/` (and the IPC server `libs/generic/ipc-endpoint-server/src/server.ts`)
* Telemetry orchestration: `recordTelemetry` in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-stack.ts`
* Window-key + ceiling computation: host-injected `computeQuotaWindow` (engine default `libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-types.ts:defaultComputeQuotaWindow`; Papercusp policy `packages/agent-mcp/src/quota-policy.ts:papercuspComputeQuotaWindow`)

## Future Intel-tab queries

[Section titled “Future Intel-tab queries”](#future-intel-tab-queries)

The planned `/harness/<slug>?tab=intel` page reads `tool_invocations` for the four sub-tabs:

* **Spawns** — tree of `spawn_id → parent_spawn_id` to visualize agent lineage
* **Pack** — recent `repomix.pack` / `code2prompt.pack` calls per feature
* **Diff** — `code2prompt.diff` results linked from feature panel
* **Graph** — gitnexus query/context/impact (when the GitNexus bridge ships)

The current schema supports all of these without modification — and some already shipped: the `tool_invocations_spawn_tree` and `tool_invocations_artifacts` views back the Spawns / Pack / Diff data, with read routes under `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/harness/` (`intel-spawn-tree.ts`, `intel-artifacts.ts`). The remaining work is query views, not new tables.
