## Search-provider keys

[Section titled “Search-provider keys”](#search-provider-keys)

Not tools — env vars. Set in `/settings/api-keys` → “Search providers”; orchestrator injects the decrypted env into every spawned agent’s `process.env`. 14 supported providers:

```plaintext
TAVILY_API_KEY, PERPLEXITY_API_KEY, BRAVE_API_KEY, JINA_API_KEY,
MOONSHOT_SEARCH_API_KEY (Kimi), ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (search), GEMINI_API_KEY,
CODEX_API_KEY, ZAI_API_KEY, EXA_API_KEY, PARALLEL_API_KEY, KAGI_API_KEY,
SYNTHETIC_API_KEY, SEARXNG_ENDPOINT (+ TOKEN / BASIC_USERNAME / BASIC_PASSWORD)
```

## How to invoke

[Section titled “How to invoke”](#how-to-invoke)

### From an OMP shell ([superuser-mode](./superuser-mode))

[Section titled “From an OMP shell (superuser-mode)”](#from-an-omp-shell-superuser-mode)

```plaintext
omp> call mcp__papercusp-su__papercusp:list_workspaces
omp> call mcp__papercusp-su__gitnexus:list_repos
omp> call mcp__papercusp-su__repomix:pack with target_dir /tmp/some-repo
```

### From curl (HTTP transport)

[Section titled “From curl (HTTP transport)”](#from-curl-http-transport)

```bash
TOK=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)


# Plugin tools — under /api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>
curl -X POST "http://localhost:3070/api/plugins/repomix/pack?superuser=1&workspace=default&harness=sheets" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOK" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"include":["README*"]}'


# Plugin tools — wildcard workspace (per-call ?workspace= override or arg)
curl -X POST "http://localhost:3070/api/plugins/gitnexus/list_repos?superuser=1" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOK" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}'


# Built-in tools — under /api/agent-tools/<group>/<verb> (require principal bearer, not superuser bearer)
curl -X POST "http://localhost:3070/api/agent-tools/intel/spawn_tree" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <principal-bearer>" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"harness":"sheets","limit":10}'
```

### From MCP transport

[Section titled “From MCP transport”](#from-mcp-transport)

```bash
curl -X POST "http://localhost:3070/api/mcp?superuser=1" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOK" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"papercusp:list_workspaces","arguments":{}}}'
```

## Discovering schemas at runtime

[Section titled “Discovering schemas at runtime”](#discovering-schemas-at-runtime)

Every tool’s `inputSchema` is JSON Schema (Zod 4 → `z.toJSONSchema`). Browse them:

```bash
$ curl -s http://localhost:3070/api/plugins/tools | jq '.tools[] | {name, inputSchema}'
```

Or pretty-printed in the dashboard at `/settings/plugins/tools`.

# Transports

> How HTTP, MCP, and in-process callers all reach the same function. The dispatcher is one; only the framing differs.

## The three transports

[Section titled “The three transports”](#the-three-transports)

| Transport           | Used by                                               | Path                                                         |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **HTTP** (plugin)   | Dashboard fetches, agent HTTP fallback                | `POST /api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>`                          |
| **HTTP** (built-in) | Dashboard fetches with bearer                         | `POST /api/agent-tools/<scope>/<verb>`                       |
| **MCP**             | Spawned agents over `mcp-handler` SSE/streamable-http | `POST /api/mcp` and `POST /api/sse`                          |
| **In-process**      | Direct TS imports, server actions                     | `import { lookupByMcpName }` then call `tool.fn(input, ctx)` |

All four go through the same `dispatchProjectedTool` in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-projected.ts`. The same role/capability/quota/timeout/telemetry behavior applies.

## How HTTP requests reach a function

[Section titled “How HTTP requests reach a function”](#how-http-requests-reach-a-function)

The catch-all routes are stupidly simple:

1. `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/plugins/catchall.ts` receives the request (the Hono host catch-all — migrated off the retired Next.js `app/api/plugins/[...path]/route.ts`)
2. Looks up the tool by `lookupByHttpPath(req.pathname)` — if not found, 404
3. Validates the HTTP method against the manifest’s `expose.http.methods` (default `['POST']`) — if not allowed, 405
4. Builds a `UnifiedToolContext` from URL spawn params + headers + the host’s resolver impls (spawn, secret, projectDir resolver). If no `run` param/header was supplied, a fresh `runId` is generated server-side so `ctx.askUser` / `ctx.publishState` can install — they gate on `workspaceId + runId`. SSE callers had this since T2.2; the JSON path got parity in the pass-9 audit.
5. If `Authorization: Bearer ...` present, resolves it to a principal and tx (no-op for plugins; required for built-ins)
6. Hands off to `dispatchProjectedTool`
7. Maps the resulting `DispatchProjectedResult` to status code + JSON body

The streaming path is the same except step 7 — when `Accept: text/event-stream` is on the request, the response is a `ReadableStream` of SSE events. Each `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` call from the function emits one event. **Replay-on-reconnect** (Last-Event-ID + X-Papercusp-Run-Id) is handled in `handleHttpToolRequestStreaming` (http-projection.ts): when both headers are present and the tool has a replay-buffer hit, it serves the buffered tail, emits `event: done` with `{resumed: true, replayed: N}`, and closes the sink — no re-dispatch (the original run already aborted on disconnect, by design).

## How MCP requests reach a function

[Section titled “How MCP requests reach a function”](#how-mcp-requests-reach-a-function)

Slightly more involved because we use `mcp-handler` as a transport library.

1. `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/transport/index.ts` (Hono `/api/:transport`, migrated off the retired Next.js `app/api/[transport]/route.ts`) wires a `createMcpHandler` server with `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/list`, `prompts/list` etc.
2. `tools/list` iterates `listMcpProjections(role)` — projection registry filtered by the calling role from URL params. Returns `{ name, description, inputSchema }` for every visible tool.
3. `tools/call` looks up by `lookupByMcpName(name)`, builds a `UnifiedToolContext` (similar to HTTP, but the spawn context comes from the URL on the SSE connection), and calls `dispatchProjectedTool`.
4. The dispatcher returns; the MCP SDK serializes the result into the JSON-RPC envelope.

Streaming on MCP works via `notifications/progress` — when the client sent a `progressToken` in `_meta`, every `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` becomes one notification. mcp-handler routes those over the open SSE connection.

## How in-process callers reach a function

[Section titled “How in-process callers reach a function”](#how-in-process-callers-reach-a-function)

The projection registry is exported. Any TypeScript module on the server can do:

```ts
import { lookupByMcpName } from '@papercusp/agent-mcp';


const tool = lookupByMcpName('repomix.pack');
if (!tool) throw new Error('not registered');
const result = await tool.fn(
  { target_dir: '/some/path' },
  {
    workspaceId: 'default',
    harnessSlug: 'sheets',
    role: 'architect',
    runId: 'R',
    spawnId: 'inproc',
    log: console.log,
    progress: () => {},
    signal: new AbortController().signal,
    spawn: pluginSpawnImpl,
    secret: secretImpl,
    projectDir: '/some/project',
    stateDir: '/some/project/.papercusp',
  },
);
```

This bypasses the dispatcher — no role check, no quota, no telemetry. Use when you genuinely want to call the function as a function, not as a tool. For consistency, prefer routing through `/api/plugins/...` even from server-side code so gating + telemetry stay uniform.

## The signed URL params

[Section titled “The signed URL params”](#the-signed-url-params)

When a request hits an HTTP plugin route or the MCP transport, the framework reads these query params (or equivalent `X-Papercusp-*` headers):

| Param          | Required for             | Purpose                                                                                           |
| -------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `workspace`    | Always                   | RLS scoping; `app.workspace_id` GUC                                                               |
| `harness`      | Path-resolving tools     | Looks up `projectDir` / `stateDir` via `loadHarnessRegistry()`                                    |
| `role`         | Plugin-tool role gate    | One of: `worker, validator, scoper, architect, reviewer, debugger, operator, documenter, curator` |
| `run`          | All non-worker quotas    | `window_key = 'run:<id>'`                                                                         |
| `chunk`        | Worker quotas            | `window_key = 'chunk:<id>'`                                                                       |
| `spawn`        | Telemetry attribution    | Unique per orchestrator spawn                                                                     |
| `feature`      | Optional context         | Passed to `tool_invocations.feature_id` for Intel UI                                              |
| `parent_spawn` | Optional Phase 9 lineage | Captured for spawn-of-spawn telemetry                                                             |
| `exp`          | **Signature envelope**   | Unix epoch seconds; URLs past `exp` are rejected                                                  |
| `sig`          | **Signature envelope**   | HMAC-SHA256 over the canonical sorted other params, base64url-encoded                             |

The orchestrator bakes all params into the per-spawn `.mcp.json` it writes before launching an agent process, **HMAC-signing the seven baked params plus `exp`** so the dispatcher refuses to honor a rewritten role. The agent’s MCP client then carries them on every request without the agent ever having to know about them. See [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing) for the full scheme; the minting end lives at `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/spawn-mcp.ts:writeSignedSpawnMcp()`.

## Default exposure

[Section titled “Default exposure”](#default-exposure)

If a manifest entry omits `expose.*`, the framework picks defaults:

* `expose.mcp.name` → `<short-pluginName>.<tool.name>` (drops `@scope/` prefix)
* `expose.http.path` → `/api/plugins/<short-pluginName>/<tool.name>`

So `@papercupai/repomix` plugin’s `pack` tool gets `repomix.pack` over MCP and `/api/plugins/repomix/pack` over HTTP. You only declare `expose.*` to override these — for instance, to host the same tool at a non-default URL for backwards compat.

If you only set `expose.mcp` and not `expose.http`, the tool is MCP-only. If only `expose.http`, HTTP-only. The framework requires at least one.

## Streaming progress

[Section titled “Streaming progress”](#streaming-progress)

Both transports thread `ctx.progress(pct, msg?)` through:

```ts
// Tool function
ctx.progress(0,   'starting');
ctx.progress(25,  'fetched manifest');
ctx.progress(75,  'transformed');
ctx.progress(100, 'done');
```

On MCP (when client passed `_meta.progressToken`):

```plaintext
notifications/progress { progressToken, progress: 25, total: 100, message: 'fetched manifest' }
```

On HTTP (when client sent `Accept: text/event-stream`):

```plaintext
event: progress
data: {"progress":25,"total":100,"message":"fetched manifest"}
```

The function code is identical for both. Tools that don’t call `ctx.progress` work fine — the receiver just gets the final result. `ctx.progress` is a thin alias over the more general `ctx.emit` primitive described next.

## Typed event streams

[Section titled “Typed event streams”](#typed-event-streams)

For tools that need richer streaming than `progress(pct, msg)` — LLM token deltas, mid-stream tool-call announcements, parsed sub-results — declare a typed event vocabulary in the manifest and emit via `ctx.emit(name, data)`:

```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'architect.chat',
  args: z.object({ message: z.string() }),
  events: {
    delta:     z.object({ text: z.string() }),
    tool_call: z.object({ name: z.string(), input: z.unknown() }),
    cost:      z.object({ usd: z.number() }),
  },
  requirePrincipal: false,
  roles: ['operator'],
  timeoutSec: 600,
  idleTimeoutSec: 120,
  capability: 'harness:write',
  handler: async (input, ctx) => {
    for await (const ev of runAgentChat({ promptText: input.message })) {
      if (ev.type === 'delta')     ctx.emit('delta', { text: ev.text });
      else if (ev.type === 'tool_call') ctx.emit('tool_call', { name: ev.name, input: ev.input });
      else if (ev.type === 'result')    ctx.emit('cost', { usd: ev.costUsd });
    }
    return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: 'turn complete' }] };
  },
});
```

### Projection table

[Section titled “Projection table”](#projection-table)

| Wire                                           | When emit(‘delta’, payload) is called                                                                                                                                        | When handler returns                              | When handler throws                           |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| **HTTP/SSE** (`z.string()` schema)             | `event: delta\ndata: <payload as raw text>` (one or more `data:` lines per SSE spec for multi-line)                                                                          | `event: done\ndata: <ToolResult.content as JSON>` | `event: error\ndata: { code, message }`       |
| **HTTP/SSE** (object schema)                   | `event: delta\ndata: <JSON.stringify(payload)>`                                                                                                                              | same                                              | same                                          |
| **MCP**                                        | `notifications/papercusp/event { progressToken, event: 'delta', data: payload }` (always JSON-encoded — JSON-RPC carries strings as quoted strings inside the params object) | `tools/call` response with ToolResult             | `tools/call` response with `isError: true`    |
| **In-process (`dispatchProjectedToolStream`)** | `{ kind: 'event', name: 'delta', data: payload }` (handler-supplied; no transcoding)                                                                                         | `{ kind: 'done', result }`                        | `{ kind: 'error', error: { code, message } }` |

### Wire format per event — schema-inferred

[Section titled “Wire format per event — schema-inferred”](#wire-format-per-event--schema-inferred)

The framework inspects each declared event’s Zod schema at registration time and picks the on-the-wire encoding:

* `z.string()` → **raw text**. The payload is the text; multi-line content gets split into multiple `data:` lines per SSE spec, joined back by `parseSseStream`. Use for high-frequency token streams (LLM deltas, log lines) — no JSON.stringify on emit, no JSON.parse on consume, smaller bytes per frame.
* Any object/union/etc. → **JSON-encoded**. Use for structured events (suggestions, tool\_calls, cost summaries).

```ts
events: {
  delta:      z.string(),                              // raw on the wire
  tool_call:  z.object({ name: z.string(), input: z.unknown() }),  // JSON
  cost:       z.object({ usd: z.number() }),           // JSON
  suggestion: SuggestionSchema,                        // JSON
}
```

The MCP transport always JSON-encodes (JSON-RPC doesn’t have a raw-text channel inside a notification’s `params`); the classification only affects the SSE wire. Clients consuming over MCP see `data: '<the text>'` as a string field; over SSE for the same event, they see `data: <the text>` without quotes.

### Content-type hints via `.describe()`

[Section titled “Content-type hints via .describe()”](#content-type-hints-via-describe)

Any text-based format works through `z.string()` — XML, CSV, YAML, NDJSON, Markdown, plain logs are all just text-shaped on the wire; the framework doesn’t care what the bytes inside the string represent. The producer formats, the consumer parses.

When a tool wants to advertise *which* text format it emits, attach a `.describe()` annotation. It round-trips through `tools/list` as the JSON-Schema `description` field:

```ts
events: {
  diff_patch: z.string().describe('application/xml'),
  log_line:   z.string().describe('text/plain'),
  json_token: z.string().describe('application/json'),
  csv_row:    z.string().describe('text/csv'),
}
```

`tools/list` returns `events.diff_patch = { type: 'string', description: 'application/xml' }`. Clients pick a parser off the description. No wire-format change — the SSE event stays `event: diff_patch\ndata: <text>`.

The MCP transport dual-fires when `name === 'progress'`: every `ctx.emit('progress', ...)` (or `ctx.progress(...)` via the alias) produces *both* `notifications/papercusp/event` and the spec-standard `notifications/progress`. Built-in MCP UIs that watch the standard progress channel still get a signal; Papercusp-aware clients also receive the typed-event payload.

### Reserved event names

[Section titled “Reserved event names”](#reserved-event-names)

The framework reserves these wire-level names (`RESERVED_EVENT_NAMES` in `tool-projection.ts`); the `defineTool` `events` generic refuses them at compile time (`UserEvents<T>`) and `registerProjectedTool` re-checks at register time so JSON-manifest plugins also fail loudly:

* `done` — framework auto-emits when the handler returns (payload: ToolResult content array).
* `heartbeat` — `@papercusp/sse` emits every 15s for keepalive.
* `result` — pre-2026-05-12 legacy terminal name; reserved for collision avoidance.
* `chunk` — framework auto-emits when the handler returns a result carrying an `outputRef` (large-output scratch ref).
* `card` — framework-emitted `ctx.askUser` card payloads; cards ride the state channel, so reserving the name keeps a plugin from intercepting another tool’s askUser flow (see [Cards](#cards-interactive-mid-run-prompts) below).

`progress` and `error` are intentionally *not* reserved. `progress` is user-emittable via the `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` sugar, which itself routes through `ctx.emit('progress', ...)` — tools declare a schema for it so the wire kind is inferred. The framework auto-emits `event: error` on handler throw, but a handler may also `ctx.emit('error', { message })` mid-stream for non-fatal errors. The canonical case is `runAgentChat` yielding `{type:'error'}` events that don’t terminate the stream.

### Discoverability

[Section titled “Discoverability”](#discoverability)

`tools/list` surfaces each tool’s events as JSON-Schema, so clients can render typed event streams without out-of-band knowledge:

```jsonc
{
  "name": "architect.chat",
  "description": "...",
  "inputSchema": { ... },
  "events": {
    "delta":     { "type": "object", "properties": { "text": { "type": "string" } } },
    "tool_call": { "type": "object", "properties": { "name": { "type": "string" }, "input": {} } },
    "cost":      { "type": "object", "properties": { "usd": { "type": "number" } } }
  }
}
```

Standard MCP clients that don’t know about the `events` field simply ignore it.

### Idle timeout

[Section titled “Idle timeout”](#idle-timeout)

`idleTimeoutSec` augments the wall-clock `timeoutSec`: the dispatcher aborts the handler when the gap between `ctx.emit` calls exceeds the cap. Catches wedged child processes that have stopped producing output but haven’t formally hung. `0` or `undefined` disables.

### Strict-streamable

[Section titled “Strict-streamable”](#strict-streamable)

The HTTP catch-all returns `406 Not Acceptable` if a client sends `Accept: text/event-stream` against a tool that has **none** of:

* declared `events` (typed event channel), or
* declared `state` (state-shaped, see [`ctx.publishState`](./state-tools.mdx)), or
* `expose.mcp.streaming === true` (explicit opt-in).

Prevents clients from opening an SSE connection for a one-shot result. The `state` trigger matters because state-shaped tools need a `runId`-bearing ctx (`ctx.publishState` only installs when `workspaceId + runId` are both present), and the SSE branch is the path that injects a fresh `runId` via `searchParams.set('run', ...)`. State tools that fell through this predicate before the pass-9 fix returned 406 in spite of having a perfectly valid wire shape.

### Cards (interactive mid-run prompts)

[Section titled “Cards (interactive mid-run prompts)”](#cards-interactive-mid-run-prompts)

Cards are first-class framework primitives — **not** an emergent pattern that piggybacks on `ctx.emit`. The handler calls `ctx.askUser(spec)` and blocks until the user submits, declines, or the run is cancelled. The card payload travels on the **state channel** (`state-snapshot` events on `GET /api/operator/state-snapshot`), not on the per-tool event ring buffer.

```ts
const r = await ctx.askUser({
  prompt: 'Apples or bananas?',
  dataSchema: z.object({ picks: z.tuple([z.enum(['apples', 'bananas'])]) }),
  presentation: { kind: 'radio', options: [
    { id: 'apples', label: 'Apples' },
    { id: 'bananas', label: 'Bananas' },
  ]},
});
// r.action: 'submit' | 'decline' | 'cancel'
// r.payload (when submit): validated against dataSchema
```

The user’s click `POST`s to `/api/operator/conversations/:id/card-response`; the card-correlator resolves the deferred and the handler returns the response value to its caller. Tools no longer echo their args back to the client — the response value IS the user’s pick.

The wire-level event name `'card'` is reserved at `registerProjectedTool` (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/tool-projection.ts:RESERVED_EVENT_NAMES`); a tool declaring `events: { card: ... }` throws at register time. This prevents plugins from intercepting `ctx.askUser` flow by name collision on the events channel.

Full reference: [ctx.askUser](./ask-user.mdx). Implementation files: `libs/generic/tooldef/src/{card-correlator,state-channel,workspace-lifecycle}.ts` (the `askUser` ctx wrapper itself lives in the `ctx-bindings` step of `dispatch-stack.ts`) + `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/operator/{state-snapshot,card-response,run-cancel}.ts` (the wire paths are still `/api/operator/state-snapshot` and `/api/operator/conversations/:id/{card-response,run-cancel}`).

## Result formats — token-efficient serialization

[Section titled “Result formats — token-efficient serialization”](#result-formats--token-efficient-serialization)

A `ToolResponse.data` is no longer always `JSON.stringify`’d into `content[0].text`. The result serializer (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/serialize-result.ts`, the single source of truth for every transport) picks a **token-efficient format** server-side and labels it. Plan: `token-efficient-tool-result-formats-2026-06-06`.

**Format selection (delivered, not requested).** The model never names a format — efficiency is a deterministic server-side choice:

* **Server default** — the MCP transport (the agent-facing surface, where the LLM reads `content[0].text`) defaults to **compact**; every other transport (HTTP catch-all, in-process, IPC) defaults to lossless **JSON**. “Compact” resolves to the best format the data’s shape can be safely rendered in: **TOON** for arrays, JSON for single objects. TOON is a JSON-lossless superset that renders uniform arrays as CSV-style rows — ≈ −20–35% tokens on real list payloads.
* **Eligibility** — when a tool declares an output schema (`defineTool({ result: z.array(...) })`), `@papercusp/result-encoding`’s `analyzeSchema` computes the capability set once at registration: a flat array of scalar-only objects → `{json,toon,csv,tsv,md}`; an array with nested/heterogeneous rows → `{json,toon}`; a non-array → `{json}`. No schema → the TOON runtime auto-encoder still gives a compact path.
* **Negotiation override** — set by the *client process*, not the model. HTTP: `?format=` or `Accept` (`application/toon`, `text/csv`, `application/json`). MCP: `_meta.format` on the `tools/call` params, or `?format=` on the connection URL. The requested format is intersected with the tool’s capability set; an unsupported request falls back to the best representable format and labels the downgrade (`_meta.formatFallback`).

**The response contract.** Every compact payload self-identifies so the model never parses an unlabeled one:

* `content[0].text` carries the rendering prefixed with a `format: <fmt>` marker (JSON, the assumed default, is left unmarked). TOON additionally carries its own self-describing `[N]{cols}:` header — which is also where the **row count** lives (so list tools drop any `{ ok, count }` wrapper).
* `_meta.format` records the format machine-readably; `_meta.nextCursor` / `_meta.degraded` / `_meta.degradedReasons` carry the pagination/degraded **envelope** — routed OUT of the tabular body so compact formats are safe for paginated list tools.
* `structuredContent` (opt-in via `?structured=1` / `_meta.structured`) carries the lossless structured JSON for UI/programmatic consumers — gated OFF by default so the model never pays for both the compact text AND the JSON.

**Lossless guarantee.** `@toon-format/toon` is lossless in the common case but has round-trip edge cases (pathological keys; certain string values with structural characters in its nested form). The encoder VERIFIES the round-trip (`encodeToonChecked`: encode → decode → deep-compare) and falls back to JSON whenever it doesn’t hold — the model is never handed a compact payload that doesn’t decode back to the input. See the agent-insight [Parsing tagged compact tool results](/internal/docs/agent-insights/compact-tool-result-formats).

MCP `tools/list` advertises a tool’s `outputSchema` (spec-aligned) and a Papercusp `resultFormats` extension (its capability set) so a client knows what it may negotiate.

## The three context types

[Section titled “The three context types”](#the-three-context-types)

The codebase has three context types floating around — same field set, different supersets. Knowing which is which helps when tracing types through the dispatcher and transport adapters.

| Type                           | Lives at                                      | Used by                                                                       | Streaming?                                                   |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `UnifiedToolContext`           | `libs/generic/tooldef/src/tool-projection.ts` | The dispatcher canonical context. All transport adapters build one.           | Yes — `emit`, `progress`.                                    |
| `ToolContext` (plugin-sdk)     | `packages/plugin-sdk/src/index.ts`            | Plugin tool handlers (`PluginToolMap`).                                       | Yes — `emit`, `progress` (mirrored from UnifiedToolContext). |
| `ToolContext` (legacy, engine) | `libs/generic/tooldef/src/types.ts`           | Legacy principal-gated `defineTool` handlers — `{ principal, tx, log }` only. | No — these don’t stream.                                     |

When `defineTool({ requirePrincipal: false, … })` is called (role-gated), the handler receives `UnifiedToolContext` directly. When `defineTool({ … })` is used with default `requirePrincipal: true`, the wrapper synthesizes the legacy `ToolContext` from the unified one — `emit`/`progress` are dropped because legacy built-ins don’t stream.

## Trust model

[Section titled “Trust model”](#trust-model)

The per-spawn URL params are **HMAC-signed** end-to-end. The orchestrator mints with the shared key in `harness_shared.operator_secrets`; the dispatcher verifies before honoring any role claim. A worker that rewrites `?role=worker` → `?role=operator` produces an invalid signature, the request is rejected with `request_rejected: spawn_sig_invalid_signature`, and the attempt lands in `harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures`. See [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing) for the full scheme and threat model.

Layered defences still apply:

* The operator binds to `127.0.0.1` (`PAPERCUSP_BIND_HOST` defaults to loopback). Only local processes can hit `/api/plugins/*` or `/api/[transport]`.
* Built-in tools still require a bearer principal when accessed without a spawn ctx. They throw `UnauthorizedToolError` (HTTP 401) when none is present.
* `.mcp.json` is written mode 0600; per-spawn worktree dirs are mode 0700.

The signing scheme defends against prompt-injected workers rewriting URL params. It does **not** defend against same-UID code reading the signing key from PG, replaying another spawn’s still-valid URL, or any of the other same-UID escalation paths catalogued in [Spawn-URL signing → Threat model](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing#threat-model). Off-loopback exposure still needs a real principal/auth layer in front; that’s separate work.

### Desktop IPC: webview is in-boundary

[Section titled “Desktop IPC: webview is in-boundary”](#desktop-ipc-webview-is-in-boundary)

The desktop Tauri app uses a fourth transport — endpoint IPC over a Unix domain socket (Linux/macOS) or named pipe (Windows). The Tauri webview opens a `Channel<T>` through Rust to the Node sidecar’s IPC server (`libs/generic/ipc-endpoint-server/src/server.ts`); the round-trip skips localhost HTTP entirely. See [`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-ipc/PROTOCOL.md`](https://github.com/papercupai/papercup/blob/main/packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-ipc/PROTOCOL.md) for the wire format.

IPC calls **skip HMAC signature verification**. The trust boundary is different from the signed-URL HTTP path:

* The signed-URL model defends against a spawned subprocess rewriting its own `?role=...` query param. That subprocess is untrusted code (often a prompt-injected worker) running in a separate process.
* The webview is *not* a separate process in the same threat sense — it’s spawned by the same Tauri parent that spawned the Node sidecar, runs the same trusted UI code, and lives in the same process tree. Rewriting “its own role” is a category error: the webview is the role.

So the IPC adapter synthesizes a fixed `principal: { role: 'operator', workspaceId: <active-workspace> }` and dispatches without verifying any signature. The same dispatcher (role gates, rolesQuota, telemetry, idle/wall-clock timeouts) still runs — only the cryptographic verification step is bypassed. All other defenses (loopback bind, file modes, `.mcp.json` permissions) continue to apply.

What this does **not** apply to:

* **MCP-spawned agents** (claude-code / omp subprocesses) — they go through `/api/mcp` and `/api/sse` over loopback HTTP with signed URLs. They’re untrusted same-UID code, exactly the threat the signing scheme targets.
* **The non-Tauri webapp** (`:3070` test surface, mobile RN clients) — these are not in-boundary; they use HTTP+SSE.

The transport column in `tool_invocations` records which path each call took (`ipc` / `http` / `mcp` / `in_process`), so post-incident review can distinguish the in-boundary fast path from the signed-URL slow path.

# Voice modality

> How tools declare which surface they make sense from, and how the EL Conv AI voice integration interacts with the framework.

# Voice modality

[Section titled “Voice modality”](#voice-modality)

Tools can declare a `modality` field stating which surfaces they’re meaningful from — `'text'` (chat sidebar, harness chat panel), `'voice'` (the ElevenLabs Conv AI integration), or both. The framework’s prompt-assembly layer filters tools out of catalogs they don’t belong in.

## Default behaviour

[Section titled “Default behaviour”](#default-behaviour)

```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'tasks:list',
  // modality omitted → defaults to ['text', 'voice']
  args: TaskListArgs,
  handler: async (input, ctx) => { … },
});
```

A tool without a declared modality is available from **both** surfaces — it appears in the catalog rendered for text *and* for voice. (An earlier text-only default silently emptied the voice catalog for every tool that didn’t opt in, so the default was flipped to `['text', 'voice']`.)

## Declaring a voice-capable tool

[Section titled “Declaring a voice-capable tool”](#declaring-a-voice-capable-tool)

```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'operator:converse',
  modality: ['text', 'voice'],
  args: ConverseArgs,
  handler: async (input, ctx) => { … },
});
```

The catalog renderer will include this tool in both text and voice surfaces.

## Declaring a text-only tool explicitly

[Section titled “Declaring a text-only tool explicitly”](#declaring-a-text-only-tool-explicitly)

```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'some:button_only_tool',
  modality: ['text'],  // REQUIRED to keep it out of voice — the default is both
  // This drops the tool from voice catalogs.
  args: SomeArgs,
  handler: async (input, ctx) => { … },
});
```

This is a **real** carve-out, not just documentation: because the default is `['text', 'voice']`, a tool that should never reach a voice surface must declare `modality: ['text']` — otherwise it shows up in voice catalogs too.

## What the framework does NOT do

[Section titled “What the framework does NOT do”](#what-the-framework-does-not-do)

The framework’s modality concept is **prompt-assembly metadata only**. The framework:

* ✅ Filters the rendered tool catalog by the caller’s modality (via `renderToolsCatalog(role, names, modality)`)
* ✅ Surfaces `modality` on the `tools/list` MCP response so MCP clients can filter independently
* ❌ Does NOT auto-narrate `progress` / `done` events for voice surfaces
* ❌ Does NOT enforce modality at call-time — a voice surface can still invoke a text-only tool if it forces the call

The “narration” model from the original Phase 4 plan was a poor fit for the EL Conv AI integration. See [the spike memo](./../plans/voice-modality-spike-2026-05-13.md) for the analysis.

## How the EL Conv AI integration actually works

[Section titled “How the EL Conv AI integration actually works”](#how-the-el-conv-ai-integration-actually-works)

The browser opens a WebRTC session to EL’s hosted Conv AI agent (Claude Haiku via BYO-LLM). When the agent decides to “ask the operator,” the EL SDK invokes our `ask_operator` clientTool handler in the browser:

packages/operator-core/lib/voice-engines/elevenlabs-conv.ts

```ts
tools.ask_operator = async (params) => askOperatorViaSse(params);
```

`askOperatorViaSse`:

1. POSTs `/api/agent-mcp/operator-converse` with the conversation history + the new user turn.
2. Drains the SSE stream into an `assembled` string.
3. Extracts the `<say>...</say>` body from the assembled text.
4. Returns that string to EL.
5. EL speaks the string via TTS.

The contract with EL is **one string in, one string out** per turn. EL is not subscribing to a typed-event channel — it reads the clientTool function’s return value.

## The `<say>` tag protocol

[Section titled “The \<say> tag protocol”](#the-say-tag-protocol)

The operator brain (Claude Sonnet 4.x running our prompt) wraps voice-mode replies in `<say>...</say>` tags. The brain may also emit other tags that the system parses:

| Tag                                                                         | Purpose                                        | Where parsed                                                      |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `<say>spoken text</say>`                                                    | TTS body. Required for voice turns.            | Client (`askOperatorViaSse`) extracts the body and returns to EL. |
| `<set_mode>active\|passive</set_mode>`                                      | Lifecycle hint.                                | Server + client (`operator-converse-tags.ts`).                    |
| `<sleep duration_minutes="N" reason="…">`                                   | ”Stay silent for N minutes” (capped at 1 day). | Server + client.                                                  |
| `<spawn role="..." harness="..." feature="..." chunk="..." extras="K=V" />` | Server-side orchestrator dispatch.             | Server (`parseOperatorTurn`); never returned to EL.               |

## Sanitizer

[Section titled “Sanitizer”](#sanitizer)

The client-side `askOperatorViaSse` warn-logs when a voice turn arrives without a `<say>` tag — that’s the silent-regression class where TTS would speak raw markup including `<set_mode>` / `<spawn>` tags verbatim. Console message:

```plaintext
[el-conv:ask_operator] voice turn returned without <say> tag; the raw body will be spoken via TTS: <text>
```

If you see this in production, the brain’s voice-mode prompt regressed.

## Cards on voice — `fallbackText`

[Section titled “Cards on voice — fallbackText”](#cards-on-voice--fallbacktext)

The bespoke-card-improvements arc (`ctx.askUser`) added a state channel that delivers card payloads to chat surfaces. Voice doesn’t render cards — there are no buttons to click — but a tool that emits a card during a voice turn still wants the user to hear *something*.

The `CardSpec.fallbackText` field bridges this gap. When set, the operator-converse SSE forwarder picks up `state-snapshot` events and appends each card’s `fallbackText` (or `prompt` as a fallback) to the spoken response:

```ts
ctx.askUser({
  prompt: 'Did you mean X or Y?',
  dataSchema: z.object({ choice: z.enum(['x', 'y']) }),
  presentation: { kind: 'radio', options: [...] },
  fallbackText: 'Did you mean X or Y?',   // voice surfaces speak this
});
```

Gating (audit5+): the `operator-converse` SSE only forwards `state-snapshot` events when `body.modality === 'voice'`, and only forwards snapshots with at least one openCard carrying `fallbackText`. This avoids cross-conversation leak (a text turn’s card would otherwise be spoken in a concurrent voice turn) and keeps state-shaped tools (`ctx.publishState` without cards) off the voice path.

`chat:ask_choice` is available from **both** surfaces — it declares no `modality`, so it defaults to `['text', 'voice']`. On a voice turn its `fallbackText` (the question + options) is spoken, and by default the user still clicks the card on the chat surface to answer. A single-select card that sets `voiceAnswerable: true` (e.g. the silence-nudge “Ready” card) goes further: the client-side `voice-card-router` matches the user’s spoken pick against the option labels/ids and submits it via `/card-response` — so voice **can** now answer those cards hands-free (gated by the `cardAnsweringEnabled` voice preference). Multi-select and non-`voiceAnswerable` cards still require a click.

[Section titled “See also”](#see-also)

* [Transports](./transports.mdx) — how typed events project across HTTP / MCP / IPC
* [Spike memo](./../plans/voice-modality-spike-2026-05-13.md) — why the original “ctx.narrate” design didn’t fit

* `packages/operator-core/lib/operator-converse-tags.ts` — the tag parser

# Writing a tool

> Recipe for writing a tool end-to-end — picking the right shape, declaring the manifest entry, and verifying both transports.

> **Webapp retired (2026-05-14).** Any `localhost:3055` or `localhost:3070` URL on this page is only reachable while the **Tauri dev shell** is running. Start it with `cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev`.

## The two shapes

[Section titled “The two shapes”](#the-two-shapes)

Before writing any code, decide which shape your tool needs:

### Built-in (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/**`)

[Section titled “Built-in (packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/\*\*)”](#built-in-packagesoperator-corelibagent-tools)

Use when **the tool needs a real authenticated principal**. Bearer token in the request → resolved to a principal with workspace ID and a capability set. The wrapper throws `UnauthorizedToolError` (HTTP 401) if no principal is present.

* Most built-ins live in `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/<group>/<verb>.ts`; the smaller read-side set lives in `packages/agent-mcp/src/tools/**`.
* Used today by: dashboard-only operations (settings reads/writes, credentials, marketplace tokens, budget, preferences)
* **Agents cannot call built-ins** today — agents pass URL spawn context, not a bearer token. If you make a tool a built-in, the dashboard sees it; agents do not.
* Auto-projected by `defineTool({ name, capability, args, handler })`. No manifest, no plugin folder.

### Plugin (`libs/papercusp/plugins/<name>/`)

[Section titled “Plugin (libs/papercusp/plugins/\<name>/)”](#plugin-libspapercusppluginsname)

Use when **agents must be able to call the tool** from their spawn URL. No principal required; gating is via role allowlist + per-window quota. Trust comes from the orchestrator’s URL-baking guarantee.

* Used today by: every plugin in `libs/papercusp/plugins/` — repomix, fetch-plus, code2prompt, firecrawl-bridge
* Manifest lives in `papercusp.json`; handlers in `index.ts`’s `tools` export.

### Decision rule

[Section titled “Decision rule”](#decision-rule)

> *Will an agent in a spawn ever call this with just URL params?* If yes → plugin. If no → built-in.

If both — agent **and** dashboard — need it, plugin is correct. The dashboard can call the same `/api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>` URL the agent does. Loopback trust is the same boundary either way.

## The 6-step recipe

[Section titled “The 6-step recipe”](#the-6-step-recipe)

Every new tool follows the same six steps. Skip any of them and you ship a broken tool.

### Step 0 — `set_config` discipline (if your tool reads/writes workspace-scoped PG tables)

[Section titled “Step 0 — set\_config discipline (if your tool reads/writes workspace-scoped PG tables)”](#step-0--set_config-discipline-if-your-tool-readswrites-workspace-scoped-pg-tables)

Use this pattern. Always.

```ts
await sql.begin(async (tx) => {
  await tx.unsafe(`SELECT set_config('app.workspace_id', $1, true)`, [ctx.workspaceId]);
  // ...your queries...
});
```

**Never** write `SET LOCAL app.workspace_id = $1`. PG’s `SET` command does not accept bind parameters; you’ll get a silent `syntax error at or near "$1"` and your quota/telemetry will fail open.

### Step 1 — Write the function (typed, no transport awareness)

[Section titled “Step 1 — Write the function (typed, no transport awareness)”](#step-1--write-the-function-typed-no-transport-awareness)

```ts
import type { ToolContext } from '@papercusp/plugin-sdk';


export async function fetchSomething(
  input: { url: string; depth?: number },
  ctx: ToolContext,
): Promise<ToolResult> {
  // No header reads. No Response objects. Cancel via ctx.signal.
  if (ctx.signal.aborted) throw new Error('cancelled');
  ctx.progress(10, 'starting');
  // ...
  return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: '...' }] };
}
```

What the `ctx` argument has:

* `workspaceId, harnessSlug, role, runId, spawnId` — URL spawn context. `runId` is always present for HTTP-projected calls (defaulted by the catch-all when no `?run=` is supplied) so the state-channel hooks below always install.
* `featureId?, chunkId?, parentSpawnId?` — optional spawn context
* `projectDir, stateDir` — resolved by the framework via `loadHarnessRegistry()`
* `log(msg)` — appends to run.log.jsonl with plugin attribution
* `signal` — `AbortSignal` for the dispatcher’s timeout / cancellation
* `progress(pct, msg)` — alias over the typed-event channel; emits MCP `notifications/progress` (always) AND `notifications/papercusp/event` (always) on MCP, plus `event: progress` on HTTP SSE
* `emit(name, payload)` — typed event channel. Declare the vocab via `defineTool({ events: { ... } })`. See [Typed event streams](./transports.mdx#typed-event-streams).
* `askUser(spec)` — mid-run interactive prompt; blocks until the user submits/declines/cancels. Returns the validated user payload. Installed when `workspaceId + runId` are set. See [ctx.askUser](./ask-user.mdx).
* `publishState(snapshot)` — push the current tool state to the state-channel SSE. Installed when the tool declared `state: ZodType<S>` AND ctx has `workspaceId + runId`. Validated against the declared schema. See [state-shaped tools](./state-tools.mdx).
* `spawn?(bin, argv, opts)` — capability-gated subprocess
* `secret?(name)` — async secret resolver (env vars, encrypted PG)
* `principal?, tx?` — only set for built-in tools called with a bearer

### Step 2 — Write the manifest entry

[Section titled “Step 2 — Write the manifest entry”](#step-2--write-the-manifest-entry)

For plugins, this goes in `libs/papercusp/plugins/<name>/papercusp.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "do_thing",
  "description": "One-sentence description. Lead with the verb. Mention what to use it instead of.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "url": { "type": "string" } },
    "required": ["url"]
  },
  "capabilities": ["http:fetch:example.com"],
  "roles": ["worker", "architect"],
  "rolesQuota": { "worker": { "perChunk": 1 }, "architect": { "perRun": 5 } },
  "timeoutSec": 60,
  "guidance": {
    "when": "When the user asks you to <X>; pair with <Y> for the chained-list case.",
    "notWhen": "Not for <Z> — use <other_tool> instead.",
    "chaining": "After <prerequisite_tool> if you need its id; before <successor_tool>."
  }
}
```

Notes:

* **Write JSON Schema directly.** Do not reach for `zodToJsonSchema` — it returns `{}` against Zod 4. If you have a Zod schema, use Zod 4’s built-in `z.toJSONSchema(schema)`.
* **`capabilities` is descriptive for plugin tools** today (used by tooling/Intel UI). Built-in tools have it enforced via the principal’s capability set.
* **`roles` is enforced.** Workers use `perChunk` quotas (resets per chunk); everyone else uses `perRun` (resets per orchestrator run).
* **Reads usually don’t need a quota.** Only set `rolesQuota` for: external API spend, PG write bursts, subprocess fan-out.
* **`timeoutSec` defaults to 60** if omitted. The dispatcher aborts via `ctx.signal` when it fires.
* **`guidance` is optional but strongly recommended.** Rendered into the [prompt-assembly tools catalog](/internal/docs/agents/prompt-assembly#section-2--tools-catalog) so every role that’s allowed to call the tool gets the same `when` / `notWhen` / `chaining` framing without you having to write it in N role files. Built-in tools pass `guidance` to `defineTool({...})` as a sibling of `capability`. Omit it and the catalog falls back to description-only.

### Step 2.5 — If you need a new PG schema, apply the migration manually

[Section titled “Step 2.5 — If you need a new PG schema, apply the migration manually”](#step-25--if-you-need-a-new-pg-schema-apply-the-migration-manually)

The system PG (`:5432`) is **not wired into the embedded-pg migration runner**. New SQL files do not run automatically.

```bash
# 1. Write libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/048-my-new-table.sql
# 2. Apply manually:
PGPASSWORD=harness_admin_pwd psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U harness_admin -d papercusp -f libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/048-my-new-table.sql


# 3. Verify:
PGPASSWORD=harness_admin_pwd psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U harness_admin -d papercusp -tAc "SELECT to_regclass('harness_shared.my_new_table')"
```

Skip this and your tool will return 200 in dev because reads/writes silently fail.

### Step 3 — curl HTTP transport

[Section titled “Step 3 — curl HTTP transport”](#step-3--curl-http-transport)

```bash
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3055/api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>?harness=sheets&workspace=default&role=architect&run=R&spawn=S' \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{...}'
```

The seven URL params (`harness, workspace, role, feature, chunk, run, spawn`, plus optional `parent_spawn`) are how the framework knows your spawn context. Without them, you get partial context and several gates will fail open or closed unexpectedly.

### Step 4 — curl MCP transport

[Section titled “Step 4 — curl MCP transport”](#step-4--curl-mcp-transport)

```bash
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:3055/api/mcp?harness=sheets&workspace=default&role=architect&run=R&spawn=S' \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"<plugin>.<tool>","arguments":{...}}}'
```

The MCP `name` is dotted (`<plugin>.<tool>`) for plugin tools, colon-namespaced (`<scope>:<verb>`) for built-ins. Both are valid.

### Step 5 — Verify telemetry row landed

[Section titled “Step 5 — Verify telemetry row landed”](#step-5--verify-telemetry-row-landed)

```bash
PGPASSWORD=harness_admin_pwd psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U harness_admin -d papercusp -c \
  "SET app.workspace_id='default'; SELECT tool_name, role, status, duration_ms FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
```

Should show `status='ok'` and a real duration. Note the `SET app.workspace_id` — the table has RLS, so reads without the GUC return zero rows.

### Step 6 — Smoke test the gates

[Section titled “Step 6 — Smoke test the gates”](#step-6--smoke-test-the-gates)

```bash
# Quota: fire perChunk+1 with the same chunk → second is 429.
for i in 1 2; do curl -X POST '.../my/tool?...&role=worker&chunk=Q' -d '{...}'; done


# Role gate: call with a role NOT in roles[] → 403.
curl -X POST '.../my/tool?...&role=validator' -d '{...}'   # if validator not allowed


# Refresh and confirm host error count unchanged
curl -X POST http://localhost:3055/api/plugins/host/refresh | jq '.status.errors'
# expect: 2  (the two pre-existing unrelated errors). If higher → you broke something.
```

## After every plugin manifest or handler edit

[Section titled “After every plugin manifest or handler edit”](#after-every-plugin-manifest-or-handler-edit)

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3055/api/plugins/host/refresh
```

The projection registry is module-level state. HMR is unreliable. If you don’t refresh, you’re testing stale code and won’t know.

## Don’t write tools for these

[Section titled “Don’t write tools for these”](#dont-write-tools-for-these)

* Voice WSS (true bidirectional stream — agent ↔ user audio mid-call). Use the ElevenLabs Conv AI integration.
* File uploads >5MB (multipart isn’t wired)
* Browser-state actions (no server function to project; use `ui:dispatch` instead — those are client commands, not tools)

LLM streaming output *is* fine — declare typed events on the manifest and the framework projects them over HTTP/SSE and MCP. See [Typed event streams](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/transports#typed-event-streams).

Mid-run server-asks-client is *also* fine — use `ctx.askUser(spec)` (the state channel ships the prompt out-of-band; the handler blocks on a deferred until the user clicks). See [ctx.askUser](./ask-user.mdx).

If you find yourself wanting to wrap one of the three remaining above, stop and ask. The contract was deliberately kept narrow.

# Configuration

> Where harness configuration lives today — blueprint shape + declared params, the PG-stored instance layer delivered via HARNESS_CONFIG_JSON, and the effective-config overlay.

The first-generation harness was configured by one hand-edited `.harness/config.json`. Today configuration is split into two layers with a declared, validated surface between them — and **the config file is gone**.

## The two layers

[Section titled “The two layers”](#the-two-layers)

**1. The blueprint (the shape).** A harness is instantiated from a blueprint (`libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/<id>/blueprint.yaml`), which declares the *shape*: roles, spine, triggers, gates, dispatch policy, plus

* **`knobs`** — shape-level defaults (e.g. the coding blueprint sets `harnessKind: coding`, `requiresRepo: true`, `debuggerThreshold: 3`), and
* **`params`** — the *declared tunables*: a keyed record where each key is a dot-path into the instance config (`debugger.threshold`, `parallelWorkers.useChunkLoop`, `parallelWorkers.workingStateCheck`, …) carrying `label` / `type` / `min`/`max` / `options` / `default` / `group` / `affects` / `description`. Params **union across `extends`**: `base` declares the universal ones (dispatch, backend); a child blueprint adds its own (the coding blueprint’s worker/typecheck/debugger knobs are coding-only). Schema: `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/blueprint/schema.ts`.

**2. The instance config (the overrides).** Per-harness values live in the **workspace-PG store**, not in a file. At spawn time the operator assembles the instance config and delivers it solely via the `HARNESS_CONFIG_JSON` env transport — `.papercusp/config.json` is **deprecated to zero and not read** (`deprecate-harness-config-json-2026-06-06`; the `harness:migrate-config-json` tool exists to absorb a legacy file into the PG store).

## How the effective config resolves

[Section titled “How the effective config resolves”](#how-the-effective-config-resolves)

`effective-config.ts` overlays blueprint knobs **under** the instance config — instance overrides always win, merged by a deep-merge where nested objects merge recursively and scalars/arrays replace. The overlay carries only the residual knob keys (`promptOverrides`, `aiBackend`, `parallelWorkers`, `scoper`, `snapshotRetention`); already-migrated knobs (`maxCostUsd`, `debuggerThreshold`, dispatch concurrency) have their own resolution paths and are deliberately excluded so nothing double-applies.

## Reading and writing configuration

[Section titled “Reading and writing configuration”](#reading-and-writing-configuration)

The schema-driven layer in `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/blueprint/params.ts` is the one supported read/write path:

* **`resolveParamViews`** — the current effective value for each declared param (instance override if present, else the param’s `default`).
* **`validateParamPatch`** — rejects keys that aren’t declared (no arbitrary config writes), type/range/option-checks each value, and **skips `secret` params** — secrets route through the credential store, never the config.
* **`applyParamPatch`** — writes the validated patch at each dot-path, dropping values equal to their default so the stored instance config stays minimal.

Because param keys *are* the historical config paths, no data migration was needed — existing overrides already sit at the declared key-paths; they’re now declared + validated rather than freeform.

The UI for all of this is the schema-driven **harness settings panel** (`BlueprintSettingsPanel`, gated by the `papercusp-blueprint-aware-settings` [flag](/internal/docs/posthog/feature-flags)): it introspects the harness’s blueprint `params` and renders controls per declared group — which is why a research or gym harness shows its own tunables instead of a hardcoded coding form.

## Mapping from the legacy config (for old-timers)

[Section titled “Mapping from the legacy config (for old-timers)”](#mapping-from-the-legacy-config-for-old-timers)

| Legacy `.harness/config.json` field  | Today                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `models.<role>` / backend choice     | `aiBackend.*` (residual overlay key; per-param declared)                                                |
| `promptOverrides.<role>`             | survives as a residual overlay key                                                                      |
| `debugger.threshold`                 | declared param `debugger.threshold` (blueprint knob default 3)                                          |
| `parallelWorkers.*`                  | declared params (`useChunkLoop`, `workingStateCheck`, …)                                                |
| `snapshotRetention`                  | residual overlay key                                                                                    |
| `smokeTest.*`                        | gate machinery exists, runner not yet ported — see [Smoke-test gate](/internal/docs/harness/smoke-test) |
| `checkpoints.*`                      | retired — `CHECKPOINT` finalizes as escalation; milestone gates are `needs-human` plan items            |
| `branchIsolation.*` / lane worktrees | retired with the run-loop — see [Worktrees & isolation](/internal/docs/harness/worktrees)               |

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* [Roles](/internal/docs/harness/roles) — what the blueprint’s spine wires
* [Storage policy](/internal/docs/system/storage-policy) — why the instance layer is PG, not a file

# Decision telemetry & ghost rate

> Every director decision verb is persisted and auditable, and unparseable decisions are tracked as "ghosts" — a health signal, not an invisible stall.

Each iteration of a feature pipeline ends with the deciding agent emitting one **decision verb**. The harness treats that stream of verbs as first-class telemetry: every decision is persisted, and outputs that fail to parse as a known verb are counted as **ghosts** — because a failed parse means the engine saw no decision at all.

## The decision-verb model today

[Section titled “The decision-verb model today”](#the-decision-verb-model-today)

The per-feature **director** (`libs/papercusp/packages/harness/prompts/director.md`) emits `NEXT_WORKER` / `NEXT_ARCHITECT` / `NEXT_VALIDATOR` / `DONE` / `ESCALATE`. The durable pipeline interprets the parsed verb through the blueprint spine’s `deriveNext` interpreter (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-workflow.ts`), so what each verb *does* is declared by the blueprint, not hardcoded.

The full verb vocabulary (including legacy/global verbs) is still classified defensively in `classifyDecision` (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-decide.ts`) so a stray verb never dead-ends a pipeline: lifecycle verbs dispatch a role, `DONE`/`ESCALATE` finalize, benign global verbs stop cleanly, and genuinely unsupported verbs (parallel-lane forms, `NEXT_HARNESS`) warn and stop. `classifyDecision` is retained as the **golden-reference oracle**: `derive-next-equivalence.test.ts` asserts the `coding` blueprint’s spine never silently drifts from it. `CHECKPOINT` is deprecated — it now finalizes as an escalation (milestone gates became `needs-human` plan items).

## Persistence: the decisions timeline

[Section titled “Persistence: the decisions timeline”](#persistence-the-decisions-timeline)

Decision events persist to Postgres (`harness_shared.harness_decisions`) via `POST /api/internal/decision-event` (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/internal/decision-event.ts`, bearer-token-authenticated per harness), each row carrying timestamp, verb, args, iteration, and an `isGhost` flag. The UI reads the chronological timeline through the `harnessDecisions.byHarness` sync resolver (`packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts`).

## Ghost rate

[Section titled “Ghost rate”](#ghost-rate)

The deciding agent sometimes wraps its verb in a markdown fence or decorates it; the parser strips what it can, but an unrecognized output is a **ghost** — the engine saw no decision. In the bash era, tracking `ghosts / total` surfaced a real masked bug: \~8% of orchestrator outputs were being silently ghost-classified; one anti-fence prompt rule dropped it below 1%. The lesson stuck: parse failures must be a visible rate, not silent stalls.

Today the harness health read computes ghost rate from the run log’s `ORCH decision:` lines against the known-verb set (`packages/operator-core/lib/harness-readers.ts` — `NEXT_WORKER`, `NEXT_VALIDATOR`, `NEXT_ARCHITECT`, `ESCALATE`, `CONVERTED`, `DONE`), and **`low_ghost_rate`** (ghosts ≥ 10% fails) is one of the composite health checks alongside `features_present`, `not_escalated`, `no_pending_checkpoints`, `smoke_test_clean`, `recent_activity`, and `not_stuck`.

## Why this is uncommon

[Section titled “Why this is uncommon”](#why-this-is-uncommon)

Most agent frameworks treat orchestrator output as opaque — a parse failure just looks like an idle loop. Persisting every verb and exposing the ghost rate as a health signal lets a prompt regression show up on a dashboard within one mission instead of as a mysterious stall three missions later.

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* [Why fresh contexts per role](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/fresh-contexts) — the decision verb is how “try again” works without conversational memory
* [Orchestrator + pending\_events](/internal/docs/spec/orchestrator) — the durable pipeline that consumes these decisions

# Why a curator role

> Without compaction, raw observations grow unboundedly — a dedicated role owns distilling them into bounded, auto-injected memory.

The curator is the harness’s memory-compaction role: the one place where noisy raw observations get distilled into the bounded, durable memory every other role reads. It is the only role allowed to *delete* memory. Without it, the append-only observation log grows linearly with iterations and no other role has the bandwidth to read it.

The design predates the current engine (it was one of the original bash-harness roles) and survived into the blueprint era nearly unchanged.

## When the curator fires

[Section titled “When the curator fires”](#when-the-curator-fires)

In the `coding` blueprint (`libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/coding/blueprint.yaml`), the curator sits at the end of the spine (`scoper → architect → worker → validator → reviewer → documenter → curator`) and runs in the finalize recipe on **both** terminal outcomes: `onDone: [curator, postCuratorOutputs, documenter, archive]` and `onEscalate: [curator]`. Same contract as the original design: terminal events always get a curation pass.

## What the curator does (per its persona)

[Section titled “What the curator does (per its persona)”](#what-the-curator-does-per-its-persona)

The persona (`libs/papercusp/packages/harness/prompts/curator.md`) is explicit and ordered:

1. **Process pending issues first.** Validator findings land as pending issues; the curator triages them through the operator’s merge endpoint (dedupe by code-pointer + title, attempt counters on duplicates, auto-close stale ones).
2. **Merge raw observations into `MEMORY.md`** — the full curated store at `.papercusp/memory/MEMORY.md`, organized under fixed headings, deduplicated, bounded at \~200 lines.
3. **Re-derive `summary.md`** — `.papercusp/memory/summary.md`, **hard-capped at 40 lines / \~800 tokens**, auto-injected into every future role’s prompt (it rides the cacheable preamble — see [Why prompt-cache-dominant](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/prompt-cache)).
4. **Truncate `raw.md`** — `.papercusp/memory/raw.md` is the append-only one-liner log any role writes to; after curation only a short recent-history tail remains.
5. **Maintain per-role identity files** — `identity/<role>.md` carries lessons *across* missions (MEMORY.md is mission-scoped). The orchestrator mirrors these into Postgres (`harness_shared.identity_files`) via `POST /api/internal/identity-snapshot`, so the durable, queryable copy is the PG row; the curator authors by writing the file.

## Why compaction is a separate role

[Section titled “Why compaction is a separate role”](#why-compaction-is-a-separate-role)

Other frameworks bundle memory maintenance into every agent. The result: workers spend tokens deciding what’s worth remembering, different workers disagree about what matters, and mid-mission deletions churn shared state. Splitting compaction into one role gives:

* **One place to review** the “what should we remember” prompt.
* **Atomic mutations** — the curator runs, and every subsequent spawn sees the new memory.
* **Auditable history** — `raw.md` is the working set; `MEMORY.md` is what the curator distilled from it.
* **Bounded growth** — the 40-line summary and \~200-line store mean the system can’t ingest more than later spawns can afford to re-read.

Any role appends to `raw.md` without coordination; the curator decides where an observation belongs (mission memory vs cross-mission identity). The worker flags; the curator files.

## Where this stands today

[Section titled “Where this stands today”](#where-this-stands-today)

Memory compaction is the curator’s pipeline job, and curation has also grown an operator-level read surface: the `curation:*` tools (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/curation/` — `curation:feed`, `curation:change-feed`, `curation:state-of-hive`) project completed work and fleet-wide meta-patterns for supervising agents. The same instinct — distill the noisy stream into a bounded, grounded digest — applied one level up.

Personal/cross-client semantic memory is a separate system (the `memory:*` tools over the canonical PG store); the curator owns the *harness’s* working memory. See [Memory](/internal/docs/harness/memory) for the full layering.

# Why fresh contexts per role

> Every spawn is a fresh agent process that re-derives state from durable stores — drift-resistance over efficiency, with the prompt cache making it affordable.

Every role invocation in the harness pipeline is a **fresh agent process** with no shared in-memory state. A spawn gets its prompt assembled from scratch (`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/prompt-build.ts` — fed to the agent CLI via stdin for `claude`, via an `@file` argument for `omp`), does its job, and exits. Nothing conversational carries over to the next spawn; durable state lives in Postgres (work items, messages, plans, memory) and is re-read each time.

This is a deliberate design decision carried over from the first harness generation, and it has survived two engine rewrites (bash run-loop → TS run-loop → the DBOS pipeline) unchanged.

## The case for shared context (what we don’t do)

[Section titled “The case for shared context (what we don’t do)”](#the-case-for-shared-context-what-we-dont-do)

A long-running agent that maintains one conversation across iterations has theoretical advantages: it remembers what it just tried, reuses intermediate reasoning, and doesn’t re-read the same files. In practice, every long-running agent measured during the bash-harness era drifted — hour-1 instructions lose weight against hour-3 code, and the agent starts agreeing with its own earlier bad decisions because they’re already in its context.

## The case for fresh contexts (what we do)

[Section titled “The case for fresh contexts (what we do)”](#the-case-for-fresh-contexts-what-we-do)

* **No drift.** Every invocation reads canonical state from the durable stores — there is no stale conversational residue to argue with.
* **Reproducibility & debuggability.** A spawn can be replayed with the exact prompt it saw; `buildPromptParts` exposes the assembled halves so tests can assert byte-stability (the prefix-hash assertion in `prompt-build.ts`).
* **Per-role specialization.** Each role gets a tightly-scoped persona (`libs/papercusp/packages/harness/prompts/<role>.md`) without dragging in another role’s history.
* **Crash-safety.** A dead spawn loses nothing that matters: the work item, its comments, and the message inbox hold the state a successor needs.

## What replaces conversational memory

[Section titled “What replaces conversational memory”](#what-replaces-conversational-memory)

The bash era replaced “remember our conversation” with files on disk; the current system replaces it with durable, queryable stores, re-injected into each fresh prompt:

| Need                  | Carried by                                                                                                                                                                   |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| What is the task?     | The work item + plan context, injected per-spawn                                                                                                                             |
| What happened before? | Feature history + the durable message inbox (`messages:*`)                                                                                                                   |
| Hard-won role lessons | Per-role identity files (`identity/<role>.md`) + curated memory (`memory/summary.md`), both in the prompt preamble — see [Curator](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/curator) |
| ”Try again”           | A re-dispatch is simply a new fresh spawn with updated state                                                                                                                 |

## The cost question

[Section titled “The cost question”](#the-cost-question)

A naive read of “fresh context” is “you pay full prompt tokens every spawn.” The Anthropic prompt cache changes the math — and the current prompt assembler is explicitly structured for it: a **byte-stable cacheable preamble** (role prompt → overrides → shared guides → identity → curated memory, ordered by descending stability) followed by a **volatile tail** (live substrate context, runtime context, brief) appended after the preamble so it never invalidates it (`prompt-build.ts` header, “Cache discipline”).

In the bash era this design measured a **99.94% cache hit rate** (180M cache-read vs 106K fresh-input tokens over a 5-iteration mission) — the cost of “fresh” was effectively zero. The numbers and the levers are on [Why prompt-cache-dominant](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/prompt-cache).

## Tradeoffs we accept

[Section titled “Tradeoffs we accept”](#tradeoffs-we-accept)

* **No conversational repair.** A role can’t say “you misunderstood, try again” to itself; correction arrives as new durable state (a validator verdict, a message, an updated work item) read by the next fresh spawn.
* **Cache-read fees.** Even cached, tokens aren’t free — cheaper than fresh-input by an order of magnitude, but not zero.
* **Startup I/O.** Every spawn re-assembles its prompt and re-queries state. Negligible next to LLM latency.

## Where this stands today

[Section titled “Where this stands today”](#where-this-stands-today)

The DBOS pipeline (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/`) spawns each pipeline role as a one-shot agent process via the shared launch spec (`packages/operator-core/lib/role-launch-spec.ts`); interactive role sessions (`psu --role <role>`) ride the same spec. Long-lived *chat* surfaces (the operator, oracle) are conversations by design — the fresh-context rule is about the autonomous pipeline, where unattended drift is the failure mode.

# Decision log (harness design history)

> The chronological design decisions of the first-generation harness, which of them survive in the current engine, and where decisions are recorded today.

This page preserves the design-decision history of the **first-generation (bash) harness** — the rationale trail that shaped the current system — and maps which decisions survive in today’s engine. Historical entries are kept as written; they describe the system *as it was*.

## Where decisions are recorded today

[Section titled “Where decisions are recorded today”](#where-decisions-are-recorded-today)

This log is frozen history. Current design decisions live on **plans** — each plan document carries a `## Decisions` section of dated `D-NNN` entries (written via `plans:add-decision`), and the event-maintained rationale projection (`rationale:feed`) serves the topic-keyed “why” across plans, work items, and insights. If you’re about to record a decision, put it on the relevant plan, not here.

## The bash-era decision log (historical)

[Section titled “The bash-era decision log (historical)”](#the-bash-era-decision-log-historical)

| When    | Decision                            | Rationale (as recorded)                                                                   |
| ------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Initial | **bash + claude as the runtime**    | No agent-runtime opinion; \~1500 lines of supervisor anyone can read in an afternoon.     |
| Initial | **Disk-only state**                 | Any role can be invoked from a fresh shell and re-derive everything.                      |
| Initial | **Fresh context per role**          | No drift across iterations; the prompt cache absorbs the cost (99.94% hit rate observed). |
| Initial | **Per-role markdown prompts**       | Improvements compound without code changes; cache-key-stable.                             |
| Initial | **Curator role**                    | Without compaction, raw memory grows unboundedly.                                         |
| Mid     | **Plan-reviewer gate**              | Catches scope drift before any worker fires.                                              |
| Mid     | **Debugger role**                   | Stuck features (attempts ≥ 3) deserve root-cause analysis, not blind retry.               |
| Mid     | **Crosscheck role**                 | A different model re-validates the validator’s pass; catches “confidently wrong”.         |
| Late    | **Cost-cap removed**                | Miscounted spend + owner wanted unbounded cost; soft-warn, later disabled.                |
| Late    | **TDD iron law in validator**       | Behavioral assertions need a test that failed before the change.                          |
| Late    | **”Boil the lake” principle**       | Sprawling roles got an explicit “do fewer things perfectly” section.                      |
| Late    | **Evidence rule**                   | Every PASS claim must quote source output; reports without evidence revert to failing.    |
| Late    | **Identity file per role**          | Cross-mission append-only memory; curator promotes recurring patterns.                    |
| Late    | **Named checkpoints**               | Pre-agreed milestones gate progress, distinct from escalations.                           |
| Late    | **Git worktrees**                   | Each parallel lane gets its own filesystem dir; no git race possible.                     |
| Late    | **Service smoke-test**              | Real curl + service startup before declaring DONE.                                        |
| Late    | **Two-mode parallelism**            | `lane` (different features) vs `competition` (same feature, validator picks winner).      |
| Late    | **Decisions timeline + ghost rate** | Orchestrator parse-ghost telemetry as a first-class signal.                               |

## Which of these survive today

[Section titled “Which of these survive today”](#which-of-these-survive-today)

Verified against the current engine:

* **Fresh contexts, prompt-cache discipline, curator** — survive as core design, each with its own page: [fresh-contexts](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/fresh-contexts), [prompt-cache](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/prompt-cache), [curator](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/curator).
* **Per-role markdown prompts** — survive at `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/prompts/<role>.md` with layered resolution (see [Roles](/internal/docs/harness/roles)).
* **Validator disciplines** — the **default-reject disposition** and the **evidence rule** survive verbatim in the validator persona (`prompts/validator.md`: “Your default is *reject*”; “EVIDENCE RULE” — every positive claim backed by quoted executable evidence, else `[FAIL]`).
* **Debugger + crosscheck** — survive as blueprint roles in `blueprints/coding/blueprint.yaml`: the debugger is a *reactive overlay* that fires before a worker retry once `knobs.debuggerThreshold` attempts accrue; crosscheck is an opt-in quality gate (`NEXT_CROSSCHECK`).
* **Decision telemetry + ghost rate** — survives; see [Decision telemetry](/internal/docs/harness/decisions-timeline).
* **Named checkpoints** — **deprecated**: `CHECKPOINT` now finalizes as an escalation; milestone gates are `needs-human` plan items.
* **Competition mode** — removed (replaced by the synthesizer pre-cutover, itself dormant since the run-loop retirement); lane-style isolation lives on — see [Worktrees & isolation](/internal/docs/harness/worktrees).
* **Disk-only state** — superseded: Postgres is the runtime store-of-record (see [Storage policy](/internal/docs/system/storage-policy)); the fresh-shell re-derivability *goal* survives, now via PG + the operator API.

## Later eras (condensed)

[Section titled “Later eras (condensed)”](#later-eras-condensed)

Two further decision clusters in the original log concerned systems that are now fully retired, kept here as one-line summaries: the **org layer** (five fixed LLM directors with typed message kinds and file-based state under `~/.restart-org/` — retired; its jobs live in work items, coord, and the Pot operator) and the **public-site extraction** (a slim public repo + Cloudflare-Workers static hosting for papercupai.com — site retired to `_retired/papercup/`). The full tables remain in this page’s git history and the retired source (`_retired/papercup/`).

## Decisions explicitly rejected (historical, still instructive)

[Section titled “Decisions explicitly rejected (historical, still instructive)”](#decisions-explicitly-rejected-historical-still-instructive)

| Rejected                                         | Why                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| AutoGPT-style infinite loop                      | Drift catastrophe; supervised iterations with explicit decision verbs instead.                                                                                                     |
| LangChain orchestration                          | Heavyweight runtime + abstractions we didn’t need.                                                                                                                                 |
| External task-source integration (Linear/Notion) | Owner explicitly declined an external task source.                                                                                                                                 |
| Vector-DB memory for the harness loop            | Bounded markdown memory was sufficient at harness scale. (Semantic memory later arrived as a *separate* system — the `memory:*` store — without replacing curated harness memory.) |
| Discord/Slack as the control surface             | Couples the harness to one chat UI; HTTP API + dashboard instead.                                                                                                                  |
