| Tmux-based agent messaging                       | Couples state to a terminal multiplexer.                                                                                                                                           |

# Why prompt-cache-dominant

> The harness is designed so the Anthropic prompt cache absorbs the cost of fresh-context-per-role — prefix stability is an explicit, tested property of the prompt assembler.

The harness spawns a [fresh agent process per role invocation](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/fresh-contexts). That is only affordable because the prompt assembler is designed for Anthropic’s prompt cache: keep the expensive prefix byte-stable across spawns, and only a small volatile tail is fresh-billed.

## The design, in the current code

[Section titled “The design, in the current code”](#the-design-in-the-current-code)

`buildPromptParts` (`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/prompt-build.ts`) assembles every pipeline spawn’s prompt as two halves — the file’s header documents this as the explicit “cache discipline”:

* **Cacheable preamble** — byte-stable across spawns of the same role, ordered by *descending stability* so a change invalidates the smallest possible suffix: the role’s prompt file → per-role config override → tools playbook + shared guides → shared-base constants → per-role identity (`identity/<role>.md`, cross-mission, append-oriented) → curated memory (`memory/summary.md`) last, because it changes most often.
* **Volatile tail** — per-spawn content (live substrate context, runtime context, brief, plan context, feature history) appended *after* the preamble so it never invalidates it.

The split is exposed precisely so tests can assert the preamble is byte-identical across volatile-input changes (the prefix-hash assertion in `prompt-build.ts`’s test suite). Prefix stability is a **tested invariant**, not a hope.

Cache behavior is also observable: every sampled spawn records `cache_read_tokens` and `cache_creation_tokens` alongside input/output tokens and cost to Postgres (`usage-sample-pg.ts`), so a cache-hit-rate regression is a queryable signal.

## What the bash era measured

[Section titled “What the bash era measured”](#what-the-bash-era-measured)

The numbers that motivated this design (measured on the first-generation bash harness, 5-iteration mission, 13 role invocations):

| Metric             | Value                                                |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Cache read tokens  | 180,049,624                                          |
| Fresh input tokens | 106,471                                              |
| **Cache hit rate** | **99.94%**                                           |
| Output tokens      | 24,533                                               |
| Total cost         | \~$0.31 (vs \~$3.10 if everything were fresh-billed) |

A non-cached harness cost \~10× more. The cache hit rate was treated as a primary observability signal — a sudden drop means *something is rewriting state the design expects to be stable*.

## How to keep the hit rate near 100%

[Section titled “How to keep the hit rate near 100%”](#how-to-keep-the-hit-rate-near-100)

The levers are the same today as in the bash era, mapped to current surfaces:

1. **Stable role prompts.** Don’t edit `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/prompts/<role>.md` mid-mission; each edit costs one cache-miss spawn per role.
2. **Append-oriented identity files.** The curator appends to `identity/<role>.md` rather than rewriting (its persona instructs exactly this), so each change shifts the cache key minimally.
3. **Bounded curated memory.** `memory/summary.md` is hard-capped (40 lines / \~800 tokens, enforced by the curator persona) and sits **last** in the preamble — a curator pass costs one miss, then subsequent spawns hit again.
4. **Volatile content at the end.** Anything per-spawn rides the tail, never the preamble.

What still breaks the cache: editing prompt sources mid-run, rewriting (vs appending) identity/summary files, or switching model mid-mission (the cache is keyed on model).

## Where this stands today

[Section titled “Where this stands today”](#where-this-stands-today)

The discipline was re-audited and re-asserted in the DBOS era (`token-usage-reduction-audit-2026-06-09` P-009 — the header of `prompt-build.ts` cites it): the preamble/tail split, the stability ordering, and the prefix-hash test all live in the current assembler. The same instinct applies beyond spawn prompts — e.g. long-lived interactive sessions schedule their idle wake-ups around the cache TTL — but the load-bearing, tested implementation is the pipeline prompt assembler above.

# Glossary (harness runtime)

> The runtime terms you meet working with a live harness, each traceable to the defining code.

Runtime terms, alphabetical, each pointing at its defining code. For spec-level/product vocabulary (Install, Goal, Plugin, marketplace `kind`, …) see [Vocabulary](/internal/docs/spec/vocabulary); for the user-facing brand lexicon (Hive/Queen/bee display strings) see the `papercusp-the-hive` [flag](/internal/docs/posthog/feature-flags) — those are presentation-layer names over the code terms below.

**Bee** · The generic “do this task” agent of the hive blueprint — carries no pipeline spine and no chunk requirement, unlike `worker`. — `packages/agent-mcp/src/role-config.ts`

**Blueprint** · A harness’s declarative shape: roles, spine, triggers, gates, dispatch policy, `knobs`, and declared `params`. Built-ins extend `base`. — `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/`, schema in `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/blueprint/schema.ts`

**Brain** · The RBAC *principal* role marking the operator’s own orchestration intelligence — gates spawn-approval tools at the dispatch layer. Not an agent role. — `role-config.ts :: BRAIN_PRINCIPAL_ROLE`

**Chunk** · A feature-family work-item kind: a feature sub-unit sized for one worker turn, executed by the worker chunk loop (per-chunk file locks + a typecheck gate). — `packages/operator-core/lib/work-items.ts`

**Claim / lease** · Taking ownership of a work item (`work_items:claim`); a live lease with a dead holder is an *orphaned claim*, surfaced by `fleet:assignments`.

**Curator** · The memory-compaction pipeline role; the only role that deletes harness memory. — [Why a curator](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/curator)

**Decision verb** · The single verb a deciding agent emits per iteration (`NEXT_WORKER` / `NEXT_ARCHITECT` / `NEXT_VALIDATOR` / `DONE` / `ESCALATE`); interpreted by the blueprint spine. — [Decision telemetry](/internal/docs/harness/decisions-timeline)

**Director** · The persona that emits per-feature decision verbs in the durable pipeline. A prompt file, not an `AGENT_ROLES` id. — `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/prompts/director.md`

**Dispatch** · The blueprint-declared policy for when/what the engine runs next; concurrency knobs resolve via their own path (not the effective-config overlay). — `blueprints/*/blueprint.yaml`

**Effective config** · Blueprint knobs overlaid *under* the per-harness instance config (instance wins). — [Configuration](/internal/docs/harness/config)

**Escalation** · A pipeline finalizing with `ESCALATE`: the `on-escalate` hook fires and the `onEscalate` recipe (default: curator) runs; the harness surfaces the reason for a human. — `packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-finalize.ts`

**Feature** · The classic feature-family work-item kind (`F-NNN`), routed through the coding blueprint’s spine. — `work-items.ts`

**Finalize recipe** · The blueprint’s `gates.finalize` step list run on terminal outcomes (`onDone` / `onEscalate`). — `blueprints/coding/blueprint.yaml`

**Ghost** · A deciding-agent output that fails to parse as a known decision verb; tracked as a rate and a health signal (`low_ghost_rate`). — `packages/operator-core/lib/harness-readers.ts`

**Harness** · One managed work pipeline (repo + work queue + runs), instantiated from a blueprint; slug-identified.

**Hook** · An out-of-band shell script at `.papercusp/hooks/<name>.sh` run at pipeline boundaries. — [Lifecycle hooks](/internal/docs/harness/hooks)

**Identity file** · `identity/<role>.md` — cross-mission per-role lessons, PG-mirrored to `harness_shared.identity_files`. — [Memory](/internal/docs/harness/memory)

**Instance config** · Per-harness overrides stored in workspace-PG and delivered via the `HARNESS_CONFIG_JSON` env transport; `.papercusp/config.json` is deprecated and not read. — `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/effective-config.ts`

**Knobs** · Shape-level defaults a blueprint declares (e.g. `debuggerThreshold: 3`). — `blueprints/coding/blueprint.yaml`

**Params** · A blueprint’s *declared tunables*, keyed by instance-config dot-paths, unioned across `extends`; the schema-driven settings layer validates writes against them. — `blueprint/params.ts`

**Phase** · One of up to three worktrees per project — `staging` (the main path), `testing`, `production` (sibling `<path>--<phase>` checkouts). — `packages/operator-core/lib/harness-phases.ts`

**Planner** · An interactive plan-authoring session role (drafts one plan via `plans:*`); not the spec-level Planner pipeline role. — `role-config.ts`

**Queen** · The steering intelligence of a hive/Pot — schedules, places, and prioritizes work (the role the lexicon surfaces as “Queen”); distinct from the watching `sentinel`. — `role-config.ts` (sentinel entry)

**Redundancy / replica** · BOINC-style multi-dispatch of one work item to independent replicas with a judge step (`work_items:set_redundancy` / `claim_replica` / `judge_redundancy`); feature-family only.

**Role** · A named agent function with its own persona + tool surface. The runtime registry is `AGENT_ROLES`. — [Roles](/internal/docs/harness/roles)

**Run / spawn** · One agent invocation: the spawn is the envelope (workspace

* harness + role + work item + signed MCP URL), the run is the execution; tracked in `harness_shared.spawned_agents`.

**Sentinel** · The read-mostly fleet watcher (stuck spawns, lock hogs, coord staleness); its only writes are alarms. — `role-config.ts`

**Spine** · The blueprint’s declared role-routing model; the `deriveNext` interpreter maps (state, decision verb) → next action. — `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/blueprint/derive-next.ts`

**Summary memory** · `.papercusp/memory/summary.md` — curator-maintained, 40-line cap, auto-injected into every pipeline spawn. — [Memory](/internal/docs/harness/memory)

**Task** · An issue-family work-item kind recording delegated work; excluded from the default `issues:*` listing. — `work-items.ts`

**Work item** · The unified unit of work, one type discriminated by `kind`: feature family (`feature` / `research-task` / `chunk`) + issue family (`bug` / `change` / `task`), served by the `work_items` UNION view over the per-kind tables (migration 159). — `packages/operator-core/lib/work-items.ts`

**Workspace** · One Papercusp install: many harnesses, one PG database, one credential set.

# Lifecycle hooks

> Out-of-band shell scripts in .papercusp/hooks/ that the DBOS finalizer runs at mission boundaries — plus how plugin hooks fire alongside them.

Lifecycle hooks are user-supplied shell scripts that the harness runs at fixed pipeline boundaries. Drop an executable script at `<project>/.papercusp/hooks/<name>.sh` and the engine invokes it when the matching event fires. The runner is `runHook()` in `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/hooks.ts`: it looks up `<stateDir>/hooks/<name>.sh`, skips silently if the file is missing or not executable (owner-execute bit), runs it with `cwd` set to the project directory, captures combined stdout+stderr to `<stateDir>/logs/hooks/<unix-seconds>-<name>.log`, and logs a non-zero exit as a warning — a failing hook never halts the mission. On Windows the script needs `bash` on `PATH` (Git for Windows ships one); the desktop bootstrap surfaces that prerequisite.

## Why hooks instead of in-prompt actions

[Section titled “Why hooks instead of in-prompt actions”](#why-hooks-instead-of-in-prompt-actions)

This is design intent carried over from the first harness generation, and it still holds: hooks are **out-of-band**. They consume no tokens, add no latency to any LLM call, and fire **deterministically** — not “if the agent decides to”. Anything you’d otherwise bolt onto a role prompt as “and also send a Slack message” belongs in a hook, keeping each prompt focused on the role’s one job.

## Hooks that fire today

[Section titled “Hooks that fire today”](#hooks-that-fire-today)

The legacy bash run-loop fired twelve hook events; that loop is retired (`libs/papercusp/_retired/orchestrator-run-loop/`). In the current DBOS pipeline, hooks fire from the **finalizer** — the step list that `planFinalization()` builds when a feature pipeline ends in DONE or ESCALATE (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-finalize.ts`). Two hook names are wired:

| Hook          | Fires                                                                                      | Event-specific env                                       | Call site                    |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `on-escalate` | Pipeline finalizes with **ESCALATE**, before the `onEscalate` recipe roles run             | `REASON`, `PROJECT_DIR`, `STATE_DIR`                     | `orchestrator-runner.ts:641` |
| `afterDone`   | Pipeline finalizes **DONE** (and the done-gates pass), after the `onDone` recipe roles run | `TRIGGER=done`, `FEATURE_ID`, `PROJECT_DIR`, `STATE_DIR` | `orchestrator-runner.ts:657` |

A blocked DONE (an open needs-human plan item) skips the whole finalization step list, hook included.

`runHook()` itself accepts any name — the engine isn’t limited to these two — but no other call site exists in the live tree, so no other event fires. The pre/post-worker, validator, smoke, checkpoint and competition hooks from the bash era retired with the run-loop.

### The `afterDone` builtin

[Section titled “The afterDone builtin”](#the-afterdone-builtin)

`afterDone` has a TS builtin behind it: when **no** user hook script ran, the finalizer calls `notifyParentOnDone()` (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/notify-parent-done.ts`), which posts a `Completion` message to this harness’s sealed parent once the feature queue drains — so a parent that spawned this harness as a child learns the sub-work is done. A per-harness `hooks/afterDone.sh` **overrides the builtin entirely** (parity with the retired bash builtin resolver). Plugin hooks fire regardless (below).

## Environment a hook receives

[Section titled “Environment a hook receives”](#environment-a-hook-receives)

On top of the event-specific variables in the table, `runHook()` auto-injects context so scripts can query the operator instead of scraping harness files (`hooks.ts:100–111`):

* `HARNESS_SLUG` — the current harness slug (defaults to the project directory’s basename when not passed explicitly)
* `WORKSPACE_ID` — the active workspace, when known
* `OPERATOR_BASE` — operator API base URL; defaults to `$PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_BASE`, then `http://localhost:3055`

The full process environment is inherited too; the caller’s explicit env wins over the injected values on conflict.

**Hooks must not read harness state from the filesystem.** Files like `lanes.json` no longer exist at runtime — PG is the runtime store-of-record (see [Storage policy](/internal/docs/system/storage-policy)). The contract in `hooks.ts` is: query the operator API instead.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Example: .papercusp/hooks/afterDone.sh — look up feature state via the API
features=$(curl -fsS "$OPERATOR_BASE/api/harness/$HARNESS_SLUG/features")
status=$(echo "$features" | jq -r '.[] | select(.id == "'"$FEATURE_ID"'") | .status')
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Example: .papercusp/hooks/on-escalate.sh — page a Slack channel
curl -X POST -H 'Content-type: application/json' \
  --data "{\"text\":\"Mission escalated: $REASON\"}" \
  "$SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL"
```

Make scripts executable (`chmod +x`) — a non-executable file is skipped without error.

## Plugin hooks fire alongside

[Section titled “Plugin hooks fire alongside”](#plugin-hooks-fire-alongside)

User hook scripts are per-harness; **plugins** hook the same lifecycle globally. At the `afterDone` step the finalizer also calls `firePluginHook()` (`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/plugin-hooks.ts`), which discovers plugins under `<projectDir>/plugins/`, `~/.papercusp/harnesses/*/plugins/` and `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/` and invokes the named hook on each via the `papercusp-fire-hook` CLI — one child process per plugin, so a misbehaving plugin can’t crash the pipeline. Output lands in `<stateDir>/logs/plugins.log`; failures are logged and ignored. Plugin hooks fire whether or not a user hook script ran. The in-process plugin host has a separate lifecycle surface (`plugins:fire_event` tool / `firePluginLifecycle`) — see [Plugins](/internal/docs/spec/plugins).

## Managing hook scripts over the API

[Section titled “Managing hook scripts over the API”](#managing-hook-scripts-over-the-api)

`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/harness/hooks.ts` exposes CRUD for hook scripts: `GET /api/harness/:slug/hooks` (list known hooks with content + executable bit), `PUT`/`DELETE /api/harness/:slug/hooks/:name` (write with `chmod 755` / remove), and `GET /api/harness/:slug/hook-logs/:logId` to read a hook-run log. The `hooks:known` tool returns the same name list.

**Known staleness:** that name list comes from `getKnownHooks()` (`packages/operator-core/lib/known-hooks.ts`), which greps `orchestrator/src/main-loop.ts` for `runHook(` calls — but `main-loop.ts` was retired with the run-loop, so the grep finds nothing and the function falls back to `['pre-worker']`. Today the API therefore lists only `pre-worker` (a hook that never fires) and rejects writes to `on-escalate`/`afterDone` (the two that do). `runHook()` itself never consults this list, so scripts created directly on disk work regardless. Treat `known-hooks.ts` as needing a re-point at the live call sites.

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* [Orchestrator + pending\_events](/internal/docs/spec/orchestrator) — the DBOS pipeline whose finalizer fires these hooks
* [Plugins](/internal/docs/spec/plugins) — plugin lifecycle states and hook handler semantics
* [Storage policy](/internal/docs/system/storage-policy) — why hooks query the API instead of reading harness files

# Memory

> The three memory layers — curator-maintained harness working memory, the semantic memory store behind memory:*, and procedural knowledge in agent-insights — and what carries live state instead.

“Memory” in Papercusp is three different systems with three different jobs. Confusing them causes drift, so the boundaries are the point of this page.

## 1. Harness working memory (curator-maintained files)

[Section titled “1. Harness working memory (curator-maintained files)”](#1-harness-working-memory-curator-maintained-files)

Each harness keeps a small, bounded set of memory files under `.papercusp/memory/` — the direct descendants of the first-generation design:

* **`raw.md`** — append-only one-liner observations; any role writes here without coordination.
* **`MEMORY.md`** — the curated mission-scoped store (\~200-line bound), merged from raw observations by the curator.
* **`summary.md`** — hard-capped at 40 lines / \~800 tokens and **auto-injected into every pipeline spawn’s prompt** (it rides the cacheable preamble of `prompt-build.ts` — see [Why prompt-cache-dominant](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/prompt-cache)).
* **`identity/<role>.md`** — per-role lessons that carry *across* missions; the orchestrator mirrors them into Postgres (`harness_shared.identity_files`) via `POST /api/internal/identity-snapshot`, making PG the durable, queryable copy.

Only the [curator](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/curator) compacts or deletes these; everyone else appends.

## 2. Semantic memory (`memory:*` — the cross-client store)

[Section titled “2. Semantic memory (memory:\* — the cross-client store)”](#2-semantic-memory-memory--the-cross-client-store)

Durable facts that should survive sessions and be recalled by *every* client (Claude / Codex / OMP / spawned agents) live in the semantic memory store behind the `memory:remember` / `memory:search` / `memory:list` / `memory:forget` / `memory:update` tools.

* **Canonical store:** Postgres — `harness_shared.memory_canonical` (embedded rows; `last_surfaced_at` powers injection dedup).
* **Swappable backend:** the store core is the generic `@papercusp/memory` lib behind a `MemoryBackend` seam; the operator registers concrete backends in `packages/operator-core/lib/memory/configure.ts` — `mem0` (the canonical PG store), `claude-file` (the `~/.claude` topic-file store), and **`hybrid`**, which fuses the claude-file lexical leg with the mem0 cosine leg via cosine-gated reciprocal-rank fusion; hybrid **writes** always delegate to the mem0 leg, so PG stays canonical.
* **Live selection:** which backend serves is an operator-wide setting (`harness_shared.operator_settings`, key `memory_backend`), changeable from the settings UI with no restart; resolution is persisted setting → `PAPERCUSP_MEMORY_BACKEND` → `mem0` (`packages/operator-core/lib/memory/backend-selection.ts`).
* **Injection:** relevant memories are surfaced into a session pre-turn (`packages/operator-core/lib/memory/injection.ts`), with a per-session watermark over `last_surfaced_at` so the same memory isn’t re-pushed turn after turn.

Scoping: pass a `harness_slug` for project facts; omit it for personal facts. Client-local file memories (e.g. Claude Code’s topic files) are a per-client layer — the shared store is the one every agent recalls from.

## 3. Procedural knowledge (agent-insights)

[Section titled “3. Procedural knowledge (agent-insights)”](#3-procedural-knowledge-agent-insights)

Runbooks — “how X works / how to not lose an hour on Y” — are **docs, not memory rows**: PR-reviewed MDX under [agent-insights](/internal/docs/agent-insights). Short facts go to semantic memory; multi-step explanations go here.

## What is NOT memory: live state

[Section titled “What is NOT memory: live state”](#what-is-not-memory-live-state)

In-flight state belongs to its own systems, never to a memory store: work items carry task state, **coord** carries presence/intents/handoffs, plans carry decisions (projected by `rationale:feed`). The legacy instinct “write it to a file so the next role sees it” maps today to “write it to the durable store the next spawn queries” — see [Storage policy](/internal/docs/system/storage-policy).

## Choosing the right layer

[Section titled “Choosing the right layer”](#choosing-the-right-layer)

| You have…                                  | Put it in                                         |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| A one-liner observation mid-mission        | `.papercusp/memory/raw.md` (curator will file it) |
| A durable preference / convention / gotcha | `memory:remember` (semantic store)                |
| A multi-step runbook                       | an agent-insights page                            |
| Task progress, blockers, hand-offs         | the work item / coord — not memory                |
| A design decision                          | the plan’s `## Decisions` (D-NNN)                 |

# Roles — the operational reference

> Every built-in agent role — where it's defined, where its persona lives, and when it fires.

This is the operational reference for agent roles: what exists *now*, where each is defined, and when each fires. For the spec-level model (the four core roles and install shapes) see [The four core roles](/internal/docs/spec/roles).

## The registry

[Section titled “The registry”](#the-registry)

**`AGENT_ROLES`** in `packages/agent-mcp/src/role-config.ts` is the single runtime source of truth for built-in role ids — tool `roles:` allowlists, quota keys, and `byRole` guidance all key off it. The set is open: plugins contribute namespaced `<plugin>:<role>` ids at runtime.

The built-ins, grouped as the file orders them:

| Group         | Roles                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Pipeline      | `scoper` · `architect` · `worker` · `validator` · `reviewer` · `debugger` · `documenter` · `curator`                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Chat surfaces | `operator` · `oracle`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Hive          | `bee` (the generic “do this task” agent — no pipeline spine, no chunk requirement) · `planner` (interactive plan-authoring session)                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Cross-cutting | `orchestrator` · `promote` · `security-reviewer` · `infra-reviewer` · `crosscheck` · `ui-qa` · `auditor` (read-only adversarial screen for remote-authored features) · `merge-resolver` (git-sync conflict resolution) · `release-manager` (deploy go/no-go) · `sentinel` (read-mostly fleet watcher) |

Two adjacent ids that are *not* agent roles: **`brain`** (`BRAIN_PRINCIPAL_ROLE`) is an RBAC role on the operator’s own *principal* — “only the brain approves spawns” is enforced at the dispatch layer, never carried by a spawned agent — and the per-feature **director** is a persona (`prompts/director.md`) that emits the decision verbs (`NEXT_WORKER` / `NEXT_ARCHITECT` / `NEXT_VALIDATOR` / `DONE` / `ESCALATE`; see [Decision telemetry](/internal/docs/harness/decisions-timeline)) rather than an `AGENT_ROLES` entry.

## Personas and layered resolution

[Section titled “Personas and layered resolution”](#personas-and-layered-resolution)

Spawn personas live at `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/prompts/<role>.md`, layered with `base/<role>.md` plus kind/department overrides per the resolution rules in that directory’s `README.md`. The directory carries more personas than `AGENT_ROLES` lists — blueprint-specific roles (`researcher`, `research-director`, `gym-director`, `migration-director`, `transformer`, `judge`, …) are resolved by their blueprints. Chat roles (`operator`, `oracle`) are assembled differently — by `packages/operator-core/lib/prompt-assembly.ts` from `apps/operator/prompts/<role>.persona.md` + the generated tools catalog.

## When pipeline roles fire (the `coding` blueprint)

[Section titled “When pipeline roles fire (the coding blueprint)”](#when-pipeline-roles-fire-the-coding-blueprint)

The blueprint (`libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/coding/blueprint.yaml`) declares the wiring:

* **Spine:** `scoper → architect → worker → validator → reviewer → documenter → curator` — each work item’s kind/state determines the next role; the spine’s `deriveNext` interpreter consumes the director’s decision verbs.
* **Reactive overlay:** the `debugger` fires *before a worker retry* once a feature accrues `knobs.debuggerThreshold` failed attempts — read-only root-cause notes for the next worker.
* **Opt-in quality gates:** `tester` / `security` / `crosscheck` / `ui-qa`, e.g. `NEXT_CROSSCHECK` re-validates a pass with a different model.
* **Finalize recipe:** `onDone: [curator, postCuratorOutputs, documenter, archive]`; `onEscalate: [curator]` — the curator always runs on terminal outcomes (see [Why a curator](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/curator)).

Other blueprints are different shapes on the same engine — `blueprint:catalog` lists what each one runs.

## How a role spawn happens

[Section titled “How a role spawn happens”](#how-a-role-spawn-happens)

The DBOS pipeline (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/`) dispatches each role as a fresh one-shot agent process (see [Why fresh contexts](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/fresh-contexts)), built from the same `buildRoleLaunchSpec` (`packages/operator-core/lib/role-launch-spec.ts`) that powers interactive role sessions (`psu --role <role> [--feature F-NNN]`) — one prompt/tools/ feature/backend spec, two entry points.

## Role disciplines that survive from the first generation

[Section titled “Role disciplines that survive from the first generation”](#role-disciplines-that-survive-from-the-first-generation)

Verified in the current persona files:

* **Validator: default-reject.** “Your default is *reject*. The worker has to earn approval” (`prompts/validator.md`).
* **Validator: the evidence rule.** Every positive claim must quote executable evidence (an HTTP body, a DB row, a log line — “something that could not exist without the feature being present”); a claim with no producible evidence is `[FAIL]`, overriding any “looks reasonable” intuition (`prompts/validator.md`, “EVIDENCE RULE”).
* **Curator: sole memory compactor.** Only the curator deletes/compacts harness memory ([details](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/curator)).

The first-generation “role design rules” — one job per role, read-mostly where possible, default-skeptical gates — are visible throughout the current registry (the `auditor` and `sentinel` are explicitly read-only/read-mostly by design, per their `role-config.ts` entries).

# Smoke-test gate

> The DONE-blocking smoke gate — why it exists, what's wired today (the gate machinery + health signal), and what still awaits its port (the runner).

Validators verify code-level claims; they don’t always start the real service and hit real endpoints. A feature can “pass” — unit test green, contract documented, migration applied — while the deployed service 500s from config drift, a missing env var, or a startup race. The **smoke-test gate** exists to catch that class of failure *before* a pipeline declares DONE. The principle (“quality through truth”: verify service startup, don’t trust test output alone) came from the first harness generation and still holds.

## What is wired today

[Section titled “What is wired today”](#what-is-wired-today)

**The gate.** The durable finalizer’s planner (`planFinalization` in `packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-finalize.ts`) treats the smoke result as a first-class DONE gate, exactly like an open `needs-human` plan item: when `smokeEnabled` is set and `smokePassed === false`, finalization is **blocked** — no curator/documenter recipe runs and the pipeline does not complete.

**The health signal.** The harness health read (`packages/operator-core/lib/harness-readers.ts`) includes `smoke_test_clean` among its composite checks: it fails whenever a `smoke-failure.md` sentinel exists in the harness state dir, so a failed smoke run is visible on every health surface.

**The hooks.** `on-smoke-pass` / `on-smoke-fail` remain valid [lifecycle-hook](/internal/docs/harness/hooks) names the engine can run (`runHook()` accepts any name), with tests covering the smoke-hook env shape.

## What is NOT yet wired: the runner

[Section titled “What is NOT yet wired: the runner”](#what-is-not-yet-wired-the-runner)

The piece that actually *executes* a smoke test — start the service if needed, curl the configured URLs, write the pass/fail sentinel — was a main-loop-internal of the retired engine and has **not been ported** to the durable pipeline. The runner call site passes the gate explicitly off (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-runner.ts`:

> “Smoke gate is config-gated-off for \~all harnesses; not yet ported into the durable finalizer (`runSmokeTest` is a main-loop-internal). Tracked as a Phase F follow-up; pass not-run so it never blocks here.”

— `smokeEnabled: false, smokePassed: null`). Until that follow-up lands, nothing in the live tree writes `smoke-pass.md`/`smoke-failure.md`, so `smoke_test_clean` only fires on sentinels left by earlier engines or written out-of-band.

In short: **gate machinery live, runner pending.** If you need a service-level check on a harness today, the supported route is the testing surface (the project’s own test/E2E suites — see [Testing](/internal/docs/testing)) rather than the harness smoke config.

## The bash-era design (reference for the port)

[Section titled “The bash-era design (reference for the port)”](#the-bash-era-design-reference-for-the-port)

For whoever picks up the follow-up, the retired runner’s behavior — still the right shape — was: read the smoke config (`urls` of `{ url, expectStatus, expectText? }`, optional `startupCmd` + `startupWaitSeconds`), start the service if the first URL isn’t responding, curl each URL, then on all-pass write the pass sentinel (clearing any failure sentinel) and on any-fail write `smoke-failure.md` and reopen the most-recently-passed feature as failing. Gating ran in two modes: `onDone` (block mission completion) and `onFeaturePass` (revert a feature before the documenter runs, so docs are never generated for a broken state).

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* [Lifecycle hooks](/internal/docs/harness/hooks) — `on-smoke-pass` / `on-smoke-fail`
* [Decision telemetry](/internal/docs/harness/decisions-timeline) — the health-check family `smoke_test_clean` belongs to

# Steering & chat

> Which surface to use to steer running agents — durable messages, role-scoped chats, live coord nudges, turn interruption, and human gates.

The first-generation harness had one steering surface: a chat box in the retired web UI. Today steering is several purpose-built surfaces; picking the right one matters because they differ in durability, latency, and who reads them.

## Which surface for which job

[Section titled “Which surface for which job”](#which-surface-for-which-job)

| You want to…                                                        | Use                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Leave durable direction/context for whoever works a feature next    | `messages:send` (work-item-scoped)                              |
| Have an interactive conversation with a role agent inside a harness | `agent_chats:*`                                                 |
| Nudge a *live* agent right now (or wake an idle one)                | `coord:send` (with `wake: true`)                                |
| Make a running agent stop / wrap up                                 | `turn:interrupt`                                                |
| Answer a question an agent asked                                    | the decision card / `conversations:answer` / `coord` escalation |
| Steer the whole Pot (not one agent)                                 | the operator chat surface                                       |

## Durable messages — `messages:*`

[Section titled “Durable messages — messages:\*”](#durable-messages--messages)

`messages:send` (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/messages/send.ts`) writes a durable message that survives across spawns — the right surface for inter-agent hand-offs and human direction tied to work. Messages are **work-item-scoped**: with `to_feature_id` set they form that feature’s thread; without it they’re harness-level (`packages/agent-mcp/src/tools/messages/inbox.ts`). Every fresh spawn working that item reads the thread via `messages:inbox` — this is how direction reaches a [fresh context](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/fresh-contexts) that didn’t exist when you wrote it.

## Role-scoped chats — `agent_chats:*`

[Section titled “Role-scoped chats — agent\_chats:\*”](#role-scoped-chats--agent_chats)

For an interactive back-and-forth with a role agent inside a harness (the “pair” primitive): `agent_chats:create` opens a persistent chat, `agent_chats:chat` streams a turn (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/agent_chats/chat.ts` — transcripts, cost rollup, and feature-lock checks handled server-side), and `agent_chats:send_message` is the fire-and-forget non-streaming append used by autonomous dispatches. Use this when you want a conversation; use `messages:*` when you want durable direction.

## Live coordination — `coord:*`

[Section titled “Live coordination — coord:\*”](#live-coordination--coord)

`coord:send` reaches a *live* (or wakeable) agent’s coordination inbox; deltas are injected into the recipient mid-turn after its tool calls. With `wake: true` it re-invokes an idle agent — agents are armed for inbox-wake at session start, and a wake that woke nobody returns a `woken: 0` warning rather than failing silently. `coord:escalate` raises a durable escalation a human (or the operator) must resolve. Don’t use coord for state that must outlive the session — that’s what messages and work items are for.

## Turn interruption — `turn:interrupt`

[Section titled “Turn interruption — turn:interrupt”](#turn-interruption--turninterrupt)

To make a running agent stop, `turn:interrupt` (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/turn/interrupt.ts`) supports two modes — operator-mediated, reason-required, audited, and storm-rate-limited:

* **cooperative** — injects a high-priority `yield` line into the target’s coord stream; the agent finishes its atomic step, releases locks, checkpoints state, and ends its turn.
* **force** — ends the turn *now*, mid-thought (Ctrl+C to a managed pty / SIGINT headless); no checkpoint is guaranteed.

You cannot interrupt your own turn.

## Human gates: questions, escalations, approvals

[Section titled “Human gates: questions, escalations, approvals”](#human-gates-questions-escalations-approvals)

Agents pause for humans through structured gates rather than free chat: a mid-tool decision card (`ctx.askUser` / `chat:ask_choice`; with the `papercusp-inbox-durable-escalations` flag the card is also mirrored to a durable coord escalation so it can be answered later from the inbox), knowledge-first questions routed by topic (`coord:ask` → a conversation answered via `conversations:answer`), pipeline escalations (`harness:escalation` surfaces the blocker; resolution re-enters the pipeline), and plan items marked `needs-human` (which also block a DONE finalization — see [Smoke-test gate](/internal/docs/harness/smoke-test) for the gate family).

## Observing without steering

[Section titled “Observing without steering”](#observing-without-steering)

`fleet:bee_mail` renders what a specific agent has received/sent (the bee-dossier view) — for *inspection*, not for reading your own inbox (`coord:inbox`) or deriving who’s-on-what (`fleet:assignments`). The fleet-wide steering surface — scheduling, placement, prioritization — is the operator/Queen’s job; see [Operator persona](/internal/docs/agents/operator-persona).

# Worktrees & isolation

> Where git worktrees are (and deliberately are not) used today — phase worktrees, transient scratch envs for verification, and the shared-tree rule for the dev fleet.

The first-generation harness used a git worktree per parallel lane (`.harness/worktrees/<feature-id>/`) so concurrent workers couldn’t race each other’s `git checkout`. That mechanism retired with the bash loop, but the underlying idea — *give a unit of work its own filesystem view instead of fighting over HEAD* — survives in three distinct, narrower forms.

## 1. Phase worktrees (staging / testing / production)

[Section titled “1. Phase worktrees (staging / testing / production)”](#1-phase-worktrees-staging--testing--production)

A harness project can have up to three phased worktrees (`packages/operator-core/lib/harness-phases.ts`):

* **staging** → the project’s main path
* **testing / production** → a sibling checkout at `<path>--testing` / `<path>--production`, or an explicit per-phase `path` override carried on the project’s workspace-registry entry (not read from `config.json` — `deprecate-harness-config-json-2026-06-06`)

Every `?phase=` API route resolves through `phasePath()`, and the FS watcher mirrors all three worktrees into `harness_shared.*` with a `phase` column. Agents resolve a phase’s absolute path with the `harness:phase_path` tool. The multi-phase surface is gated by the `papercusp-harness-phases` [feature flag](/internal/docs/posthog/feature-flags).

## 2. Transient scratch worktrees for verification

[Section titled “2. Transient scratch worktrees for verification”](#2-transient-scratch-worktrees-for-verification)

The worker chunk loop wants to typecheck a worker’s pending edits **before** committing them, in a tree that can’t see other concurrent workers’ WIP. The primitive is `scratch-env.ts` (`libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/scratch-env.ts`): create a transient git worktree at integration HEAD, apply the worker’s pending edits for its locked files, symlink the heavy gitignored cache dirs (`node_modules`, `.turbo`, …) back to the main repo so caches stay warm, run the check, tear down. Setup is \~60 ms; `git worktree prune` at setup self-heals orphans from crashed runs; many workers can hold scratch envs simultaneously.

This is the direct descendant of the legacy lane-worktree insight: parallel workers sharing one working tree contaminate each other’s verification signal, and a cheap throwaway worktree is the cleanest cross-platform fix.

A sibling primitive, `tmpfs.ts`, hands subprocesses RAM-resident scratch *directories* for their inputs (`/dev/shm` on Linux) — state is PG-canonical, but external agent CLIs still need a path on disk to read.

## 3. What deliberately does NOT use worktrees: the dev fleet

[Section titled “3. What deliberately does NOT use worktrees: the dev fleet”](#3-what-deliberately-does-not-use-worktrees-the-dev-fleet)

For Papercusp’s own development, concurrent agents work **one shared checkout on `staging`** — no per-agent worktrees, no feature branches. Isolation comes from coordination instead of tree-splitting: the per-edit file-lock hook serializes same-file edits (`locks:*`), declared intents make work visible (`coord:*`), and a background git-sync routine owns commit + push. The trade — messy interleaved history for zero merge-reconciliation tax — is deliberate; see the repo guide (`CLAUDE.md`, “Branch discipline”).

The two models coexist because they solve different problems: worktrees isolate *machine verification* (a typecheck must not see foreign WIP); locks + coord serialize *human-scale collaboration* (two agents shouldn’t edit one file at once, but they *should* see each other’s work immediately).

## Historical note: competition mode

[Section titled “Historical note: competition mode”](#historical-note-competition-mode)

The bash harness briefly ran a Conductor-inspired **competition mode** — N workers attacking the same feature in sibling worktrees, the validator picking a winner. It was replaced pre-cutover by the **synthesizer** (read every lane’s diff, compose one shipping branch), which has itself been dormant since the legacy run-loop retired (`libs/papercusp/_retired/orchestrator-run-loop/`). Today’s analogue for “multiple independent attempts, judged” is work-item **redundancy** (replica dispatch + `work_items:judge_redundancy`), which operates at the work-item layer rather than the git layer.

## Related

[Section titled “Related”](#related)

* [Decision log](/internal/docs/harness/decisions/log) — the original worktree decision and its rationale
* [Storage policy](/internal/docs/system/storage-policy) — why state moved off the filesystem even as worktrees stayed for code

# Marketplace implementation

> Ship state of papercuspai.com — what's live, what's planned, what's still missing.

> **Webapp retired (2026-05-14).** Any `localhost:3055` or `localhost:3070` URL on this page is only reachable while the **Tauri dev shell** is running. Start it with `cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev`.

Superseded — describes the retired papercuspai.com marketplace

This page documents the standalone **`papercuspai.com` marketplace** (`papercupai/papercusp-registry`, Cloudflare Pages + Tunnel + a Hono `marketplace-api` on `:3057`) as of the 2026-04-27 handoff. That public marketplace surface is **no longer the current distribution path.**

What replaced it: the in-app **Cupboard** — a GitHub-backed listing service served by `apps/operator-public` (Cloudflare Workers + Hono + D1), with the desktop operator owning the listing UI. Listings span four kinds (`harness | blueprint | snapshot | plugin`); publish/install flow through the `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/cupboard.ts` operator routes and the `apps/papercusp-publish` Worker, with agent verbs `blueprint:*` (`catalog`/`create`/`extend`/`validate`) and `snapshots:*` (`get`/`list`). Read the rest of this page as a historical record of the earlier design, not the current system.

Handoff notice — last updated 2026-04-27

This page is the canonical handoff document for marketplace implementation. If a future agent or operator picks up the work, **read this in full first**. Specifically:

1. The OAuth client\_secret was leaked in a chat session and **may not have been rotated yet** — check `~/.papercusp/marketplace-secrets.env` and rotate at github.com → Developer Settings → Papercusp Marketplace.
2. The marketplace was extracted to its own repo `papercupai/papercusp-registry` (private) — **NOT in `papercupai/papercusp` anymore**.
3. Both `localhost:3055` and `papercuspai.com` exist intentionally; see “Two surfaces, often confused” below.
4. The CF API token at `~/.cloudflare-token` lacks Tunnel:Edit and (likely) R2:Edit scopes. Tunnel + R2 changes need user action in CF dashboard.

The marketplace is the public-facing component of Papercusp described in [§11 Distribution](/internal/docs/spec/distribution). This page tracks what’s actually shipped vs. what’s still spec’d-only.

## Two surfaces, often confused

[Section titled “Two surfaces, often confused”](#two-surfaces-often-confused)

There are **two distinct user-facing apps** in this project, both legitimate, both needed. They serve different audiences:

| Surface                          | URL                       | Source                                                                                                                                          | Audience                                     | Purpose                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Substrate operator dashboard** | <http://localhost:3055>   | `libs/papercusp/apps/web/` (in [papercupai/papercusp](https://github.com/papercupai/papercusp) submodule)                                       | Anyone running their own Papercusp install   | Manage local API keys, browse the catalog with installed-state, view harness state, sign in for publishing |
| **Public marketplace**           | <https://papercuspai.com> | `../papercusp-registry/apps/marketplace-site/` (in [papercupai/papercusp-registry](https://github.com/papercupai/papercusp-registry) submodule) | Anyone on the internet discovering Papercusp | Browse the catalog read-only, read docs, see featured packages, get install instructions                   |

### Why both exist (not a duplicate, not a stale-link mistake)

[Section titled “Why both exist (not a duplicate, not a stale-link mistake)”](#why-both-exist-not-a-duplicate-not-a-stale-link-mistake)

* The substrate operator UI is **part of every Papercusp install** — anyone self-hosting gets it. Its `/marketplace` page hits a LOCAL `/api/marketplace/catalog` route, which proxies to `api.papercuspai.com/catalog` and adds local install state (“you have this installed”, “newer version available”, etc.). That’s only meaningful if you have an install.

* The public marketplace at papercuspai.com is **install-free** — it just shows the catalog. No login, no install state, no API keys. Anyone evaluating Papercusp lands here first.

The substrate UI and public site share the same data source (`api.papercuspai.com`) but render different concerns. **Not a stale duplicate.**

## Architecture (current state)

[Section titled “Architecture (current state)”](#architecture-current-state)

```plaintext
papercuspai.com  (Cloudflare Pages — static Next.js export)
   │
   │ runtime fetch (CORS-allowed origin)
   ▼
api.papercuspai.com  (Cloudflare Tunnel — public ingress)
   │
   │ tunnel → cloudflared (token mode)
   │   tunnel UUID c53515b3-edfe-4e99-813b-e3916ae9d02c (papercupai-api)
   ▼
http://localhost:3057  (marketplace-api — Hono on Node)
   │   ../papercusp-registry/apps/marketplace-api/
   │
   │ filesystem read
   ▼
~/.papercusp/marketplace-storage/<slug>/<version>/
   ├── papercusp.json          (manifest)
   ├── README.md               (rendered on detail page)
   └── <slug>-<version>.tar.gz (the install)
```

### Endpoints implemented in marketplace-api

[Section titled “Endpoints implemented in marketplace-api”](#endpoints-implemented-in-marketplace-api)

```typescript
GET    /healthz                          → "ok"
GET    /catalog                          → { catalog: [{...manifest, versions[]}], storageRoot }
GET    /catalog/:slug                    → { slug, versions, latest: manifest }
GET    /catalog/:slug/:version           → { slug, version, manifest, readme }
GET    /download/:slug/:version          → tarball stream (application/gzip)
POST   /publish/:slug/:version           → multipart upload (manifest + tarball + readme)
DELETE /catalog/:slug/:version           → unpublish (dev-only)
```

POST `/publish` is currently in **open** mode (no auth). It supports a PAT-auth mode via `PAPERCUSP_MARKETPLACE_AUTH=pat` that verifies the Authorization header against the GitHub user API and records the verified login as `publishedBy`.

### Marketplace site features

[Section titled “Marketplace site features”](#marketplace-site-features)

* **Landing page** (`/`) — live-fetches 3 featured packages from `/catalog`; “How it works” section; “Publish your own harness” CTA with sample command.
* **Catalog grid** (`/marketplace/`) — live fetch + client-side search by name/description/author. Cards show name, version, author, description, role count, plugin count.
* **Package detail** (`/marketplace/[slug]/`) — manifest + rendered README; install command with copy button; download tarball link; sidebar listing roles (with preferred models), plugins, schema files, version history, substrate compat range.
* **Docs** (`/docs/`) — quickstart placeholder with CLI install/run commands. Full reference link to spec site.

## Implementation plan — by spec section

[Section titled “Implementation plan — by spec section”](#implementation-plan--by-spec-section)

For each spec’d feature in §11, this is the planned implementation route. Items are ordered by priority (auth → reliability → UX → discovery → governance).

### Phase M1 — Auth on publish (§11.6)

[Section titled “Phase M1 — Auth on publish (§11.6)”](#phase-m1--auth-on-publish-116)

**Goal:** Anyone publishing under `@user/foo` must prove ownership of GitHub user `user`.

**Plan:**

1. Add GitHub OAuth app at `github.com/papercupai` (or repurpose existing). Redirect URI: `https://api.papercuspai.com/v1/auth/github/callback`.

2. Add session middleware to marketplace-api (signed cookies; HMAC key from env).

3. New endpoints:

   * `GET /v1/auth/github/login` → redirect to GitHub authorize URL
   * `GET /v1/auth/github/callback` → exchange code, verify token, set session cookie
   * `GET /v1/auth/me` → return verified GitHub identity
   * `POST /v1/auth/logout` → clear cookie

4. Modify `POST /publish/:slug/:version`:

   * Reject if no session cookie OR session’s GitHub login doesn’t match the `@owner` namespace prefix in `:slug`.
   * Stamp manifest with `publishedBy: <github-login>` server-side.

5. CLI `papercusp publish` — open browser to `/v1/auth/github/login`, capture session cookie, persist to `~/.papercusp/credentials.json` (mode 0600).

6. Rejection messages must be specific: `"foo/bar" requires GitHub user "foo"; you're authenticated as "baz"`.

**Estimate:** 3-4 hours work. CSRF protection, scope validation, retry-on-token-expiry are the hard parts.

### Phase M2 — R2 storage backing ✅ CODE SHIPPED (gated, awaiting credentials)

[Section titled “Phase M2 — R2 storage backing ✅ CODE SHIPPED (gated, awaiting credentials)”](#phase-m2--r2-storage-backing--code-shipped-gated-awaiting-credentials)

**Status:** All code paths shipped. Activates the moment R2 credentials are added to the env. **No code changes needed when the user has the bucket + token.**

**What shipped:**

* New module `apps/marketplace-api/src/r2.ts` — S3-SDK against R2 endpoint; `isR2Configured()`/`putFile`/`putBytes`/`presign`/`exists`/`deleteKey`. Lazy client init, throws clearly if env missing.
* Schema delta `sql/006-r2-backing.sql` — adds `r2_key`, `r2_signature_key`, `r2_uploaded_at` columns to `package_versions` (idempotent).
* `POST /publish/:slug/:version` — after the FS write, also uploads tarball + `signature.json` to R2 (best-effort, non-fatal). Records `r2_key` in DB. Response now includes `r2: { key }` or `r2: { configured: false }`.
* `GET /download/:slug/:version` — when R2 is configured AND the version has been uploaded there, redirects to a 60s presigned URL (or to `R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL/<key>` when set). Falls back to FS streaming otherwise.
* New endpoint `GET /v1/storage/status` — returns `{ configured, account?, bucket?, publicBaseUrl? }` for ops visibility.
* New endpoint `POST /v1/storage/backfill-r2` — operator-token-gated; uploads up to 100 unbackfilled versions per call. Idempotent (skips versions with `r2_key` already set).
* npm deps added: `@aws-sdk/client-s3`, `@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner`.

**To activate:**

1. Create R2 bucket in Cloudflare dashboard (account `f896982ea2f6d507e4f29eeecbd26e94`)

2. Generate an R2 API token (R2 → Manage API Tokens → “Object Read & Write” on the bucket)

3. Append to `~/.papercusp/marketplace-secrets.env`:

   ```plaintext
   R2_ACCOUNT_ID=f896982ea2f6d507e4f29eeecbd26e94
   R2_BUCKET=papercusp-marketplace-tarballs
   R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<from token>
   R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<from token>
   # Optional: R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL=https://r2.papercuspai.com (if you set up a public bucket / CDN)
   ```

4. `bin/overmind-all restart marketplace`

5. Verify: `curl localhost:3057/v1/storage/status` → `"configured": true`

6. Backfill existing tarballs: `curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $PAPERCUSP_MARKETPLACE_OPERATOR_TOKEN" localhost:3057/v1/storage/backfill-r2`

After backfill, all downloads transparently 302-redirect to R2. Future publishes dual-write FS + R2.

**Verified:** marketplace-api boots cleanly in disabled mode (`[r2] disabled — set ...`); `/v1/storage/status` returns `{"configured":false}`; `/download/...` still serves from FS. No regressions.

### Phase M2.5 — Postgres metadata table

[Section titled “Phase M2.5 — Postgres metadata table”](#phase-m25--postgres-metadata-table)

**Goal:** Replace `listSlugs` / `listVersions` filesystem walks with a Postgres-backed catalog.

**Schema** (in `papercusp_marketplace` schema):

```sql
CREATE TABLE packages (
  slug          TEXT PRIMARY KEY,         -- @owner/package
  owner         TEXT NOT NULL,            -- verified GitHub login
  description   TEXT,
  homepage      TEXT,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  retracted     TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'  -- 'active' | 'deprecated' | 'withdrawn' | 'quarantined'
);


CREATE TABLE package_versions (
  slug              TEXT REFERENCES packages(slug),
  version           TEXT NOT NULL,
  manifest_json     JSONB NOT NULL,
  readme_md         TEXT,
  install_shape     TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'iterative' | 'scheduled' | 'reactive' | 'passive'
  capability_tiers  JSONB,                  -- { low: N, medium: N, high: N } counts
  service_pins      JSONB,                  -- { tasks: '^1.0', secrets: '^2.0', ... }
  signature         TEXT NOT NULL,          -- Ed25519 base64
  tarball_size      BIGINT NOT NULL,
  tarball_sha256    TEXT NOT NULL,
  tarball_r2_key    TEXT NOT NULL,
  published_by      TEXT NOT NULL,          -- GitHub login
  published_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  yanked_at         TIMESTAMPTZ,
  yanked_reason     TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (slug, version)
);


CREATE INDEX idx_package_versions_published_at ON package_versions(published_at DESC);
```

**Estimate:** 1 hour for schema + 1 hour migrating reads. Bundle with M2.

### Phase M3 — Tarball signing (Ed25519)

[Section titled “Phase M3 — Tarball signing (Ed25519)”](#phase-m3--tarball-signing-ed25519)

**Goal:** Detect tampering between publish and install.

**Plan:**

1. Generate marketplace’s Ed25519 keypair; private key stored at `~/.papercusp/marketplace-key.pem` on the marketplace-api host (mode 0600); public key published at `https://api.papercuspai.com/v1/keys/marketplace.pub`.

2. At publish:

   * Compute SHA-256 of the tarball.
   * Sign `${slug}\n${version}\n${sha256}\n${published_by}\n${published_at}` with the marketplace key.
   * Store the signature in `package_versions.signature`.

3. At install:

   * CLI fetches the marketplace public key (cached locally with TTL of 1 day).
   * Verifies signature against the metadata it received from `/catalog/:slug/:version`.
   * Independently SHA-256 the downloaded tarball and verify it matches the signed sha256.

4. Failure modes:

   * Signature invalid → install hard-fails with “tarball tampered or marketplace key changed”.
   * Public key fetched but doesn’t match cached → CLI prompts user to confirm rotation (single line, audit logged).

**Estimate:** 2 hours. The crypto is `tweetnacl`-grade primitives.

### Phase M4 — Search + tags (Typesense) ✅ SHIPPED real fuzzy search

[Section titled “Phase M4 — Search + tags (Typesense) ✅ SHIPPED real fuzzy search”](#phase-m4--search--tags-typesense--shipped-real-fuzzy-search)

**Status:** Live with Typesense backend; falls back gracefully to LIKE-based SQL when Typesense is unavailable.

**What shipped:**

* New module `apps/marketplace-api/src/typesense.ts` — collection schema, `indexPackage` / `unindexPackage` / `searchTypesense`
* `marketplace_packages` collection (slug, description, owner, latest\_version, capabilities\[], plugins\[], shape, retracted, downloads\_30d, updated\_at)
* `/v1/search?q=…&shape=…` hits Typesense first with fuzzy matching (2-typo tolerance + prefix), falls back to SQL LIKE on failure
* `&shape=` filter facet (iterative / scheduled / reactive / passive)
* Response includes `backend: 'typesense' | 'sql'` so callers know which path served them
* Sync hooks: every `POST /publish/...` upserts the doc; every `withdraw`/`quarantine` removes it; `unwithdraw`/`unquarantine`/(un)`deprecate` re-syncs the retracted state
* Operator endpoint `POST /v1/admin/reindex-typesense` — bulk re-index existing packages (idempotent)

**Verified:** typo `codign` correctly resolves to `papercup-coding` (“Did you mean?” semantics for free); responses through tunnel show `backend: 'typesense'`.

### Phase M5 — Update / uninstall flows (§11.7, §11.8)

[Section titled “Phase M5 — Update / uninstall flows (§11.7, §11.8)”](#phase-m5--update--uninstall-flows-117-118)

**Goal:** `papercusp update <name>` and `papercusp uninstall <name>` work per spec.

**Plan:**

1. Substrate-side state: `installed_plugins` table tracking `{ slug, version, applied_migration_index, granted_capabilities, install_path, installed_at }`.

2. CLI `papercusp update <slug>` flow per [§11.7](/spec/distribution/#117-update-flow):

   * Fetch latest version from marketplace
   * Diff capabilities (added/removed/renamed/major)
   * Prompt only for additions (unless major version → re-prompt all)
   * Snapshot old version to `~/.papercusp/installed/<slug>/.snapshots/<old-version>/` (manifest + schema dump + granted-caps)
   * Apply new migrations from `applied_migration_index`
   * Reconcile routines (delete renamed, insert new, update existing in-place)
   * Replace plugin code on disk

3. CLI `papercusp uninstall <slug>` flow per [§11.8](/spec/distribution/#118-uninstall-flow):

   * Default: stop code, leave data
   * `--purge-data`: also drop plugin schema

4. CLI `papercusp rollback <slug>`: re-mount snapshot version (DB rollback is user’s responsibility — substrate doesn’t run down-migrations).

**Estimate:** 5-6 hours. The capability-diff logic is the hard part; everything else is filesystem + Postgres mechanics.

### Phase M6 — Retraction (§11.9)

[Section titled “Phase M6 — Retraction (§11.9)”](#phase-m6--retraction-119)

**Goal:** Server-side package status — Deprecated / Yanked / Withdrawn / Quarantined.

**Plan:**

1. Add `retracted` column to `packages` (already in M2.5 schema).

2. Add `yanked_at` / `yanked_reason` to `package_versions` (already in M2.5 schema).

3. New endpoints:

   * `POST /v1/packages/:slug/deprecate` (owner-only)
   * `POST /v1/packages/:slug/withdraw` (owner OR operator)
   * `POST /v1/packages/:slug/quarantine` (operator-only)
   * `POST /v1/packages/:slug/versions/:version/yank` (owner OR operator)

4. Marketplace-api list endpoints (`/catalog`, `/v1/search`) filter by `retracted` status:

   * `deprecated` → still returned with a flag in the response
   * `yanked` versions → hidden from listings
   * `withdrawn` packages → hidden from listings
   * `quarantined` packages → hidden + tarball returns 410 immediately

5. Substrate periodically polls `/v1/installed-status?slugs=A,B,C&versions=...` (every hour) to detect retractions of installed plugins. On `quarantined`, auto-pause routines from that plugin and surface UI alert.

6. Public audit log at `papercuspai.com/security/quarantines` (page generated at build, sourced from `/v1/admin/quarantine-log`).

**Estimate:** 3-4 hours including the polling client in the substrate.

### Marketplace operator dashboard ✅ SHIPPED

4. Site uses `popularity` field (last 30 days’ downloads) to:

   * Sort the catalog grid by default (most-downloaded first)
   * Compute a “Trending this week” section (biggest week-over-week % gainers).

5. Stats are public; no PII.

**Estimate:** 2-3 hours.

### Phase M10 — Size & bandwidth quotas (§11.10)

[Section titled “Phase M10 — Size & bandwidth quotas (§11.10)”](#phase-m10--size--bandwidth-quotas-1110)

**Goal:** Enforce the per-package, per-publisher, per-IP limits to prevent abuse.

**Plan:**

1. **Per-package limits at upload:**

   * Reject `POST /publish` early if `Content-Length` > 50 MB.
   * Validate manifest size ≤ 64 KB before parse.
   * Validate README size ≤ 256 KB after extraction.

2. **Per-publisher quotas** — table `publisher_quotas { github_login, day, publishes_count, total_bytes }`:

   * 50 publishes/day check at upload time.
   * Aggregate-storage check by summing `package_versions.tarball_size` for all of the publisher’s packages.

3. **Per-IP throttling** — middleware on the marketplace-api Hono router:

   * In-memory `Map<ip, { count, windowStart }>` with 1-minute windows for read endpoints.
   * For `/download/`, hourly windows.
   * For `/publish/`, per-authenticated-user windows (not IP).
   * Returns HTTP 429 with `Retry-After` header.

4. **Cloudflare-side rate limit rules** for the `api.papercuspai.com` zone. Currently no token scope to configure these via API; must be added via CF dashboard.

**Estimate:** 3-4 hours (most of it is plumbing the in-memory rate limiter and the publisher-quota table).

### Phase M11 — Catalog webhooks (§11.11)

[Section titled “Phase M11 — Catalog webhooks (§11.11)”](#phase-m11--catalog-webhooks-1111)

**Goal:** CI / mirrors / external monitors get notified on catalog events.

**Plan:**

1. Schema:

   ```sql
   CREATE TABLE webhook_subscriptions (
     id              TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
     owner           TEXT NOT NULL,           -- '@avi' or '*' (operator only)
     url             TEXT NOT NULL,
     events          TEXT[] NOT NULL,         -- ['version.published', ...]
     secret          TEXT NOT NULL,           -- HMAC key
     created_by      TEXT NOT NULL,           -- GitHub login that registered it
     created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
     last_delivery   TIMESTAMPTZ,             -- updated on success
     consecutive_fails INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
     disabled_at     TIMESTAMPTZ
   );


   CREATE TABLE webhook_deliveries (
     id              TEXT PRIMARY KEY,        -- 'wh_evt_01J6...' (event id)
     subscription_id TEXT REFERENCES webhook_subscriptions(id),
     event           TEXT NOT NULL,
     ts              TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
     payload         JSONB NOT NULL,
     attempt         INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
     status_code     INT,
     completed_at    TIMESTAMPTZ
   );
   ```

2. Endpoints:

   * `POST /v1/webhooks` — register subscription; auth-gated (only namespace owner can subscribe to events for that namespace).
   * `DELETE /v1/webhooks/:id` — owner-only.
   * `GET /v1/webhooks` — list subscriber’s webhooks + delivery history (last 100 attempts each).

3. Producer side: `version.published`, `version.yanked`, `package.withdrawn`, `package.quarantined` events insert into `webhook_deliveries` with attempt=0 within the publish/retract transaction.

4. Worker process: long-lived loop polls `webhook_deliveries` where `completed_at IS NULL`, dispatches with HMAC-SHA-256 signature header, retries per spec schedule. Could run inside marketplace-api or as separate microservice; start in marketplace-api.

5. After 90 days of failed delivery, mark subscription `disabled_at`. Send one warning email (via Resend or similar) before disable.

**Estimate:** 4-5 hours. The worker loop is the hard part — must be exactly-once enough that owners can dedup confidently.

### Phase M12 — Vendored / offline install (§11.12)

[Section titled “Phase M12 — Vendored / offline install (§11.12)”](#phase-m12--vendored--offline-install-1112)

**Goal:** `papercusp pack` produces a self-contained mirror; substrate can install from `file://` URL.

**Plan:**

1. **CLI command** `papercusp pack <slug>[@<version>] [<slug2>]... --output <dir>`:

   * Authenticates against the configured registry.
   * For each requested package, downloads the tarball + manifest + README.
   * If signed (per §11.5/M3), bundles the signature file too.
   * Bundles the marketplace’s public verification key.
   * Writes a `marketplace-snapshot.json` with the catalog state as of pack time (lets the offline substrate respond to “what versions exist?” queries).
   * Writes `index.json` per package (the “latest” pointer + version list).

2. **Substrate resolver changes** in `@papercusp/cli`:

   * `papercusp config set registry file:///path/to/dir/` accepted.
   * Loader uses `node:fs/promises` for `file://` URLs; same JSON shapes as HTTP.
   * Signature verification works identically (the public key is bundled).

3. **Refresh tooling**:

   * `papercusp pack --refresh <existing-mirror-dir>` — re-fetches all packages currently in the mirror, updating to latest.
   * `papercusp pack --diff <existing-mirror-dir> <other-dir>` — show what changed between two pack snapshots.

**Estimate:** 5-6 hours. The `file://` resolver + bundled public key are the new mechanics; rest is filesystem walks.

### Phase M13 — Multi-registry resolution (§11.13)

[Section titled “Phase M13 — Multi-registry resolution (§11.13)”](#phase-m13--multi-registry-resolution-1113)

**Goal:** Support scope-based registry routing, no automatic fallback.

**Plan:**

1. CLI parses `~/.papercusp/config.json` for `registries[]`.

2. For each install/update/lookup request, walk the list:

   * Find the first registry whose `scope` matches the requested package.
   * Issue the request to ONLY that registry.
   * On failure: if `trustOnFail` is `false` (default), return error to user; if `true`, log warning and try next.

3. Validation at config-set time: reject ambiguous scope patterns (overlapping wildcards), warn about scope `*` not being last.

4. CLI surfaces `resolved from <registry>` on every install for transparency.

**Estimate:** 1-2 hours. Almost entirely CLI logic; no server-side changes.

### Phase M14 — SBOM attestation (§11.14)

[Section titled “Phase M14 — SBOM attestation (§11.14)”](#phase-m14--sbom-attestation-1114)

**Goal:** Verified packages can attach an SPDX or CycloneDX SBOM at publish time; marketplace surfaces it with vulnerability scanning.

**Status:** Live in production.

**What shipped:**

* Schema `papercusp_marketplace.{package_version_sboms, package_version_vulnerabilities}` + view `v_package_vuln_summary`

* SBOM ingest (`POST /v1/packages/:slug/:version/sbom`, JSON body): auto-detects SPDX-2.3 vs CycloneDX-1.5, validates JSON, caps at 5 MB, hashes with sha256

* Background scan worker (60s tick): pops `scan_status='pending'`, extracts package URLs from SBOM, batch-queries osv.dev `/v1/querybatch`, persists vulns with severity bucketing

* Endpoints:

  * `GET /v1/packages/:slug/:version/sbom` — metadata + summary
  * `GET /v1/packages/:slug/:version/vulnerabilities` — full vuln list (sorted by severity)

* CLI: `papercusp publish --sbom <path>` flag (uploads after publish, queues scan)

* Marketplace site:

  * `SbomBadge` next to version pill (”✓ No CVEs” green / ”⚠ N CVEs” amber/red by worst severity)
  * `SbomSection` at the bottom of detail page (severity chips + collapsible vuln list with deep links to cve.org / github.com/advisories)

**Verified end-to-end:** seeded an SBOM for `signed-test@0.1.0` (lodash\@4.17.20 + minimist\@1.2.5 components) → osv.dev returned 6 GHSAs (5 lodash + 1 minimist) → all persisted, summary aggregated, exposed at <https://api.papercuspai.com/v1/packages/signed-test/0.1.0/sbom> + /vulnerabilities.
