| Marketplace quarantines or retracts any version of `(P, G)`                                                                              | All trust entries for `(P, G)` cleared. Future encounters require fresh approval.                                                                                                                                          |
| Marketplace quarantines a *different* plugin `(P, OtherPlugin)`                                                                          | All trust entries for `(P, OtherPlugin)` cleared. **Trust on `(P, G)` is preserved** unless that plugin was also flagged. The pure-publisher-quarantine sledgehammer is reserved for evidence of publisher-key compromise. |
| Marketplace publishes a publisher-key compromise advisory                                                                                | All trust entries for any `(P, *)` cleared.                                                                                                                                                                                |

### Ownership transfer

[Section titled “Ownership transfer”](#ownership-transfer)

Per-(publisher, plugin) trust is keyed on the **publisher’s signing-key fingerprint** as recorded in the marketplace’s per-version metadata. When a plugin’s ownership transfers (e.g., npm-style maintainer addition or hand-off), the new version’s `publisher_id` differs from the cached trusted version’s. The substrate detects this and treats the new encounter as fresh:

```text
@papercupai/aws-lambda 0.2.0 ships from a different publisher key than
@papercupai/aws-lambda 0.1.5 (which you trusted on 2026-04-01).


  Old key fingerprint: SHA256:abc...  (last trusted 2026-04-01)
  New key fingerprint: SHA256:xyz...


This may be legitimate (publisher rotated their key — see Marketplace
attestations below) or it may be unauthorized (publisher's key was
compromised). Re-approve only if you can confirm the rotation.
```

This closes the xz-utils-in-miniature attack class: an attacker becoming a maintainer of an already-trusted plugin doesn’t inherit the prior maintainer’s trust.

### Key rotation

[Section titled “Key rotation”](#key-rotation)

A publisher rotating their own signing key (legitimate operation, e.g., yearly key rotation) needs to be distinguishable from a compromise. Solution: **rotation events are countersigned by the marketplace’s infrastructure key**.

```json
{
  "kind": "key-rotation",
  "publisher": "@papercupai",
  "old_key_fingerprint": "SHA256:abc...",
  "new_key_fingerprint": "SHA256:xyz...",
  "rotated_at": "2026-05-12T18:00:00Z",
  "reason": "scheduled rotation",
  "marketplace_signature": "..."
}
```

The substrate refuses to display a “publisher rotated their key” prompt unless `marketplace_signature` validates against the marketplace’s **pinned infrastructure key** (the substrate ships with this pinned; rotating it requires a substrate update). An attacker who compromised a publisher’s signing key cannot forge a rotation event, because they don’t have the marketplace’s infrastructure key.

When a valid rotation event is observed, the substrate prompts:

```text
@papercupai rotated their signing key on 2026-05-12.
Marketplace confirms the rotation (signature verified).
Reason: scheduled rotation


Re-trust future signed scripts from @papercupai for plugins:
  ☐ @papercupai/cloudflare-pages   (last trusted 2026-04-01)
  ☐ @papercupai/aws-lambda          (last trusted 2026-03-15)
  ☐ @papercupai/github-repo         (last trusted 2026-04-12)


Re-trust applies one plugin at a time.
```

User can re-trust per-plugin or skip. The “trust this plugin’s future scripts” toggle is unchecked by default after every rotation event.

### Compromise + revocation

[Section titled “Compromise + revocation”](#compromise--revocation)

If a publisher’s key is compromised (signaled by marketplace publishing a `key-compromise` advisory, also countersigned by the marketplace’s infrastructure key):

| Event                                                                          | Effect                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Marketplace publishes `key-compromise` for fingerprint `K`                     | Substrate refuses to verify any signature against `K`. All trust entries for any plugin signed by `K` flagged `signing_key_compromised: true`.          |
| User invokes a plugin with a compromised signing key                           | Plugin actions and hooks blocked; settings UI shows compromise notice + “this plugin is unsafe to run; uninstall and switch to a different signing key” |
| Publisher publishes new versions signed with a fresh, marketplace-attested key | Substrate accepts these as a new publisher\_id; user re-approves on first encounter                                                                     |

## Consent flow

[Section titled “Consent flow”](#consent-flow)

When the user is about to fork a snapshot containing plugins with provisioning, or when they enable a plugin with `provision.setup`, the operator shows:

```text
Approve setup script for @papercupai/aws-lambda
─────────────────────────────────────────────────


Will run: ./provision/setup.sh   (sha256: a1b2c3...)
Display name: Provision AWS Lambda + API Gateway
Description: Creates a Lambda function, an API Gateway HTTP API, and
             the IAM role binding them.


Signed by:    @papercupai (5 previous versions trusted by you)
Sandbox:      bubblewrap (Linux); restricted filesystem + network
Outbound:     lambda.us-east-1.amazonaws.com,
              execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com,
              iam.amazonaws.com
Timeout:      5 min


  [ Show full script source ▼ ]


Static analysis: 0 warnings.


This script will run in a sandbox with the listed restrictions. The
substrate will:
  ✓ Stream all output into a terminal pane you can watch live
  ✓ Capture stdout/stderr to the audit log
  ✓ Track created resources for teardown
  ✓ Refuse to run if the script's hash doesn't match the signed manifest


  ☐ I have reviewed the script.
  ☐ Trust future signed scripts from @papercupai (one-click approve next time)


  [ Approve and run ]    [ Cancel ]
```

For unsigned scripts, the dialog is louder, the “trust future” toggle is hidden, and the consent text says “**Unsigned**. The script’s source has not been verified by any publisher.”

## Re-run policy

[Section titled “Re-run policy”](#re-run-policy)

`setup` runs **once per (harness, plugin) pair** until the configHash changes (see [Idempotency](#idempotency-contract)). Once it succeeds, re-running requires the user to explicitly click “Re-provision” in the plugin settings *or* the configHash to differ.

If `setup` fails partway through:

* The state file (whatever was written so far) is kept.
* The plugin is marked `setup-failed` in the operator UI.
* The user sees the audit log and the partial state.
* They can re-run setup explicitly (script must be idempotent enough to handle the partial state).

## Teardown semantics

[Section titled “Teardown semantics”](#teardown-semantics)

`papercusp plugin uninstall <slug> [--purge-grants]` (which walks every harness the plugin is enabled in) triggers `teardown` if declared. The flow:

```text
Uninstall @papercupai/aws-lambda from harness `my-store`
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


This plugin's teardown script will be run. It will delete:


  • aws.lambda.function   arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123:function:my-fn
  • aws.iam.role          arn:aws:iam::123:role/my-fn-role
  • aws.apigatewayv2.api  abc123


These resources will no longer be available after teardown.


  ☐ I have backed up anything I need to keep
  ☐ Approve and run teardown


  [ Run teardown ]    [ Skip teardown (orphan resources) ]    [ Cancel ]
```

If the user picks “Skip teardown”, the plugin is uninstalled but the substrate writes an orphan-resources marker so a later “clean up orphaned resources” command can find them.

## Verify semantics

[Section titled “Verify semantics”](#verify-semantics)

`verify` runs:

* After `setup` succeeds (immediate confirmation)
* On every operator boot (best-effort, async)
* **When the plugin’s tile is foreground in the operator UI** (visibility-aware) — periodic background polling is *not* the V1 default. Round-3 review noted that 10-min interval polling at scale (5 plugins × 100 harnesses) hits cloud-API rate limits. Foreground-only polling reduces this to “checks happen when the user is looking.”
* On demand from the plugin settings UI (“Check health” button)
* Optionally on a periodic background timer if `verify.intervalSec` is set; default is unset (foreground-only).

`verify` should be fast (seconds) and read-only. It exits 0 for “healthy”, 1 for “degraded but functional”, 2 for “broken”. The substrate surfaces these in the plugin’s harness-toolbar tile and in the dashboard summary.

## Audit logging

[Section titled “Audit logging”](#audit-logging)

Every script run writes to `<harness>/.papercusp/audit/provision-runs/<ts>-<plugin>-<phase>.log`:

```plaintext
=== papercusp provision run ===
plugin: @papercupai/aws-lambda
version: 0.1.0
phase: setup
script: ./provision/setup.sh
script-hash: sha256:a1b2c3...
sandbox: bubblewrap
network: restrict (allowed: lambda.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, ...)
started: 2026-05-08T20:14:32.123Z
runId: prov-abc123


=== environment ===
PAPERCUSP_HARNESS_SLUG=my-store
PAPERCUSP_PROJECT_DIR=/home/me/projects/my-store
PAPERCUSP_PLUGIN_DIR=/home/me/.papercusp/global-plugins/@papercupai/aws-lambda
PAPERCUSP_CFG_REGION=us-east-1
(secrets redacted)


=== output ===
::papercusp::progress {"step": "iam-role", "pct": 25}
[setup] Creating IAM role aws-lambda-role-my-store...
... (full stream) ...
::papercusp::progress {"step": "done", "pct": 100}


=== exit ===
exitCode: 0
durationMs: 47230
stateWritten: yes
stateBytes: 412
```

### Retention

[Section titled “Retention”](#retention)

Audit logs are forensic — they’re consulted when something goes wrong (unexpected cloud bill, suspected compromise, “what changed since last month”), and the time horizon for noticing those problems is months, not days.

**V1 default**: 1 year retention, 50 MB per (harness, plugin) cap, oldest-first eviction within the cap.

The size cap protects against a runaway plugin spamming logs; the duration protects the actual use case. Provisioning runs are rare (often once per harness lifetime), so a year of logs is typically under 10 MB per harness. V1.1 formalizes the policy and adds UI surfaces for browsing older audit entries.

### Per-plugin override

[Section titled “Per-plugin override”](#per-plugin-override)

Plugins doing terraform-class provisioning (K8s cluster bootstrap, multi-resource Terraform applies) can legitimately emit hundreds of MB. The 50 MB default would silently evict useful debugging context.

```json
{
  "provision": {
    "setup": {
      "auditLogCapMb": 500
    }
  }
}
```

Surfaced in the consent dialog as a discrete line: “**This plugin requests up to 500 MB of audit space.**” Lets legitimate plugins request capacity while flagging it as a thing the user should notice.

### Fail-loud on encrypted-locked volumes

[Section titled “Fail-loud on encrypted-locked volumes”](#fail-loud-on-encrypted-locked-volumes)

`<harness>/.papercusp/audit/provision-runs/` may live on an encrypted volume that’s locked at boot (LUKS, FileVault, EncFS). If the substrate can’t write to the audit dir, it **fails loud**: setup is refused, operator banner shows “audit volume unavailable; unlock the volume or run with `PAPERCUSP_NO_AUDIT=1` (not recommended).” Silent audit-swallowing is forbidden — the audit trail is the only record of what scripts did, and losing it silently is a worse failure mode than refusing to run.

## Relationship to compute:exec:\*

[Section titled “Relationship to compute:exec:\*”](#relationship-to-computeexec)

The existing SDK provides a `compute:exec:<bin>` capability for plugins that need to shell out from action handlers. Build scripts are a separate mechanism with different properties:

| Surface                                              | Capability-gated?                                                   | Sandbox?                           | Consent flow?                              | Lifecycle                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `compute:exec:<bin>` (action shell-out)              | Yes — declared per-binary in the manifest, enforced at the DI proxy | Capability sandbox + bin allowlist | Granted at install time                    | Runs whenever the action is invoked                           |
| `provision.{setup, teardown, verify}` (build script) | No — declared as a `provision` block, lifecycle-bound               | OS-level sandbox (bwrap on Linux)  | Per-script-hash approval at install / fork | Runs once at setup, once at teardown, periodically for verify |

Both coexist. A plugin can use `compute:exec:git` for in-action git operations *and* `provision.setup` for one-time AWS provisioning. The distinction:

* Action shell-outs are routine, capability-gated calls plugged into the normal action path (single binary, sandboxed).
* Build scripts are lifecycle infrastructure events with consent ceremony, full output streaming, and resource lifecycle tracking.

V1.1 will add explicit cross-references between the two in the SDK docs.

## Helper library: `provision/lib.sh`

[Section titled “Helper library: provision/lib.sh”](#helper-library-provisionlibsh)

The substrate ships a small helper library that plugin scripts source. Its path is provided to the script in `$PAPERCUSP_RUNTIME_LIB` (source is `packages/operator-core/lib/provision/runtime/lib.sh`); scripts source it by the standard pattern:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
. "$PAPERCUSP_RUNTIME_LIB"


papercusp_progress "step:iam-role" "creating role $ROLE_NAME"
ROLE_ARN=$(aws iam create-role ...)
papercusp_record_resource "aws.iam.role" "$ROLE_ARN"


papercusp_progress "step:lambda" "creating function $FN_NAME"
FN_ARN=$(aws lambda create-function ...)
papercusp_record_resource "aws.lambda.function" "$FN_ARN"
```

### Helpers exposed in V1

[Section titled “Helpers exposed in V1”](#helpers-exposed-in-v1)

| Helper                                                | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `papercusp_progress <step> <message>`                 | Emits a `::papercusp::progress` marker. UI renders a structured progress bar.                                                                                                                   |
| `papercusp_warn <message>`                            | Emits a `::papercusp::warn` marker. UI renders a yellow indicator.                                                                                                                              |
| `papercusp_error <message>`                           | Emits a `::papercusp::error` marker. UI renders a red indicator (script may still continue or exit).                                                                                            |
| `papercusp_record_resource <kind> <id> [<meta-json>]` | Appends `{kind, externalId, recordedAt, metadata?}` to the resource WAL (via `$PAPERCUSP_RECORD_FIFO`) *immediately* (not at success). Substrate uses this for partial-failure rollback.        |
| `papercusp_state_set <key> <value>`                   | Sets a key in `state.json` `outputs` (same FIFO, `$op: "state_set"`).                                                                                                                           |
| `papercusp_render_templates`                          | Walks `$PAPERCUSP_PROJECT_DIR` for `*.tmpl` files, renders each via `envsubst` with the script’s exported env, writes the de-suffixed result, removes the `.tmpl` source. Skips VCS/build dirs. |

### Partial-failure rollback via `record_resource`

[Section titled “Partial-failure rollback via record\_resource”](#partial-failure-rollback-via-record_resource)

Real provisioning scripts often create resources in dependency order. If step 3 of 5 fails, the substrate already knows about the 2 successful resources because they were recorded at the time of creation:

```text
Setup script @papercupai/aws-lambda failed at step "lambda" (exit 1).


The script created these resources before failing:
  • aws.iam.role           arn:aws:iam::123:role/my-fn-role
  • aws.iam.role-policy    my-fn-policy


Tear down these resources before re-trying setup?
  [ Yes — run teardown ]    [ No — keep them, fix the script first ]    [ Audit log ]
```

If the user picks teardown, the substrate runs `teardown.sh` with a state.json containing only the recorded-so-far resources. Plugin authors don’t have to write defensive “did this fail in stage X?” logic in setup; partial state is captured and tear-downable.

`papercusp_record_resource` writes are atomic appends to a write-ahead log; the substrate compacts them into `state.json`’s `createdResources` array on next read. This means even a hard kill of the script (SIGKILL) preserves what was recorded.

### Teardown contract: plugin’s `teardown.sh` is the dispatcher

[Section titled “Teardown contract: plugin’s teardown.sh is the dispatcher”](#teardown-contract-plugins-teardownsh-is-the-dispatcher)

Resource kinds (`aws.iam.role`, `aws.lambda.function`, etc.) are plugin-author vocabulary, not substrate-defined types. `teardown.sh` receives the recorded resources via `state.json` and dispatches per kind:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
. "$PAPERCUSP_RUNTIME_LIB"


# Read recorded resources from state.json (passed via $PAPERCUSP_PLUGIN_STATE)
mapfile -t RESOURCES < <(jq -c '.createdResources[]' "$PAPERCUSP_PLUGIN_STATE")


# Tear down in REVERSE creation order (LIFO)
for resource in "${RESOURCES[@]}" | tac; do
  kind=$(echo "$resource" | jq -r .kind)
  id=$(echo "$resource" | jq -r .id)
  case "$kind" in
    aws.lambda.function)
      aws lambda delete-function --function-name "$id" || \
        papercusp_warn "lambda delete failed: $id"
      ;;
    aws.iam.role)
      aws iam delete-role --role-name "$id" || \
        papercusp_warn "role delete failed: $id"
      ;;
    *)
      papercusp_warn "unknown kind in teardown: $kind ($id)"
      ;;
  esac
done
```

The substrate does **NOT** interpret resource kinds in V1. It hands the plugin’s `teardown.sh` the recorded list and expects the plugin to do the right thing. If `teardown.sh` doesn’t handle a `kind`, the resource is reported as orphaned in the audit log + the user-visible orphan-banner (see [Skip teardown banner](#skip-teardown-banner-v11)).

V2+ may add a substrate-level dispatcher with built-in handlers for common cloud resource kinds. V1 keeps the contract simple: plugin author owns the dispatch.

## Run timing (V1.1)

[Section titled “Run timing (V1.1)”](#run-timing-v11)

V1 always runs `setup` at install / fork time. V1.1 adds a manifest field to control when setup fires:

```json
{
  "provision": {
    "setup": {
      "path": "provision/setup.sh",
      "runAt": "fork"          // "fork" (default) | "install" | "first-action"
    }
  }
}
```

### Behavior per surface when setup hasn’t yet run

[Section titled “Behavior per surface when setup hasn’t yet run”](#behavior-per-surface-when-setup-hasnt-yet-run)

The `setup-required` state affects every plugin surface, not just actions:

| Surface                                         | Behavior when setup hasn’t run                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Action invocation**                           | Substrate returns `{ok: false, error: "setup-required", setupUrl: "..."}`. Matches existing capability-denied shape. UI shows a “this plugin needs initial setup” banner with a one-click button. No UI hang.                                                       |
| **Lifecycle hook fire** (e.g., `onMissionDone`) | Hook event is **queued** (FIFO, capped at 10 events per `(plugin, harness)`). After setup completes within `setupCompletionWindowMin: 30` (default), queued events replay in order. After 30 min or 10-event overflow, dropped events are written to the audit log. |
| **Routine fire** (cron-style scheduled)         | Same queue-and-replay as hooks, with the same 10-event cap.                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Incoming webhook**                            | Substrate responds 503 to the webhook caller. **Not queued** — incoming webhooks shouldn’t accumulate, and the external caller can retry with their own backoff. Audit log records the rejection.                                                                   |

### Queue overflow surfacing

[Section titled “Queue overflow surfacing”](#queue-overflow-surfacing)

The 10-event hook queue cap is a real ceiling. When events are dropped:

* Audit log entry per dropped event (kind, payload, original-fire-time, drop-reason)
* **Persistent badge on the plugin’s settings tile**: “N hook events dropped during setup. \[View audit log]” — until user explicitly acknowledges by clicking the badge

The badge prevents the silent-drop failure mode where the user has no idea their plugin missed events because setup took too long.

### Run-timing options

[Section titled “Run-timing options”](#run-timing-options)

(The shipped SDK `runAt` enum is `'fork' | 'install' | 'first-action'`; `"install"` runs setup at plugin-install time rather than at fork. The `"manual"` mode described here is a design target not yet in the enum.)

`runAt: "manual"` puts setup behind a “Run setup” button in plugin settings, never auto-fires. Useful for heavyweight optional plugins (e.g., a plugin that provisions a managed K8s cluster — defer until the user explicitly opts in).

`runAt: "first-action"` defers setup until the first action / hook / routine that needs it. The first such fire returns `setup-required` (for actions) or queues + prompts (for hooks/routines). Useful for plugins where many users install but only some end up using the provisioned infra.

## Skip-teardown banner (V1.1)

[Section titled “Skip-teardown banner (V1.1)”](#skip-teardown-banner-v11)

When a user picks “skip teardown” during uninstall, the orphan-resources marker is written and the plugin is removed. To prevent silent cost leak (a user who skipped teardown in haste and forgot), the operator’s home tile surfaces a passive banner after 7 days:

```text
You have 3 orphan resources from 2 uninstalled plugins.
   • aws.lambda.function (from @papercupai/aws-lambda, uninstalled 14 days ago)
   • aws.iam.role × 2


Run `papercusp orphans cleanup` to inspect and (optionally) tear them down.
```

No budget enforcement here — that’s V1.1’s `budgetCap` work. This is just visibility for “I forgot I left infra running.” V1.1 line item.

## Plugin “host activity” settings tile (V1)

[Section titled “Plugin “host activity” settings tile (V1)”](#plugin-host-activity-settings-tile-v1)

A plugin that uses both `compute:exec:<bin>` (for in-action shell-outs) *and* `provision.{setup,...}` (for one-time provisioning) has two distinct host-execution surfaces with two consent flows. From the user’s point of view that’s confusing — “this plugin runs scripts on my host” is true twice.

The plugin’s settings tile gains a single **“Host activity”** section listing both:

```text
Host activity
─────────────────────────
Provisioning scripts (one-time, with consent gate):
  ✓ provision/setup.sh    (run 14 days ago, exit 0)
  ✓ provision/verify.sh   (last run 2 min ago, healthy)
    provision/teardown.sh  (not yet run)


In-action shell-outs (runs on every action invocation, capability-gated):
  • git, gh                   (compute:exec:*)
```

Single visual surface, two underlying mechanisms. User sees the full host-activity surface in one place; substrate’s internal capability distinction stays as documented.

## What’s NOT in V1

[Section titled “What’s NOT in V1”](#whats-not-in-v1)

| Item                                        | Why deferred                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `provision.setup.costEstimateAdvisory`      | The two reviewers correctly flagged this as theater: a number with no enforcement is worse than no number. **V1.1** adds `provision.setup.budgetCap: { aws: { monthlyUsd: 5 } }` wired to AWS Budgets via a substrate helper (\~150 LOC, AWS-only). When that lands, costs are *enforced*, not advertised. |
| Layer-7 network proxy with TLS interception | V1 enforces network restrictions via the OS sandbox (bwrap blocks the syscall when a host is undeclared). V2 adds a layer-7 proxy with TLS interception for richer per-request observability.                                                                                                              |
| Encrypted-at-rest token storage             | V1 target is single-user dev/desktop; encryption-at-rest matters for shared-host scenarios that aren’t the V1 target.                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `runAt` scheduling                          | V1.1, per above. V1 always runs at install/fork.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Interactive subprocess support              | V2 may relax with a richer interactive-prompt protocol; V1 forbids.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Per-cloud `budgetCap` helpers beyond AWS    | V2. AWS-Budgets ships in V1.1 as the dogfood; GCP/Azure/Cloudflare follow as plugin authors demand them.                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Marketplace moderation gate                 | The plan acknowledges this as a known gap (no review currently happens at publish time). A separate spec doc will cover the moderation layer.                                                                                                                                                              |

## Open issues moved to dedicated review

[Section titled “Open issues moved to dedicated review”](#open-issues-moved-to-dedicated-review)

The remaining design questions (cross-platform commitments, signing infrastructure rollout, multi-publisher trust accumulation) are in the [Open Questions](./open-questions) page with explicit V1 / V1.1 / V2 disposition.

# OAuth integration

> A generic substrate-level OAuth helper so plugins can mark a credential field as oauth, and users get a "Connect" button instead of pasting tokens. Plugins read tokens via ctx.oauth.token() — substrate handles refresh and 401 retry transparently.

Rounds 2–6 review feedback incorporated

* `ctx.oauth.token(field)` helper — refresh + 401 retry-once transparent to plugin authors
* **Promise-cache for concurrent refresh** — 10 actions firing in parallel share one in-flight refresh request rather than racing
* Pasted tokens (hybrid mode) get **scope verification via provider introspection** before being accepted
* **State is a URL parameter, NOT a cookie** — corrects a wording bug from earlier drafts; concurrent OAuth flows have independent state tokens (HMAC-signed, single-use nonce server-side)
* **Single-tenancy callout** — V1 OAuth assumes single-tenant operators; multi-tenant hosted papercusp.com requires separate OAuth apps per tenant or rate-limit handling (V1.1)
* **Library decision (`arctic`) gated on supply-chain audit** — adopting OAuth library to save LOC is the wrong reason given this plan is about supply-chain hygiene

## Why OAuth

[Section titled “Why OAuth”](#why-oauth)

The current credential UX for BYO plugins is paste-a-token-into-a-field. Users have to:

1. Read the plugin’s docs to learn what scopes they need.
2. Navigate to the provider’s token-creation UI.
3. Manually pick scopes (often selecting too many “to be safe”).
4. Copy-paste a sensitive string.
5. If the token expires, repeat all four steps.

OAuth replaces all of that with one button click. Plus:

* Provider-side audit trail of which app got authorized.
* Refresh-token mechanics for long-lived authorization.
* Standard revocation flow (user revokes papercusp’s app, all derived tokens die).

## Manifest surface

[Section titled “Manifest surface”](#manifest-surface)

A `configSchema` field can declare OAuth support inline:

```json
{
  "github_token": {
    "type": "string",
    "secret": true,
    "oauth": {
      "provider": "github",
      "scopes": ["repo"],
      "tokenType": "access"
    }
  }
}
```

When the operator’s `/settings/plugins` page or the snapshot-fork completion UI sees this annotation, it renders a **Connect with GitHub** button instead of a password input. Click → OAuth dance → field gets populated by the substrate.

The field is still a plain `string` and a plain `secret`. OAuth is just *how* the value gets filled. Plugins that prefer to support both can leave the field editable; users who want to paste a PAT can click “advanced” and do that. (See “Hybrid mode” below.)

### Field reference

[Section titled “Field reference”](#field-reference)

| Field            | Required | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `provider`       | yes      | Must be a substrate-registered provider. V1 supports `github`. V2 adds `slack`, `linear`, `notion`, `jira`.                                                                                                                               |
| `scopes`         | yes      | Array of provider-specific scope strings. The substrate forwards these unchanged in the authorize URL.                                                                                                                                    |
| `tokenType`      | no       | `access` (default), `refresh`, or `both`. Determines what gets stored in the config. `refresh` is required if the plugin needs to operate without re-auth for >24h.                                                                       |
| `userInfoFields` | no       | Optional list of extra fields to populate from the provider’s user-info endpoint, e.g. `["login", "email"]` for GitHub. The substrate writes them as `<field>_user_<key>` in the plugin config (e.g. `github_token_user_login: "alice"`). |

## Substrate-level provider config

[Section titled “Substrate-level provider config”](#substrate-level-provider-config)

Each provider is a one-time platform-owner registration. Config lives at:

```text
~/.papercusp/oauth-apps.json
{
  "github": {
    "clientId": "Iv1.abc123",
    "clientSecretFile": "/etc/papercusp/oauth/github-secret",
    "authorizeUrl": "https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize",
    "tokenUrl": "https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token",
    "userInfoUrl": "https://api.github.com/user",
    "redirectUri": "http://localhost:3055/api/oauth/callback?provider=github"
  }
}
```

Sensitive values (`clientSecret`) live in a separate file with `0600` perms. The substrate reads them at start, never logs them, never includes them in audit output.

For production, `redirectUri` should be HTTPS — `http://localhost` is the dev/desktop default. Production deployments override via `PAPERCUSP_HOST` env var or the substrate’s site config.

## Endpoints

[Section titled “Endpoints”](#endpoints)

```text
GET /api/oauth/start?provider=<p>&plugin=<plug>&harness=<h>&field=<f>
  → 302 to provider authorize URL with HMAC-signed state in the URL `state` parameter


GET /api/oauth/callback?provider=<p>&code=<c>&state=<s>
  → exchanges code for token
  → writes token to plugin's per-harness config[field]
  → redirects to /settings/plugins?connected=<plugin>


POST /api/oauth/verify-paste
  → hybrid mode: introspect a pasted PAT's granted scopes against the
    plugin's required scopes (exact/superset accept, subset reject)
```

### State design (URL parameter, not cookie)

[Section titled “State design (URL parameter, not cookie)”](#state-design-url-parameter-not-cookie)

State lives in the URL `state` parameter end-to-end. **No cookies are used in the OAuth flow.** This means concurrent flows (user opening 3 OAuth tabs simultaneously to install 3 plugins from a fresh fork) have independent state values — no cookie collision is possible.

State token is:

* HMAC-signed with a substrate-only secret
* 5min expiry
* Single-use (server-side nonce table; first callback consumes the nonce)
* Includes `(plugin, harness, field, providerHost)` as keyed claims

The HMAC + nonce combination prevents both CSRF (state can’t be forged without the substrate’s secret) and replay (each state can only be consumed once).

## Provider matrix

[Section titled “Provider matrix”](#provider-matrix)

| Provider   | OAuth available | Scopes for our plugins                                  | Notes                                                                        |
| ---------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| GitHub     | ✓               | `repo` (private + public access), `read:user`           | OAuth App or fine-grained PAT both work; OAuth App is what the spec assumes. |
| Slack      | ✓               | `incoming-webhook`, `chat:write`                        | Each Slack workspace authorizes once.                                        |
| Linear     | ✓               | `read`, `write`                                         | Linear’s OAuth scopes are coarse.                                            |
| Notion     | ✓               | (Notion uses public-integration mode, no scopes per se) | Slightly different flow — no `scope` param, integration ID is the scope.     |
| Jira       | ✓               | `read:jira-work`, `write:jira-work`                     | Atlassian’s OAuth 2.0 (3LO) flow; uses `audience` param.                     |
| Cloudflare | ✗               | —                                                       | CF doesn’t expose OAuth for API tokens. BYO token only.                      |

V1 ships GitHub. V2 sweeps the rest in one PR after the V1 surface is proven.

## Hybrid mode (paste OR connect)

[Section titled “Hybrid mode (paste OR connect)”](#hybrid-mode-paste-or-connect)

Default UX shows the Connect button when `oauth` is declared. But a power user might want to paste a PAT instead (e.g., for a service account). Settings UI offers an “Advanced: paste token” expander:

```text
github_token *
  [ Connect with GitHub ]
  ▼ Advanced


  Or paste a token directly:
  [ ghp_••••••••••••••••••••••• ]
```

### Paste-PAT scope verification

[Section titled “Paste-PAT scope verification”](#paste-pat-scope-verification)

When the user pastes a token, the substrate hits the provider’s introspection endpoint to verify the granted scopes match what the plugin’s manifest requires:

| Provider   | Introspection endpoint                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Notes |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- |
| **GitHub** | `GET /applications/<client_id>/token` (OAuth Apps) — substrate Basic-auths with the OAuth app’s client\_id+secret to inspect any token issued by it. For fine-grained PATs, hit `GET /user` and read the `X-OAuth-Scopes` header. | V1    |
| Slack      | `auth.test` returns scopes in response headers                                                                                                                                                                                    | V2    |
| Linear     | GraphQL `viewer { id }` errors with explicit scope-required messages                                                                                                                                                              | V2    |
| Notion     | `/v1/users/me` echoes integration capabilities                                                                                                                                                                                    | V2    |
| Jira       | `/rest/api/3/myself` + `accessible-resources`                                                                                                                                                                                     | V2    |

Verification rules:

| Granted scopes                                       | Substrate behavior                                                                                                              |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Exactly the requested set                            | Accepted silently                                                                                                               |
| Superset of requested (more permissions than needed) | Accepted with a warning toast: “this token has more scopes than the plugin needs; consider creating a more narrowly-scoped one” |
| Subset of requested (missing required scopes)        | **Rejected.** Toast names the missing scopes. User regenerates and re-pastes.                                                   |
| Token doesn’t belong to this OAuth app’s client\_id  | Rejected for OAuth-app PATs. Allowed for fine-grained PATs (no client\_id binding exists).                                      |

The plain input writes the token to the same config field. The substrate doesn’t care which path produced the token — both end up at `config.github_token`.

## Refresh mechanics

[Section titled “Refresh mechanics”](#refresh-mechanics)

Plugin authors never think about expiry. Instead of reading `config.github_token` directly, action handlers call

```typescript
const token = await ctx.oauth.token('github_token');
const r = await fetch('https://api.github.com/...', {
  headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
});
```

The substrate’s `ctx.oauth.token(field)` helper:

1. Reads the stored token from `config[field]`.
2. Checks `config[field + '_expires_at']`.
3. If `expires_at` is past, or within 5 minutes of expiring, hits the provider’s refresh endpoint *before* returning. Updates `config[field]` and `config[field + '_expires_at']` atomically.
4. Returns the (possibly-refreshed) access token.

If a plugin still gets a 401 from the provider (e.g., the token was revoked between refresh and use), the helper retries once: invalidates the cached token, hits the refresh endpoint fresh, returns the new token. A second 401 surfaces to the plugin as a normal error, plus the substrate flags `oauth_expired: true` on the config so the operator UI shows a “reconnect” button.

### Storage

[Section titled “Storage”](#storage)

For providers that issue refresh tokens (`tokenType: "refresh"` or `"both"`), the substrate stores both the access token and the refresh token plus the access-token expiry:

```json
{
  "github_token": "ghp_access_token",
  "github_token_refresh": "ghp_refresh_token",
  "github_token_expires_at": "2026-05-08T20:14:32Z"
}
```

These fields are siblings inside the same plugin-config JSON. They share the same `secret: true` flag for snapshot purposes (all three are stripped together).

### Concurrent refresh storm

[Section titled “Concurrent refresh storm”](#concurrent-refresh-storm)

If 10 actions fire in parallel and the access token is past `expires_at`, all 10 calls would naively hit the provider’s refresh endpoint simultaneously. Provider rate-limits would bite; some refreshes would fail; the user would see a flurry of “reconnect needed” errors.

The substrate caches an in-flight `Promise<token>` per `(plugin, harness, field)`:

```typescript
// Inside ctx.oauth.token() helper
const inFlight = refreshCache.get(key);
if (inFlight) return inFlight;       // share the in-flight refresh


const promise = doRefresh().finally(() => {
  refreshCache.delete(key);
});
refreshCache.set(key, promise);
return promise;
```

Concurrent callers wait on the same Promise. The first refresh wins; the rest get the result. Provider sees one refresh request, not ten.

### Offline / desktop-laptop scenario

[Section titled “Offline / desktop-laptop scenario”](#offline--desktop-laptop-scenario)

The original draft proposed a 30-minute background job that proactively refreshes near-expired tokens. The reviewer correctly noted that doesn’t help the desktop case where the laptop is closed for a week — the background job hasn’t run, the next action’s first call is past `expires_at`, the plugin gets a 401 with no chance to react.

The `ctx.oauth.token(field)` helper covers this case directly: **every action invocation** does an expiry check + refresh-if-needed before returning the token. The action’s first network call always uses a token that was either fresh enough to skip refresh, or just-refreshed.

The 30-minute background job remains as a *secondary* optimization for long-running operators (so the very first action after a long idle isn’t delayed by the refresh round-trip), but it’s no longer the load-bearing mechanism. Plugins that go through the `ctx.oauth.token()` helper are safe even if the background job never runs.

### When refresh fails

[Section titled “When refresh fails”](#when-refresh-fails)

If refresh fails (revoked authorization, provider outage), the substrate marks the plugin’s config as `oauth_expired: true` and surfaces a “reconnect” button in the plugin’s settings tile. The plugin’s own action handlers can also detect this state by checking `config[field + '_expired']` if they want to show a richer “reconnect needed” message in their own UI.

## Revocation

[Section titled “Revocation”](#revocation)

Two revocation paths:

1. **From the operator UI**: clicking “Disconnect” on a plugin’s settings clears `config[field]` + calls the provider’s revoke endpoint (best-effort) + marks the plugin as needing-auth. (The dedicated disconnect route is not yet broken out as its own endpoint; clearing the field via the existing `PUT /api/plugins/config` path is the current mechanism.)
2. **From the provider’s UI**: user revokes papercusp’s app on github.com → next API call from the plugin returns 401 → substrate marks `oauth_expired: true` → user re-clicks Connect.

Either way, the plugin’s own data on the provider side is preserved; only papercusp’s authorization is gone.

## Implementation

[Section titled “Implementation”](#implementation)

| Surface                                                                  | Change                                                                                                               | LOC   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- |
| `@papercusp/plugin-sdk`                                                  | `oauth` field on the property schema + `PluginOAuthRequirement[]` manifest entries.                                  | \~15  |
| `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/oauth/start.ts`        | Generate state, redirect to provider authorize URL.                                                                  | \~60  |
| `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/oauth/callback.ts`     | Exchange code, fetch user info, write to plugin config.                                                              | \~100 |
| `packages/operator-core/lib/oauth/{providers,token,state,storage-fs}.ts` | Provider registry (GitHub), token-exchange + `ctx.oauth.token()` refresh logic, HMAC state, fs-backed token storage. | \~120 |
| `apps/operator/app/settings/plugins/page.tsx`                            | Render Connect button when `oauth` is declared on a field.                                                           | \~50  |
| `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/oauth/verify-paste.ts` | Hybrid mode — introspect a pasted PAT’s scopes against the plugin’s required scopes.                                 | \~40  |

Total: **\~385 lines.** Slightly bigger than the share-semantics work, slightly smaller than build-scripts. (Implemented: `ctx.oauth.token()` lives in `packages/operator-core/lib/oauth/token.ts`, wired from `plugin-host-runtime.ts`; the three `/api/oauth/*` routes and the provider registry are shipped. A dedicated `/api/oauth/disconnect` route is not yet broken out — see [Revocation](#revocation).)

## Multi-tenancy callout (V1.1)

[Section titled “Multi-tenancy callout (V1.1)”](#multi-tenancy-callout-v11)

V1 OAuth assumes a single-tenant operator (one Papercusp install → one user → one OAuth app per provider). For self-hosted papercusp.com serving multiple users:

* **All users share the same OAuth app’s redirect URI.** GitHub TOS may consider this fine for first-party apps, but rate-limits are per-app, shared across all users. A burst of OAuth flows from one popular template could exhaust the rate limit for everyone.
* **No per-tenant isolation** of OAuth state at rest — all stored at `~/.papercusp/harnesses/<slug>/plugin-configs/<plugin>.json` for the operator’s single user.

V1.1 plan:

* Per-tenant OAuth apps (each tenant registers its own GitHub/Slack/etc. app, recorded in tenant config)
* Per-tenant rate-limit budgeting in the substrate
* Tenant-scoped storage paths

V1 ships single-tenant only. The substrate prints a warning at startup if it detects a multi-user host (per [shared-host detection](./build-scripts#single-user-host-detection)) and recommends self-hosting a separate operator per user.

## Library decision: `arctic` vs roll-our-own

[Section titled “Library decision: arctic vs roll-our-own”](#library-decision-arctic-vs-roll-our-own)

Earlier drafts of this plan proposed adopting `arctic` (Lucia’s OAuth provider library) to save \~150 LOC of provider-specific token-exchange boilerplate. **This is now gated on a supply-chain audit**, given the plan as a whole is about supply-chain hygiene:

| Audit step       | What’s checked                                                                                                |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Direct deps      | How many top-level deps does arctic add? Are they widely-used or boutique?                                    |
| Transitive deps  | Total dep tree size; flag any dep with single-maintainer status or unsigned releases                          |
| Maintainer count | How many active maintainers? Single-maintainer libraries are higher xz-utils-precedent risk                   |
| Signing posture  | Does `arctic` publish signed npm releases? Provenance attestations?                                           |
| Coverage         | Does arctic cover Atlassian 3LO including the `audience` parameter quirk?                                     |
| Lock posture     | Pin the exact arctic version + record sha256 in substrate’s lockfile; explicit re-audit on every version bump |

Outcomes:

* **Arctic passes audit** → adopt with audit recorded as a `LIBRARY_AUDIT.md` entry. V1 OAuth ships with arctic. Total OAuth surface \~250 LOC (was 385).
* **Arctic fails audit** → roll our own provider implementations. V1 OAuth ships with \~385 LOC of in-house provider modules. Slightly more substrate code but zero new supply-chain link.

The wrong path is “adopt arctic to hit the LOC budget without doing the audit.” LOC is not a hard target; supply-chain hygiene is.

## Open questions

[Section titled “Open questions”](#open-questions)

1. **Where does the OAuth client\_secret live?** A separate `~/.papercusp/oauth/<provider>-secret` file with `0600` perms is what’s proposed. Some operators may prefer environment variables (k8s-style). Should both be supported?
2. **Multi-tenancy**: if the operator is hosted publicly (not self-hosted), every user shares the same OAuth app’s redirect URI. Is that fine? Or do we shard providers per tenant?
3. **PKCE**: required for public clients. Substrate is a confidential client (has a secret), so PKCE is optional but harmless. Probably worth implementing for defense-in-depth.
4. **Token storage at rest**: tokens currently land in plain JSON in `~/.papercusp/harnesses/<slug>/plugin-configs/<plugin>.json`. For a multi-user host, encrypting at rest would matter. Out of V1 scope?
5. **Per-plugin OR per-harness OR per-user authorization**: GitHub OAuth gives the same access regardless of which harness asks; we just write the token to a different per-harness config. Should the substrate offer to *share* an authorization across harnesses (one GitHub Connect, applies to all your harnesses)? Trade-off: convenience vs. blast radius if one harness’s config leaks.

See [Open Questions](./open-questions).

# Open questions and V1/V1.1/V2 split

> Each design decision rated by impact and assigned to V1 (gates "safe to release publicly"), V1.1 (improves the system, ships fast-follow), or V2 (separate workstream). Updated through round 6.

Rounds 2–6 review feedback incorporated

Six review rounds have shaped this list. The V1 set has grown from the original \~1,500 LOC estimate to **\~2,000–2,100 LOC honest** as defensive features (PG lock, bwrap smoke test, helper library, security advisory consultation, key-rotation attestation) have been folded in. The V1 launch criterion has also been **reframed**: “vetted-publisher alpha” not “public marketplace launch” — the latter requires the moderation layer covered in V1.1+.

Send sign-off reviewers to the [sign-off checklist](#sign-off-checklist) at the bottom.

V1 launch criterion: “**shippable to a vetted-publisher alpha** where the worst a malicious vetted-publisher can do is fail at the consent gate or be sandboxed.” Anything that fails to meet that criterion is V1; anything that improves the system but isn’t a security or correctness gate is V1.1+.

Public marketplace launch is V1.1+, gated on the moderation layer.

## V1 — gates “safe to release to a vetted-publisher alpha”

[Section titled “V1 — gates “safe to release to a vetted-publisher alpha””](#v1--gates-safe-to-release-to-a-vetted-publisher-alpha)

### Idempotency, safety, sandboxing

[Section titled “Idempotency, safety, sandboxing”](#idempotency-safety-sandboxing)

| Item                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Why V1                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Idempotency contract: done-marker hashes `(configHash, scriptHash, pluginVersion)`; `aliases` for renames + `null` for removals; structural fields default to forcing re-provision; `skipReprovisionOnPatch` governs `pluginVersion` only, never `scriptHash` | Re-runs silently corrupt state; edits to `region`/`accountId` orphan resources; a malicious patch with same major.minor and `skipReprovisionOnPatch: true` cannot slip through because the script-hash always forces re-consent |
| Sandbox by default for *all* scripts                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Without it, build scripts are an unconditioned arbitrary-code-execution vector for any approved publisher (npm event-stream / xz-utils precedent). Signing proves provenance, not safety.                                       |
| **Linux: bwrap with bundled binary + install-time smoke test**                                                                                                                                                                                                | Bundled bwrap covers distro variance; smoke test catches kernels with disabled unprivileged user namespaces. Failure → permanent `sandbox_available: false` → signed-only mode for substrate’s lifetime                         |
| **macOS: sandbox-exec + signed-only mode (no unsigned scripts at all)**                                                                                                                                                                                       | sandbox-exec is deprecated but functional — meaningful boundary against accidents. Refusing unsigned scripts on macOS plugs the “unsigned + no real sandbox” gap                                                                |
| **Network policy floor**: 169.254.0.0/16, 127.0.0.0/8, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, ::1, fd00::/8 always blocked, regardless of `allowedHosts` or `cloudProvider`                                                                                             | Closes IMDS-credential exfiltration and lateral-movement attack classes                                                                                                                                                         |
| **`cloudProvider: { id, region }` presets** with monthly signed update channel + region templating                                                                                                                                                            | Replaces the old `network: "open"` mode which gave plugins effectively unbounded outbound network access. Per-region presets close the cross-region leak surface.                                                               |
| **Static-analysis warnings** on common destructive patterns (`curl \| bash`, `sudo`, `rm -rf $HOME`, `eval` of untrusted input, `chmod -R 777`, base64-blob-smuggle)                                                                                          | Cheap and high-signal; catches “I copy-pasted destructive command and didn’t notice” failure mode                                                                                                                               |

### Trust, signing, and consent

[Section titled “Trust, signing, and consent”](#trust-signing-and-consent)

| Item                                                                                                                                 | Why V1                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Trust granularity per-(publisher, plugin)** keyed on signing-key fingerprint                                                       | Coarser-grained trust silently gives @publisher’s malicious new plugin the same trust as their existing benign one                                                                |
| **Ownership transfer invalidates trust** — different `publisher_id` on a new version triggers fresh consent                          | Closes the xz-utils-in-miniature attack class                                                                                                                                     |
| **Key rotation events must be marketplace-countersigned**                                                                            | ”Publisher rotated their key, re-trust?” prompt is otherwise a phishing surface; without marketplace’s infrastructure-key signature the prompt is just trust-me-bro-from-attacker |
| **Quarantine clears trust** for the affected `(publisher, plugin)`. Publisher-key compromise advisory clears all of `(publisher, *)` | Cached trust must die when marketplace flags anything bad                                                                                                                         |
| **`papercusp plugin install --dev`** path with per-machine ad-hoc signing key + `dev: true` trust flag                               | Plugin authors can iterate on macOS / signed-only platforms without publishing each save to a marketplace                                                                         |

### Recovery, lifecycle, observability

[Section titled “Recovery, lifecycle, observability”](#recovery-lifecycle-observability)

| Item                                                                                                                                                | Why V1                                                                                                                                                                      |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **PG-backed `harness_shared.operator_claims`** for setup locking with PG advisory locks + heartbeat-renewed `expires_at`                            | File-based locks don’t survive multi-machine harness sharing (laptop ↔ desktop split-brain)                                                                                 |
| **`papercusp_record_resource <kind> <id>`** helper that writes to `state.json` immediately                                                          | Plugin authors aren’t infra engineers; partial-failure rollback should not require defensive idempotency-handling logic in setup.sh                                         |
| **Recovery contract**: stale-lock detection prompts cleanup before re-trying setup; partial-failure offers automatic teardown of recorded resources | Killed/crashed setup leaves undiagnosable orphan resources                                                                                                                  |
| **Teardown contract**: plugin’s `teardown.sh` is the dispatcher; receives recorded resource list via `state.json` and dispatches per `kind`         | Locks Path 1 explicitly so plugin authors don’t ship empty teardown.sh assuming substrate magic                                                                             |
| **OAuth `ctx.oauth.token(field)` helper** with pre-emptive refresh + 401 retry-once + Promise-cache for concurrent-refresh storm                    | Every plugin reinvents refresh logic poorly; offline-laptop case produces inscrutable failures; concurrent calls without Promise-cache race the provider’s refresh endpoint |
| **PAT scope introspection** (V1 GitHub)                                                                                                             | Hybrid-mode pastes silently produce under-scoped tokens that break action handlers at runtime                                                                               |
| **OAuth state in URL parameter, not cookie** (HMAC + single-use nonce)                                                                              | Cookies collide on concurrent flows; URL state is per-flow by construction                                                                                                  |
| **Hook / routine queue-and-replay** when fired before setup completes; queue cap of 10 with persistent badge on overflow                            | Without queueing, hooks silently fail; with silent overflow, user has no signal                                                                                             |
| **Webhook reject** (503) when fired before setup completes; not queued                                                                              | Incoming webhooks shouldn’t accumulate; external caller retries with their own backoff                                                                                      |

### Snapshot, schema, identity

[Section titled “Snapshot, schema, identity”](#snapshot-schema-identity)

| Item                                                                                                                                                             | Why V1                                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Schema evolution**: per-property `aliases` array for both renames (`["oldName"]`) and removals (`[null]`), walked from current installed plugin’s manifest     | A single plugin version bump silently breaks every snapshot pinned to the old version                                                             |
| **`versionPin: { mode: "exact" }` is the reproducible default** (legacy `pluginVersionPinned: true` maps to it)                                                  | Pinning is the right default; alias-walk only happens on explicit “fork against latest” opt-in. Drastically reduces alias-map maintenance burden. |
| **`securityAdvisories` field** on marketplace catalog per-version; fork-time prompt loud when pinned version has open advisory                                   | Pinning a vulnerable version is otherwise a vulnerability vector                                                                                  |
| **`secret`** + **`snapshotPolicy: "include" \| "strip" \| "warn-and-prompt"`** with strip default; `--include-secrets` flag at publish + per-secret confirmation | Plugin authors otherwise hardcode secrets into project files for demos, defeating the purpose                                                     |
| **`shareable: false`** + JSON-Schema `pattern` for format validation by convention                                                                               | Format validation prevents fork-time typos in account IDs, region names, etc.                                                                     |
| **Snapshot manifest `requiresProvisioning: true`** + plugin-version pinning at fork against marketplace tampering                                                | Substrate has no signal to gate the consent flow; tampered plugin tarballs bypass the signed-manifest chain                                       |
| **Tarball format change** (additive `.shape.json` companions) explicitly acknowledged                                                                            | Even additive changes are format changes; backward-compat is “no `.shape.json` = all fields shareable”                                            |

### Audit, hosts, and policy

[Section titled “Audit, hosts, and policy”](#audit-hosts-and-policy)

| Item                                                                                                                                                                                          | Why V1                                                                                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Audit log defaults**: 1 year retention, 50 MB per (harness, plugin) cap, oldest-first eviction; **per-plugin `auditLogCapMb` override** in manifest surfaced in consent dialog              | Forensic logs consulted months later; legitimate terraform-class plugins need higher caps with explicit consent        |
| **Audit log fail-loud** on encrypted-locked filesystems                                                                                                                                       | Silent audit-swallowing is a worse failure mode than refusing to run                                                   |
| **Single-user host detection**: primary `who \| sort -u \| wc -l > 1`; secondary passwd UID-≥-1000 + `/home/<n>/` + login-shell filter; one-time acknowledgement banner on shared-host        | V1 explicitly targets single-user dev/desktop; without enforcement, threat model silently doesn’t hold on shared hosts |
| **Vetted-publisher allowlist process documented**: GitHub issue at github.com/papercupai/papercusp-publishers; reviewed within N business days; allowlist published; appeals via issue thread | Without a public process, “vetted alpha” is opaque-by-default — defeats the moderation framing                         |
| **Interactive-subprocess ban**: `requiresInteractive: false` enforced; substrate refuses scripts that read from stdin or open browsers mid-run                                                | `aws sso login`-style scripts hang the operator with no UI feedback                                                    |
| **Visibility-aware `verify` polling**: foreground-only by default, no periodic background polling unless explicitly opted in                                                                  | 5 plugins × 100 harnesses × 10-min polling = 3,000 cloud-API calls/hour just for health checks; rate-limit collateral  |
| **Plugin “host activity” settings tile**: shows both `compute:exec:*` and `provision.*` surfaces side-by-side                                                                                 | ”This plugin runs scripts on my host” was true twice via two consent flows; single tile reduces confusion              |

**V1 LOC honest total: \~2,000–2,100 LOC.** Adopting `arctic` for OAuth (post supply-chain audit) reduces by \~150 LOC.

## V1.1 — improves the system, ships fast-follow

[Section titled “V1.1 — improves the system, ships fast-follow”](#v11--improves-the-system-ships-fast-follow)

| Item                                                                                                                           | Why deferred                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Phasing inversion (share-semantics PR before OAuth PR)                                                                         | Pure PR ordering, not new code                                                                                                |
| Cost: drop field for V1, add `provision.setup.budgetCap` + AWS-Budgets helper                                                  | Real feature with teeth; \~150 LOC plus per-cloud helpers. Dropping for V1 is the right call (no enforcement = theater)       |
| `compute:exec:*` vs build-scripts docs clarification                                                                           | Pure docs; V1 substrate ships, V1.1 adds the explanatory cross-references                                                     |
| Audit log policy formalization + browse-logs UI                                                                                | V1 ships sane defaults; V1.1 adds settings UI                                                                                 |
| `runAt: "fork" \| "install" \| "first-action"` for `provision.setup` (shipped SDK enum; `"manual"` is a further design target) | V1 always runs at fork; V1.1 adds the install / first-action escape hatches                                                   |
| Skip-teardown 7-day passive banner (“you have N orphan resources”)                                                             | Visibility-only; not a safety gate                                                                                            |
| github-repo dogfood (re-implement repo creation as build script)                                                               | Smaller dogfood than cloudflare-pages-hosted; exercises full stack (OAuth + share-semantics + provisioning) more economically |
| **Marketplace moderation layer** (separate spec doc)                                                                           | V1 ships safely under vetted-publisher alpha; public marketplace launch is V1.1+ gated on moderation                          |
| **Per-tenant OAuth multi-tenancy** (separate OAuth apps per tenant; per-tenant rate-limit budgets; tenant-scoped storage)      | V1 single-tenant. Multi-tenant hosted papercusp.com is V1.1+                                                                  |
| Cross-platform per-script paths: `setup.path.linux` / `setup.path.darwin`; bashism linter at publish time                      | V1 supports a single platform-agnostic `setup.path`; V1.1 adds explicit per-platform with linter                              |
| Copy-edit: sync index.mdx vs open-questions.mdx                                                                                | Trivially fixable                                                                                                             |

**V1.1 LOC: \~500.**

## V2 — separate workstreams

[Section titled “V2 — separate workstreams”](#v2--separate-workstreams)

| Item                                                                                            | Why V2                                                                                                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **macOS Tauri sidecar with restricted entitlements** (`Info.plist`-declared)                    | Defense-in-depth on top of V1’s sandbox-exec; the operator already runs on Tauri so the surface exists                                          |
| Per-cloud `budgetCap` helpers beyond AWS (GCP, Azure, Cloudflare)                               | Ship AWS in V1.1; add others as plugin authors demand                                                                                           |
| Layer-7 network policy proxy with TLS interception                                              | V1 enforces via OS sandbox + cloudProvider presets; V2 adds richer per-request observability (requires CA cert provisioning, real install pain) |
| Encrypted-at-rest token storage                                                                 | Only matters for shared-host scenarios that aren’t the V1 target                                                                                |
| AST-level static analysis on provision scripts                                                  | V1 pattern matcher catches dumb-pattern attacks; AST-level catches more sophisticated ones (per-language parsers required)                      |
| Windows sandboxing (Job objects + restricted tokens)                                            | V1 is Linux-primary, macOS-supported, Windows-banner-only                                                                                       |
| Substrate-level teardown dispatcher (substrate knows how to delete `aws.lambda.function`, etc.) | V1 keeps `teardown.sh` as the dispatcher; V2 adds built-in handlers for common kinds                                                            |

## Sign-off checklist

[Section titled “Sign-off checklist”](#sign-off-checklist)

Before V1 implementation begins, these need explicit sign-off:

* [ ] **V1 list above is the full set** — anything in V1.1 that should actually be V1?
* [ ] **V1 line-count target (\~2,000–2,100 LOC)** is realistic
* [ ] **Sandbox-by-default for all scripts** is the locked design
* [ ] **`bwrap` bundling + install-time smoke test** — substrate ships its own copy
* [ ] **macOS: signed-only mode + sandbox-exec, no unsigned-script path** in V1
* [ ] **`PAPERCUSP_DEV_UNSIGNED=<sha256>`** + `papercusp plugin install --dev` is the only macOS dev escape
* [ ] **Network policy floor (IMDS + RFC1918 + loopback) always blocks**, regardless of `allowedHosts` or `cloudProvider`
* [ ] **`cloudProvider` presets with region templating** + monthly signed update channel
* [ ] **Trust per-(publisher, plugin)** keyed on signing-key fingerprint
* [ ] **Ownership transfer invalidates trust**
* [ ] **Key-rotation events marketplace-countersigned**
* [ ] **Cost field dropped from V1**; budget enforcement comes via real `budgetCap` helper in V1.1
* [ ] **Audit retention defaults** (1y / 50MB cap) + `auditLogCapMb` per-plugin override + fail-loud on encrypted-locked volumes
* [ ] **`aliases` covers both renames and removals**
* [ ] **`versionPin: { mode: "exact" }` is the reproducible default** (legacy `pluginVersionPinned: true` maps to it); security advisories prompt loudly at fork
* [ ] **`runAt: "first-action"` synchronization contract** (action returns `setup-required`; hooks queued + replayed; webhooks 503’d) is the locked design
* [ ] **Default for structural-vs-operational fields is `structural`**
* [ ] **`papercusp_record_resource` helper** + plugin’s `teardown.sh` as dispatcher
* [ ] **PG-based `operator_claims` lock** (not file-based) for multi-machine fork safety
* [ ] **`who`-based shared-host detection** + one-time acknowledgement banner
* [ ] **Vetted-publisher allowlist process documented** as part of V1 launch criterion
* [ ] **`arctic` adoption gated on supply-chain audit**; rolled-our-own is the fallback
* [ ] **Phasing**: share-semantics + OAuth ship in one PR; build-scripts in a second PR
* [ ] **V1.1 follow-up list** is acceptable as fast-follow

Once these are checked, implementation begins. The order is:

1. **PR 1** (\~600 LOC): Snapshot share-semantics + OAuth substrate + GitHub provider + `ctx.oauth.token()` helper + paste-PAT scope check + version pinning (`versionPin`) + security-advisory consultation
2. **PR 2** (\~1,400–1,500 LOC): Build-script lifecycle (manifest, runner, sandbox with bwrap-bundling + smoke test, audit, recovery via PG, consent flow, cloudProvider presets, network floor, trust per-(publisher, plugin) with rotation/transfer, hook queue-and-replay, single-user-host detection, helper library) + dogfooded against the existing `cloudflare-pages-hosted` Worker deploy
3. **PR 3** (V1.1 onward): github-repo refactored to use build scripts + `runAt` scheduling + `budgetCap` + AWS-Budgets helper + skip-teardown banner + marketplace moderation layer (separate spec)

## Long-tail design questions

[Section titled “Long-tail design questions”](#long-tail-design-questions)

1. **`secret: true` implying `shareable: false`?** Round-1 reviewer said keep separate. Standing.
2. **Array-shaped configs** (`apiKeys: [...]`) — fine to require named-field objects.
3. **`.shape.json` location** — next to the redacted config.
4. **PKCE for OAuth** — defense-in-depth, V1.1.
5. **OAuth client\_secret storage** — V1 supports both `clientSecretFile` (`0600`) and env-var.
6. **Concurrent setup for multi-plugin snapshots** — V1 sequential; `parallel: true` opt-in deferred.
7. **`state.json` resource validation** — V1 trusts the script; plugin authors build into `verify`.
