* It does not bypass capability checks. A plugin that needs `secrets:read:FOO` in production needs it in dev too.
* It does not change the wire format of any DI service or hook payload. What works in dev works in install — modulo environment differences.
* It does not auto-publish. Publishing is always `papercusp publish`, an explicit user action.

**Plugin SDK scaffolding.**

```plaintext
$ papercusp plugin init my-plugin --template cloudflare-stack


==> Creating ./my-plugin/
package.json
papercusp.json
index.cjs
provision/setup.sh
README.md
...


==> Done. Next:
cd my-plugin && papercusp plugin lint
```

`papercusp plugin init` copies an existing reference plugin (default `cloudflare-stack`) and rewrites every reference to the new slug; `—template <slug>` picks a different starter and `—from-path <dir>` forks a local checkout. Because the scaffold is a real first-party plugin under `libs/papercusp/plugins/`, the output is verifiable from source.

# 14. Plugin marketplace — design proposal (v1, post-review-round-2)

Status: historical design record — superseded by the in-app Cupboard

This page is the original design rationale for a standalone plugin marketplace. The plugin **distribution** model it proposes (a `kind` discriminator on `papercusp.json`, install-time capability consent, per-harness enable, the `actions` primitive, lockfiles) has shipped — but the storefront is now the **in-app Cupboard** (`apps/operator-public` = `@papercusp/cupboard-worker`, a Cloudflare Worker + D1, live at `cupboard.papercusp.com`), not a `papercuspai.com/marketplace/` site. The Cupboard is a single catalog with four listing **kinds** — `plugin` (install), `blueprint` (fork), `snapshot` (fork), and `harness` (join) — exposed over HTTP (`/api/cupboard/*`), with no `cupboard:*` MCP verbs. Plugins install to `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/<slug>/` and mount under `/api/plugins/<name>/`. Treat the URLs, package names (`papercusp-marketplace`, `papercusp-plugin-sdk`), and `~/.papercusp/installed/` paths below as the historical proposal’s wording, not current identifiers; the concepts map onto the Cupboard. Read this for the *why*; see the [authoring quickstart](/internal/docs/spec/plugin-quickstart) for the *how* today.

## 14.0 Why this exists

[Section titled “14.0 Why this exists”](#140-why-this-exists)

The marketplace today distributes **harness templates** — reusable recipes that spin up concrete harness instances (papercup-coding, papercup-org). They ship with their own roles, model preferences, and project layout.

But templates can’t share **integrations**. If `papercup-coding` wants “one-click publish to Cloudflare Pages”, that integration is either baked into the template (forcing every coding harness in the world to know about Cloudflare) or has to be implemented separately by every template author. Same for vscode-server, Slack notifications, Postgres schema management, etc.

This is why every mature plugin ecosystem has a **plugin marketplace** distinct from a **theme/template marketplace**: WordPress separates plugins from themes; VS Code separates extensions from project templates; Backstage separates plugins from app shells.

Papercusp needs the same split. Templates are recipes; plugins are horizontal capabilities that any template can pull in.

## 14.1 Templates vs plugins — the ontological split

[Section titled “14.1 Templates vs plugins — the ontological split”](#141-templates-vs-plugins--the-ontological-split)

|                | **Harness template**                                           | **Plugin**                                                              |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| What it is     | Recipe for spinning up a harness                               | Horizontal capability any harness can use                               |
| Cardinality    | 1 template → N harness instances                               | 1 plugin install → mounted into N harness instances                     |
| Install scope  | Per-instance (each `papercusp run` produces a fresh instance)  | Per-machine (installed globally; enabled per harness instance)          |
| Examples       | papercup-coding, papercup-org, “research-org”, “habit-tracker” | cloudflare-pages, vscode-server, slack-notifier, gemini-narrator        |
| Composition    | One template per harness                                       | Multiple plugins per harness instance                                   |
| Manifest field | `kind: 'template'` (default)                                   | `kind: 'plugin'`                                                        |
| Closest analog | WordPress *themes*; npm-create-\*                              | WordPress *plugins*; VS Code *extensions*                               |
| Lifecycle hook | `papercusp run` — instantiates a harness from the template     | Substrate boot — discovers + mounts global-plugins for active harnesses |

Both share the marketplace pipeline (catalog, signing, retraction, namespaces, reviews, SBOMs, authors, webhooks). They diverge only in the runtime model: templates produce instances; plugins extend instances.

## 14.2 Research summary — 8 plugin systems studied

[Section titled “14.2 Research summary — 8 plugin systems studied”](#142-research-summary--8-plugin-systems-studied)

| System             | Sandbox                                         | Capability model                                                        | Distribution                          | Hook system                                       | Composition                              |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| **VS Code**        | Out-of-process extension host + iframe webviews | Manifest `activationEvents` + `contributes`; \~30 surfaces              | Bespoke marketplace, \~50k extensions | Typed event API (`vscode.workspace.onDidChange*`) | `extensionDependencies`                  |
| **WordPress**      | None                                            | None (full host privileges)                                             | Bespoke + npm-style; 60k+ plugins     | `add_action` / `add_filter` priority numbers      | Hook-priority composition                |
| **Backstage**      | None                                            | DI container `ApiRef` typed services                                    | npm packages, build-time              | React context + DI                                | Plugins ship npm packages with peer-deps |
| **Figma**          | iframe + UI iframe + manifest network allowlist | Strongest of survey: manifest declares network domains; iframe enforces | Bespoke marketplace                   | postMessage RPC                                   | Limited                                  |
| **Obsidian**       | None (full Node + DOM)                          | All-or-nothing at install (cautionary tale)                             | Bespoke “community plugins”           | Vault events + Plugin API                         | Plugins commonly conflict                |
| **Slack apps**     | Hosted webhook                                  | OAuth scopes (coarse)                                                   | App directory                         | Event subscriptions                               | None                                     |
| **Astro / Vite**   | None (build-time)                               | None                                                                    | npm                                   | Build hooks                                       | Linear pipeline                          |
| **Probot / Hubot** | Hosted GitHub App / chat bot                    | Coarse permissions                                                      | npm scaffolding                       | Webhook events                                    | Each app independent                     |

### The two failure modes to avoid

[Section titled “The two failure modes to avoid”](#the-two-failure-modes-to-avoid)

1. **Obsidian / WordPress’s “no sandbox”** — host trivially exploitable by malicious or buggy plugin. Both retroactively bolted on capability prompts.
2. **Backstage’s “build-time only”** — installs require rebuild + redeploy. Backstage 2.0 is rebuilding the plugin model around runtime loading.

Papercusp’s spec already commits to: iframe sandboxing for v2 UI plugins (Figma’s model), runtime install with capability consent (Chrome Web Store style), capability strings at the DI boundary (VS Code × Cap’n Proto). This proposal builds on that foundation.

## 14.3 The four design pillars

[Section titled “14.3 The four design pillars”](#143-the-four-design-pillars)

### 14.3.1 Reuse the marketplace pipeline; add a `kind` discriminator

[Section titled “14.3.1 Reuse the marketplace pipeline; add a kind discriminator”](#1431-reuse-the-marketplace-pipeline-add-a-kind-discriminator)

`papercusp.json` adds:

```json
{ "kind": "plugin", "name": "@papercupai/cloudflare-pages", "version": "0.1.0", ... }
```

`papercusp publish` is kind-agnostic. The catalog stores `kind` in the package row. The marketplace site filters at `/marketplace/?kind=template|plugin` (default both). Search and authors all work without code changes.

`papercusp install` checks the `kind`:

* `template` → registers in `~/.papercusp/registry.json` (already implemented)
* `plugin` → unpacks to `~/.papercusp/global-plugins/<slug>/` (already implemented in plugin-loader); the substrate’s plugin-runtime mounts on next `papercusp run`

Both flows go through the same publish + signing + retraction infrastructure. Operators get the same ops dashboard counts. Authors see “5 templates and 12 plugins published” on their profile.

### 14.3.2 Plugin lifecycle: install-time consent, harness-time mount

[Section titled “14.3.2 Plugin lifecycle: install-time consent, harness-time mount”](#1432-plugin-lifecycle-install-time-consent-harness-time-mount)

A plugin is **installed once globally** — capability-consent prompt at that point. Then **mounted at runtime** into every harness instance whose template `requires` it (or that the user enables via `papercusp plugin enable cloudflare-pages --harness sheets-clone`).

This matches WordPress’s “active plugins per site” + Backstage’s “plugins mounted into the app”.

### 14.3.3 New primitive: `actions` (button-shaped, presence-determined runtime)

[Section titled “14.3.3 New primitive: actions (button-shaped, presence-determined runtime)”](#1433-new-primitive-actions-button-shaped-presence-determined-runtime)

The current SDK has hooks, routes, UI, routines, schema. Missing: a user-triggered action that the harness UI can surface as a button.

```typescript
export interface ActionDefinition {
  /** Stable name within the plugin. */
  name: string;
  /** Display label in UI. */
  label: string;
  /** Lucide icon name. */
  icon?: string;
  /** Where to surface — multiple allowed. Per-id capabilities gate each surface. */
  surfaces: Array<'harness-sidebar' | 'harness-toolbar' | 'feature-row'>;
  /** Capabilities required (must be a subset of plugin's manifest capabilities). */
  capabilities: Capability[];
  /** JSON schema for parameters; UI auto-generates a form (see §14.3.5). */
  paramsSchema?: JsonSchema;
  /** Maximum execution time. Defaults to 30s. */
  defaultTimeoutSec?: number;


  /**
   * Server-side declaration. Presence (alone or alongside `clientHandler`)
   * determines that this action has a server runtime. The actual handler is
   * registered imperatively from the plugin's `init()` via
   * `plugin.actions.register(name, handler)`. The manifest carries no
   * function references — they don't survive serialization or postMessage.
   */
  serverHandler?: { timeoutSec?: number };


  /**
   * Client-side declaration. Presence determines that this action has a
   * client runtime. The component is mounted in the iframe's plugin-bridge
   * and the click is dispatched to it.
   */
  clientHandler?: { component: string };


  // Note: actions are strictly USER-CLICKED. There is no `autoOn` field.
  // To auto-fire an action on a substrate event (e.g. `mission.done`), the
  // plugin ships a routine that internally invokes the same handler the
  // action button calls. One trigger registry (routines), one event
  // capability namespace (`events:listen:*`), one audit trail.
}
```

**Runtime is presence-determined**:

* `serverHandler` only → server runtime (Node-only, full DI, capability-checked)

* `clientHandler` only → client runtime (iframe, postMessage RPC, network-bound capabilities)

* Both present → **hybrid** (substrate routes preview to client, commit to server)

  * **v1 rejects manifests with both** at load time, with a clear `not-yet-implemented: hybrid actions` error
  * **v1.5 lifts the rejection** — no manifest schema change at any point

This pattern mirrors VS Code’s `contributes.commands` (declarative) + `commands.registerCommand` (imperative). It avoids the “function in JSON manifest” trap and keeps a clean migration path to iframe sandboxing.

Three properties make actions worth their own primitive vs reusing routines/hooks:

1. **They’re user-discoverable.** A button in the dashboard. Routines and hooks are invisible to the end user.
2. **They have parameters.** A “Publish” button needs to know the target. JSON-schema → auto-form.
3. **They have execution status.** Async with a progress indicator. Routines fire-and-forget; hooks are passive.

WordPress has admin actions, VS Code has commands, Slack has slash commands, Backstage has Actions Catalog. We need our equivalent.

### 14.3.4 Capability consent UI at install time

[Section titled “14.3.4 Capability consent UI at install time”](#1434-capability-consent-ui-at-install-time)

```plaintext
Install @papercupai/cloudflare-pages 0.1.0?


You are installing a plugin — it will be enabled into your harness instances
and run alongside the template's logic.


This plugin will be granted:
  ▸ HIGH   secrets:read:CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN
           — read your Cloudflare API token at deploy time
  ▸ MEDIUM http:fetch:api.cloudflare.com
           — make HTTPS requests to Cloudflare's API
  ▸ LOW    ui:harness-action:publish
           — register a "Publish" button in your harness dashboard
  ▸ LOW    ui:harness-sidebar:cloudflare-publish
           — claim the "cloudflare-publish" sidebar slot
  ▸ LOW    storage:plugin-private
           — store deploy history in plugin-private filesystem


Tier summary (per §10.6.1): 1 high · 1 medium · 3 low


Signed by: @papercupai (verified)
SBOM: no known CVEs (scanned 2026-04-27)


[Install]  [Cancel]
```

Adapted from Chrome Web Store / iOS App Store consent screens, using the capability tiers we already have (§10.6.1). The first line names what kind of artifact is being installed (plugin vs template) so users understand the runtime implications.

### 14.3.5 Capability granularity — per-id everywhere

[Section titled “14.3.5 Capability granularity — per-id everywhere”](#1435-capability-granularity--per-id-everywhere)

All UI capabilities are **per-id**, matching the per-id collision-resolution rule from §10.5. A plugin claiming `ui:dashboard-tab:foo` can mount one tab named `foo`; mounting `bar` requires a separate `ui:dashboard-tab:bar` capability.

This makes the consent prompt name what’s actually being claimed:

| Capability                | What it grants                                        |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `ui:dashboard-tab:<id>`   | One tab in the dashboard tab strip                    |
| `ui:sidebar-item:<id>`    | One sidebar entry in the harness chrome               |
| `ui:harness-action:<id>`  | One action surface (button, menu item)                |
| `ui:harness-route:<slug>` | One full-route mount under `/harness/<slug>`          |
| `ui:plugin-config-panel`  | Override the auto-generated config form (see §14.3.7) |

The previous coarse `ui:dashboard-tab` (no id) was *proposed* for removal here. In the shipped SDK, the coarse no-id forms (`ui:dashboard-tab`, `ui:sidebar-item`, `ui:harness-route`, `ui:tui-pane`) are what landed — the per-id capability granularity in this section is design intent, not the current `Capability` type.

### 14.3.6 Server-runtime resource isolation

[Section titled “14.3.6 Server-runtime resource isolation”](#1436-server-runtime-resource-isolation)

Server-runtime action handlers run as Node code inside the substrate process. The iframe sandbox (§10.4) does not apply. To prevent one plugin from degrading the whole harness:

* **Per-action timeout** — `defaultTimeoutSec` on the action (default 30s); substrate cancels via `AbortSignal` threaded through `ctx.signal`.
* **No `process:spawn` capability in v1** — see §14.3.6.1 below.
* **Soft heap budget** — substrate polls `process.memoryUsage()` per harness; if a plugin’s RSS jumps >256 MB above its baseline during a handler call, the action is cancelled and the harness logs a budget violation.
* **Postgres connection cap** — plugin’s `ctx.db` proxy holds at most one connection per concurrent action invocation; long-running queries get the same `AbortSignal` as the action.

#### 14.3.6.1 No `process:spawn` capability in v1

[Section titled “14.3.6.1 No process:spawn capability in v1”](#14361-no-processspawn-capability-in-v1)

A `process:spawn` capability — even per-binary (`process:spawn:git`) — is unsafe. Common binaries have config flags that spawn other binaries (`git -c core.fsmonitor=<attacker-binary>` is the canonical example; the same trick works for `ssh`, `docker`, `npm`, `node`). Per-(binary, args-pattern) capabilities would re-implement sudoers, which is not a thing we want to maintain.

Instead, follow the architecture §10 already commits to: every capability resolves to a method on a substrate-provided typed service. Apply the same posture for subprocess needs:

* **v1 has no `process:spawn` capability.**
* The substrate offers typed wrappers for the common cases: `git: GitService`, `docker: DockerService`, `shell: { execTrustedCommand(name: TrustedBinary, args) }` where `TrustedBinary` is a substrate-curated enum.
* Plugins that need a binary that isn’t wrapped → contribute an SPI extension upstream, or live without it in v1.

`process:spawn` can be revisited in v1.5 if real plugins prove the typed-service approach insufficient. Don’t lead with the foot-cannon.

### 14.3.7 paramsSchema / configSchema dialect commitment

[Section titled “14.3.7 paramsSchema / configSchema dialect commitment”](#1437-paramsschema--configschema-dialect-commitment)

Every place this proposal says “UI auto-generates a form” needs a precise contract or it silently degrades to “we ship a generic form, every serious plugin overrides it” (the WordPress experience).

**Commitments:**

1. **Dialect**: JSON Schema Draft 2020-12, **strict subset**:

   * Allowed: `object`, `array`, `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `enum`, `oneOf` for tagged unions
   * Allowed: `format` for `email`, `uri`, `hostname`, `date-time`, `uuid`
   * Disallowed: `$ref` to external URIs (security + offline use); `if/then/else`; `not`; `additionalProperties: <schema>`
   * Disallowed: regex `pattern` containing backreferences (ReDoS class)

2. **Companion `uiSchema`** sibling using RJSF’s vocabulary (widgets, hints, ordering). Optional. Plugin author writes:

   ```json
   {
     "paramsSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "domain": { "type": "string", "format": "hostname" } } },
     "uiSchema":     { "domain": { "ui:placeholder": "myapp.example.com", "ui:autofocus": true } }
   }
   ```

3. **Escape hatch — `ui:plugin-config-panel` capability**: plugins that need full control register their own React component for the config UI. The substrate calls into it via the iframe-bridge (or directly in v1 trusted server-runtime case).

This is what Backstage and VS Code arrived at after years of “auto-form” debt. Spec it now.

## 14.4 Worked example: `@papercupai/cloudflare-pages`

[Section titled “14.4 Worked example: @papercupai/cloudflare-pages”](#144-worked-example-papercupaicloudflare-pages)

papercusp.json

```json
{
  "kind": "plugin",
  "name": "@papercupai/cloudflare-pages",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "One-click publish your harness's project output to Cloudflare Pages.",
  "papercusp": "^0.1.0",
  "license": "MIT",


  "capabilities": [
    "secrets:read:CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN",
    "secrets:read:CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID",
    "http:fetch:api.cloudflare.com",
    "ui:harness-action:publish",
    "ui:harness-sidebar:cloudflare-publish",
    "events:listen:mission.done",
    "storage:plugin-private"
  ],


  "configSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "pages_project":         { "type": "string", "title": "Pages project name", "minLength": 1 },
      "build_dir":             { "type": "string", "title": "Build output dir", "default": "dist" },
      "custom_domain":         { "type": "string", "format": "hostname", "title": "Custom domain (optional)" },
      "auto_publish_on_done":  { "type": "boolean", "title": "Auto-publish on mission complete", "default": false }
    },
    "required": ["pages_project"]
  },
  "uiSchema": {
    "pages_project": { "ui:placeholder": "myapp" },
    "custom_domain": { "ui:placeholder": "myapp.example.com" }
  },


  "actions": [
    {
      "name": "publish",
      "label": "Publish to Cloudflare Pages",
      "icon": "rocket",
      "surfaces": ["harness-sidebar"],
      "capabilities": ["secrets:read:CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN", "http:fetch:api.cloudflare.com"],
      "serverHandler": { "timeoutSec": 120 }
    }
  ],


  "routines": [
    {
      "name": "auto-publish-on-done",
      "trigger": { "kind": "event", "event": "mission.done" },
      "targetAction": "publish",
      "enabledIfConfig": "auto_publish_on_done"
    }
  ]
}
```

index.ts

```typescript
import type { Plugin, PapercuspContext } from '@papercusp/plugin-sdk';


async function publishHandler(ctx: PapercuspContext, params: unknown) {
  const token = await ctx.api.secrets.read('CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN');
  const accountId = await ctx.api.secrets.read('CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID');
  const projectName = ctx.config.pages_project;
  const buildDir = join(ctx.projectDir, ctx.config.build_dir ?? 'dist');


  // Honour the AbortSignal from the substrate (timeout / user-cancel)
  const r = await ctx.api.fetch(`https://api.cloudflare.com/...`, {
    signal: ctx.signal,
    /* ... */
  });


  // Write to the per-action audit log via context
  await ctx.audit('publish.success', { url: `https://${projectName}.pages.dev` });


  return { ok: true, result: { url: `https://${projectName}.pages.dev` } };
}


export default {
  name: '@papercupai/cloudflare-pages',
  version: '0.1.0',
  papercusp: '^0.1.0',
  capabilities: [...],
  configSchema: {...},
  actions: [{ name: 'publish', /* ... */ serverHandler: { timeoutSec: 120 } }],


  init(ctx) {
    // Imperative registration — no function in the manifest.
    ctx.actions.register('publish', publishHandler);
  },
} satisfies Plugin;
```

User flow:

1. `papercusp install @papercupai/cloudflare-pages` → consent screen → installed globally
2. `papercusp plugin enable cloudflare-pages --harness sheets-clone` → form for `pages_project`, etc.
3. User goes to `/harness/sheets-clone` → “Publish to Cloudflare Pages” button in sidebar
4. Click → progress modal → success URL

For auto-publish on mission complete: the routine declared in the manifest fires when the substrate emits `mission.done`. The routine handler invokes the same `publishHandler` function the action button does — single code path, single audit trail.

`papercup-coding`’s template manifest just adds:

```json
{ "recommends": ["@papercupai/cloudflare-pages@^0.1"] }
```

The install flow then suggests “papercup-coding works well with cloudflare-pages — install it too?” but doesn’t force.

## 14.5 Existing tab classification — what should be plugin vs core?

[Section titled “14.5 Existing tab classification — what should be plugin vs core?”](#145-existing-tab-classification--what-should-be-plugin-vs-core)

The current papercusp dashboard has **8 tabs**: proposals, dashboard, summary, docs, vscode, pi, insights, config. Each needs a classification: keep in core, or extract to a plugin?

The principle: **a tab is core if every harness — coding, research-org, content-pipeline, marketing-bot, anything — would benefit from it**. A tab is a plugin if it’s specific to one template family or external integration.

| Tab           | Today’s content                                          | Recommended                              | Rationale                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **dashboard** | Feature queue, agents, logs, issues — the main canvas    | **CORE**                                 | This IS the harness UI. Every harness has features+agents+logs. Plugins contribute INTO it via `dashboardTabs`/`sidebarItems`. If this were a plugin, harnesses with no plugins would have nothing to show. |
| **summary**   | High-level changelog of what’s been built                | **CORE**                                 | Generic across all templates. A research-org harness wants “what got researched”; a content-pipeline wants “what got published”; coding wants “what features shipped”. Same primitive.                      |
| **insights**  | Features count, cost, tokens, iterations                 | **CORE**                                 | Universal harness metrics. Every harness pays for tokens; every harness has iterations.                                                                                                                     |
| **config**    | Per-instance configuration                               | **CORE**                                 | Every harness needs config. Plugins contribute their own config sections via `configSchema`.                                                                                                                |
| **proposals** | AI-generated scope expansion suggestions for the SPEC.md | **CORE for v1**, defer extraction        | See §14.6 — proposals isn’t a UI tab extraction, it’s an authorization-model question.                                                                                                                      |
| **docs**      | iframe of project docs (fumadocs on :4325)               | **PLUGIN** (`@papercupai/fumadocs`)      | Optional integration with an external docs server. Templates that don’t generate docs shouldn’t see this tab.                                                                                               |
| **vscode**    | iframe of code-server on the project dir                 | **PLUGIN** (`@papercupai/vscode-server`) | Code-server is heavyweight + only useful when there’s code to edit. Research, marketing, support harnesses don’t need it.                                                                                   |
| **pi**        | iframe of the pi (omp) interactive coding agent          | **PLUGIN** (`@papercupai/pi-companion`)  | Pi is one specific external tool. Would be like baking “ChatGPT side panel” into Slack.                                                                                                                     |

### Where this proposal disagrees with the maintainer’s initial take

[Section titled “Where this proposal disagrees with the maintainer’s initial take”](#where-this-proposal-disagrees-with-the-maintainers-initial-take)

The maintainer suggested:

* Core: pi, insights, Config
* Plugins: proposals, dashboard, summary, docs, vscode

This proposal disagrees on three of them:

1. **`dashboard` should stay CORE, not become a plugin.** The dashboard is the composition surface — it’s where plugins’ actions and tabs render. Making it a plugin would mean “harness with no plugins = empty UI” which breaks the first-run experience and the “core works without plugins” guarantee.
2. **`summary` should stay CORE.** Every harness benefits from “what got done”; the implementation is template-agnostic (read features+goals from state, render a timeline). Pulling it into a plugin would force every template author to either reimplement it or depend on the same plugin (a tax on adoption).
3. **`pi` should be a PLUGIN, not core.** Pi/omp is one specific external tool; not all harnesses use it. Treating it as core would tie papercusp to one external tool.

**The dashboard nuance**: the dashboard *chrome* (tab strip, panel layout, action surfaces) stays core. The dashboard’s *primary panel* (feature queue for coding ≠ briefing pipeline for research-org) is contributed by the active template via a `defaultDashboardPanel` UI contribution. Templates ship their own dashboard panel; the chrome stays core.

## 14.6 Migration plan — porting tabs to plugins

[Section titled “14.6 Migration plan — porting tabs to plugins”](#146-migration-plan--porting-tabs-to-plugins)

The migration is straightforward because each tab is already an isolated React component in `apps/papercusp/app/harness/`. Each plugin extraction is:

1. Move the component file into `libs/papercusp-marketplace/seeds/papercupai/<plugin-name>/src/`
2. Wrap it in a `Plugin` export with appropriate per-id capabilities
3. Replace the inline `activePanel === 'X'` render with a `dashboardTabs` contribution
4. Publish via the seed-publish pipeline (service token model)
5. Add to `papercup-coding`’s `recommends:` so existing users get it on install

Per-tab effort estimate (post-Phase-P2):

| Tab → Plugin                                | Lines                     | Capabilities                                                 | Est              | Status         |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------- | -------------- |
| `vscode` → `@papercupai/vscode-server`      | \~10 (iframe)             | `ui:harness-tab:vscode` + config `code_server_url`           | 30 min           | **Pilot — P5** |
| `docs` → `@papercupai/fumadocs`             | \~10 (iframe)             | `ui:harness-tab:docs` + config `docs_url`                    | 30 min           | P7             |
| `pi` → `@papercupai/pi-companion`           | \~150 (PiPanel)           | `ui:harness-tab:pi` + typed-services for child-process needs | 1.5h             | P7             |
| `proposals` → `@papercupai/scope-proposals` | substrate-protocol change | New: plugin authorization to mutate harness-canonical state  | DEFERRED to v1.5 | See note       |

**Why proposals is deferred to v1.5**: proposals isn’t a UI panel extraction. The blocker is **the write side** — today `apply_proposal_to_spec` is substrate code mutating substrate-canonical state (SPEC.md, the goals tree). For proposals to live in a plugin, the substrate has to authorize a plugin to mutate harness-canonical state, which is a real authorization-model question (not “let plugins call substrate functions” — those exist via the DI proxy — but “let plugins overwrite the harness contract”). Designing that authorization model is its own milestone; until then, proposals stays core.

Total v1 migration effort (vscode + docs + pi): \~2.5h of straightforward refactoring once the action + tab plugin primitives are in place.

The migration is **non-breaking** because:

* Each tab keeps its component code, just relocates
* The dashboard chrome already has a generic `dashboardTabs` slot
* Plugins are loaded at substrate boot; existing harnesses see them on next `papercusp run`
* Templates that haven’t been republished still work (they just don’t get the new tabs until users explicitly install the plugins)

## 14.7 Implementation roadmap

[Section titled “14.7 Implementation roadmap”](#147-implementation-roadmap)

Order matters; later items depend on earlier.

**Status — 2026-04-27**: P1 → P8 shipped + operator dashboards for `audit.action_executions` (drill-down + webhooks) and plugin grants (`granted-capabilities.json` + `extended-grants.json` with revoke). **Seven** in-tree reference plugins (`@papercupai/{vscode-server, cloudflare-pages,pi-coding,fumadocs,slack-notifier,postgres-manager, notion-export}`) published to the local marketplace; full publish → catalog → install → enable → lockfile round-trip verified end-to-end with the service-token CI flow. Drill-down drawer has **Detail** + **History** tabs + a **Retry** button (re-invokes via the substrate CLI, mirrors the result back into `audit.action_executions`) + a **diagnose→remediate** affordance that surfaces a “revoke grants for this plugin” shortcut when an error message looks capability-related. Per-plugin audit page at `/papercusp-marketplace-ops/plugins/<slug>` aggregates every audit row across all action names with per-action filter chips. Top-of-page sticky nav links the four sections (Stats / Recent / Plugin grants / Action failures) with a red-pill count when there are recent failures. Webhook subscriptions are managed inline (operator-token-gated; create with event-type chips, disable/enable/delete per row, expandable per-row delivery log). `papercusp lock {check,upgrade-all,prune}` closes the lockfile-hygiene loop on the CLI; `lock prune` cascades transitive-orphan removal. Capability- aware install diff shows `+added` / `-removed` per cap before the consent prompt fires when there’s a prior grant. Per-harness audit page mirrors the per-plugin one — drill in from the harness column in the grants table to see every action invocation across all plugins on that harness. Both the per- harness and per-plugin pages show a cross-pivot grants table linking back to the other axis. History tab surfaces a per-row “vs prior” diff hint (same / +N / -M / \~K) so flaky-but-equivalent vs flaky-and-different is visible at a glance. Webhook deliveries sub-table is sortable by status / attempt / ts and gains a per-row replay button that resets a delivery to attempt 0. The drawer is deep-linkable via `?drawer=<auditId>`; back/forward syncs the open state naturally. Grants table supports multi-select + bulk-revoke and renders capability pills color-coded by tier (high=red, medium=amber, low=grey). Recent-action-failures table is now substring-filterable by harness, plugin, or error message. Persistent operator audit log (`audit.operator_actions`) records every operator-token-gated mutation and surfaces in a new dashboard panel with substring filtering. Grants table supports tier filter chips (high/medium/low) so operators can isolate the dangerous grants. Audit log + grants table both have CSV export for offline records. Webhook subscriptions can rotate their HMAC secret with a one-shot reveal modal. Marketplace Ed25519 signing key has an inspect + rotate surface that archives the old key (timestamped) and continues serving signatures already minted against archived keys. Test coverage: 27 plugin-loader action tests + 7 hot-reload + 12 lockfile + 7 lock-resolve + 15 consent + 7 plugin-cli + 9 grants = **84 passing**. Bonus operator surfaces: `papercusp plugin invoke <slug> <action>`, `papercusp plugin watch <slug>`, `papercusp upgrade-pin <slug>`, marketplace-ops Action-executions card + Recent-action-failures table + per-row drill-down drawer, a 30-second poller that emits `action.failed` / `action.timeout` webhook deliveries from `audit.action_executions`, and a **Plugin grants** card + per-harness table with revoke + sticky “extended to all” un-stick.

Live state: `audit.action_executions` migration applied to the running `papercusp` Postgres DB (incl. `webhook_emitted_at` column for scanner idempotency); `/v1/admin/overview` includes `actionExecutions`, `/v1/admin/action-executions/:id` returns full row detail; the grants dashboard reads `~/.papercusp/{granted-capabilities,extended-grants}.json` server-side (no token needed; operator filesystem is the boundary). P9+ open (publishing the in-tree reference plugins, more reference plugins, action history view inside the drill-down drawer, retry-from-drawer).

[Section titled “Phase P3.5 — papercusp.lock per-instance lockfile (\~3h) ✅ shipped”](#phase-p35--papercusplock-per-instance-lockfile-3h--shipped)

* **Bonus**: `papercusp upgrade-pin <slug> [--harness <slug>]` — re-pins a withdrawn/quarantined plugin to its latest active version. Closes the loop on the lockfile error message that suggests this command.

### Phase P4.5 — Action handler failure semantics (\~2h) ✅ shipped

[Section titled “Phase P4.5 — Action handler failure semantics (\~2h) ✅ shipped”](#phase-p45--action-handler-failure-semantics-2h--shipped)

* Per-action timeout enforced via `AbortSignal` (default 30s, override via `defaultTimeoutSec`)
* Idempotency keys derived from `(harness-slug, action-name, trigger-source-id)` so substrate restarts mid-action don’t double-publish
* New table `audit.action_executions { id, harness_slug, plugin_name, action_name, started_at, completed_at, status, error_msg, trigger_source }` mirroring existing `audit.hook_executions`
* Failure UX: persistent audit row + a banner on the action’s surface
* Routine that failed-action: backoff per spec §9 (existing routine retry policy applies)

### Phase P8 — Hot-reload for plugin development (\~3h, optional) ✅ shipped (with caveat)

[Section titled “Phase P8 — Hot-reload for plugin development (\~3h, optional) ✅ shipped (with caveat)”](#phase-p8--hot-reload-for-plugin-development-3h-optional--shipped-with-caveat)

* `HotReloader` class in `packages/papercusp-plugin-loader/src/hot-reload.ts` watches plugin dirs (recursive), debounces bursts, emits `changed` + `reloaded` + `error` events.
* CLI surface: `papercusp plugin watch <slug> [--src <dir>]` — useful for plugin authors iterating in-tree.
* **Caveat**: under `tsx` the ESM cache isn’t invalidated by query-string bust, so the `reloaded` event fires with the original module contents. The `changed` event still fires correctly and is the right signal for a “restart needed” workflow. Full content-fresh hot-reload would require either spawning a fresh tsx child per reload or using `tsx watch` to restart the harness — left for v1.5.

[Section titled “Phase P9+ — More reference plugins, marketplace polish”](#phase-p9--more-reference-plugins-marketplace-polish)

**Total Phase P1-P7 estimate: \~16-20 hours** to a working “one-click publish” loop with three core tabs migrated to plugins.

## 14.8 Tradeoffs

[Section titled “14.8 Tradeoffs”](#148-tradeoffs)

* **vs. Backstage’s build-time-only:** we pay for runtime loading with the iframe sandbox v2 work and per-instance config UI. Worth it — the marketplace pitch needs runtime install.
* **vs. WordPress’s full-trust plugins:** we pay for the capability system with manifest verbosity and consent friction. Worth it — we won’t have an Obsidian-style retroactive cleanup.
* **vs. VS Code’s command system:** we collapse “commands” + “API contributions” into one `actions` primitive. VS Code distinguishes because their plugins do many non-action things (language servers, decorations, etc). Our plugins are smaller-surface; one primitive suffices.
* **vs. Slack’s hosted apps:** we run plugins **on the user’s substrate**, not on our infrastructure. The capability sandbox makes this safe-ish; it also means plugins can do things hosted ones can’t (read project files, work offline).
* **`actions` vs reusing `routines`:** distinct surfaces, single trigger registry. Actions = user-clicked buttons (with parameters, status UI). Routines = scheduled/event-fired (cron, webhook, substrate event). A routine that targets an action (`targetAction: 'publish'`) is the same code path as the user-clicked action, with `trigger-source` differing in the audit row.
* **No `process:spawn` capability in v1:** plugins that need subprocess access use typed substrate services or contribute upstream. Trade flexibility for safety; lift in v1.5 if proven necessary.

## 14.9 Resolved decisions

[Section titled “14.9 Resolved decisions”](#149-resolved-decisions)

These were open questions in the v1 draft and resolved through review.

### 14.9.1 Plugin scope: per-machine install + per-harness enable

[Section titled “14.9.1 Plugin scope: per-machine install + per-harness enable”](#1491-plugin-scope-per-machine-install--per-harness-enable)

Plugins are installed once globally (`papercusp install <slug>`). They’re enabled per harness instance via `papercusp plugin enable`. This matches every comparable system (VS Code, WordPress active-plugins-per-site, Backstage).

### 14.9.2 Granted-capabilities scope: per-(plugin, version, harness-slug) with sticky extension

[Section titled “14.9.2 Granted-capabilities scope: per-(plugin, version, harness-slug) with sticky extension”](#1492-granted-capabilities-scope-per-plugin-version-harness-slug-with-sticky-extension)

The decision: **strict per-(plugin, version, harness-slug)** as the default. **Sticky “extend to other harnesses” affordance at second-use**.

Concrete consent flow:

1. **First grant** (e.g. `secrets:read:CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` for harness `sheets-clone`): one prompt, granted for `sheets-clone` only. Recorded in `granted-capabilities.json` as `{plugin: 'cloudflare-pages', version: '0.1.0', harness: 'sheets-clone', cap: 'secrets:read:CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN'}`.

2. **Second grant of the same cap from a different harness** (e.g. enabling the plugin on `random-research-spike`): the prompt now offers two buttons:

   * **Grant for this harness only** — adds `harness: 'random-research-spike'` row
   * **Grant for all current and future harnesses on this machine** — wildcards the harness slug (`harness: '*'`); future harnesses re-evaluate without re-prompting

3. **Update with new capability** (e.g. plugin v0.2.0 adds `secrets:read:CLOUDFLARE_PAGES_API_TOKEN`): per §10.8 update flow, prompt for the new capability only; existing grants survive.

This gives strict isolation by default (no silent cross-harness leakage), one prompt for the common case (one-harness-per-plugin), and an explicit opt-in for the convenience case.

Three alternatives considered + rejected:

* **Uniform per-machine** (simplest, every plugin marketplace does it) — accepts that secrets installed for harness A are usable by harness B on the same box.
* **Uniform per-(plugin, version, harness-slug)** with a “remember for all” checkbox at first prompt — one consent surface; the high-cost case is the explicit unchecked default.
* **Tier-graded scope** (low per-machine, medium per-(machine, plugin, version), high per-(machine, plugin, version, harness-slug)) — three different scope semantics is too much complexity to ship without two consent surfaces designed first.

The chosen path balances safety (strict default) and friction (one-prompt common case) without inventing new prompt surfaces.

### 14.9.3 Default dashboard panel ownership

[Section titled “14.9.3 Default dashboard panel ownership”](#1493-default-dashboard-panel-ownership)

Templates contribute their default dashboard panel via a `defaultDashboardPanel` UI contribution in the template’s manifest. Render order: template’s panel first; plugins’ tabs appended.

### 14.9.4 First-party vs community parity

[Section titled “14.9.4 First-party vs community parity”](#1494-first-party-vs-community-parity)

`@papercupai/*` plugins get prominence (verified badge, default ranking) but no extra capabilities. Same security model for everyone.

### 14.9.5 Forwards-compatibility with iframe sandbox v2

[Section titled “14.9.5 Forwards-compatibility with iframe sandbox v2”](#1495-forwards-compatibility-with-iframe-sandbox-v2)

The action handler’s runtime location is **explicit in the manifest** via `serverHandler` / `clientHandler` presence (§14.3.3). Plugin authors don’t rewrite anything when the iframe sandbox lands; the loader resolves to the right execution path based on what’s in the manifest.

### 14.9.6 Lockfile retraction interaction

[Section titled “14.9.6 Lockfile retraction interaction”](#1496-lockfile-retraction-interaction)

Three retraction states map to three lockfile behaviors:

| State         | Author intent                                                                 | Lockfile reaction                                                                           |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `deprecated`  | ”still works, prefer X going forward”                                         | Warn at `papercusp run`, proceed normally                                                   |
| `withdrawn`   | ”I removed this, but please don’t break grandfathered installs”               | Warn loud at `papercusp run`, require `--allow-withdrawn` flag to actually run              |
| `quarantined` | ”this version is actively unsafe — security issue or supply-chain compromise” | Refuse to run, force `papercusp upgrade-pin <plugin>` to bump to next non-retracted version |

Same rules apply to `recommends` entries: a recommends pointing at a quarantined plugin is **stripped from the suggestion UI entirely** (not shown with a warning).

### 14.9.7 Lockfile transitivity

[Section titled “14.9.7 Lockfile transitivity”](#1497-lockfile-transitivity)

The rule: **every line in the lockfile is something the user explicitly chose to be in their world**.

* **Hard `requires`** are pinned transitively in the lockfile (npm/cargo behavior). The plugin author tested against a specific dep version; surprises are bugs.
* **`recommends` are NOT in the lockfile until the user accepts them.** Once accepted, they enter the lockfile and pin transitively from then on (the recommended plugin’s own `requires` get pinned).
* An un-accepted `recommends` showing up after a template version bump re-prompts but doesn’t pin until acceptance.

This invariant makes lockfiles legible to humans, which matters more for a marketplace than for npm.

### 14.9.8 `recommends` UX touch-points

[Section titled “14.9.8 recommends UX touch-points”](#1498-recommends-ux-touch-points)

* **CLI**: `papercusp install <template>` shows the recommends list with `--with-recommends` (default off) and `--no-recommends` flags
* **Web admin**: modal at template-install completion with checkboxes
* **Re-evaluation**: on `papercusp run` if the lockfile shows recommends mismatching the current template version, prompt; on a template version bump, the install flow re-shows the recommends diff
* **Persisted state**: track which recommends were “skipped” so we don’t keep re-asking (`~/.papercusp/skipped-recommends.json`)

## 14.10 Plugin → plugin dependencies

[Section titled “14.10 Plugin → plugin dependencies”](#1410-plugin--plugin-dependencies)

Both `requires` and `recommends` are valid at **both** template and plugin manifest levels:

```json
// In a plugin's papercusp.json
{
  "kind": "plugin",
  "name": "@papercupai/cloudflare-pages-history",
  "requires": ["@papercupai/cloudflare-pages@^0.1"]
}
```

Resolution at install time:

1. Substrate computes the transitive closure of `requires`
2. Substrate prompts user for capability consent for ALL plugins in the closure
3. If any plugin in the closure is `quarantined`, refuse install; if any is `withdrawn`, require explicit override
4. On install, all transitive `requires` enter the lockfile (per §14.9.7)
5. `recommends` from the leaf packages are surfaced separately (per §14.9.8) and not pinned until accepted

This matches VS Code’s `extensionDependencies` + `extensionPack` semantics. The retraction-aware install flow (§14.9.6) applies uniformly to all plugins in the closure.

# 15. Snapshots — share working harness state via marketplace (v1.2)

Status: shipped — but the cross-machine transport is the Cupboard, NOT Gitea/Cosign

**Snapshots** — sharing a working harness instance (template + state) so other developers can fork and continue it. **Local capture + restore** shipped (`libs/papercusp-export-state/`; the snapshot endpoint routes `create` / `instantiate` / `publish` / `retract` under `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/snapshots/`; the `snapshots:list` / `snapshots:get` agent tools).

**Cross-machine sharing also shipped — but via the in-app Cupboard, not the Gitea/Forgejo + ORAS + Cosign + papercuspai.com design that sections 15.3–15.8, 15.10, 15.21–15.23 describe.** A snapshot is published to the Cupboard (`apps/operator-public`, Cloudflare Workers + D1) as a `listing_kind='snapshot'` whose tarball is **content-addressed by SHA-256** and stored in **R2** (`snapshots/<hash>.tar.gz`); a consumer forks it via `fork-from-cupboard` (`…/routes/snapshots/fork-from-cupboard.ts`). Auth is a **GitHub bearer** (validated against `api.github.com/user`), publisher trust is the GitHub repo-permission signal + an optional Ed25519 device-pubkey ↔ login gist attestation — **not** Cosign/Sigstore/Rekor, `tenantId`/`tenantSecret`, or OCI manifests. There is no Gitea instance.

Treat the Gitea/OCI/Cosign/ORAS material below, and the `papercuspai.com/snapshots` marketplace UI, as **superseded design history**; the redaction / capture-pass / restore-pass / migration / abuse-and-moderation reasoning (§15.4–15.6, §15.9, §15.11, §15.24) remains the conceptual reference. Eight rounds of architectural research and critique have been incorporated.

**This is a different feature from §16 (Publishing).** Snapshots ship the entire working harness (DB rows + filesystem + git history) to a marketplace for other operators to fork. Publishing ships a static-site bundle of build output to a public web URL for end users. Both features are real and both ship. They share infrastructure (auth, redaction, audit log) but have distinct artifact formats, audiences, and lifecycles. The dashboard exposes two top-right buttons: **Save snapshot** (this spec) and **Publish website** (§16). See §15.13 for the full sibling-feature comparison.

Changes in v1.2 (from v1.1 review feedback, rounds 7-8)

**Correctness:**

* §15.6 step 7e: shared-row IDs now slug-prefixed (option b) — eliminates the silent-corruption case where same-id-different-bytes collisions fired on common paths (e.g., divergent PM curation between machines)
